  variance with loadings .70, .60, .30 or .775, .645, .155; 500 samples
  of N = 60 drawn after `set.seed(1)`; percentile intervals from B = 999
  resamples), the lower limit exceeded the population omega in 11.6 and
  13.1 percent of the samples that yielded an estimate (413 and 352 of
  the 500), against the nominal 2.5.

- **The analytic
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  records the `improper` rule it was given** in its `bootstrap`
  attribute rather than the engine’s default. It fits no model, so no
  replication can be improper.

- **The bootstrap reports no interval when most replications fail the
  distinct-case rule.** The standard error and limits are `NA` when more
  than half of the replications have too few distinct cases for the
  coefficient. Near that rule’s bound, the resamples kept are selected
  for repeating the fewest rows; at the bound they are only reorderings
  of the data and give an interval with no width. The `bootstrap`
  attribute counts these refusals in `too_few_cases`, including in its
  `jackknife` record. This rule applies throughout the engine. The
  separate `require_half` rule withholds an interval whenever fewer than
  half return a value, whatever the reason; it holds for every caller
  (the element `require_half` of the `bootstrap` attribute is always
  `TRUE`), as the entry on the bootstrap family’s half-return
  requirement states. The number of replications a request must ask for
  is set by the rule of the next section, One Rule for Bootstrap
  Replications. A bias estimate for H is reported only when its interval
  is formed.

- **A bootstrap warning describes limits only when they exist.** With
  fewer than two returned values, or when either rule above withholds
  the interval, the warning and printed line say that no interval is
  reported and give no caution about its limits. The caution names an
  improper solution only when one was kept. A refusal quoted with its
  count loses its trailing period inside the parentheses.

- **An unobserved column in a replication is named separately from a
  constant one.** No observed value leaves its variance and covariances
  unidentified; a single value leaves its variance zero. Both are
  counted and quoted by name. A bootstrap of `reliability_H(fit = )`
  follows the fit’s own missing data method: complete-data and listwise
  fits use the rank of the sample covariance matrix, FIML and two-stage
  fits use the saturated model’s case rule, and pairwise fits use
  neither case-count rule. Its messages describe the resample without
  claiming that the supplied fit’s data were refused.

### One Rule for Bootstrap Replications

- **Every function that runs bootstrap or Monte Carlo replications
  requires a sufficient number of them, counts the ones it uses, and
  says so in the result.** A percentile limit is a quantile of the `B`
  replications and is located by the replications that lie beyond it. An
  interval read from quantiles is now run only when `B` puts at least 10
  replications beyond each limit, and never with fewer than 100: 200,
  400, and 2000 replications at the 90, 95, and 99 percent levels. A BCa
  interval, whose limits the bias correction and the acceleration move
  farther into the tails, is run only with 50 beyond each nominal limit:
  1000, 2000, and 10000. An interval built from the standard deviation
  of the replications (`"bootstrap_se"`, `"bootstrap_se_logistic"`)
  needs 100, and so does a Monte Carlo *p*-value. A one-sided bound and
  a reference quantile need 10 beyond their one quantile (200 at the
  95th percentile). A `B` below the number required is refused before
  anything is computed, with an error of class `dmar_count_invalid`
  whose message states the number and the count behind it:
  `mediate(d, "x", "m", "y", B = 200)`, the call of the 1.0.x help
  example, returned 0.1816 \[0.1163, 0.2684\] and now stops with “‘B’
  must be a single whole number of at least 400. A 95% interval read
  from the quantiles of the replications has 2.5% of them beyond each
  limit, and an interval is reported only when at least 10 replications
  lie beyond each limit (10 / 0.025 = 400). To run fewer for exploration
  or a demonstration, see ?dmar_bootstrap.”; with `B = 400` it returns
  0.1816 \[0.1165, 0.2592\], the numbers DMAR 1.0.0 returned for
  `B = 400`. The numbers of the rule were computed for DMAR (the tail
  area a limit cuts off has a relative standard deviation of about 30
  percent with 10 replications beyond it, whatever the shape of the
  bootstrap distribution; at 400 replications a 95 percent limit of a
  bell-shaped distribution varies from run to run by about 0.13
  bootstrap standard errors); no published source is cited for them, and
  the new help page
  [`?dmar_bootstrap`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_bootstrap.md)
  gives the reasons.
- **The functions and what each accepted before.** The rule governs
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  (percentile, BCa, and Monte Carlo intervals; the Sobel interval draws
  nothing and `B` is not read for it),
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  and
  [`plot_mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_mediation_mbco.md)
  (Monte Carlo),
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md),
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md),
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md),
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md),
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md),
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md),
  [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md),
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md),
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md),
  [`ci_ratio_of_means()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_ratio_of_means.md),
  [`ci_ratio_of_means_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_ratio_of_means_paired.md),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md),
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md),
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md),
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md),
  and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md).
  Before, a `B` was accepted from 2 in the reliability family,
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md),
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md),
  and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md);
  from 100 in
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md),
  the kappa functions,
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md), the
  ratio functions,
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  and
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md);
  and was not checked at all in
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md), and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md).
  A fractional `B` was accepted and truncated by
  [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md),
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md),
  and
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  (`cohen_kappa(B = 250.5)` ran 250 replications) and is now refused.
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  required a `B` of at least 100 whatever the interval and now reads `B`
  only for `ci_method = "monte_carlo"`.
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  keeps its own minimum of 1000, which the rule raises to 2000 at the 99
  percent level.
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md) needs
  200 at the default level (100 to 199 were accepted),
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md)
  and
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  200 at the 95th percentile (`factor_count(B = 0)` still omits the
  reference), and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md) 100.
  The planners that run an interval inside each simulated study follow
  the rule too:
  [`ss_aipe_indirect_effect()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_indirect_effect.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity.md)
  hold `B` to it under `method = "monte_carlo"` (400 at the 95 percent
  level, where 100 was accepted by the planner and the sensitivity
  function made no check; under `method = "closed_form"`, which draws
  nothing, `B` need only be a whole number), and the default `B` of
  [`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  is now `NULL`, resolved to the larger of 200 and one and a quarter
  times the number the interval method and the level require: 500 for
  `"percentile"`, 2500 for `"bca"`, and 200 for the two bootstrap
  standard error methods at the 95 percent level, where the default was
  200 for all four. The quarter is room for replications that return no
  value: the number required is held to the request, so a simulated
  study that loses a few replications still reports its interval, and
  with the quarter its limits still rest on about the number required.
  Its run time is proportional to `G` times `B`, so a percentile check
  takes about two and a half times as long by default and a BCa check
  twelve and a half times. With the exploratory option the three
  planners give one warning for the call, not one for each simulated
  study, and their results carry the attributes `B`, `B_used`,
  `n_dropped`, `B_required`, and `bootstrap_status`, which record the
  request each simulated study ran.
- **No default is changed, and some defaults do not serve every level.**
  The default `B = 1000` of
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md),
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md),
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md),
  and of
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  under `missing = "mi"` serves the 90 and 95 percent levels and not
  `conf_level = 0.99`, which needs 2000; the default of
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  does not serve `ci_method = "bca"` (2000 at 95 percent); and the
  default `B = 2000` of
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  serves a 99 percent percentile interval exactly and not a 99 percent
  BCa interval (10000). In each case the refusal names the number to
  pass.
- **A replication that returns no value is dropped, counted, and
  reported, everywhere.** Five functions removed such replications
  without a count or a warning:
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  (a Monte Carlo draw at which an effect is not a finite number),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md), and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  (a refit that failed or a value that is not finite). They now give one
  warning of class `dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped`, as the others
  do.
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md), and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  removed a missing value for one statistic only, so the intervals of
  one call could rest on different replications; a replication without a
  value for any statistic is now dropped for all of them (see Changes to
  Earlier Results). The warnings that were unclassed now carry the
  class, and every one carries the fields `B`, `B_used`, `n_dropped`,
  `B_required`, `share_dropped`, `caution`, and `status`. When the
  dropped replications number at least the share of `B` beyond one limit
  (2.5 percent at the 95 percent level) the warning adds a caution, the
  rule the reliability family already applied, because they could then
  decide by themselves where that limit falls.
- **The number required is counted on the request, not on the
  replications that remain.** `B` is held to the count before anything
  is computed, and that is the whole of the count rule. A request that
  meets it and then loses replications still reports its interval: the
  warning states how many were dropped, and when those that remain are
  fewer than the number required it says so and says to request more
  (“The 400 required are counted on the number requested (400), not on
  the number that remained; the 397 that remained are fewer, so request
  more bootstrap replications where some can fail, enough that at least
  400 remain.”). The two rules about shares then decide: more than half
  dropped withholds the interval, and dropped replications that reach
  the share of `B` beyond one limit bring the caution. A constrained
  bifactor model of six tests of `holzinger_swineford` with
  `ci_bifactor_indices(B = 400, seed = 63)` and one improper replication
  set aside reports the intervals of its 15 indices from the 399 that
  return a value. Where replications can fail, ask for more than the
  minimum; the defaults do at the 95 percent level.
- **The warnings of the reliability family’s bootstrap name the function
  that was called.**
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md),
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  (with and without `missing = "mi"`),
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md),
  and
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  share one bootstrap engine, whose warnings began with the count (“3 of
  400 bootstrap replications were set aside …”) and now begin with the
  function (“reliability_omega(): 3 of 400 bootstrap replications were
  set aside …”), as the warnings of the other functions under the rule
  do. The condition carries the name in the field `fun`.
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md)
  passes its call on, so its warning names the function that ran the
  bootstrap.
- **The bootstrap warnings of
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md),
  and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md)
  name the function too.** These three compose their own account of a
  run (the factors, the reference data sets, the reasons a sample was
  set aside), and it began with the count (“2 of 200 bootstrap
  replications were set aside …”). It now begins with the function
  (“average_variance_extracted(): 2 of 200 …”), so every warning under
  the rule says where it came from. A note that
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  prints from its parallel analysis begins “parallel_analysis():”.
- **The messages about Monte Carlo draws say “draws” throughout.**
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  and
  [`plot_mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_mediation_mbco.md)
  draw the estimates from their estimated sampling distribution. Their
  caution and their note on an exploratory run spoke of “replications”
  and of “the bootstrap distribution”; they now speak of draws and of
  the distribution of the draws, as the rest of each message does.
- **Too few usable replications withhold the interval; they no longer
  stop the call.** When more than half of the replications were dropped
  the limits are `NA`, the estimate and every other row are returned,
  and the warning has the new class `dmar_bootstrap_insufficient`.
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md),
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md),
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md), and
  the two ratio functions stopped with an error when fewer than 100
  replications remained, and
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  when fewer than two did. With a predictor that is nonzero in one of 20
  cases, `mediate(B = 150, seed = 113)` stopped with “Only 91 of 150
  bootstrap replications returned a finite indirect effect”; the same
  call with `B = 400` now returns the indirect effect 0.5959 with limits
  from the 240 replications that remain and the warning that 240 is
  fewer than the 400 required, and with `B = 2000` it returns \[0.1319,
  0.9613\] from 1267 replications, as before.
- **Every result that ran replications records them the same way.** The
  attributes `B` (requested), `B_used` (the number the interval rests
  on), `n_dropped`, `B_required`, and `bootstrap_status` (`"complete"`,
  `"dropped"`, `"exploratory"`, `"insufficient_count"`, or
  `"insufficient_share"`) are on every such result;
  [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md),
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md),
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  and
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  had no `B` attribute, and
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md),
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md),
  and
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  recorded no counts under these names.
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  carry them as elements of the fitted object, and
  [`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) and
  [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html) state them in one
  line. The rows `B` and `B_used` of
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  and the row `B_used` of
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md)
  are kept. The `bootstrap` attribute of the reliability family keeps
  every element and gains `required`, `bootstrap_status`, and `B_used`;
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md)
  gains `B_required` and `bootstrap_status` in its `sem_fit` list.
  [`dmar_metadata()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_metadata.md)
  returns `required` and `status` in its `bootstrap` element. The line
  under a table of the ratio functions reads “Bootstrap: 2000
  replications, 1283 used (717 dropped; at least 400 must be requested).
  A dropped replication had a denominator of zero”;
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  prints the corresponding line for its Monte Carlo interval, and the
  tables of
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md),
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md),
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  and
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  print “Bootstrap: 400 replications, 400 used (0 dropped; at least 400
  must be requested)” beneath them when a bootstrap was run.
- **A BCa interval is held to the count where its limits finally sit.**
  After the replications are run, the count of 10 is applied at the two
  quantile positions the bias correction and the acceleration give, and,
  like the count of the request, it is held to the number requested.
  When `B` puts fewer than 10 replications beyond one of them, no BCa
  interval is reported (limits `NA`, class
  `dmar_bootstrap_insufficient`, with the positions as `positions` and a
  suggested `B` as `B_suggest`). This applies to
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  the kappa functions, the ratio functions, and the reliability family.
  In the probe behind the rule this happened in at most 14 percent of
  data sets at `B = 2000` (an indirect effect with 50 cases and small
  paths) and in 0 to 3 percent of the other conditions; the positions
  asked for more than 10,000 replications in about 1 percent of the data
  sets of that hardest condition (4 of 400, the largest count 32,909)
  and in none of the others. The count the positions take is what the
  result records as `B_required` and what the warning carries, in every
  family; the reliability family recorded the 2,000 of the request
  beside a message that stated the larger count, and printed no reason
  under the table, and now records and prints the count at the positions
  (“5105 are required where the bias correction and the acceleration
  place the limits, so no BCa interval is reported”).
- **What a withheld interval, a single bound, and a note look like.** A
  bootstrap interval of
  [`ci_ratio_of_means()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_ratio_of_means.md)
  or
  [`ci_ratio_of_means_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_ratio_of_means_paired.md)
  that the rule withholds prints “Percentile bootstrap interval: no
  interval is reported.” in place of a line that called the missing
  interval “the whole line”, and its `confidence_set` attribute and
  `tidy()` column are `NA`. The messages call a one-sided bound a bound
  and the reference quantile of
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md)
  and
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  a reference quantile; a BCa interval with unequal tail areas is
  refused with a sentence that names the smaller nominal tail area,
  where it named two positions the request did not have;
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  gives the exploratory mark under its own name;
  `parallel_analysis(percentile = 50)` and
  `factor_count(percentile = 50)` stop with a message that names
  `percentile`, where it named `conf_level`. A warning about a run in
  which nothing was dropped (in the reliability family, a BCa interval
  replaced by the percentile interval, or replicates that are all the
  same value; in
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  and
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md),
  the function’s account of improper replications kept or of reference
  fits that warned) was unclassed and has the class
  `dmar_bootstrap_note`. The `B` attribute of the reliability family is
  an integer, as the other counts are (it was a double when `B` was
  given as one). In an exploratory run below the required number the
  reliability family no longer passes on “extreme order statistics used
  as endpoints” from
  [`boot::boot.ci()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/boot/man/boot.ci.html) beside
  its own warning, which already says how few replications each limit
  rests on, and
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  no longer pass on lavaan’s count of bootstrap runs that failed beside
  the classed warning that reports the same replications with the
  counts.
  [`plot_mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_mediation_mbco.md)
  returns a plot, which carries no attributes, and its warnings no
  longer say that the counts are recorded in the result.
- **[`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md)
  and
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md)
  refuse a BCa interval that is not defined.** The acceleration needs
  kappa with each case left out. A leave-one-out kappa that is undefined
  (chance agreement 1) was removed without a word and the acceleration
  computed from the rest. The call now stops with an error of class
  `dmar_bca_undefined` (a `dmar_refusal`) that names the cases, as
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  does; the same class is given when every bootstrap estimate falls on
  one side of the sample estimate or the acceleration is not finite.
  `ci_method = "percentile"` does not need these quantities.
- **`options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)` runs fewer
  replications, and marks the result.** A first look, a help page
  example, and a simulation over many data sets do not need a reportable
  interval from each run. Under the option a `B` from 2 up is accepted;
  the result records `B_required` and has `bootstrap_status`
  `"exploratory"`, the line under the table says that the interval is
  below the number required for a reported interval, and every call
  gives a warning of class `dmar_bootstrap_exploratory`. The share rule
  still applies. The examples of
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md),
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md),
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md),
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md),
  whose replications each refit a model, set the option, run their small
  `B`, and restore it; the examples of
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  and
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md)
  (now `B = 400`), of
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md)
  and
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  (`B = 200`), and the BCa example of
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  (`B = 2000`) meet the requirement. The vignettes `missing_data` (six
  intervals, `B = 200` before) and `DMAR`
  ([`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md),
  `B = 50` before) run the required numbers.
- **[`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md)
  gives one warning about the samples it sets aside.** It gave two when
  no *p*-value was formed, one for the samples set aside and one for the
  missing *p*-value; it gives one, with the class that says which case
  it is.
- **New help page
  [`?dmar_bootstrap`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_bootstrap.md).**
  It states the rule and its reasons, what is recorded and where, the
  treatment of BCa intervals, the exploratory option, the conditions
  with their fields, and a table of the functions with their kind,
  default `B`, and the number required at the 95 percent level.

### Coefficient H From a Fitted Model

- **[`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  computes coefficient H from a fitted model, raw data, or a covariance
  matrix, and its interval now uses the full covariance matrix of the
  estimates.** In 1.0.0 the function took standardized loadings and, for
  an interval, their marginal standard errors, the diagonal of the
  covariance matrix of the loading estimates. Those estimates are
  correlated in any fitted factor model, so that interval could be too
  narrow or too wide: on one-factor ML and MLR fits (`std.lv = TRUE`) of
  seven blocks of `holzinger_swineford` tests (1, 2, 4; 6, 7, 9; 10, 12,
  13; 1–4; 5–9; 14–19; and 20–24) the standard error from the full
  matrix is 0.75 to 1.29 times the one from the diagonal under ML and
  0.69 to 1.16 under MLR. H is now computed from the fitted loadings,
  residual covariances, and factor variance. It does not depend on how
  the factor was identified, and when residuals inside the block are
  correlated it is the maximal reliability of Gabler and Raykov (2017).
  Its delta method variance runs over every free parameter with the
  fit’s own covariance matrix of the estimates (standard, robust, FIML,
  or WLSMV), under either `ceq.simple` setting of a fit whose equality
  constraints come from labels or `group.equal`, and it reproduces the
  `H_<factor>` row of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  and lavaan’s own delta method for H defined with `:=`. The new
  arguments come after the 1.0.0 ones: `fit` (any factor of a lavaan
  confirmatory or structural model measured by observed items, named
  with `factor`, and any group, named with `group`); `data` (the
  single-factor model fitted as
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  fits it, with `missing` and `aux`); `S` and `N`; `vcov_loadings`;
  `ci_method`; `B`; `seed`; and `ncpus`. The default interval is the
  Wald interval on the logit scale, with the robust maximum likelihood
  standard error for `data`, the maximum likelihood one for `S`, the
  fit’s own for `fit`, and for `loadings` the one their `vcov_loadings`
  (or `se_loadings`) gives; standardized loadings with neither carry
  nothing an interval can be formed from and give the estimate alone
  (`ci_method = "none"`), with a line under the table saying what an
  interval needs. The four bootstrap methods refit the model on every
  replication, and their `bootstrap` attribute carries the estimated
  bias of the sample H, which runs upward (Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, &
  McIntosh, 2019). On the fit path the model is refitted to the fit’s
  own rows before any resample is drawn, and the call stops unless that
  refit reproduces the estimate; every refit starts from the fit’s
  estimates. A fit with sampling weights or a cluster variable, which a
  resample of rows cannot carry, is refused, and the delta method
  interval, which uses the fit’s own standard error, is named in its
  place. The refits of a fitted model are not checked for three items
  whose correlations admit no single-factor solution, so such a resample
  is counted as improper when lavaan stops at a solution that has run
  away and as non-finite when it does not converge; from data it is
  counted in `improper` and in `no_solution`, as
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  counts it. A fit for which H is not defined stops with the remedy
  named: an item that also loads on another factor or is regressed on
  another variable, a higher-order factor, an observed covariate
  predicting the factor, an improper solution, or three items whose
  correlations admit no single-factor solution. A loading or regression
  fixed or constrained to zero is not one: a model written with
  `0*item`, or with `a*item` and `a == 0` (directly or through a chain
  such as `a == b` with `b == 0`), gets the H of the model written
  without it. A bifactor fit, whose items load on more than one factor,
  is refused with a message that names the index
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  reports, its `maximal_reliability` attribute, and
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md).
  Every call but the 1.0.0 form (see Changes to Earlier Results) returns
  the reliability family table (`estimate`, `se`, `ci_lower`,
  `ci_upper`, `conf_level`, `N`, `N_complete`, `n_items`; class
  `dmar_reliability`, coefficient `"H"`). Attributes name the factor,
  the group, the metric (`"latent_response"` for ordered items), the
  basis of the standard error, what came with standardized loadings
  (`vcov_supplied`), and the standardized loadings, and the printed
  table says which factor of a model it describes.
  `reliability(type = "H")` dispatches to it; auto-detection never
  chooses it. From data, a fit that lavaan stops with an error is
  reported with lavaan’s message, as
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  reports it.

### The Bifactor Model

- **[`fa_bifactor()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_bifactor.md)
  is new.** It fits the bifactor model, a general factor on every item
  and two or more group factors, each on its own items, with every
  factor uncorrelated with the others and its variance fixed at 1,
  described as
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  describes a model: the items of each group factor are named in
  `factors`, the general factor’s name in `general`, and items on the
  general factor alone in `general_only`. It shares
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)’s
  engine, interface, and fit rows: raw data (by full information maximum
  likelihood, the default, or after listwise deletion) or a covariance
  matrix with its N, ML or MLR, `equal_loading`, `equal_error`, and
  `equal_intercept` within a factor, and the five outputs, `"fit"`
  returning the lavaan fit that
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md),
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md),
  and
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  take. Beside the loadings, error variances, and intercepts the table
  reports, with a delta method standard error and a confidence interval
  each, omega and omega_H for the total score; omega and omega_HS for
  each subscale; ECV, H, and the maximal reliability for every factor;
  and PUC, which depends on the structure alone and has no interval.
  Omega, omega_H, and omega_HS are the reliabilities of sums of the
  items as scored, the coefficients
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  and `semTools::compRelSEM()` compute, where
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  keeps the standardized metric (on the help page’s 15 Holzinger and
  Swineford tests, omega_H is 0.552 for the sum of the scores and 0.577
  for the sum of the standardized scores); ECV, H, the maximal
  reliability, and PUC are
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)’s.
  The standard errors of the indices lavaan can define are its own; the
  maximal reliability’s is the delta method’s with numerical
  derivatives, and every limit is formed on the logit scale and lies
  within (0, 1). A structure outside the model, or one that is not
  identified, is refused before anything is fit, with an error of class
  `dmar_bifactor_unidentified` (a `dmar_refusal`) that names the factors
  or items and says in its `reason` element which kind of refusal it is:
  fewer than two group factors and an item on two group factors are
  outside the model (`"scope"`; a general factor beside one group
  factor, with items on the general factor alone, is identified, but the
  subscale indices need two or more); an item listed twice, under one
  group factor or under a group factor and in `general_only`, and names
  that clash are `"names"`; and a group factor of one item or of two
  with free loadings, and two group factors whose general loadings the
  data fix only up to a scale (two groups of three items each with
  nothing on the general factor alone, as on six of the Holzinger and
  Swineford tests, where lavaan cannot invert the information matrix),
  are `"unidentified"`. Every model with two group factors that is fit
  gives a warning of class `dmar_bifactor_empirical` on empirical
  underidentification (Green & Yang, 2018), once the arguments and the
  data have passed their checks, so a call that then fails does not get
  it. When lavaan’s information matrix is singular, whether the observed
  information of a FIML fit or the expected information of a listwise
  fit or of a covariance matrix, every standard error, test, and
  interval is `NA`, the maximal reliability’s included, with a warning;
  lavaan inverts such a matrix without complaint, and the maximal
  reliability’s delta method would otherwise give a standard error of 0.
  Ordered items are refused with a pointer to
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  for the latent response metric, and `wald_df = "missing_information"`,
  calibrated on one factor models, is refused as well. An improper
  solution leaves the maximal reliabilities, and the H and omega rows it
  makes undefined, `NA` with a warning.

- **[`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  and
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  take items on the general factor alone.** An item that loads on the
  general factor and on no group factor, which DMAR 1.0.x refused, now
  counts in the general factor’s ECV, omega, omega_H, H, and maximal
  reliability and in PUC, whose pairs with it are uncontaminated, and in
  no subscale, when the fit has two or more group factors. A fit with
  one group factor is refused by both (see Changes to Earlier Results).

### The Second-Order Model

- **[`fa_second_order()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_second_order.md)
  is new.** It fits the second-order factor model, first-order factors
  on their own items and one or more second-order factors on their own
  first-order factors, named in `factors` and `second_order`; several
  second-order factors are always correlated (uncorrelated second-order
  factors are not offered). The model is identified as lavaan’s
  `std.lv = TRUE` identifies it, every second-order factor’s variance
  and every first-order factor’s disturbance variance fixed at 1, and it
  shares
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)’s
  engine, interface, and fit rows: raw data (by full information maximum
  likelihood, the default, or after listwise deletion) or a covariance
  matrix with its N, ML or MLR, `equal_loading`, `equal_error`, and
  `equal_intercept` within a first-order factor and
  `equal_second_order_loading` within a second-order factor, and the
  five outputs. The table reports the first-order and second-order
  loadings, the error variances, and the intercepts; then, for each
  second-order factor, omega and omega_H for the sum of its items and
  its ECV, H, maximal reliability, and PUC, and for each first-order
  factor omega and omega_HS for its subscale score and the ECV, H, and
  maximal reliability of its disturbance, each with a delta method
  interval whose limits are formed on the logit scale (PUC has none);
  then the fit rows. The indices are those of
  [`fa_bifactor()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_bifactor.md)
  computed from the Schmid-Leiman loadings the estimates imply (Schmid &
  Leiman, 1957; Yung, Thissen, & McLeod, 1999), which the
  `schmid_leiman` attribute gives in the standardized metric, item by
  item. Structures outside the model or not identified, and names that
  clash, are refused before anything is fit with an error of class
  `dmar_second_order_unidentified` (a `dmar_refusal`) whose `reason`
  element says which, as for
  [`fa_bifactor()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_bifactor.md):
  a first-order factor of one item, a second-order factor of one
  first-order factor, and one second-order factor over two first-order
  factors without equal loadings are `"unidentified"`; an item on two
  first-order factors and a first-order factor under two second-order
  factors are `"scope"`; and an item or factor listed twice under one
  factor, a first-order factor under none, and clashing names are
  `"names"`. With exactly three first-order factors under one
  second-order factor (or two with equal loadings) the second-order
  structure is just identified, and a line under the table states that
  condition in words and says that the model then fits as the correlated
  factors model of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  does whenever the factor correlations have a positive product and
  imply standardized loadings below one (on nine Holzinger and Swineford
  tests, a chi square of 85.31 on 24 degrees of freedom under both).
  Incomplete data under FIML in which no case observes two first-order
  factors together are refused when the pairs observed together do not
  identify the second-order loadings (three first-order factors under
  one second-order factor with one such pair), and fit when they do
  (four). In this parameterization a standardized second-order loading
  reaches one only as its loading runs off toward infinity, and lavaan’s
  optimizer can stop on the way short of the maximum, with other
  second-order loadings drifted far off, or not converge; so the model
  is fit a second time in a parameterization whose boundary is a point
  (each first-order factor on the scale of its second-order factor, the
  variance of its disturbance there bounded below at zero, every
  equality constraint of the call imposed exactly), and the larger
  likelihood is reported, two log likelihoods within 1e-6 per case being
  taken as the same maximum whatever the number of cases. On one
  second-order factor over spatial, verbal, and speed tests and t24,
  t25, and t26 of `holzinger_swineford`, the first fit stopped at a chi
  square of 251.77, where the maximum is 169.77. A standardized
  second-order loading of one at the maximum, a Heywood case at the
  second order, leaves that factor’s second-order loading and its
  loadings on its disturbance without a finite estimate and the rows of
  its disturbance undefined, all `NA`, while the other rows and the fit
  rows are those of the maximum (the standard errors holding the loading
  at one, and absent, with a warning, under `se = "bootstrap"`); and a
  correlation of two second-order factors beyond one leaves every
  maximal reliability `NA`. Each gives a warning that names it, with the
  values in the `improper_second_order` attribute, as a negative error
  variance is handled in
  [`fa_bifactor()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_bifactor.md).
  Under FIML, `output = "summary"` of a fit with a loading at one shows
  lavaan’s robust CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and GFI as `NA`, since lavaan cannot
  form them for a fit computed without the optimizer, with one warning
  in place of lavaan’s three. Each first-order factor is reported with
  loadings that sum to a positive value, and then each second-order
  factor with second-order loadings that do. The help shows the
  likelihood ratio test of the second-order model against the bifactor
  model in which it is nested (Yung et al., 1999; Chen, West, & Sousa,
  2006), through
  [`lavaan::lavTestLRT()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/lavaan/man/lavTestLRT.html)
  on the `output = "fit"` objects of
  [`fa_second_order()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_second_order.md)
  and
  [`fa_bifactor()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_bifactor.md).
  The function is named for the structure it fits because the sources
  call the orthogonal layered model of the bifactor family the
  hierarchical factor model.

### Intervals for the Bifactor Indices

- **[`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  is new.** It gives nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals for
  the indices
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  reports: ECV, omega, omega_H, omega_HS, and coefficient H for each
  factor they apply to, and the maximal reliability of each factor,
  which
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  returns beside its table. PUC depends only on which items share a
  group factor and has no interval. Each replication resamples the rows
  the fit used (under full information maximum likelihood, every
  incomplete row with its missing data pattern), refits the model with
  the fit’s own parameter table and options, and reads every index from
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  on the refit, so the intervals rest on the same replications (under
  `improper = "keep"`, those of the maximal reliability on the proper
  ones among them); before any resample is drawn, the call checks that
  such a refit reproduces the point estimates. The percentile interval
  is the default (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016) and the BCa interval
  is available. `B = 1000`, `seed`, and `ncpus` work as in the
  reliability family, and the draws and the fate of every replication
  travel in the `bootstrap` attribute. Improper replications are set
  aside by default (`improper = "drop"`), unlike the reliability
  family’s default. A solution, the fit’s or a replication’s, is
  improper when
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  flags it or lavaan’s post-estimation check fails, a check made on the
  model’s own parameters for a fit with auxiliary variables (lavaan’s
  `aux`), as
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  makes it: lavaan’s own check also tests the residual covariances of an
  auxiliary variable, which are not positive definite once it is related
  to the general factor strongly enough, however proper the bifactor
  solution. On a bifactor model of 15 Holzinger and Swineford tests (a
  general factor on tests 1 to 9 and 14 to 19, with spatial, verbal, and
  memory group factors on tests 1 to 4, 5 to 9, and 14 to 19;
  `seed = 113`), 212 of 1,000 replications were improper and their omega
  ran as high as 26.5; keeping every one of them would have put the
  upper limit of the 95 percent interval for omega at 13.7 rather than
  0.902. `improper = "keep"` uses an improper replication only when
  every index it gives but the maximal reliability is defined and a
  proportion. The maximal reliability, which is not defined for an
  improper solution, rests on the proper replications under either rule,
  so its interval is the same under both, and an improper point estimate
  reported under `"keep"` has none. Coefficient H is not defined when a
  standardized loading reaches one (see Changes to Earlier Results), and
  such a replication is set aside under either rule. Every replication
  set aside is counted and named (improper, not converged, an error, an
  ordered item that lost a category in the resample), and a caution is
  printed when they reach the tail area of an interval. As throughout
  the bootstrap family, an index’s interval requires at least half of
  the `B` replications, and at least two, to return a value for it;
  otherwise its `se` and limits are `NA`, and the warning and the
  printed line say so. Multiple-group, clustered, and weighted fits,
  fits to a covariance matrix, and fits that did not converge are
  refused. So are the fits
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  refuses, among them a fit with an item on two group factors. The H it
  bootstraps is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), not
  the maximal reliability of the factor, which has rows of its own (on
  the help page’s model run with `B = 50` in place of its 10 and
  `seed = 113`, the general factor’s maximal reliability is 0.678
  \[0.646, 0.734\] beside the index’s 0.769 \[0.741, 0.808\]). The
  sample values of both run upward (Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, & McIntosh,
  2019), so the `bootstrap` attribute carries the bootstrap estimate of
  each index’s bias (the mean of the replicates its interval uses minus
  the estimate), and the printed table gives it for H and the maximal
  reliability. On the same example with `B = 200` (the same seed) it is
  0.031 for the first group factor’s maximal reliability and 0.019 for
  its H, against 0.005 for its omega. The printed table says what ECV
  and omega mean for a group factor. The table has one row per index and
  factor, with `estimate`, `se`, `ci_lower`, and `ci_upper`; `tidy()`
  and `glance()` give one row per index and one row of counts and
  settings.

### Categorical Omega Without mvtnorm, and With Incomplete Items

- **Categorical omega no longer needs `mvtnorm`.**
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  and the per-factor categorical omega of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  sum a bivariate normal probability over every pair of thresholds of
  every pair of items (Green & Yang, 2009, Eq. 21). Through 1.0.1 each
  probability was its own call to `mvtnorm::pmvnorm()`, so categorical
  omega stopped for a user without `mvtnorm`, a suggested package, and
  those calls took most of the time of a bootstrap replication. DMAR now
  computes the probabilities itself, all at once, by the method of
  Drezner and Wesolowsky (1990) as refined by Genz (2004), the algorithm
  `mvtnorm` applies in two dimensions. The two agree to within 4e-16 on
  a grid of 2,873 points. Every categorical omega checked is unchanged
  to the rounding of its sums, by at most 9e-16: Green and Yang’s ten
  population designs, six to 24 Holzinger and Swineford tests cut into
  two to seven categories under both denominators,
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)’s
  per-factor omega, and a seeded bootstrap. Within about 1e-7 of a
  correlation of one `mvtnorm` loses accuracy, and within about 1e-10 it
  returns the limit at one (an error of up to 2.2e-6, at both limits
  zero); DMAR’s computation matches the exact values there. Only a
  communality or a polychoric correlation that close to one reaches that
  region. At 12 items with 7 categories the assembly takes 0.002 s
  rather than 0.37 s, so a bootstrap replication takes about 0.07 s
  rather than 0.43 s, and a BCa interval at the default `B = 10000`
  about 12 minutes rather than 70 on the machine where this was
  measured. No argument, default, or output shape changes, and `mvtnorm`
  leaves Suggests.

- **[`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  analyzes incomplete items by pairwise deletion or by multiple
  imputation.** Through 1.0.1 it analyzed only the complete rows. It
  gains `missing = c("listwise", "pairwise", "mi")`, `aux`,
  `impute = c("pmm", "polr")`, and `imputations = 5`, appended after
  `ncpus`. `"listwise"` stays the default and returns the same results
  as before.

  `"pairwise"` estimates each threshold from the rows that observe its
  item and each polychoric correlation from the rows that observe both
  items (lavaan’s pairwise deletion). With no covariates in the model it
  is consistent only when values are missing completely at random, as
  listwise deletion is (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010). Under missingness at
  random it is biased (Shi, Lee, Fairchild, & Maydeu-Olivares, 2020),
  and the printed table says so.

  `"mi"` imputes the items by chained equations with mice (now in
  Suggests): predictive mean matching by default, or the proportional
  odds model. Auxiliary variables named in `aux` are predictors in the
  imputation model only, and a row with no observed item is imputed when
  an auxiliary variable is observed on it, and `N` counts it. The
  estimate is the mean of categorical omega over the imputations of the
  observed data. Its interval is the bootstrap then impute interval of
  Schomaker and Heumann (2018): each of `B` bootstrap samples of the
  incomplete rows is imputed `imputations` times, and the percentile
  interval of the replicate means is the confidence interval. BCa is
  refused. The items reach mice as plain integer codes, so a column read
  with haven, which carries value labels, and a factor whose labels are
  whole numbers are imputed as those numbers. Every incomplete item is
  imputed, including one observed together with another on only two or
  three rows, as in a planned missing design with a small overlap; the
  check by which mice sets aside a variable almost perfectly correlated
  with another would otherwise leave it with its missing values. An item
  with a single observed value is refused, and an item mice still does
  not impute stops the call by name. Turning that check off would also
  keep an auxiliary variable that duplicates another, so the auxiliary
  variables are screened first. One whose multiple correlation with the
  columns observed on every row that observes it (the items and the
  auxiliary variables kept before it) reaches .999, mice’s own threshold
  for a pair, carries no information beyond the predictors already in
  the model and is left out, with a message. Kept together, two or more
  such variables would make mice fall back to a ridge penalty and impute
  unstably. When mice still applies its ridge penalty, the warning says
  how often (`ridge` in the `imputation` attribute).

  The point estimate is formed from at least 20 imputations, and more
  when von Hippel’s (2020) quadratic rule asks for more, and averages
  those that return a value. The rule is applied to the upper limit of
  the fraction of missing information that the replications themselves
  estimate. A call with a bootstrap makes the most imputations the rule
  can ask for (201) and fits every one before the bootstrap runs, so
  nothing found in a completed data set of the observed data can discard
  a finished bootstrap.

  A completed data set with no categorical omega, an improper (Heywood)
  solution above all, is set aside and counted, as a bootstrap
  replication is, and the estimate averages the rest. The call stops
  only when fewer than half return a value, the criterion of Lim and
  Cheung (2022) for a failed analysis. Stopping on any one would fail
  with probability 1 - (1 - p)^M, for a share p of improper sets among M
  imputations. Imputation produces such solutions when the observed data
  have none, if two items are skewed in opposite directions and values
  are missing among the few respondents who determine their polychoric
  correlation. On the help page’s incomplete items under the model
  implied denominator (`missing = "mi"`, `ci_method = "percentile"`,
  `B = 200`, `seed = 1`), 26 of the 201 completed data sets of the
  observed data were improper, while the complete data and pairwise fits
  were proper (the complete rows leave two polychoric correlations
  undetermined and the loadings unidentified, so listwise deletion
  stops). An improper set has the largest loadings, so setting it aside
  lowers the estimate a little. The warning, the printed lines, and the
  `imputation` attribute (`imputations_returned`,
  `imputations_set_aside`, `status`) say how many were set aside and
  why.

  A bootstrap replication computes the same statistic as the point
  estimate: it averages those of its completed data sets that return a
  value, and it is set aside only when fewer than half do. A rule
  requiring every completed data set to return a value would set a
  replication aside with probability 1 - (1 - p)^M for a share p of sets
  returning none, which grows with `imputations`. Under this rule the
  share goes to zero as `imputations` grows when fewer than half of the
  sets fail. It does not fall steadily, though: an odd number of
  imputations needs one more set to return a value than the even number
  below it, so it sets more replications aside. The warning therefore
  names an even number when any set was set aside. In the bootstrap of
  the help page’s incomplete items above, a quarter of the replications’
  completed data sets returned no value. Applied to the first two,
  three, four, and five imputations of each replication (the
  `replicate_estimates` element of the `imputation` attribute), the rule
  set aside 12.5, 21, 14.5, and 20% of the replications, where requiring
  every set would set aside 35.5, 45.5, 48.5, and 52.5%. The replicate
  by imputation estimates form an unbalanced one-way analysis of
  variance (Searle, Casella, & McCulloch, 1992). The warning and the
  `imputation` attribute (`replicate_sets_set_aside`) count the
  completed data sets set aside within the replications kept. As for the
  other treatments, no interval is reported when fewer than half of the
  replications return a value.

  The result’s `imputation` attribute carries the imputations, the
  fraction of missing information, and how much imputation noise widens
  the interval. A replication whose imputation fails is set aside and
  counted under a new reason, `imputation`, and a seed gives the same
  result for any `ncpus`. A completed data set whose fit lavaan stops
  with an error is set aside under `"error"`, and the warning quotes
  lavaan’s message.

  In a Monte Carlo simulation described on the help page (10 items at n
  = 300, about a fifth of the values missing at random), predictive mean
  matching came closest to the complete data estimate, ahead of the
  proportional odds model, pairwise deletion, and listwise deletion.

- **`B` defaults to `NULL` in
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  and
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md).**
  For every existing call it means 10000, the default written before.
  Under `missing = "mi"`, where each replication imputes the data and
  refits on every completed data set, it means 1000. When no item value
  is missing, `missing = "mi"` has nothing to impute and returns the
  complete data result, whose bootstrap takes that path’s default of
  10000; the message says so.

- **[`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md)
  forwards each family function’s missing data treatment.** `missing` is
  now `NULL` by default and forwarded as given, so each family function
  checks it against its own choices (listwise, FIML, or two-stage for
  alpha and omega; listwise or FIML for H; listwise, pairwise, or
  multiple imputation for categorical omega). `missing`, `aux`, and the
  new `impute` and `imputations` reach
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md).
  KR-20 still refuses `missing` and `aux`.

### Fit, Precision, and Comparison of Structural Equation Models

- **CFA help states the standard errors each estimator receives.**
  `se = "standard"` supplies inverse-information standard errors: normal
  theory for ML, MLR, and GLS, and Browne’s asymptotically distribution
  free ones for WLS. Ordered items request `robust.sem` in its place.
  MLR otherwise needs `se = "robust.huber.white"` for sandwich standard
  errors under FIML. From a covariance matrix, `robust.sem` with ML
  needs the asymptotic covariance of the moments in `NACOV`. This
  corrects the description; no result changes.

- **[`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md)
  is new.** It gives the chi square test of exact fit a reference
  distribution that does not assume normal data: the model based
  bootstrap of Bollen and Stine (1992), which transforms the data so
  that the fitted model holds in them exactly, resamples the transformed
  rows `B` times, refits the model to each sample, and reports the share
  of bootstrap statistics at least the observed one as `p_bootstrap`,
  with the Wilson interval for its Monte Carlo error (its limits print
  to the four decimal places of the *p*-value) and the counts of samples
  used, improper, and failed. With complete data it is lavaan’s
  `bootstrapLavaan(type = "bollen.stine")`, resample for resample when
  the seed given here is passed to lavaan as its `iseed` (with lavaan
  run serially; lavaan called without `iseed` draws its own seed from
  the caller’s random number stream). With incomplete data fitted by
  FIML it transforms the rows so that the saturated FIML estimates on
  the transformed data are the model implied moments, by the two
  transformations of Savalei and Yuan (2009): one matrix for every
  missing data pattern (the default) or pattern by pattern with each
  pattern’s own moments. Both are solved on the variables divided by
  their saturated standard deviations, so the result does not depend on
  the units of the variables; it differs element by element from the
  same transformations solved in raw units (as semTools’ `bsBootMiss()`
  solves the common one), though both make the model hold exactly. Every
  bootstrap sample keeps the missing values of the rows it draws, so the
  model is refitted by FIML. The transformed data are checked: the
  largest saturated estimating equation and the largest mean residual at
  the model implied moments are recorded, and
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  on the transformed data returns the fitted moments. Replications are
  drawn before any refit, so a seed gives the same result whatever
  `ncpus` is. A sample’s solution is improper when lavaan’s
  post-estimation check finds a negative variance estimate or a
  covariance matrix that is not positive definite; for a fit with
  auxiliary variables (lavaan’s `aux`) the check is made on the model’s
  own parameters, as for the fit itself (see the
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  entry). Fits to summary statistics, ordered indicators, non-ML
  estimators, two-level and clustered models, sampling weights,
  two-stage fits, fits conditional on observed exogenous variables, fits
  whose analysis data keep missing values without FIML (pairwise
  deletion), and fits without a standard test statistic are refused with
  the reason, as an error of class `dmar_exact_fit_bootstrap_scope` (a
  `dmar_refusal`) whose `reason` element names it (a fit whose cases
  lavaan removed by listwise deletion is bootstrapped on its complete
  cases, as it was fitted, with a warning); a missing data pattern too
  small for the pattern transformation is refused with class
  `dmar_pattern_too_small`, which carries the pattern, its counts, and
  its group, and a transformation that is undefined for the data with
  class `dmar_transformation_undefined`.

- **[`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  is new.** It reports the fit of a structural equation model in one
  table of twenty-four rows: the chi square test of exact fit; the RMSEA
  with its confidence interval and the tests of close fit (Browne &
  Cudeck, 1993) and not close fit (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996);
  CFI, TLI, NFI, IFI, and RNI; the covariance SRMR; and gamma hat and
  adjusted gamma hat with their intervals, with `NA` where the input
  does not determine a row. It takes a fitted lavaan model or the
  summary statistics a paper reports. With a fitted model the default
  `version = "auto"` gives lavaan’s robust measures for a fit with a
  corrected test statistic (MLM, MLR, WLSMV, a sampling weighted fit;
  Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, & Li, 2012; Brosseau-Liard & Savalei, 2014;
  Savalei, 2018, 2021), the FIML corrected indices of Zhang and
  Savalei (2023) for a FIML fit (which approximate the complete data
  RMSEA and CFI and are not corrections for nonnormality), and the
  standard measures for a normal theory ML fit of complete data; with
  auxiliary variables (lavaan’s `aux` under FIML) the SRMR is over the
  model’s own variables, since lavaan’s SRMR averages in the auxiliary
  variables, whose residuals of about zero make it lower for the same
  model; the printed footer names the version and why it was chosen. A
  fitted model keeps lavaan’s sample size multiplier, so its values
  equal lavaan’s (for the scaled version, those lavaan gives under
  `rmsea.scaled.mplus = TRUE`); summary input takes
  `sample_size_convention = "N-1"` by default, the convention of
  [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md)
  (pass `"N"` for a statistic from lavaan or Mplus), and `n_groups` for
  Steiger’s (1998) multiple group RMSEA. The default `conf_level` is
  0.90, the conventional level of the RMSEA interval, whose two limits
  decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 that the table
  reports beside it; the help page explains why, and `conf_level = 0.95`
  gives a 95 percent interval. A fitted model that did not converge is
  refused with an error of class `dmar_not_converged`, and one whose
  solution is inadmissible with a refusal of class `dmar_inadmissible`
  that names the negative variance estimate, or the covariance matrix
  that is not positive definite (that of the latent variables, of the
  residuals of the observed variables, or of the residuals of the
  structural part of the model), as lavaan’s post-estimation check finds
  them. With auxiliary variables (lavaan’s `aux` under FIML) the check
  is made on the model’s own parameters: lavaan’s own check also tests
  the residual covariances of the auxiliary variables, which it models
  as saturated correlates, and that block is not positive definite once
  an auxiliary variable is related to a factor strongly enough (for one
  factor whose items have uncorrelated residuals, and an auxiliary
  variable related to them only through the factor, a correlation above
  .33 between the two when the maximal reliability of the items is .9),
  however proper the model’s solution. Auxiliary variables are
  recognized when they are given through lavaan’s `aux`; saturated
  correlates written into the model by hand are judged with the rest of
  theta.
  [`sem_residual_fit()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_residual_fit.md),
  [`sem_information_criteria()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_information_criteria.md),
  [`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md),
  [`ecvi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ecvi.md), and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md)
  share the check, and
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  judges a fit with auxiliary variables by it.

- **[`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  reports the robust measures of a mean and variance adjusted statistic,
  a CFI of 1 for a saturated model, and no measure of a ULS fit of
  continuous data that changes with the units of the variables.** In the
  examples, the three-factor model of nine Holzinger and Swineford tests
  is visual perception, cubes, and lozenges; paragraph comprehension,
  sentence completion, and word meaning; and addition, counting groups
  of dots, and straight and curved capitals, fit to
  `holzinger_swineford` by
  [`lavaan::cfa()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/lavaan/man/cfa.html) with
  `std.lv = TRUE`.

  - **MLMVS.** lavaan computes no robust measures beside the older mean
    and variance adjusted statistic (`estimator = "MLMVS"`, or
    `test = "mean.var.adjusted"`). Savalei (2018) shows that the robust
    RMSEA and CFI of Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, and Li (2012) and
    Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2014) do not depend on which corrected
    statistic accompanies them. Each subtracts c df from the ML
    statistic, with c = tr(U Gamma)/df, which is that statistic’s
    scaling constant times its degrees of freedom over df. So `"auto"`
    reports the robust version of such a fit, computed by DMAR, with the
    interval and close fit tests of Brosseau-Liard et al. (2012, Eq. 10)
    and a robust gamma hat. The values equal lavaan’s for the same model
    fitted by MLM. For the three-factor model by MLMVS the RMSEA is .091
    with 90 percent interval (the default) \[.070, .113\], the CFI .932,
    and gamma hat .958, where the scaled measures `version = "scaled"`
    gives are .089 \[.066, .113\] and .734. A saturated fit with this
    statistic is reported in the robust version as well. Nothing is
    computed from its undefined scaling constant there, and the footer
    attributes the corrections to Brosseau-Liard et al. without saying
    DMAR computed them.
  - **Continuous ML without robust measures.** Where lavaan offers a
    scaled statistic but no robust measures for a continuous ML fit,
    `"auto"` reports the standard version, with a warning; a bootstrap
    test, which carries no scaled statistic, gets the standard version
    without one. The standard version estimates the population values of
    the ML measures, as the robust one does and the scaled one does not
    (Savalei, 2018).
  - **Saturated models.** A model with no degrees of freedom and a
    statistic of zero has a CFI and an RNI of 1 in every version, and in
    the standard and scaled versions its NFI and IFI take their values
    at a statistic of zero (the robust version has none). lavaan’s
    robust CFI and RNI are formed with a scaling constant of 0/0 and
    come out `NA`, or a value only by rounding.
  - **ULS with continuous data.** The ULS statistic, (N - G) times the
    ULS fit function, is in the units of the squared covariances, and a
    measure of fit must not change when every variable is multiplied by
    the same number. lavaan forms the robust RMSEA of a ULSM or ULSMV
    fit of continuous data by putting that statistic into a correction
    derived for the ML fit function, so multiplying every variable by k
    multiplies it by k^2: 16.1 for the three-factor model by ULSM on the
    raw scores, and 0.161 with every score divided by 10. That RMSEA,
    its interval, and its close fit tests are `NA`. So are those of the
    standard version, whose CFI, TLI, RNI, and IFI set the degrees of
    freedom against the same statistic and are `NA` too (lavaan’s
    standard CFI is .977 for the raw scores and .979 for the scores
    divided by 10); its NFI, a ratio of two such statistics, is
    reported. When the model restricts the means, the ULS fit function
    adds the squared mean residuals to the squared covariance residuals,
    which are in other units, and every RMSEA row and incremental index
    of every version is `NA`: with the intercepts of paragraph
    comprehension and word meaning constrained equal in the same model
    (`meanstructure = TRUE`), lavaan’s robust CFI is .979 for the raw
    scores and .972 for the scores divided by 10, and its scaled RMSEA
    .160 and .181. The `chi_square` row and the SRMR are kept. The
    robust CFI, TLI, and RNI and the scaled measures of a model with
    free means do not depend on the units and are reported, though no
    cutoffs have been developed for them (Savalei, 2018). So are the
    measures of a fit by `estimator = "ULS"` alone, tested by Browne’s
    residual statistic, when its estimates do not change with the units.
    When restrictions link the means and covariances through shared
    parameters, as equal loadings and intercepts do through latent
    means, ULS estimates change with the units. Browne’s statistic at
    those estimates and its indices change too; RMSEA and incremental
    indices are withheld. The valid test statistic and SRMR remain. A
    warning, the `uls` element of the `sem_fit` attribute, and a line of
    the printed footer say which rows are `NA` and why.

- **The scaled version of
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  puts the scaled statistic in the standard formulas.** Its RMSEA
  interval and its tests of close and not close fit are computed from
  the `chi_square` and `df` rows of the same table (Brosseau-Liard,
  Savalei, & Li, 2012, Eqs. 11 and 13; Savalei, 2018, Table 1). These
  are the values EQS and Mplus report, and the ones lavaan gives under
  `rmsea.scaled.mplus = TRUE`. lavaan’s default for a Satorra-Bentler,
  Yuan-Bentler, or mean and variance adjusted statistic refers the
  unscaled statistic to the noncentral chi square on tr(U Gamma) degrees
  of freedom, c df with c = tr(U Gamma)/df as in the previous entry (for
  a Satorra-Bentler or Yuan-Bentler statistic, whose degrees of freedom
  are df, c is the scaling constant itself): the same point estimate,
  but an interval and p-values that the rows beside them do not imply.
  The two differ little when c is near 1: for the three-factor model by
  MLR, c = 0.98, and the 90 percent interval is \[0.0728, 0.1150\]
  against lavaan’s default \[0.0726, 0.1152\]. They differ much when c
  is not near 1: for the same model on multivariate *t* data with 4 df
  (each pupil’s centered scores multiplied by `sqrt(4 / rchisq(301, 4))`
  after `set.seed(1)`), c = 1.80, the interval is \[0.0506, 0.0950\]
  against \[0.0562, 0.0892\], and the p-value of close fit .046 against
  .013. A scaled and shifted statistic (MLMV, WLSMV) gets lavaan’s own
  values. For an MLMVS fit, whose scaled measures `version = "scaled"`
  reports, the interval is \[0.0659, 0.1125\] against lavaan’s default
  \[0.0684, 0.1098\]; `"auto"` reports the robust measures of such a
  fit, which DMAR computes.

- **Gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat come with intervals, and gamma hat
  has a robust version.** The rows `gamma_hat_ci_lower`,
  `gamma_hat_ci_upper`, `adjusted_gamma_hat_ci_lower`, and
  `adjusted_gamma_hat_ci_upper` of
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  are the noncentrality limits of the RMSEA interval mapped to each
  index (Steiger & Fouladi, 1997, pp. 251–252, whose 90 percent interval
  of .972 to .997 for the adjusted index in their worked example the
  tests reproduce). For a robust ML fit of complete continuous data
  (MLM, MLR, MLMV, and MLMVS, whose robust measures DMAR computes since
  lavaan does not), the robust version reports gamma hat from the robust
  noncentrality, with limits from the robust RMSEA interval: 0.956, with
  the 90 percent interval \[0.935, 0.973\] that the default `conf_level`
  gives (\[0.931, 0.976\] at `conf_level = 0.95`), for the three-factor
  model by MLR. The help page says that gamma hat is lavaan 0.7-3’s
  `gfi_lrt`, which lavaan reports only when asked by name, and not the
  `gfi` lavaan prints, which is computed from Browne’s residual based
  statistic (for the same fit, the standard gamma hat, lavaan’s
  `gfi_lrt`, is 0.957 and its `gfi` 0.959). Only NFI and IFI have no
  robust version.

- **Gamma hat is `NA` where Steiger’s result does not reach.** The
  result is for covariance structures. A fitted model that restricts the
  means gets `NA`, with the reason recorded in the `sem_fit` attribute.
  Examples are a growth model, or intercepts constrained equal (under
  either `ceq.simple` setting), constrained to a constant, entered in a
  linear constraint, tied to a loading, or held at the bound of an
  inequality constraint, which lavaan’s degrees of freedom do not count.
  Whether the means are restricted is read from the derivatives of the
  model’s moments, with the constraints that bind at the estimates
  imposed. Free means change nothing. Summary input whose `df` exceeds
  p(p + 1)/2, which only restricted means can produce, gives `NA` with a
  warning, where the formula would give an adjusted gamma hat above
  gamma hat. Below that bound summary input carries nothing that shows
  restricted means, and supplying `p` states that the model is a
  covariance structure. A sampling weighted fit gives `NA` too, since
  its statistic is a weighted pseudo likelihood ratio statistic.
