- **A fit without a corrected statistic is described from lavaan’s
  options.** `"auto"` reports its standard measures under a reason that
  names the estimator and the data. Some standard statistics have no chi
  square reference distribution: an ordered fit by DWLS or ULS with the
  standard test alone (the default test of those estimators, which WLSMV
  and ULSMV extend with a corrected one) and a DWLS or ULS fit of
  continuous data whose test was set to `"standard"` (lavaan’s default
  for continuous data adds Browne’s residual based statistic, which is
  chi square under normality), to which lavaan gives no p-value, and a
  sampling weighted fit whose test was set to `"standard"`, a weighted
  pseudo likelihood ratio statistic whose p-value lavaan reports all the
  same. For such a fit a warning says that the statistic is not chi
  square distributed and names the remedy (a corrected test, or for
  continuous data leaving out `test = "standard"`), and
  `version = "robust"` refuses the fit with the same advice. Full WLS
  for ordered data is the exception. Its statistic is asymptotically chi
  square (Browne, 1984; Muthén, 1984) and lavaan reports its p-value, so
  its standard measures are reported without a warning, and a request
  for the robust version says that they are the ones to report. A
  continuous fit tested by a chi square statistic is described by its
  estimator (a normal theory ML or GLS fit, an asymptotically
  distribution free WLS fit, or a least squares fit tested by Browne’s
  residual based statistic) rather than as a normal theory fit.

- **[`equivalence_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_rmsea.md)
  is new.** It tests whether the population RMSEA is below a bound
  chosen in advance: the test of not close fit (MacCallum et al., 1996)
  read as an equivalence test by Yuan, Chan, Marcoulides, and Bentler
  (2016). It reports the 1 - 2 alpha interval, whose upper limit is
  their T-size RMSEA, with the p-value and a verdict, and takes
  `n_groups` and `sample_size_convention` (default `"N-1"`).

- **[`sem_residual_fit()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_residual_fit.md)
  is new.** It reports the unbiased SRMR of Maydeu-Olivares (2017) with
  its standard error and confidence interval (90 percent by default, as
  lavaan’s, which pairs with the test of close fit at .05), the test of
  exact fit (with the standard error that holds under exact fit only),
  an optional test of close fit, the SRMR of the mean residuals, and the
  largest standardized residual (Maydeu-Olivares, Shi, & Rosseel, 2018).
  The residual covariance it used (normal theory, or distribution free
  for MLM and MLR) is recorded on the result. A FIML or pairwise fit of
  complete data gives the residual inference of a listwise fit with the
  same mean structure and information setting; missing values, two-stage
  fits, and fits with auxiliary variables (which change nothing in the
  model’s fit when no value is missing, but lower lavaan’s SRMR) are
  refused, and the message says which.

- **[`sem_information_criteria()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_information_criteria.md)
  is new.** It reports AIC (Akaike, 1974), BIC (Schwarz, 1978), the
  sample size adjusted BIC (SABIC; Sclove, 1987; lavaan’s `bic2`),
  Haughton’s (1988) HBIC, and the IBIC and SPBIC that Bollen, Ray,
  Zavisca, and Harden (2012) proposed and Bollen, Harden, Ray, and
  Zavisca (2014) evaluated for structural equation models, then the log
  likelihood, the number of parameters, and N, in one table in which a
  criterion not requested is `NA`. It takes a fitted lavaan model, or as
  summary input the log likelihood, the parameter count, N, and (for
  IBIC and SPBIC) the information matrices, so that a published
  comparison can be reproduced; all four rows of Table 6 of Bollen et
  al. (2014) are reproduced to within 0.015. A fit whose fit function is
  not the normal log likelihood is refused with the reason (ordered
  indicators, an estimator other than ML, the Wishart likelihood, or
  sampling weights, whose pseudo log likelihood has no justification for
  these penalties; Asparouhov, 2005), a two-level model gives AIC only,
  and automatic IBIC and SPBIC are refused for fits whose information
  matrices are not the ones the criteria are defined on. The help page
  explains that IBIC depends on the units of the observed variables and
  on how the latent variables are identified, and that SPBIC under its
  default prior depends on the identification; it also notes that the
  worked example of Bollen et al. (2012, Table 1) counts log N twice in
  IBIC.

- **[`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md)
  is new.** It ranks models fitted to the same data by one criterion
  (BIC by default) and reports each model’s difference from the best,
  its relative weight within the set (Burnham & Anderson, 2004), and,
  for the BIC family, the approximate log Bayes factor of the best model
  over it. It first checks that the log likelihoods are comparable: the
  same cases and data values (or the same summary statistics), the same
  observed variables in any order, the same groups, missing data method,
  and mean structure, and the same exogenous observed variables (with
  `fixed.x = TRUE`, the default of
  [`lavaan::sem()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/lavaan/man/sem.html), the log
  likelihood is conditional on them, and two saturated models of the
  same three variables that condition on different variables differ by
  hundreds of BIC points). A refusal names the two models and what
  differs. The two two-stage settings count as one missing data method,
  since they fit the same EM moments by the same likelihood and differ
  only in their standard errors and test, which no criterion uses; the
  `comparison` attribute records each setting used. For IBIC, and SPBIC
  under its default prior, a refusal states the rule: one identification
  for every latent variable of every model, which two models that each
  mix the two identifications in the same way do not meet.
  [`?sem_information_criteria`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_information_criteria.md)
  says the same. Weighted fits are refused; multiple group models
  (configural against metric invariance, for example) are compared by
  AIC, BIC, SABIC, and HBIC. `tidy()` and `glance()` methods come with
  it.

- **[`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reads an interval held in `<estimate>_ci_lower` and
  `<estimate>_ci_upper` rows, and gains `term`.** A
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  table holds the RMSEA’s interval in rows named for the estimate, and
  gamma hat’s and adjusted gamma hat’s the same way.
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  writes the one `term` names or, when the table holds no interval in
  another form, the first such estimate, with no *p*-value: the table’s
  *p*-values are the tests of exact, close, and not close fit. The level
  is the interval’s own when the table records it, and otherwise the
  table’s. For the three-factor model of nine Holzinger and Swineford
  tests (visual perception, cubes, and lozenges; paragraph
  comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning; addition,
  counting groups of dots, and straight and curved capitals) fit by
  [`lavaan::cfa()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/lavaan/man/cfa.html) with its
  defaults, `results_sentence(sem_fit_measures(fit), digits = 3)` is
  “rmsea = 0.092, 90% CI \[0.071, 0.114\]”, at the default level.
  `term = "rmsea"` also reaches the RMSEA of a
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  table, whose `rmsea_ci_level` row records the level of its RMSEA
  interval (its `rmsea_conf_level`, .90 by default), and gives the same
  sentence for the same model. The level is also read from the table’s
  `rmsea_conf_level` attribute, so a selection of the `rmsea`,
  `rmsea_ci_lower`, and `rmsea_ci_upper` rows, which leaves the
  `rmsea_ci_level` row out, keeps the level of its interval: for the
  model above the selection reads “rmsea = 0.092, 90% CI \[0.071,
  0.114\]”, as the full table does. The same holds for the tables of
  [`fa_bifactor()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_bifactor.md)
  and
  [`fa_second_order()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_second_order.md).
  A `term` that names no estimate with such rows is refused with the
  names of those that have them. `term` is appended after `digits`, and
  reading such rows changes no sentence written before.

- **A vignette, “SEM Fit and Model Comparison”**
  ([`vignette("sem_fit_measures")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/sem_fit_measures.md)),
  teaches these measures on one running example, the nine tests of
  Jöreskog (1969) in `holzinger_swineford`: the chi square test of exact
  fit; the RMSEA with its interval, the tests of close and not close
  fit, and why the RMSEA is reported with a 90 percent interval; the
  equivalence test and the T-size RMSEA; the sample size convention and
  the multiple group RMSEA; the incremental indices and gamma hat; the
  standard, scaled, and robust version of each measure and which one a
  robust or FIML fit reports; the unbiased SRMR and reading the
  residuals; the information criteria, including a worked example in
  which rescaling one variable reverses an IBIC verdict while BIC, HBIC,
  and SPBIC do not move; ranking candidate models with
  [`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md);
  and the ECVI. Every number in its text is computed from the fits.

### Missing Data: What the Missing Values Cost

- **[`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  is new.** For each free and each defined parameter of a full
  information maximum likelihood fit (a lavaan fit with `missing = "ml"`
  or `"ml.x"`, for example from
  `fa_confirmatory(..., missing = "fiml", output = "fit")`, or an
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) or
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  fit) it reports the fraction of missing information, 1 - SE_C^2 /
  SE_O^2 (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012), the proportion of the sampling
  variance of the estimate that is due to the missing values, with the
  effective N, N(1 - FMI), the target N, N / (1 - FMI), and the interval
  width inflation factor, 1 / sqrt(1 - FMI), which state in AIPE terms
  the precision the missing values cost. Both standard errors come from
  refits at the fit’s estimates with the optimizer off and one
  information type for both, the complete data side fit to the EM
  (unrestricted) moments with the same N and no (N - 1)/N rescaling of
  the covariance matrix, as lavaan computes them. `information` chooses
  among the three estimators of Chen and Savalei (2021):
  `"unstructured"`, the default, which cannot be negative and broke down
  least in their simulations; `"structured"`; and `"hessian"`, lavaan’s
  default, which agrees with lavaan’s `parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE)`
  to about 1e-7 when the fit runs lavaan’s EM as far
  (`em_h1_args = list(tol = 1e-10)`), and otherwise only to the
  precision of lavaan’s EM (see the first example below). The default
  therefore differs from lavaan’s. An MLR fit gets the normal theory FMI
  at its estimates, which is the ML fit’s. Multiple groups are
  supported, each row’s N following its group and its equality
  constraints, whether a constraint names labels or defined parameters
  (`ind1 == ind2` with `ind1 := a1*b1` and `ind2 := a2*b2` gives the
  rows it ties the summed N, as `a1*b1 == a2*b2` does), and the omega,
  H, and AVE that
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  defines get their FMI through their delta method variances. A
  percentile bootstrap interval is opt-in (`ci_method = "percentile"`,
  with `B` and `seed`), and the printed table says that a sample FMI is
  imprecise unless N is several hundred (Chen & Savalei, 2021). Fits
  with ordered items, an estimator outside the ML family, listwise,
  pairwise, or two-stage missing data handling, `conditional.x = TRUE`,
  more than one level, sampling weights, or no convergence are refused
  with the reason, as are lavaanList objects and rotated EFA solutions.
  `tidy()` and `glance()` methods come with it. The examples below use
  the data sets of `tests/testthat/test-fraction_missing_information.R`
  in the source package.

  - **Units.** Both refits are made with every observed variable divided
    by the power of two nearest its standard deviation, the factors
    lavaan divides by when it rescales a badly scaled fit; the parameter
    table, defined parameters and constraints included, is carried
    through the same exact map, and the standard errors are mapped back.
    The FIML refit runs lavaan’s EM estimate of the unrestricted moments
    until no mean or covariance changes by more than 1e-10 times the
    smallest variance, where lavaan’s default stops at an absolute 1e-5.
    Take lavaan’s nine Holzinger and Swineford tests in three factors,
    with x5 and x9 missing at random (`set.seed(11)`, then
    `x5[runif(301) < plogis(-1 + x4)]` and `x9[runif(301) < 0.25]` set
    to `NA`). lavaan’s own FMIs move by up to 5e-6 when its EM is run to
    1e-14 rather than 1e-5, and those of the same model by school, whose
    solution has a negative residual variance, by up to .0014. With the
    fit’s estimates held (the fit to the rescaled data made at the
    rescaled estimates with `optim.method = "none"`), the FMIs of the
    three estimators agree with those in the original units to within
    1e-9 in one group and 5e-8 by school when every variable is
    multiplied by .001, .01, 10, 1000, 10,000, or 1,000,000. Take next a
    regression of y on three predictors with values missing at random
    (200 cases of four standard normal variables correlated .5, drawn
    after `set.seed(3)`, with `x3[runif(200) < plogis(1 + 2 * x1)]` and
    `x2[sample(200, 3)]` set to `NA`), fit by
    `lavaan::sem("y ~ x1 + x2 + x3", missing = "ml", fixed.x = FALSE)`.
    Fit anew to the rescaled data, its FMIs agree with those at a
    standard deviation of 1 to within 1.3e-7 when y, x1, or x3 alone, or
    every variable, is multiplied by .001, 10,000, or 100,000, when x2
    alone is multiplied by 10,000 or 100,000 (by .001 its standard
    deviation lies just above the .001 at which lavaan rescales a fit,
    and lavaan’s fit does not converge), and when the outcome is
    multiplied by 100,000,000, where
    `mlmr(wald_df = "missing_information")` gives the degrees of freedom
    it gives at 1. lavaan’s own `parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE)`, which
    refits in the variables’ own metric, is off by up to .93 (by .04 to
    .07 for the slopes) with every standard deviation near 100,000, and
    returns NA with every standard deviation near 300,000 or with that
    of y near 10,000,000.
  - **Estimates that are not at the maximum.** The FMI is computed at
    the fit’s estimates. lavaan rescales a fit only when a standard
    deviation is .001 or less or 1000 or more, or two differ by a factor
    of 1000, and between those limits it can stop short of the maximum
    while it reports convergence. With every standard deviation of the
    regression near .003 the FMIs are off by up to .001. In the three
    factor model, identified by marker indicators, with every test
    multiplied by 100 they are off by up to .011, and by .12 multiplied
    by 500. In lavaan 0.7-3 a fit made with `ov_order = "data"` and
    rescaled by lavaan is not the maximum likelihood fit when the
    columns of the data are not in the model’s order: with x3, y, and x1
    of the regression multiplied by .004, .03, and .5 and the columns
    ordered x3, x2, x1, y, the slopes’ FMIs are .28, .22, and .70 in
    place of .06, .19, and .70. The computation takes one Newton step in
    the refit metric. When an estimate moves by more than 1e-4 of the
    larger of 1 and its size, the FMIs are computed again one step on. A
    warning is given only when an FMI changes by more than 1e-4. It
    names the parameter, likelihood gain, and largest FMI change. Units
    and `rescale_data = TRUE` are named only for a fit lavaan did not
    rescale whose standard deviations indicate that cause; variable
    order is named only for a fit lavaan rescaled. A flat small- sample
    likelihood can trigger the warning without either cause, and the
    warning does not prescribe a remedy already applied. The FIML refit
    estimates the unrestricted moments in its own order of the
    variables, so a fit made with `ov_order = "data"` that lavaan does
    not rescale gets the FMIs of the same fit in the model’s order.
  - **Models kept in their own metric, and refits that fail.** A model
    the refits cannot carry to that metric (one with composites or
    product terms, which lavaan does not rescale either) keeps its own;
    there the Hessian estimator warns when a standard deviation falls
    outside .01 to 1000, and the check for a maximum is not made. A
    refit whose information cannot be inverted stops the computation
    with a message that names the likeliest cause, in place of lavaan’s
    warning that the model may not be identified: variables too badly
    scaled for a model kept in their own metric, a predictor so far from
    zero relative to its standard deviation that its coefficients and
    the intercept are nearly collinear. Centering is named as the remedy
    only when the same model with that predictor centered has invertible
    information; an indicator or outcome’s location is not blamed. Where
    centering changes an intercept the model fixes or constrains, both
    causes are named, or a model that is not identified. The messages
    name the variables of an
    [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) or
    [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
    fit as its formula does.
  - **Solutions lavaan’s checks flag.** A fit with auxiliary variables
    entered as saturated correlates (lavaan’s `aux`, which
    `fa_confirmatory(..., aux = )` passes on) is supported. Every refit
    keeps the fit’s estimates whatever lavaan’s checks of a solution say
    of them, except for the run-away Heywood case described next. This
    covers an auxiliary fit, whose augmented residual covariance matrix
    is not positive definite by construction, two factors correlated
    above 1, and a residual variance a little below zero. lavaan’s own
    `parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE)` shrinks such a covariance to a
    correlation below 1 before it refits, and so reports the FMIs of
    other estimates: -1.62 against .25 for the covariance of two factors
    correlated 1.08 in a sample of 60. The computation stops with a
    message that says why when the refit at the estimates moves them.
    Besides a rotated solution, this happens with an improper one:
    lavaan (0.7-3) will not take as a starting point the estimates of a
    Heywood case whose negative residual variance exceeds the variable’s
    observed variance in size, and restarts from its simple starting
    values, and lavaan’s own `parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE)` then
    reports FMIs computed at those values (NA for some rows, negative
    for the intercepts), warning only that the covariance matrix of the
    estimates is not positive definite. The computation also refuses
    data with no unrestricted estimate of their means and covariances: a
    pair no case observes together, or a saturated likelihood without a
    maximum. The pair or singular subset is named, and the checks
    precede every refit. An EM iteration limit where the maximum exists
    instead gives a warning in DMAR’s words. The conditions have classes
    `dmar_fmi_never_together` and `dmar_fmi_saturated_singular`;
    `wald_df = "missing_information"` gives the same reason and names
    numeric degrees of freedom as the alternative. Refits do not repeat
    lavaan’s notice of low pairwise coverage.

- **[`missing_patterns()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/missing_patterns.md)
  and
  [`missing_coverage()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/missing_coverage.md)
  are new.** They describe the missing values before any model is fit:
  the distinct patterns of observed and missing items with their counts
  (the pattern with nothing observed kept as a row, since lavaan sets
  those cases aside), and the number and proportion of cases that
  observed each pair of items, with lavaan’s denominator, the cases with
  at least one observed item. Both return tables of the same shape
  whatever the number of items.

- **[`df_missing()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_missing.md)
  is new.** A Wald interval from full information maximum likelihood
  refers the estimate to the normal distribution; von Hippel (2016)
  showed that in small samples with missing values this reference
  distribution, not the estimate or its standard error, is what makes
  the interval too short, and that a *t* reference on degrees of freedom
  that shrink with the parameter’s fraction of missing information
  brought his intervals for regression coefficients and moments near
  nominal coverage.
  [`df_missing()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_missing.md)
  computes both of his rules from a vector of FMIs or from the table
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  returns: `method = "effective_n"`, N(1 - FMI) - k (his Eq. 31), and
  `method = "complete_df"`, df_complete(1 - FMI)(df_complete +
  1)/(df_complete + 3) (his Eq. 32), each bounded below at 3, as he
  recommends (`floor`). Neither `k` nor `df_complete` has a default,
  because the right value depends on the parameter: for a regression
  coefficient k counts the slopes and the intercept, and for a factor
  loading or omega DMAR’s calibration study chose k = 1 (see the
  `wald_df` items below). A clearly negative FMI, which the structured
  and Hessian estimators can return, is refused. Its example takes the
  FMIs from
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  on an [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md)
  fit and sets the *t* interval beside the Wald interval it replaces.

- **[`df_barnard_rubin()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_barnard_rubin.md)
  is new.** It gives Barnard and Rubin’s (1999) degrees of freedom for
  an estimate pooled over imputations, with the total variance, the
  imputations’ estimate of the FMI, the relative increase in variance,
  and both components of the formula, vectorized over parameters.
  `floor = 3` is von Hippel’s bound; `floor = 0` reproduces `mice`’s
  `barnard.rubin()`, and `df_complete = Inf` gives Rubin’s (1987)
  degrees of freedom. The between-imputation variance is passed as
  `between`, not `B`, which DMAR keeps for bootstrap counts. Both df
  functions return fixed-column tables with `tidy()` and `glance()`
  methods, and print beneath the table a line naming the rule that made
  the `df` column (with the `m` and `df_complete` used, for
  [`df_barnard_rubin()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_barnard_rubin.md))
  and the value it is bounded below at, which a knitted table carries as
  well.

- **`wald_df` refers Wald intervals to a *t* distribution.**
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md),
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  (with [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md)
  and [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md)),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md), and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  gain `wald_df = Inf`, appended after their existing arguments (after
  the `...` that
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
  its wrappers, and the mlmr pair forward to lavaan, so it must be named
  in full): the degrees of freedom of the *t* distribution their Wald
  intervals refer to. The estimate and its standard error are unchanged
  and the normal quantile is replaced by the *t* quantile (von Hippel,
  2016); in
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  and the mlmr pair the *p*-values refer to the same *t* distribution,
  so the interval and the test agree, and the ratio is reported in the
  column `test_statistic` (`z_value` in 1.0.x; see the breaking
  changes). The default reproduces every interval and *p*-value of 1.0.x
  exactly ([`qt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) and
  [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) at infinite degrees of
  freedom are [`qnorm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Normal.html) and
  [`pnorm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Normal.html)): results gain a
  `wald_df` attribute and their `tidy()` rows a `wald_df` column, `Inf`
  by default; a finite value adds a line under the printed table.
  [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html) of an
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) or
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  fit then heads its coefficient table `t value` and `Pr(>|t|)`, as
  [`summary.lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/summary.lm.html) does, with
  that line beneath the table’s significance codes. A number applies to
  every Wald interval of the call: the `"ml"`, `"mlr"`, and `"adf"`
  intervals of alpha and of the model implied omega and their
  `_logistic` variants (on the logit scale), every parameter row of the
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  tables including the standardized solution, and every coefficient of
  the mlmr pair. A finite value where the interval is not a Wald
  interval (the closed forms, the profile likelihood, a bootstrap,
  robust omega, `fa_confirmatory(output = "fit")`, `se = "none"`) is an
  error. [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md)
  and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  also accept `wald_df = "missing_information"`, von Hippel’s (2016)
  rule for regression coefficients, max(3, N(1 - FMI) -

  11. for each coefficient, with the FMI estimated from the fit as
      [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
      estimates it and k the slopes and intercept of the coefficient’s
      outcome; with complete data it gives the N - k of
      [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html). Its computation does
      not depend on the units of the variables. It warns when the fit’s
      estimates are not at the maximum of the likelihood, as lavaan’s
      can be for variables measured in small units: with every standard
      deviation of the regression of the
      [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
      entry near .003 (`mlmr(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, ci_method = "wald")`),
      the intercept’s degrees of freedom move by .15, and
      `rescale_data = TRUE`, passed through `...`, is the remedy. A
      coefficient whose fraction of missing information cannot be
      computed stops the call with the reason rather than receive NA
      degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom and the
      [`df_missing()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_missing.md)
      table they came from are attributes of the fit, and
      [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html) lists each
      coefficient’s FMI and degrees of freedom. As von Hippel published
      it, the interval pairs the maximum likelihood standard error with
      the *t* quantile, so on complete data it is shorter than the
      interval of [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) by sqrt((N -
      k)/N).
      [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
      and
      [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
      accept the keyword as well, for the loadings and omega, on the
      rule DMAR’s calibration study chose (next item);
      [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
      takes a number only.

- **`wald_df = "missing_information"` for factor loadings and omega.**
  Von Hippel’s (2016) evidence for his degrees of freedom covers
  regression coefficients and moments, not factor loadings or
  reliability coefficients, so DMAR ran a calibration study of its own.
  It lives in the source repository, `methodology/missing_data`, with
  the plan (the design and the decision rule, fixed before the run), the
  script, the results, and the per parameter summary from which every
  verdict can be recomputed; it is not in the package.

  - **Design.** The study simulated one factor models as
    [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
    writes them: 6 items at N from 30 to 200 and 12 items at N = 50 and
    100, normal data fit by ML and nonnormal data by MLR with
    Huber-White standard errors, and no missing values or 15 or 30
    percent of the values of half the items missing completely at random
    or at random, with 2000 replications in each of 60 cells. It
    compared the normal interval with *t* intervals on four of von
    Hippel’s rules under a decision rule fixed before the run, and a
    repetition of his own design reproduced his Tables 4 and 5 to within
    .012.
  - **Verdict.** His effective sample size rule with k = 1 was the
    simplest rule to pass for the loadings: over the small samples with
    missing values its coverage was .0171 from .95 on average, against
    .0247 for the normal interval; averaged over a cell’s loadings it
    was never above .9502. With missing values no single loading’s
    coverage exceeded .96 (the highest was .9595); without them the t
    reference on N - 1 reached .963, where the normal reference reached
    .962. It also passed for omega (.0180 against .0242, never above
    .9550), with normal theory and robust standard errors alike.
  - **Where it applies.**
    [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
    (with
    [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md) and
    [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md))
    and
    [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
    accept the keyword. In
    [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
    the loadings of the `"verbose"` table take the *t* reference, each
    on its own degrees of freedom, and every other row keeps the normal
    reference, since the study evaluated neither factor correlations,
    intercepts, error variances, nor the AVE and *H*; omega passed on
    its own scale, but
    [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
    now forms omega’s limits on the logit scale, where the *t* reference
    overcovered (.9645), so omega keeps the normal reference there, and
    the `"measurement"` table, which has no loading, refuses the
    keyword. In `reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied")` it
    applies to the `"ml"` and `"mlr"` intervals. With complete data,
    listwise deletion, or a covariance matrix every FMI is 0 and the
    degrees of freedom are N - 1.
  - **Example.** On the five spatial tests of `holzinger_swineford`
    (visual perception, cubes, lozenges, the second paper form board,
    and flags), two of which only the Grant-White pupils took (156 of
    the 301 values missing),
    `fa_confirmatory(missing = "fiml", wald_df = "missing_information")`
    gives the loadings of those two tests 139.8 and 143.7 degrees of
    freedom (FMI .53 and .52), the other three 246.0 to 274.9, and omega
    214.6 (FMI .28); omega’s 95% interval moves from \[.6946, .8061\] to
    \[.6942, .8064\]. In a pilot of 60 of the pupils
    (`set.seed(113); sample(301, 60)`), the model implied omega’s FMI
    under
    `reliability_omega(missing = "fiml", ci_method = "ml", denominator = "model_implied")`
    is .23, its degrees of freedom are 45.5, and its interval \[.665,
    .888\] becomes \[.662, .891\], 2.7% wider.
  - **Where it is refused.** The keyword is refused, with the reason,
    where the study did not reach: the `_logistic` intervals (on the
    logit scale the *t* reference covered up to .9645 with normal data,
    where the normal interval was already within .0044 of .95 on
    average), the ADF intervals, robust omega, the standardized
    solution, estimators other than ML and MLR, ordered items, pairwise
    deletion and two-stage estimation, standard errors other than the
    normal theory and Huber-White ones (`robust.sem` is accepted only
    under listwise deletion, or from a covariance matrix with the
    required `NACOV`; it and Satorra-Bentler tests passed through `...`
    are refused under FIML whether values are missing or not, because
    lavaan falls back to listwise deletion), and, under full information
    maximum likelihood, standard errors from any information but the
    observed information computed from the Hessian, lavaan’s default
    there and the study’s.
  - **Alpha.**
    [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
    refuses it too, since no rule passed the study’s decision rule for
    alpha: the *t* reference brought alpha’s FIML interval barely closer
    to .95 than the normal one, which was already close (.0042 against
    .0043), and covered .966 in one cell, the one where the study’s fit
    of the saturated model converged in only 53 percent of the
    replications. Without that cell the rule would have passed (.0035
    against .0042), but the rule was fixed before the run and its
    verdict stands; a number of degrees of freedom remains available.
  - **Attributes.** The degrees of freedom are the `wald_df` attribute,
    the
    [`df_missing()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_missing.md)
    table they came from is the `wald_df_table` attribute, and a line
    under the printed table names the rule, N, and the rows it applied
    to.

- **[`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  returns the maximum likelihood covariance matrix and means of
  incomplete continuous data.** These are the estimates of the saturated
  model fitted by full information maximum likelihood, the moments the
  EM algorithm converges to, computed with lavaan’s EM, run on the
  variables centered at their means and divided by their standard
  deviations, with the estimates transformed back. They are the
  unrestricted moments `lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "sampstat.h1")` returns
  for any FIML fit to the same variables. They are consistent when
  values are missing at random given the variables included, where the
  complete case matrix is consistent in general only when values are
  missing completely at random. lavaan’s EM stops when no mean or
  covariance changes by more than 1e-5, a criterion on the absolute
  change, so run in the raw metric its estimates depend on the units: on
  the regression data of the
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  entry with every variable multiplied by .001,
  `lavaan::lavCor(missing = "ml")` returns correlations off by up to
  .16, with no warning that its EM stopped short (it warns only that the
  matrix is near singular, its variances being near zero). Multiplying a
  variable by a constant multiplies the mean
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  returns, and its row and column of `S`, by that constant, and the
  estimates agree with lavaan’s own to about seven digits. A warning
  lavaan raises about the variables names them as `data` does. Columns
  named in `aux` enter the saturated model as auxiliary variables and
  are left out of what is returned, and a case observed only on its
  auxiliaries is used, as the reliability family uses it under FIML (see
  Changes to Earlier Results). The result is a list, like that of
  [`cov_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_sem.md),
  because every use of it takes the matrix: `S` (divisor N), `mu`, `N`,
  `N_complete`, `patterns`, and `converged`. A non-numeric column, a
  column with fewer than two distinct observed values, a pair of
  variables never observed together, and a pair observed together only
  in rows where one of them takes a single value (or in one row only),
  whose rows in common say nothing about how the two vary together, are
  refused by name.
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  and the reliability family refuse such pairs in the same words, from
  shared checks: the message names the method that needs the covariance,
  says what an estimate of it would rest on (lavaan only warns about a
  pair never observed together, and its estimate of that covariance is
  arbitrary), and advises leaving out one variable of each pair, an
  auxiliary variable where the pair has one. The help page explains why
  `N` is not an effective sample size for a method that treats the
  matrix as complete data (Enders & Peugh, 2004; Savalei & Bentler,
  2009). The matrix is the basis for an exploratory factor analysis or a
  parallel analysis of incomplete items.

- **A vignette, “Missing Data: What the Missing Values Cost”**
  ([`vignette("missing_data")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/missing_data.md)),
  teaches the missing data family on the six spatial tests of
  `holzinger_swineford`, two of which were given only at the Grant-White
  school. It covers the patterns of missing values and the cases behind
  each covariance; why listwise deletion needs values missing completely
  at random and FIML needs them missing at random given the model’s
  variables, shown on the real data (where listwise deletion analyzes
  one school) and on a deletion made missing at random whose complete
  data answer is known; auxiliary variables as saturated correlates
  through `fa_confirmatory(..., aux = )`, and what lavaan’s warning
  about the residual covariance matrix means there; the fraction of
  missing information of every parameter, with the effective sample
  size, the target sample size, the width inflation factor, the three
  estimators of Chen and Savalei (2021), and a bootstrap interval for
  the FMI; the EM covariance matrix of
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  as the basis of an exploratory factor analysis, and why its N is not
  an effective sample size; *t* reference distributions in small samples
  through `wald_df = "missing_information"`,
  [`df_missing()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_missing.md),
  and
  [`df_barnard_rubin()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_barnard_rubin.md);
  two-stage maximum likelihood with its residual based statistic and
  corrected fit indices; omega, alpha, and categorical omega (pairwise
  deletion and multiple imputation) from incomplete items; factor scores
  and their determinacy for each missing data pattern; and a sample size
  plan for omega made with the FMI and checked by simulation. Every
  number in its text is computed from the analyses.

### Two-Stage Maximum Likelihood for Incomplete Data

- **[`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
  [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md),
  [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md), and
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  gain `missing = "two_stage"` and `missing = "robust_two_stage"`**
  (lavaan’s spellings `"two.stage"` and `"robust.two.stage"` are
  accepted too). The model is fit to the EM estimates of the means and
  covariances, computed from every partially observed case and from any
  auxiliary variables passed as lavaan’s `aux`, which enter that first
  stage only (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Bentler, 2009). A case
  observed on an auxiliary variable but on no variable of the model is
  used too. The first stage estimates the items and the auxiliaries
  jointly and sums its likelihood over every case (Savalei & Bentler,
  2009, Eq. 10), which is what makes the estimates consistent when the
  items go missing together at random given the auxiliaries.

  lavaan’s two-stage estimator reads such a case in its first stage but
  leaves it out of its N. That N turns the per case quantities of the
  two stages into:

  - every standard error, each too large by sqrt(N_read / N);
  - the naive statistic, and the scaled statistic, corrected indices,
    and RMSEA interval built on it;
  - the log likelihood;
  - in several groups, the weight of each group in the discrepancy
    function the second stage minimizes, on which the estimates of a
    model that constrains parameters across groups depend.

  The fit is therefore computed again with the sample size set to the
  cases the first stage read, group by group. lavaan’s own formulas then
  give every value on that N, in the table and in the lavaan fits of
  `output = "fit"` and of the `"fits"` attribute.

  - In one group, and at the configural rung, the estimates do not
    depend on the count and stay lavaan’s.
  - A rung that constrains parameters across groups is estimated again
    with the counts of the cases read. These are the two-stage estimates
    with every case read, whose estimates and naive statistic semTools’
    `twostage()` gives.
  - lavaan’s [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html) of such
    a fit counts the cases as used, and `lavTestLRT()` warns that a
    difference test between it and a fit lavaan made of the same data on
    its own N is invalid.
  - A message counts such cases, and a line under the table names the N.
    When the fit cannot be computed again, a warning says instead what
    rests on lavaan’s N.

  Example: six Holzinger and Swineford tests, a spatial factor of visual
  perception, cubes, and lozenges and a verbal factor of paragraph
  comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning, with the whole
  block missing for 77 of 301 pupils at random given general
  information, the auxiliary (`set.seed(113)`, then the six tests set to
  `NA` in the rows `sample(301, 77, prob = plogis(-1.5 + 1.2 * z))`,
  with z the standardized general information score).

  - A verbal loading of 2.840 has a standard error of .190 rather than
    lavaan’s .220 (sqrt(301/224) = 1.159).
  - The robust two-stage chi square is 24.83 rather than 18.48.
  - BIC is formed with N = 301.
  - By school, 130 and 94 pupils with an observed test grow to 156 and
    145 cases read. At the scalar rung the common intercept of lozenges
    is 18.00 (SE .697) rather than lavaan’s 18.21 (SE .782). The scalar
    difference test is 14.97 on 4 df, against 10.86 from lavaan’s own
    ladder, 16.46 under FIML with the same auxiliary, and 17.44 after
    listwise deletion.
  - Setting the 77 cases aside instead would condition the analysis on
    an observed item. On the same data it moves the loading to 2.796 and
    the intercept of paragraph comprehension from 9.21 to 8.75 (9.18
    with complete data). Over 60 bootstrap resamples of the 301 pupils
    (`set.seed(2026)`), each with the block deleted in the same way, the
    intercept’s mean error against the resample’s complete data estimate
    is -0.49 with the cases set aside and -0.01 with them kept.

  The standard errors are the two-stage sandwich, normal theory or
  robust to nonnormality. After normal theory two-stage estimation the
  `chi_square` row is the residual based statistic of Savalei and
  Bentler (2009). DMAR computes it from the observed information of the
  saturated model over every case the first stage read, and their
  simulations found it to hold its rejection rate near the nominal
  level. After robust two-stage estimation the row is lavaan’s scaled
  statistic (Savalei & Falk, 2014). Simple equality constraints that
  lavaan keeps under `ceq.simple = TRUE`, passed through `...`, are
  read: the residual based statistic of such a model is that of the same
  model without `ceq.simple`.

  The `cfi` and `rmsea` rows are lavaan’s robust indices, the corrected
  indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023). They subtract from the naive
  statistic an estimate of its expectation, built from the asymptotic
  covariance matrix of the EM moments.

  - After robust two-stage estimation that matrix is the sandwich of the
    observed and first order information of the saturated model, and the
    indices are their TS V2, the version they recommend.
  - After normal theory two-stage estimation it is the inverse of the
    observed information, the form the sandwich takes under normality.
    The indices are then the normal theory analog of TS V2, which they
    did not study.
  - On nine Holzinger and Swineford tests in three factors (the spatial
    and verbal tests above, and addition, counting groups of dots, and
    straight and curved capitals), with 90 values each of sentence
    completion and straight and curved capitals deleted completely at
    random (`set.seed(1)`, then `sample(301, 90)` for each in turn), the
    RMSEA is .0869 after normal theory and .0859 after robust two-stage
    estimation.
  - Zhang and Savalei define only the RMSEA and the CFI; the `tli` and
    `nnfi` rows and the RMSEA interval are lavaan’s extension of the
    correction. A line under the table says which version it holds.

  The rung-to-rung tests of
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  are the scaled difference tests (Satorra & Bentler, 2001). `AIC` and
  `BIC` are the two-stage criteria of Lai (2021), the values
  [`sem_information_criteria()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_information_criteria.md)
  reports. The printed table says which statistic, indices, and criteria
  it reports.
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  frees the item intercepts under two-stage estimation as it does under
  FIML; through bare `lavaan()` lavaan would fix them at zero. An
  estimator other than ML, a robust `se`, ordered items, and covariance
  input are errors that name the option to use.
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)’s
  table gains a `test` attribute naming the statistic in its
  `chi_square` row, and
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  a `model_test` attribute. No existing value changes.

- **[`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  and
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md)
  gain `missing = "two_stage"`**, appended to the choices; the default
  is full information maximum likelihood when a value is missing (see
  Changes to Earlier Results). The model implied coefficients take the
  normal theory two-stage standard error under `ci_method = "ml"` and
  the robust one under `"mlr"`. Their fits go through
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
  so a case observed on an auxiliary variable alone is counted as above.

  Robust omega divides the squared sum of the two-stage loadings by the
  sum of the EM covariance matrix, with a bootstrap interval that refits
  both stages. No delta method interval is offered for it, since none
  has been studied. Each bootstrap replication fits the second stage to
  the EM moments of the resample, without the two-stage standard errors
  and scaled statistic that lavaan computes for every two-stage fit and
  no replication reads. The bootstrap replications of the model implied
  coefficients do the same. The estimates are those of a full two-stage
  fit, to rounding error, wherever the likelihood has a well defined
  maximum. On a small, heavily incomplete resample, whose likelihood is
  nearly flat or has no proper maximum, the two optimizers can stop at
  different points. A replication’s value can then differ at the
  optimizer’s tolerance, and a solution that runs away can be counted as
  not converged rather than improper, or the reverse; under either
  verdict it is among the replications the bootstrap counts as set aside
  or improper.

  Analytic alpha, a function of the first stage alone, equals its FIML
  value and interval. Two-stage estimation uses the cases FIML uses,
  every case with an observed item or an observed auxiliary variable,
  since its first stage reads a case observed on an auxiliary variable
  alone. A message counts such cases, once per call rather than once per
  bootstrap replication. When the fit of a model implied coefficient
  cannot be computed again with every case, a warning says that its
  analytic standard error is too large and that a bootstrap interval
  counts every case. On visual perception, paragraph comprehension,
  sentence completion, and word meaning, with the block deleted as in
  the example above and general information as the auxiliary, alpha
  (`ci_method = "ml"`) is .773 (SE .0235) on 301 cases, the FIML value.
  Setting the 77 aside would give .769 (SE .0242) on 224.

  `aux` names auxiliary variables of the first stage, and `aux` without
  `missing` still means FIML. The intervals refused under FIML are
  refused here too, the profile likelihood also because no likelihood of
  the observed data is maximized.

- **[`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  reports a two-stage fit with the statistic and indices
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  reports, and
  [`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md)
  compares two-stage fits by their two-stage criteria.**
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  reports the robust version, the corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei
  (2023). After robust two-stage estimation these are their TS V2. After
  normal theory two-stage estimation they are its normal theory analog,
  which lavaan forms with the inverse of the observed information of the
  saturated model where TS V2 takes the sandwich of the observed and
  first order information, and which they did not study. The
  `chi_square` row is the residual based statistic, or the scaled
  statistic after robust two-stage estimation, and the printed footer
  names the version of the indices, as
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)’s
  does. It refuses `version = "standard"` (the naive statistic, which is
  not chi square distributed) and `"scaled"`.

  The residual based statistic is refused, with a message that says what
  to do instead, for a fit with:

  - sampling weights or clustered cases;
  - an observed exogenous variable under `fixed.x = TRUE` or
    `conditional.x = TRUE`. Refit with `fixed.x = FALSE` (and with
    `conditional.x = FALSE`, since lavaan does not take
    `fixed.x = FALSE` beside `conditional.x = TRUE`), which leaves the
    estimates as they are when the exogenous variables are complete and
    otherwise also keeps the cases lavaan deletes for a missing
    exogenous variable when it conditions on them (robust two-stage
    estimation included), so the estimates then differ; to keep the
    fit’s estimates, refit on the rows the fit used, those on which
    every exogenous variable is observed, which
    `lavInspect(fit, "case.idx")` lists. The refusal is an error of
    class `dmar_two_stage_fixed_x` (a `dmar_refusal`) that carries the
    exogenous variables;
  - inequality constraints;
  - a parameter on a bound.

  Its listwise deletion warning counts only the cases lavaan deletes
  listwise; the empty cases lavaan drops under FIML or two-stage
  estimation, which carry no information, draw none.

  It warns when a two-stage fit made with lavaan has cases observed on
  an auxiliary variable but on none of the model’s variables. lavaan’s
  first stage reads such cases and its N leaves them out. The naive
  statistic, the scaled statistic and corrected indices built on it, the
  RMSEA multiplier, and the `N` row then rest on fewer cases than the EM
  moments, while the residual based statistic uses every case. The table
  reports lavaan’s values. The warning points to
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  and
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md),
  whose fits keep and count such cases, and to FIML. On the six tests
  above
  (`lavaan::cfa(model, data, std.lv = TRUE, missing = "two.stage", aux = "t5_general_information")`),
  lavaan’s N is 224 and its robust RMSEA .095; the fit
  `fa_confirmatory(missing = "two_stage")` returns for the same model
  counts 301 cases and gives .103.

  [`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md)
  reports no log evidence for two-stage criteria, which approximate no
  marginal likelihood, and refuses two-stage fits whose auxiliary
  variables differ.

- **[`sem_information_criteria()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_information_criteria.md)
  and
  [`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md)
  count every case the first stage of a two-stage fit read.** lavaan
  forms the two-stage log likelihood as its N times the complete data
  log likelihood per case at the EM estimates, and BIC, SABIC, and HBIC
  take the same N into their penalties. A case observed on an auxiliary
  variable but on none of the model’s variables moves the EM estimates
  and is left out of that N. The log likelihood and N are taken instead
  from the fit computed again with every case the first stage read.

  - In one group, and in several groups that no constraint holds
    together, the estimates stay, and each group’s log likelihood is its
    value per case times the cases read.
  - In several groups held together by a constraint, such as equal
    loadings or intercepts, the estimates move with the groups’ counts,
    and the log likelihood is the one at the two-stage estimates with
    every case read.
  - A line under the table says which, and the `sem_information`
    attribute records the counts.

  On the six tests above, fit by lavaan as in the previous entry,
  lavaan’s N for the two-factor model is 224 and its log likelihood
  -4040.25. That is 224/301 of the -5429.09 reported with N = 301, and
  BIC is 10966.61 (8183.32 from lavaan’s values). With the two schools
  as groups and equal loadings and intercepts
  (`group = "school", meanstructure = TRUE, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts")`),
  the log likelihood is -5393.34 and BIC 10957.89, against -5393.52 and
  10958.25 at lavaan’s estimates and -4020.79 and 8203.92 from lavaan’s
  values. A fit
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  or
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  returns already counts the cases and gives the same criteria, and
  [`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md)
  compares it with a lavaan fit of the same data. A warning names what
  rests on lavaan’s N only when the fit cannot be computed again.

### Factor Scores

- **[`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  is new.** It returns both standard factor scores of a fitted lavaan
  model for every row and factor: the regression score (the posterior
  mean) and the Bartlett score, or for ordered items lavaan’s empirical
  Bayes modal and maximum likelihood scores. Each comes with a per-case
  standard error and a `conf_level` interval, beside the number of the
  factor’s items the case answered, its missing data pattern, and, for
  continuous items in a fit not conditional on exogenous covariates, the
  determinacy of each score for that pattern, in one long table with one
  row per row of the data and factor. An item listed under a factor with
  its loading fixed or constrained to zero (`0*item`, or `a*item` with
  `a == 0`) is not one of that factor’s items.
  [`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html), `tidy()`, and
  `glance()` methods come with it.

  Under FIML each case is scored from its own observed items, and the
  determinacy for each pattern shows what a missing item costs; for one
  factor its square is coefficient H. Beside the regression score’s
  determinacy rho, the display and the `determinacy` and `patterns`
  attributes give 2 rho^2 - 1 (`min_score_correlation`), the lowest
  correlation two sets of scores equally consistent with the model can
  have (Guttman, 1955), reported without a line drawn. Rows the fit did
  not score (deleted listwise, with no observed item, without a group)
  stay in the table with the reason when `data` is supplied, and a frame
  that is not the rows given to the fit is refused. A row deleted
  listwise from an ordered fit is told that `missing = "pairwise"`
  scores it, since lavaan has no FIML for ordered items. A row deleted
  for a missing exogenous covariate is told, whatever the fit’s
  treatment of missing values, that `missing = "ml.x"` scores it (with
  `conditional.x = FALSE` for a fit conditional on the covariates), or
  with ordered items that no fit lavaan can score keeps it. Without
  `data`, where the two cannot be told apart, the reason in a one-group
  fit by listwise deletion names what scores each; in any other fit that
  deletes such rows it names `missing = "ml.x"` and says that supplying
  `data` identifies the reason. A case that answered none of a factor’s
  items has no Bartlett score and keeps a regression score that comes
  only from its other observed variables (the items of correlated
  factors, a covariate that predicts the factor, an outcome it
  predicts). A factor that a pattern’s observed items do not separate
  from another (a case that answered only an item two factors share) has
  no Bartlett score, rather than the minimum norm solution of lavaan’s
  generalized inverse; a factor the pattern does identify keeps its
  score.

  A fit of continuous items that keeps the incomplete cases without FIML
  is scored as a FIML fit is, each case from its own observed items,
  with the fit’s estimates. That covers a two-stage fit (lavaan’s
  `missing = "two.stage"` or `"robust.two.stage"`, or
  `fa_confirmatory(missing = "two_stage")`), whose estimates are
  consistent when the values are missing at random, as the FIML
  estimates are (Savalei & Bentler, 2009). It also covers a fit by
  pairwise deletion (`missing = "pairwise"` or `"available.cases"`),
  whose estimates require values missing completely at random. lavaan’s
  `lavPredict()` scores such a fit as complete data and leaves every
  case with a missing value without a score, so
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  computes these scores itself, by the closed forms `lavPredict()`
  applies pattern by pattern under FIML. Such a fit conditional on
  exogenous covariates is refused.

  Without a mean structure (the default for one group under listwise or
  pairwise deletion), a factor that a covariate predicts is centered
  where lavaan and FIML center it, at the slope times the covariate’s
  mean. In such a fit without an exogenous covariate, `lavPredict()`
  counts twice the mean of an observed variable that lavaan holds among
  the latent variables, which shifts by a constant every score whose
  weights involve it (the regression score of every factor related to
  it, the Bartlett score of a factor that predicts it);
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  computes those scores itself, and a higher order factor keeps lavaan’s
  Bartlett score less that constant. An observed variable regressed on
  others, such as an item with a direct effect of a covariate (the MIMIC
  model of differential item functioning) or an outcome the factor
  predicts, is held by lavaan among the latent variables, with its
  loadings among the regressions. The scores, their standard errors and
  determinacies, the check of the ML score, and the check of the
  solution take its loadings and residual variance from there, as
  `lavPredict()` does, so an item with a direct effect enters its
  factor’s Bartlett score. An observed variable that lavaan holds the
  same way but regresses on nothing, such as a criterion that covaries
  with a factor (`f ~~ z`) or a covariate of a factor that also covaries
  with another variable, is conditioned on, as an exogenous covariate
  is.

  Without regressions among the variables lavaan holds as latent, a
  variable regressed only on exogenous covariates is conditioned on as
  well, also when it covaries with a factor. With such regressions,
  `lavPredict()` gives an observed variable regressed on nothing a row
  of zeros among the loadings, leaving its covariances with the factors
  out of the scores.
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  scores these fits itself and refuses one conditional on the
  covariates. A fit with such regressions is refused when the
  disturbance of an observed variable regressed on others covaries with
  a factor or a variable the scores condition on: lavaan’s Bartlett
  score is then not conditionally unbiased, and where a factor is
  involved its regression score is not the conditional mean. The remedy
  carries the variable as a single indicator latent variable without
  fixing its loading, with its observed residual variance fixed at zero.
  This preserves the model under `std.lv = TRUE` as well. In multiple
  groups the refusal also names the intercept and residual variance and
  covariance equalities needed to preserve the constraints.

  For ordered items a factor has an ML score only where the likelihood
  of the case’s responses has a finite and unique maximum in it, which
  an exact check decides for any loading structure, cross-loadings,
  bifactor models, and observed variables regressed on the factors
  included (by Farkas’ lemma, through nonnegative least squares). Each
  of these has an `NA` ML score with the reason and keeps its EBM score:
  a factor whose observed items all sit at the end of their scales that
  their loadings point to (all in the lowest category, or all in the
  highest, for positive loadings), one whose likelihood rises without
  bound together with others, one its items cannot separate from
  another, and a higher order factor. Every other factor keeps its ML
  score, also one that shares items with a factor whose likelihood rises
  without bound: its maximum is then that of the case’s other items,
  which lavaan’s optimizer reaches within its tolerance. When lavaan’s
  default optimizer stops on the other factor and returns no score, the
  score comes from lavaan’s `nlminb` optimizer. With ordered items,
  lavaan’s EBM and ML scores omit terms from each case’s likelihood or
  prior. A fit is scored when the omitted term is constant in the
  factors: a covariate’s effect on an outcome that depends on no factor
  directly, or a fully mediated chain of continuous observed variables.
  A fit is refused for a direct effect of a covariate on a variable that
  depends on a factor directly, a regression of such a variable on an
  observed variable, or a regression on an ordered item. It is also
  refused when an observed variable lavaan holds among the loadings has
  a disturbance covarying with a factor, or a row lacks a predictor
  whose path reaches a factor without an observed mediator cutting it. A
  fit with exogenous covariates that is not conditional on them is
  refused because `lavPredict()` cannot score it. A fit of ordered items
  with residual covariances is scored with a warning, since lavaan’s EBM
  and ML scores leave those covariances out of each case’s likelihood;
  the help page gives the size of these errors in an example. Ordered
  items require lavaan 0.7-3 or newer: lavaan 0.7-2 counted the
  intercepts of ordered indicators twice in its EBM and ML scores, which
  were then wrong in any model where those intercepts are not zero (a
  multiple group model with equal thresholds, for one), so
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  refuses an ordered fit under an older lavaan.

  Auxiliary variables carried as saturated correlates are set aside, and
  the scores are computed from the indicators with the fit’s estimates,
  since conditioning on them removes true score variance. A fit that
  carries them with ordered items is refused (refit without them), as is
  one that carries them and is conditional on exogenous covariates
  (refit with `conditional.x = FALSE`). A higher order factor has no
  Bartlett score, and its reason says so, where the scores are computed
  from the indicators (auxiliary variables set aside), where the data
  have missing values and the scores are computed here for a two-stage
  fit or one by pairwise deletion (`"pairwise"` or `"available.cases"`),
  or in a fit in which lavaan gives an observed variable regressed on
  nothing a row of zeros among the loadings, since lavaan’s construction
  of that score is not repeated there. Elsewhere it keeps lavaan’s score
  (less the constant above where lavaan counts a mean twice), and its
  Bartlett standard error from lavaan is in the pattern table.

  An improper solution is scored with a warning: a negative variance
  (the residual variance of an observed variable regressed on others
  included), a covariance matrix of the factors that is not positive
  definite (a factor correlation beyond 1, for one), a residual
  covariance matrix of the continuous items that is not, or, when none
  of these holds, a residual covariance matrix of the structural part of
  the model that is not, the conditions lavaan’s post-estimation check
  flags. For ordered items lavaan computes no score for a solution with
  a negative residual variance, and the warning and the reasons say so.

  The help page says which score belongs where: regression scores for a
  predictor and Bartlett scores for an outcome, each from its own
  measurement model (Skrondal & Laake, 2001), and one-step SEM or
  structural after measurement
  ([`lavaan::sam()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/lavaan/man/sam.html); Rosseel &
  Loh, 2024, which includes Croon’s correction) as the route to
  relations among factors. Scores under missing data are discussed with
  Estabrook and Neale (2013). The help says that the Bartlett score’s
  conditional unbiasedness and the coverage of its interval hold under
  missing data only when whether an item is observed does not depend on
  the residuals of the items scored (Rubin, 1976), so not when it
  depends on the factor’s own observed items, with an example. It also
  says that the regression score’s posterior interval keeps its coverage
  when the missingness depends on the items scored, but not when it runs
  through an auxiliary variable set aside.

  A loading or regression held at zero, directly or through a chain of
  plain equalities, is read as absent. It makes no item, does not keep a
  saturated correlate from being set aside as an auxiliary variable, and
  gives the scores and reasons of the model written without it.

### Planning Under Missing Data

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  gains `fmi` and `seed`.** A reliability coefficient estimated by full
  information maximum likelihood from incomplete data has a wider
  interval at a given N than a complete data plan assumes. `fmi`
  (default 0) is the fraction of missing information anticipated for the
  coefficient, supplied by a pilot study or a comparable data set
  through
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md);
  it is not the proportion of missing values. Missing information
  multiplies the sampling variance by `1 / (1 - fmi)` (Savalei &
  Rhemtulla, 2012). The planner’s variance is V / (N - 1), so the plan
  divides the complete data N - 1 by `1 - fmi`:
  `N = (N_c - 1) / (1 - fmi) + 1`, and an FMI of .5 doubles N - 1,
  not N. With an assurance, the Monte Carlo search runs at the complete
  data (effective) size and its answer is mapped back the same way, a
  first-order approximation that the sensitivity function checks. The
  table keeps its rows; the attributes `fmi` and `necessary_N_complete`
  record the plan, and a line under the table names both. The help page
  explains where a planning FMI comes from, why a pilot’s FMI is
  imprecise (Chen & Savalei, 2021), and why the upper limit of its
  interval is the conservative planning value. The plan maps the
  unrounded complete data solution, so the formula applied to the
  printed complete data N can give a case or two more than the plan (the
  first example of the help page, six parallel items that correlate .6
  planned for a width of .10, needs 38 complete data cases and 42 at an
  FMI of .1, where the formula on 38 gives 43); the help says so. It
  also says that a pilot FMI from
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  refers to the cases the fit used, and that when the planned N counts
  every case recruited, those who will answer no item are folded in as
  `1 - (N_used / N)(1 - fmi)`. `seed` (default `NULL`) makes the
  assurance search reproducible and restores the caller’s random number
  stream on exit; without it the search draws from and advances that
  stream, as before. With `fmi = 0` the plan is the complete data plan
  and no attribute is added; the planner’s other changes are under
  Changes to Earlier Results.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  gains `fmi`, `missing_prop`, and `B`.** `fmi` is the planning value
  passed to the planner; `missing_prop` deletes each simulated item
  score completely at random with that probability and analyzes every
  replication by full information maximum likelihood, so a plan made
  with `fmi` is judged by the widths that incomplete data actually
  deliver. For four parallel items with reliability .80, a width of .15,
  and `missing_prop = .2`, the FMI of the coefficient is .184 relative
  to every case and .182 relative to the cases a fit keeps, since a
  share .2^4 = .0016 of the cases loses every item (the realized FMI,
  described below, of one FIML fit to 200,000 simulated cases:
  `ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(true_reliability = .8, n_items = 4, width = .15, specified_N = 200000, missing_prop = .2, G = 1)`
  after `set.seed(113)`). In 1,000 replications, with `set.seed(113)`
  before each call, the complete data plan (N = 74) gave `"ml"`
  intervals averaging .170 wide, and the plan made with `fmi = .184` (N
  = 91) gave .152, against .153 for the complete data plan with complete
  data. Under missing data the default interval is `"ml"`, as with
  complete data, and intervals whose standard errors ignore the missing
  values are refused. With `missing_prop` above 0, each replication that
  returns an interval also estimates the fraction of missing information
  its simulated data realized for the coefficient (the unstructured FMI
  of
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md),
  from alpha’s saturated model or omega’s single-factor model). The mean
  is reported beside the planning `fmi` as the attribute
  `mean_realized_fmi`, with the number of replications behind it in
  `n_realized_fmi`, a second line under the table, and a `realized_fmi`
  column in the per-replication file. A single sample FMI is too
  imprecise at the sizes a plan resolves to check a plan by (Chen &
  Savalei, 2021), and the mean over replications is the figure to carry
  into `fmi`. Computing it draws no random numbers, so the table’s rows
  are those of a run without it; it costs a fit and two refits per
  replication. The realized FMI is relative to every simulated case, the
  footing of the planner’s `fmi`: lavaan sets aside a case that loses
  every item, and the FMI relative to the cases it kept is folded back
  as `1 - (n_used / n)(1 - fmi_used)`. With three items at
  `missing_prop = .5`, a share .5^3 = .125 of the cases loses every
  item, so the FMI relative to the cases lavaan keeps understates the
  FMI the plan needs. `B` is the number of bootstrap resamples behind
  each replication’s interval, which was fixed at 200 whatever the
  interval; its default is the larger of 200 and the number the interval
  method and the level require, and a smaller value is refused (see One
  Rule for Bootstrap Replications). For alpha, with `fmi` and
  `missing_prop` at 0, `B` at its default, no assurance, and
  `ci_method = "bonett"`, the results are those of 1.0.x, except for
  replications whose interval lies wholly below zero (see the entry on
  clamped limits under Changes to Earlier Results); the default interval
  is now `"ml"` (see the entry there on the interval its plan was made
  for).

- **[`ss_aipe_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea.md)
  does not take `fmi`.** RMSEA is a function of the test statistic, not
  a model parameter, so no parameter’s FMI governs the noncentrality its
  interval is built on, and Savalei and Rhemtulla (2012) leave global
  measures of missing information to future research.

### Sample Size Planning for a Mean

- **[`ss_aipe_mean()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_mean.md)
  plans the sample size for the confidence interval for a single mean**,
  the mean of one sample or the mean of paired differences, which DMAR
  could not plan before:
  [`ss_aipe_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sm.md)
  plans the standardized mean, and
  [`ss_aipe_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c.md)
  requires contrast weights that sum to zero. Without an `assurance` the
  plan makes the expected width no wider than `width`, and the expected
  width is exact under normality: it uses E(S) = c4(N) sigma, where
  [`ss_aipe_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c.md)
  sets S equal to sigma, and so needs the same N as that rule or one
  fewer. With an `assurance` the realized width is no wider than `width`
  with that probability. `true_kurtosis`, on the excess scale of
  [`kurtosis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/kurtosis.md)
  so that a pilot’s value can usually be passed as it is, adjusts the
  assurance through a scaled chi square with the exact mean and variance
  of S^2; the expected width plan does not use it and warns when one is
  supplied. A pilot whose scores take nearly two values can give a
  [`kurtosis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/kurtosis.md)
  of -2 or less, which is refused, and the help page says what to pass
  instead. With a large kurtosis the assurance can be met at a very
  small N, missed over a stretch above it, and met again, so the plan is
  the smallest N from which the assurance holds at every larger N, and
  the search finds that N exactly. The answer row is `necessary_N`,
  beside the expected width at that size and the inputs.

- **[`ss_aipe_mean_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_mean_sensitivity.md)
  checks such a plan by Monte Carlo**, under a normal population or by
  resampling a vector of observed scores (`population`), which is how a
  plan meets the tails and skewness of real data, such as a pilot’s
  difference scores. It follows the sensitivity family’s arguments and
  rows, reports `mean_mean`, `median_mean`, and `sd_mean` for the
  realized means, and takes `seed` (default `NULL`), which makes a run
  reproducible and restores the caller’s random number stream on exit.
  For the help page’s pilot (the IQ gains of the control children in
  `pygmalion`, excess kurtosis 1.2), a plan for 90 percent assurance
  made under normal theory gave intervals no wider than the target of 4
  points in .870 of 1,000 replications, and the plan made with the
  pilot’s kurtosis, six children larger, in .913.

### Assurance When the Errors Are Not Normal

- **[`ss_aipe_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c.md)
  gains `true_kurtosis`.** With an `assurance`, the planner takes the
  pooled variance to follow the chi square law of normal theory, which
  holds only for normal errors. Errors lighter tailed than the normal,
  as bounded outcomes such as proportions and rating scale scores often
  are, make the pooled variance less variable than that law says, so a
  plan (for any assurance above one half) delivers more assurance than
  was requested; heavy tails make it deliver less. `true_kurtosis`
  (default 0) is the population excess kurtosis of the errors, a
  planning value on the scale
  [`kurtosis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/kurtosis.md)
  reports, and it replaces the error degrees of freedom df = J(n - 1) in
  the chi square quantile with the effective degrees of freedom 2 / (2 /
  df + true_kurtosis / (n J)), which match the variance of the pooled
  variance (Box, 1953). The default reproduces the plans of earlier
  releases exactly, and the expected width plan (no `assurance`) does
  not use the argument. An assurance plan made with a nonzero
  `true_kurtosis` keeps its one row, carries the value as the attribute
  `true_kurtosis`, says in a line under the table that its assurance
  allows for that excess kurtosis, and reports it as the column
  `true_kurtosis` of `glance()`; with `true_kurtosis = 0` no attribute
  or line is added. In a Monte Carlo check with two groups and an
  assurance of .80 (10,000 replications per condition), the plans made
  with the kurtosis supplied met the width target in .811 of the
  replications under uniform errors (excess kurtosis -1.2) and .811
  under *t* errors on 10 degrees of freedom (excess kurtosis 1), where
  the normal theory plans met it in .915 and .776. The help page
  describes the approximation and its limits, and says that
  [`ss_aipe_c_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c_sensitivity.md),
  which is unchanged, simulates normal errors.

### Common Method Variance: The Marker Adjustment With Its Interval
