- **[`common_method_adjusted_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/common_method_adjusted_r.md)
  gives every marker adjusted correlation with a confidence interval and
  the t test of Lindell and Whitney (2001), over one or more marker
  correlations.**
  [`common_method_marker()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/common_method_marker.md)
  works from the correlation matrix alone and does not take N, so its
  page left the test to the user. The new function takes `N` and returns
  one row per marker value and variable pair: the correlation, the
  adjusted correlation, its interval, and the t test on N - 3 degrees of
  freedom. The interval is the Fisher’s Z interval of
  [`ci_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md)
  carried through the adjustment, conditional on the marker correlation.
  A grid of values for `marker_r` is how the dependence of a conclusion
  on that correlation is read. With `marker_r = NULL` the smallest
  positive correlation serves as the proxy marker, as in
  [`common_method_marker()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/common_method_marker.md).
  [`common_method_marker()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/common_method_marker.md)
  is unchanged, and its page now points to the new function. A lower
  limit that the adjustment carries below -1 is set to -1; that happens
  exactly when the Fisher’s Z lower limit for the correlation falls
  below 2 r_M - 1, which with a positive marker correlation a small
  sample can produce whatever the sign of the correlation.

- **The missing-information t reference checks the fitted method.** With
  missing values,
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  refuse the keyword when lavaan fell back to listwise deletion,
  including under a Satorra-Bentler test. Complete data retain N minus
  the regression parameter count.
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  refuses `robust.sem` and Satorra-Bentler tests under FIML whether
  values are missing or not, and checks the fitted method for other
  fallbacks. The help correctly states that its default
  `se = "standard"` is normal theory for ML and MLR; an MLR test needs
  `se = "robust.huber.white"` for sandwich standard errors under FIML.
  With a covariance matrix, `robust.sem` needs the asymptotic moment
  covariance in `NACOV`. Alpha keeps its calibrated refusal of the
  keyword. The loading coverage maximum is qualified by whether values
  are missing; complete-data coverage uses t on N minus one.

- **Reliability’s missing-information diagnostics use the caller’s item
  and auxiliary names.** The warning about a fit short of its likelihood
  maximum names the parameter in words. It recommends dividing every
  item by one common constant, which preserves omega, and each auxiliary
  by its own, rather than an unavailable refit option.

- **Categorical MI diagnostics describe the interval actually formed.**
  Under bootstrap then impute, no widening or imputation-count advice is
  given for an interval that was not formed. An FMI estimated from the
  minority of replications that returned a value is labeled as such. An
  even imputation count is named only for completed data sets that
  failed, rather than an imputation failure alone.

### Multiple Comparisons

- **[`ci_dunnett_t3()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_dunnett_t3.md)
  gives Dunnett’s T3, the pairwise comparisons SPSS reports when the
  variances are not assumed equal.** Each pair has its own
  separate-variance standard error and Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of
  freedom, as in
  [`ci_games_howell()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_games_howell.md),
  and its critical value is the studentized maximum modulus for all
  a(a - 1)/2 comparisons at those degrees of freedom (Dunnett, 1980),
  the value
  [`cv_smm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_smm.md)
  returns. The adjusted p-value is that distribution’s tail beyond
  \|t\|, so it is below alpha when the interval excludes zero and not
  otherwise, to numerical precision; neither is simulated, and the
  degrees of freedom are not rounded. The table has the columns and
  class of the other post hoc intervals (`contrast`, `mean_difference`,
  `se`, `df`, `t_value`, the limits, and `p_adjusted`, class
  `dmar_post_hoc_ci`), and its display names the adjustment. It
  reproduces the Dunnett’s T3 output of SPSS for Chapter 12, Exercise 25
  of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) and agrees with
  `PMCMRplus::dunnettT3Test()`. The help explains why the formula that
  raises the single t probability to the power C is Tamhane’s T2
  (Tamhane, 1979), a different procedure whose intervals are never
  narrower, and when T3 is preferred to Games-Howell.
  [`ci_games_howell()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_games_howell.md)
  and [`cv_smm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_smm.md)
  link to it.

### Two Proportions Measured on the Same Units

- **[`ci_proportion_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_proportion_paired.md)
  gives a confidence interval for the difference between two proportions
  measured on the same units, and
  [`equivalence_proportion_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_proportion_paired.md)
  the score tests of noninferiority and equivalence on that
  difference.** Two diagnostic procedures applied to the same patients,
  or a pass rate before and after instruction for the same students,
  give correlated outcomes, and only the discordant pairs inform the
  difference, so the methods for independent proportions do not apply.
  [`ci_proportion_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_proportion_paired.md)
  takes either the two 0/1 vectors or the counts `n_10`, `n_01`, and
  `N`, and returns the score interval of Tango (1998), which inverts the
  score statistic of Nam (1997). The interval stays inside \[-1, 1\], is
  defined when no pair is discordant, and excludes 0 exactly when
  McNemar’s test without a continuity correction rejects. The Wald
  interval is available for comparison; the help shows, from the exact
  coverage of every possible table, how far short of its level it can
  fall when discordant pairs are rare.
  [`equivalence_proportion_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_proportion_paired.md)
  reports in the shape of
  [`equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_c.md),
  with the flag `nonsuperior` (the upper limit is below
  `prop_diff_upper`) as the last row and the verdict “Not relevantly
  superior only” among its outcomes. `prop_diff_upper` alone gives
  symmetric bounds; `prop_diff_lower` alone is a noninferiority test,
  whose table leaves the rows that would need an upper bound `NA` rather
  than reading them against a mirrored one. The tests reproduce Nam’s
  restricted estimates and score statistic (2.795) for the liver scan
  data he takes from McNeil, Keeler, and Adelstein (1975), and the
  limits match `PropCIs::scoreci.mp()`, against which a live comparison
  joins `tools/oracle_checks.R`.

### The Ratio of Two Means

- **[`ci_ratio_of_means()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_ratio_of_means.md)
  and
  [`ci_ratio_of_means_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_ratio_of_means_paired.md)
  give a confidence interval for the ratio of two means**, for
  independent groups and for two variables measured on the same units,
  from the raw data or from summary statistics. The default is Fieller’s
  confidence set, which inverts the *t* test of mu_1 - rho mu_2 = 0 and
  is reported as what it is: a bounded interval, the complement of an
  interval (whose gap is in the `excluded_lower` and `excluded_upper`
  rows), or the whole line, with the denominator’s *t* that decides
  which beside it. Independent groups default to unequal variances,
  inverting the Welch-type test with degrees of freedom that change with
  the ratio, so that the interval agrees with the test;
  `var_equal = TRUE` gives Fieller’s pooled interval. The paired
  function takes `cluster` for the cluster-robust covariance on Q - 1
  degrees of freedom. A `baseline` argument gives the ratio of two
  advantages over a baseline, the retained fraction of a three-arm
  noninferiority design, and `mean_baseline`, `sd_baseline`, and
  `n_baseline` give it from the three arms’ summary statistics;
  noninferiority at a fraction f holds exactly when f is below the lower
  limit of a bounded interval with a positive denominator, and the help
  says so rather than testing chosen fractions. The log-scale interval
  of the response ratio, and percentile and BCa bootstrap intervals
  (`B = 10000`, `seed = NULL`, written in base R), are offered for
  comparison; the line under a log or bootstrap interval says when the
  Fieller set at the same level is unbounded, where a bounded interval
  can undercover. `tidy()` carries the gap and the form of the set, so a
  complement is not read as the whole line, and
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  writes such a set as what it is (“99.5% confidence set: every value
  except those between 0.90 and 147.05”) rather than as “99.5% CI
  \[-Inf, Inf\]”; the sentence of every other table is unchanged. The
  log interval of a ratio whose terms are not both positive, and a
  bootstrap from summary statistics, are refused with conditions of
  class `dmar_log_ratio_undefined` and `dmar_bootstrap_needs_data`,
  which inherit `dmar_refusal`. The paired page works Fieller’s (1954)
  own example, whose set takes all three forms at three confidence
  levels.

### Equivalence and Noninferiority of a Contrast

- **[`equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_c.md)
  reports nonsuperiority.** A `nonsuperior` row, the last of the table,
  is 1 when the upper confidence limit is below `contrast_upper`: the
  contrast is then shown to be smaller than the smallest advantage that
  would matter, the mirror of `noninferior` and the decision of the
  upper one-sided test (`p_upper`, which reproduces `emmeans::test()`
  with `side = "nonsuperiority"`). The verdict gains a sixth outcome,
  “Not relevantly superior only”, checked after “Noninferior only” and
  before “Inconclusive”, which now means an interval that contains both
  bounds. This is the claim a study needs when `contrast_upper` is the
  improvement that would justify a change.
  [`plot_equivalence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_equivalence.md)
  applies the same rule through one shared helper, draws the sixth
  verdict in the palette’s sixth color, and keeps the colors of the
  other five; its legend sets each one-sided verdict beside the stronger
  one that implies it.

- **Noninferiority is planned without an upper bound, and paired designs
  are planned.**
  [`power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_c.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_equivalence_c.md)
  require `contrast_upper` only for `side = "equivalence"`. For
  `side = "noninferiority"` they take the margin, `contrast_lower`, and
  a call that gives only `contrast_upper`, as 1.0.x required of its
  `delta_upper`, still uses it as the margin, so no earlier call changes
  but for the names of the bounds. Both take a new last argument,
  `design = c("independent", "paired")`, and `c_weights` now defaults to
  `NULL` (it is still required for independent groups). With `"paired"`,
  `true_sd` is the standard deviation of the per-unit contrast scores
  (for two conditions, the difference scores), and the standard error is
  sigma / sqrt(N) on N - 1 degrees of freedom, where N is the number of
  units. Each design has its own size, because the two are different
  quantities:
  [`power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_c.md)
  takes `n_per_group` for independent groups and `N`, the number of
  units and so the total sample size, for a paired design, and refuses
  the size of the other design with a condition of class
  `dmar_argument_invalid`. The planner answers in the same terms: the
  rows of an independent plan are `necessary_n_per_group`, `total_N`,
  and `actual_power`, as in 1.0.x, and the rows of a paired plan are
  `necessary_N` and `actual_power`; `tidy()` reports the planned size
  and the power in the same columns for both. At 50 units, a difference
  score SD of 1, and a margin of .5, the noninferiority power is .9672,
  and 36 units reach .90. Independent designs give the results they did.

### A Crossed Design of Units and Raters

- **[`ss_aipe_crossed()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crossed.md)
  plans the numbers of units and raters for a fully crossed design,
  every rater scoring every unit, so that the interval for the mean is
  narrow enough at the least cost.** Units and raters are both random,
  so the variance of the grand mean is var_unit / n_u + var_rater /
  n_r + var_residual / (n_u n_r), and with n_r raters no number of units
  brings the half-width below z sqrt(var_rater / n_r); the plan reports
  that rater floor. A design costs `unit_cost` per unit, `rater_cost`
  per rater, and `judgment_cost` per score (by default the number of
  scores), and the search prices the smallest feasible number of units
  for every number of raters up to `max_raters` (or for a panel fixed by
  `n_raters`). `quantile = "t"`, the default, plans the interval
  [`ci_crossed()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_crossed.md)
  computes, with Satterthwaite (1946) degrees of freedom from the
  planning values; `quantile = "normal"` reproduces planning that uses
  the normal quantile. With the t quantile the planned width is not
  monotone in the number of units (the degrees of freedom eventually
  fall toward n_r - 1, and past a point the larger quantile outweighs
  the smaller variance), and the search takes the first feasible design.
  An `assurance` rests on the chi square approximation to the plug-in
  variance, and a plan with an assurance is never smaller than the plan
  without one, which already meets the width somewhat more than half the
  time; an assurance at or below one half returns that plan. A target no
  design within the limits meets is refused with a message naming the
  limit that binds, `max_units` or the number of raters. With judgments
  as the only cost the plan lies near the ratio n_u / n_r = var_unit /
  var_rater of Marcoulides and Goldstein (1990). The help gives the
  mapping to an information retrieval evaluation, in which the units are
  topics and the raters are relevance assessors.
- **[`ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity.md)**
  draws complete arrays from the true components at a planned or
  specified design and reports the realized widths, the proportion at or
  below the target, and the coverage of the true mean, in the return
  schema of the sensitivity family, with `seed = NULL` and
  `filename = NULL`. The planner’s arguments, its search limits
  included, pass through to it.
- **[`ci_crossed()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_crossed.md)**
  gives the interval for the mean of a complete units by raters array:
  the ANOVA estimates of the three components, a negative one set to
  zero, plugged into the variance of the grand mean, with Satterthwaite
  degrees of freedom. Its `var_unit`, `var_rater`, and `var_residual`
  rows are the planning values
  [`ss_aipe_crossed()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crossed.md)
  takes. On the four judges and six targets of Shrout and Fleiss (1979)
  it reproduces their mean squares and shows how much wider the interval
  for the mean over a population of judges is than one that treats the
  four judges as fixed.
- `tidy()` and `glance()` read `necessary_n_units` as the planned size
  of a crossed design, with `necessary_n_raters` (or
  `specified_n_raters`) kept beside it.

### Two-Phase Sampling: A Costly Measurement With an Inexpensive Proxy

- **A family for the mean of a target measurement that is costly to
  obtain, when an inexpensive proxy is available on a large pool of
  units.** The design is two-phase, or double, sampling (Neyman, 1938):
  the proxy is measured on the whole pool and the target on a random
  subsample of it, the labeled units.
  [`ci_two_phase()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_two_phase.md)
  gives the interval for the population mean of the target from the
  regression estimator, with standard error from the residual variation
  among the labeled units and the proxy’s variation over the pool,
  optional cluster standard errors whose degrees of freedom count the
  clusters among the labeled units, and units with a missing value set
  aside one by one; it refuses a target that is constant on the labeled
  units rather than report an interval of zero width.
  `method = "prediction_powered"` gives the prediction-powered estimate
  of Angelopoulos et al. (2023), which fixes the proxy’s weight at 1
  where the regression estimator learns it. The table reports the
  estimate as `mean_Y`, named for its estimand, the population mean of
  the target, with its standard error, degrees of freedom, and limits,
  and the weight the estimate gives the proxy mean of the unlabeled
  units as `proxy_weight` (the slope times N / M for the regression
  estimate, 1 for the prediction-powered one), beside `slope`,
  `correlation`, `proxy_bias`, `se_ratio_target_only`, `n_labeled`, and
  `n_pool`.
  [`ss_aipe_two_phase()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_two_phase.md)
  plans the number of labeled units for a given pool, for the expected
  width or with assurance, always leaving at least one unit with the
  proxy alone; it reports beside the plan the number needed without the
  proxy, which is the plan
  [`ss_aipe_mean()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_mean.md)
  makes, and refuses a width the pool cannot deliver rather than
  returning a missing value.
  [`ss_aipe_two_phase_cost()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_two_phase_cost.md)
  chooses both sizes: given the cost of a proxy measurement relative to
  a target measurement, it returns the least costly design in whole
  numbers whose
  [`ci_two_phase()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_two_phase.md)
  interval has an expected width no larger than the one asked for. The
  width is that of the interval as it is reported, with the *t* quantile
  on n - 2 degrees of freedom, which is the criterion
  [`ss_aipe_two_phase()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_two_phase.md)
  uses for a given pool, so that planner, given the returned pool,
  returns the returned number of labeled units; the alternative of
  measuring the target alone is the `necessary_n_target_only` plan of
  that function, and a two-phase design is returned only when it costs
  less. The search is exact: for each number of labeled units the
  smallest pool follows from the width, a convex lower bound on the cost
  (from the normal quantile, which the *t* quantile is never below) says
  which numbers of labeled units can still beat the best design found,
  and those are all examined. In 2,200 planning sets drawn at random the
  result equaled an exhaustive search over pairs of sizes every time.
  The rows are `necessary_n_labeled`, `necessary_n_pool` (0 when the
  design measures the target alone), `relative_cost` (the cost of the
  returned design over that of the target alone, both in whole numbers),
  `relative_cost_continuous` (the same ratio for fractional sizes under
  the normal quantile, which is a lower bound and is 1 at or below
  `threshold_cor`), `expected_width`, `necessary_n_target_only`,
  `threshold_cor`, and the inputs. `threshold_cor` is exact for
  fractional sizes only; above it the least costly design in whole
  numbers can still be the target alone, and is then returned. Planning
  values whose sizes cannot be represented as whole numbers, or whose
  search would examine more than 1e8 numbers of labeled units, stop with
  an error of class `dmar_two_phase_no_design`. For a width of 0.20 with
  a standard deviation of 1, a correlation of .90, and a cost ratio of
  .05, the design is 109 labeled units in a pool of 1,011, at a cost of
  159.55 target measurements against 387 for the target alone, with an
  expected width of 0.19999.
  [`ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity.md)
  evaluates a design by simulation under the family’s return schema,
  from a bivariate normal population or by resampling observed pairs; it
  reports the population target mean as `true_mean_Y`, the simulated
  estimates of it as `mean_mean_Y`, `median_mean_Y`, and `sd_mean_Y`,
  and the estimate in its per-replication file as `mean_Y`.
  [`ss_seq_two_phase()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_two_phase.md)
  evaluates the sequential stopping rule, which needs no planning
  values, in the form of
  [`ss_seq_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_c.md);
  it asks for more labeled units while the target is constant on them or
  is an exact linear function of the proxy on them, where the rule could
  stop on no evidence. The vocabulary is that of measurement (target,
  proxy, labeled units, pool); each help page says in one sentence how
  the terms map onto the evaluation of an AI system’s outputs.

- [`ss_seq_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_c.md)’s
  help page says when to use it and how it differs from the balanced
  procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018).

- **[`ss_aipe_two_phase_cost()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_two_phase_cost.md)
  refuses a `cost_ratio` that is not a single number above 0 and below 1
  with a condition of class `dmar_cost_ratio_invalid`,** which carries
  the value given.

### One Notation for the Regression and Correlation Functions

The regression, correlation, and coefficient of variation functions now
name the total sample size, the number of predictors, a planner’s
planning values, and the desired width one way. No function is renamed
and no result changes for a given model. The DMAR 1.0.x names are not
accepted; Breaking Changes in 1.1.0, at the top of this section, lists
every old and new name.

- **`p` is the number of predictors in the partial and semipartial
  correlation family, as it is in
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md),
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md), and
  [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md).**
  [`var_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_partial_r.md),
  [`var_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md),
  [`expected_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_partial_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md)
  took `J`, the number of variables partialed out. They now take `p`,
  the number of predictors in the regression of Y on X and the variables
  partialed out, so `p - 1` variables are partialed out, `p` is at least
  2, and `p = J + 1`: a partial correlation of Y and X given two other
  variables was `J = 2` and is `p = 3`. A categorical variable with *a*
  levels counts as *a* - 1 predictors. The degrees of freedom are then
  the regression ones: the raw-scale variance of a partial correlation
  divides by N - p, Fisher’s *Z* variance is 1 / (N - p - 2), the
  squared standard error of the *t* test of a semipartial correlation is
  (1 - R2_full) / (N - p - 1), and the planners return N = p +
  ceiling(z^2 V / h^2) for a half-width h. `p` holds the place `J` held,
  so a 1.0.x call that gave the count by position must add 1 to it (see
  Breaking Changes in 1.1.0). In the notation of a model comparison, `q`
  is the number of predictors removed from the full model to give the
  restricted model (q = p_full - p_restricted, the predictors being
  tested) and the number of variables partialed out is p - q; a partial
  or semipartial correlation concerns one predictor, so q = 1 and p - 1
  variables are partialed out. The help pages of the family and of
  [`ss_power_R2_change()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_change.md)
  say so, and
  [`ss_power_R2_change()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_change.md)
  reports a row `q`. No result changes for a given model.

- **`N` is the total sample size.**
  [`var_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_partial_r.md),
  [`var_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md),
  [`expected_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_partial_r.md),
  [`ci_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
  [`var_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_r.md),
  [`expected_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_r.md),
  [`equivalence_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_r.md),
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md), and
  [`var_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_cv.md)
  took `n` and take `N`, as
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md),
  [`ci_R()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
  [`cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv.md), and the
  regression functions already did;
  [`ci_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md)
  and
  [`ci_R()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
  which share a help page, now document one `N`. A size per group is
  `n_per_group` and a size per cell is `n_per_cell`; `n` alone remains
  only for one size per study or per plotted effect (`meta_r(n = )` is a
  vector of study sizes). The second position is unchanged, so
  `ci_r(.3, 100)` runs as it did; `ci_r(r = .3, n = 100)` stops with
  “unused argument”. The other functions that took a total sample size
  as `n` take `N` too
  ([`var_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_alpha.md),
  [`var_icc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_icc.md),
  [`ci_proportion()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_proportion.md),
  [`ci_eigenvalue()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eigenvalue.md),
  and the rest of the table in Breaking Changes in 1.1.0). The divisor
  of [`ecvi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ecvi.md) was
  `n` and is `multiplier`, because it is the multiplier of the fit
  function (N, or N less the number of groups), not always the total.

- **A planner names its planning value as its sensitivity function names
  the data generating value, `true_X`.** The planner treats the value as
  the truth; the sensitivity function shows what the plan delivers when
  the truth (`true_X`) differs from the value planned with
  (`supposed_X`, which was `estimated_X`).

  The planners are
  [`ss_aipe_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv.md),
  [`ss_aipe_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2.md),
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md),
  [`ss_aipe_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_r.md),
  [`ss_power_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_r.md);
  the sensitivity function
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_r_sensitivity.md),
  which took `true_r` and `estimated_r`, takes `true_cor` and
  `supposed_cor`. The planners for a regression coefficient take
  `true_reg_coef_j`
  ([`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md),
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md),
  [`ss_power_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_rc.md))
  or, for the standardized coefficient, `true_std_reg_coef_j`
  ([`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md))
  for the coefficient the plan is made for, and
  [`ss_aipe_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv.md)
  takes `true_mean` and `true_sd` where it took `mu` and `sigma`; the
  mean that
  [`ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md)
  generates data from is `true_mean`, as in
  [`ss_aipe_mean_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_mean_sensitivity.md).
  `ss_aipe_cv(true_cv = .25, width = .10, conf_level = .99)` is the
  worked example of Kelley (2007, pp. 759–760; the call is printed on
  p. 765), which gives 99; with the exact noncentral *t* distribution
  the function returns 101 (see Changes to Earlier Results). The
  full-model planning value that
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  gains in this release is `true_R2_full`.
  [`var_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_r.md),
  [`expected_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_r.md),
  and
  [`expected_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_partial_r.md),
  which evaluate a formula at a population correlation, take it as
  `true_cor` (`rho`), the name in the planners, and
  [`var_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_R2.md) and
  [`expected_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_R2.md)
  take the population squared multiple correlation as `true_R2`
  (`population_R2`), as
  [`ss_aipe_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  do;
  [`expected_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_R2.md)
  reports its value in the row `expected_R2`
  (`expected_value_population_R2`), as
  [`var_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_R2.md)
  reports `var_R2`. The null value of
  [`ss_power_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_r.md)
  was `rho_0` and is `null_cor`, as `null_R2` and `null_rmsea` are the
  null values of their planners.

- **`width` is the desired width.**
  [`ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md)
  took `w` and take `width`, as their planners do.

- **`true_cor_YX` and `true_cor_XX`.**
  [`ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_R2_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_sensitivity.md)
  took `rho_yx` and `rho_xx`, the correlations their data are generated
  from, and take `true_cor_YX` and `true_cor_XX`, the names in the
  coefficient planners.

- **Every population value of a coefficient planner carries `true_`.**
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md),
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md),
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md),
  and
  [`ss_power_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_rc.md)
  took `rho2_Y_X`, `rho2_j_X_without_j`, `rho2_Y_X_without_j`,
  `sigma_Y`, `sigma_X`, `rho_XX`, and `rho_YX` beside `b_j` or `beta_j`;
  each now has the prefix the coefficient has and names its quantity:
  `true_R2_Y_X`, `true_R2_j_X_without_j`, `true_R2_Y_X_without_j`,
  `true_sd_Y`, `true_sd_X`, `true_cor_XX`, and `true_cor_YX`, beside
  `true_reg_coef_j` or `true_std_reg_coef_j`. Cohen’s *f* squared was
  `cohen_f2` in
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md),
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md),
  and
  [`ss_power_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_rc.md)
  and is `true_f2`, the name of the row that reports it in
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_R2_change()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_change.md);
  the row of the two coefficient planners that holds its square root,
  Cohen’s *f*, was `effect_size` and is `true_f`.

- **`specified_N` in
  [`ss_power_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_r.md).**
  The sample size at which power is wanted was `N` and is `specified_N`,
  the name in
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md)
  and the name of the row the function returns.

- **The wrappers spell their arguments as the functions they call do.**
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)
  took `Rho2_j_X_without_j` and `sigma_X_j` and take
  `true_R2_j_X_without_j` and `true_sd_X`, the names in
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md);
  [`ss_power_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_rc.md)
  took `Rho2_j_X_without_j` and takes `true_R2_j_X_without_j`, the name
  in
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md).

The row for the full-model planning value of
[`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md),
new in this release, is `true_R2_full`. A row that echoes an argument
has the argument’s name, and one quantity has one row name: the desired
width is the row `width` (seven planners and
[`design_consequences()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/design_consequences.md)
called it `width_target` or `target_width`), the expected width is
`expected_width` (three planners called it `ci_width_expected`), and the
null value of
[`ss_power_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_r.md)
is `null_cor`. `necessary_N`, `specified_N`, and `total_N` keep their
names.

### Power for the Change in R Squared When Predictors Are Added

- **[`ss_power_R2_change()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_change.md)
  plans the sample size for the test that predictors added to a
  regression model contribute nothing**, the model comparison *F* test
  of a restricted model with `p_restricted` predictors against a full
  model with `p_full`, and returns the power at a `specified_N`. DMAR
  could plan the omnibus test of all predictors
  ([`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md))
  and, with fixed predictors, the test of one coefficient
  ([`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md)),
  and had no planner for a set of added predictors or for one added
  predictor when the predictors are random. The effect is given as any
  two of `true_R2_full`, `true_R2_restricted`, and `true_R2_change`, or
  as `true_f2` alone. The change in R^2 is the squared semipartial
  correlation of the added predictor when one is added and the squared
  multiple semipartial correlation of the added set when several are;
  divided by one minus the restricted model’s R^2 it is the squared
  multiple partial correlation, and Cohen’s f^2 is that partial value
  divided by one minus itself, (rho^2 full - rho^2 restricted) / (1 -
  rho^2 full). The help page sets these relations out, with the error
  degrees of freedom of the two models in the notation of Maxwell,
  Delaney, and Kelley (2027).

  With fixed predictors (`random_predictors = FALSE`) the test statistic
  is noncentral *F* with `p_full - p_restricted` and N - `p_full` - 1
  degrees of freedom and noncentrality N f^2. With one added predictor
  that is the calculation of
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md)
  (the two agree to 1e-8 on 81 combinations, and both give 50 for a
  change from .30 to .40 with five predictors and power .80), and with
  no predictors in the restricted model it is
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  (agreement to 1e-12 on 54 combinations, both predictor models). For
  five predictors that explain .25 and four added predictors that raise
  that to .30, at an alpha of .01, the power at N = 90 is .2413 and the
  sample size for power .80 is 242, the values the G\*Power 3.1 manual
  prints for that design (.241297 and 242).

  With random predictors, the default, the power comes from the
  distribution of the sample squared multiple partial correlation, which
  is that of a squared multiple correlation with the added predictors
  alone and a sample size reduced by the number of predictors in the
  restricted model (Gatsonis & Sampson, 1989, p. 518), computed with
  Lee’s (1971, Section 5.1) approximation as in
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md).
  The same design needs 250, and the power at N = 90 is .2202. Against
  the exact distribution, the power by Lee’s approximation differed by
  at most .0043 over the combinations examined (squared partial
  correlations up to .95, an alpha from .001 to .10, and one or more
  error degrees of freedom) and by at most .0004 with 25 or more error
  degrees of freedom; the necessary sample size differed from the one
  the exact distribution gives, by one case, in 20 of 1,500 searches,
  and in those the power by the exact distribution at the size returned
  was within .0011 of `desired_power`. The same holds for
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md),
  which shares the search. In a Monte Carlo with raw data (20,000
  replications in each of twelve conditions, six with random and six
  with fixed predictors) the rejection rate under the null hypothesis
  was within 2.0 standard errors of `alpha_level` and the power within
  1.9 standard errors of the value returned.

  Cohen’s (1988) noncentrality, f^2 (u + v + 1), is f^2 (N - w) for an
  increment with w predictors in the restricted model, where this
  function uses N f^2 for fixed predictors; Cohen’s value is the
  fixed-predictor call with no restricted model at a sample size of N -
  w, which the last example of the help page shows (noncentrality 6.071
  and power .2225 where N f^2 gives 6.429 and .2413), and the necessary
  sample size by Cohen’s form is at most w above the fixed-predictor
  answer (247 against 242 in that design). The result has nine rows:
  `necessary_N` or `specified_N`, `actual_power`, `noncentral_f_parm`
  (`NA` with random predictors), `true_f2` (the planning value of
  Cohen’s f^2), `true_partial_R2`, `true_R2_change`, `q` (the number of
  predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model,
  `p_full - p_restricted`), `df_1`, and `df_2`.

- **A change of zero is refused with a classed condition.**
  [`ss_power_R2_change()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_change.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  stop with a refusal of class `dmar_effect_zero` when the planning
  values give an effect of exactly zero (no sample size gives a test of
  a true null hypothesis power above `alpha_level`); the message says
  what to give instead.

### The Semipartial Correlation: Its Variance, Its Plan, and the Check of the Plan

- **[`var_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md)
  gives the first-order variance of a semipartial correlation, which
  depends on the full-model R2.** Under multivariate normality, N times
  the variance of the sample semipartial correlation tends to (1 -
  rho_sp²⁾2 - q (1 - 2 rho_sp^2), where q is the full-model R2 minus
  rho_sp^2, the squared multiple correlation of the outcome with the
  variables partialed out. DMAR 1.0.x gave (1 - r_sp²⁾2 / (N - p), which
  is that variance only when q = 0. When the variables partialed out
  explain some of the outcome, the 1.0.x value is too large if rho_sp^2
  is below 1/2 and too small if it is above: at r_sp = .3 with a
  full-model R2 of .59 the numerator is .4181 where 1.0.x used .8281,
  and at r_sp = .8 with a full-model R2 of .94 it is .2136 where 1.0.x
  used .1296. At r_sp = 0 the 1.0.x value was 1 / (N - p) whatever the
  R2, while the same function with `R2_full = .64` returned .36 / (N -
  p - 1). The new argument `under_null` (default `TRUE`) chooses between
  the two quantities that need `R2_full`: `under_null = FALSE` returns
  the first-order variance with the divisor N - p, the quantity for a
  Wald interval and for planning, and the default returns (1 - R2_full)
  / (N - p - 1) as before. The help page now describes that default as
  what it is, the squared standard error in the *t* test of X’s
  coefficient, which equals the first-order variance at rho_sp = 0; it
  is not a variance for an interval about a nonzero r_sp. No value an
  existing call returned has changed. A call without `R2_full` returns
  what it did and now warns (class `dmar_semipartial_r_no_R2_full`) that
  the value holds only when the variables partialed out explain none of
  the outcome. An `R2_full` smaller than `r_sp` squared, which no data
  can produce and which 1.0.x accepted (the 1.0.x call
  `var_semipartial_r(.9, 100, 1, R2_full = .10)` returned .0093), is
  refused with an error of class `dmar_semipartial_r_incoherent`, a
  `dmar_refusal`, that says what to pass when the two values were
  rounded. The help page states the limits of the approximation found in
  simulation: it understates the variance when \|rho_sp\| is large and
  N - p is small, and the sample semipartial correlation is biased
  toward zero by roughly rho_sp (p - 1) / (2N).

- **The help pages no longer credit (1 - r_sp²⁾2 to Olkin and
  Finn (1995) or to Algina and Olejnik (2003).** Olkin and Finn (1995)
  do not treat the semipartial correlation; their Model A is the
  difference between a squared multiple correlation with two predictors
  and a squared simple correlation, from whose delta method variance the
  result above follows for one variable partialed out (Alf and Graf,
  1999, give the difference between two squared multiple correlations
  with any number of predictors), and the pages now say so. The Yuan and
  Chan (2011) entry leaves the references of
  [`var_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md),
  since the sentence that cited it is withdrawn. Algina and Olejnik
  (2003, p. 317) are cited for what they state, that for the squared
  semipartial correlation the required sample size is largest when the
  squared multiple correlation of the restricted model is zero. The
  sentences that described the 1.0.x form as Fisher’s (1924) result
  applied by analogy, and as matching the leading 1/N behavior of the
  variance in Aloe and Becker (2012), are withdrawn; Aloe and
  Becker (2012) are cited for the effect size.

- **[`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  takes `true_R2_full`, a planning value of the full-model R2**, and
  plans from the first-order variance at that value: N = p + ceiling(z^2
  V / w^2), with V as above and w the half-width. For a planning value
  of .2, three variables partialed out (`p = 4`), and a width of .10,
  `necessary_N` is 714 with `true_R2_full = .54`, where the plan without
  it (and DMAR 1.0.x) gives

  1421. The result gains a last row, `true_R2_full`, which is NA when
        none was given. Without `true_R2_full` the plan uses the largest
        V over every full-model R2 that is possible with `true_r_sp`, so
        the sample size is sufficient whatever that R2 is (see Changes
        to Earlier Results for the cases in which this differs from
        1.0.x). The count of predictors must be a whole number, where
        the 1.0.x call
        `ss_aipe_semipartial_r(r_sp = .3, J = 1.5, width = .2)` had
        returned a `necessary_N` of 321.5. A plan with `true_r_sp = 0`
        and `true_R2_full = 1` is refused: the first-order variance is
        zero there.

- **[`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md)
  simulates a population in which the variables partialed out can
  explain part of the outcome**, through the new arguments
  `true_R2_full` (the population’s full-model R2; by default `true_r_sp`
  squared, the population 1.0.x simulated) and `supposed_R2_full` (the
  planning value passed to the planner). Under normality the
  distribution of the sample semipartial correlation depends on the
  population only through the semipartial correlation, the full-model
  R2, p, and N, so the two values describe every normal population. Its
  result gains the rows `true_R2_full` and `supposed_R2_full`. Each
  interval is now the Wald interval the planner plans for (see Changes
  to Earlier Results). In 20,000 replications of a plan for a width of
  .10, the intervals missed the true value in .053 of samples at r_sp =
  .8 with a full-model R2 of .94 (N = 331, mean width .0995) and in .051
  at r_sp = 0 with a full-model R2 of .64 (N = 556, mean width .0998);
  the Monte Carlo standard error of each rate is .002. The pages of
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  and
  [`var_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md)
  name two further conditions in which the interval misses too often: a
  full-model R2 near 1 with a small N, at any r_sp (.13 at r_sp = .1, a
  full-model R2 of .99, p = 4, and the planned N of 12), and \|r_sp\|
  above about .9 with variables partialed out that explain some of the
  outcome, where the misses fall mostly on one side even with several
  hundred observations (.064, .051 of it on one side, at r_sp = .95, a
  full-model R2 of .97, p = 2, and N = 395).

- **[`ss_aipe_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r.md)
  with `assurance` returns the smallest sample size that attains it,
  computed from the distribution of the sample partial correlation.** At
  a given sample size the width of either interval the function plans
  depends on the sample only through r and narrows as \|r\| grows, so
  the interval is no wider than the target exactly when \|r\| is at
  least a value r\* that the function solves for. The probability of
  that event is taken from the distribution function of the sample
  partial correlation, which under multivariate normality is that of a
  simple correlation from N - (p - 1) observations, written as an
  integral of a central *t* probability against a beta density (R’s
  noncentral *t* is an approximation above a noncentrality of 37.62,
  which plans for narrow intervals reach). The function returns the
  smallest sample size, at or above the one planned without `assurance`,
  at which the probability is at least `assurance`, and two rows are
  appended to the table: `assurance` and `assurance_attained`, the
  probability at the returned sample size. The search does not go below
  the plan without `assurance`, because below it the probability is not
  monotone in the sample size. DMAR 1.0.x multiplied the sample size by
  qchisq(assurance, df) / df, the step for an interval whose width is
  proportional to a standard deviation; here it gave too few cases when
  the correlation is large in absolute value and too many when it is
  small. With one variable partialed out (`p = 2`), a width of .10, and
  an assurance of .80:

  | rho | 1.0.x | now  | attained now |
  |-----|-------|------|--------------|
  | 0   | 1586  | 1539 | 1.000        |
  | .30 | 1318  | 1310 | .807         |
  | .50 | 902   | 915  | .803         |
  | .70 | 426   | 448  | .804         |
  | .85 | 135   | 151  | .807         |
  | .95 | 23    | 28   | .805         |

  The page’s example (`true_cor = .30`, `p = 3`, `width = .20`,
  `assurance = .80`) returns 338, where it returned 344. In 16 further
  conditions simulated from regression data (20,000 data sets each, the
  variables partialed out by least squares; Monte Carlo standard error
  .0015 to .0025), the 1.0.x sample sizes delivered from .139 below the
  request to .145 above it (.711 for a requested .85 at rho = .80, and
  1.000 for a requested .95 at rho = .20), and the sample sizes now
  returned from .002 to .012 above it, each within .004 of
  `assurance_attained`. At rho = 0 the plan without `assurance` already
  meets the width in every sample, and `assurance` adds nothing. No
  argument restores the earlier sample sizes.

- **[`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  with `assurance` finds the sample size by simulation, and takes `G`
  and `seed`.** The width of this interval depends on two statistics,
  the sample semipartial correlation and the sample full-model R2, so
  the function simulates them: for each sample size tried it draws `G`
  (default 20,000) samples from a multivariate normal population with
  the planning values, through the entries of the triangular factor of
  the Wishart matrix that the two statistics depend on, and takes the
  share of intervals no wider than the target. It returns the smallest
  sample size found, at or above the one planned without `assurance`, at
  which that share is at least `assurance`. Three rows are appended:
  `assurance`, `assurance_attained` (the share in a fresh set of `G`
  draws at the returned sample size, which had no part in choosing it),
  and `G`; the Monte Carlo standard error of the attained share is the
  attribute `assurance_mc_se`. The answer has Monte Carlo error: without
  `seed` two calls can differ by a few cases (eight unseeded plans for
  one condition gave 252 to 254; 40 seeded plans of each of two other
  conditions gave 470 to 473 and 306 to 310, and the probability at the
  smallest of those sizes was .897 and .895 for a requested .90), and
  `assurance_attained` can fall below the request by a few of its
  standard errors (the standard error is .003 at the default `G` and an
  assurance of .80; in 200 seeded plans the lowest value was .009 below
  a request of .90). The sample size returned is therefore the one at
  which the probability is about the request, and `assurance_attained`
  is an unbiased estimate of the probability at it. Without
  `true_R2_full` the simulated population is the one the plan without
  `assurance` is made for (variables partialed out that explain none of
  the outcome when `true_r_sp` squared is at most 1/2, a full-model R2
  of 1 otherwise). `G` and `seed` are checked and used only with
  `assurance`; `G` must be at least 100, because the step estimates a
  probability from those samples (`G = 1` returned an attained assurance
  of 0 or 1). DMAR 1.0.x multiplied by the same chi square factor as the
  partial correlation planner. With an assurance of .80 (now with
  `seed = 113`):

  | true_r_sp | true_R2_full | p   | width | 1.0.x | now | attained now (fresh draws) |
  |-----------|--------------|-----|-------|-------|-----|----------------------------|
  | .25       | not given    | 4   | .15   | 635   | 621 | .802                       |
  | .30       | .09          | 3   | .20   | 344   | 337 | .814                       |
  | .70       | .49          | 3   | .15   | 197   | 214 | .808                       |
  | .85       | .7225        | 3   | .15   | 65    | 89  | .798                       |
  | .80       | not given    | 2   | .10   | 219   | 370 | .824                       |

  (DMAR 1.0.x had no `true_R2_full`; it planned every row with variables
  partialed out that explain none of the outcome. In the last row, where
  `true_r_sp` squared is above 1/2, this release plans without
  `true_R2_full` for the full-model R2 at which the variance is largest,
  which accounts for most of the change from 219.) In 11 further
  conditions checked from data with
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md)
  (5,000 data sets each; Monte Carlo standard error .003 to .006), the
  earlier sample sizes delivered from .37 below the request to .02 above
  it (.530 for a requested .90 at a semipartial correlation of .90 and
  `true_R2_full` = .81; .574 and .623 for a requested .80 at .80 and
  -.70 with `true_R2_full` equal to `true_r_sp` squared), and the sample
  sizes now returned delivered .798 to .819 for .80, .854 to .858 for
  .85, .906 to .908 for .90, and .953 for .95. No argument restores the
  earlier sample sizes. The page still says that a plan whose sample
  size is small (a large \|r_sp\| with `true_R2_full` near `true_r_sp`
  squared) should be checked with the sensitivity function, because the
  first-order variance is too small there.

- **The count of variables partialed out must be a whole number in the
  seven functions of the partial and semipartial correlation family**
  ([`var_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_partial_r.md),
  [`var_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md),
  [`expected_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_partial_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md),
  and the two sensitivity functions). A fractional count (`J = 1.5` in
  1.0.x) had been accepted and carried into the result. The count is now
  given as the number of predictors, `p`, a whole number of at least 2
  (see “One Notation for the Regression and Correlation Functions”). The
  two sensitivity functions also check `G` (a whole number of at
  least 1) and `specified_N` (a whole number of at least p + 3 for the
  partial correlation on Fisher’s *Z* scale, whose interval needs N -
  p - 2 \> 0, and p + 2 for the raw-scale interval and for the
  semipartial).

- **[`ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity.md)
  simulates the interval that was planned, and takes `fisher_z`.** The
  planner plans the raw-scale interval, r plus or minus z (1 - r^2) /
  sqrt(N - p), unless `fisher_z = TRUE`; the sensitivity function
  planned that interval and then formed Fisher’s *Z* interval in every
  replication, so its `pct_ci_less_width` did not describe the plan. It
  now takes `fisher_z` (appended after `filename`), passes it to the
  planner, and forms the same interval in each replication; the
  raw-scale limits are not truncated, and the smallest sample size is
  p + 2 for the raw-scale interval and p + 3 for Fisher’s. The table
  carries the attribute `interval` (`"raw"` or `"fisher_z"`) and prints
  a line that names the interval. For `true_cor = supposed_cor = .70`,
  `p = 3`, `width = .20` (N = 103), 2,000 replications under
  `set.seed(7)`: mean width .203, `pct_ci_less_width` .470, and
  non-coverage .046 in DMAR 1.0.0 (Fisher’s interval at the raw-scale
  plan, with `J = 2`), and .200, .516, and .062 now; with
  `fisher_z = TRUE` the plan is 107 and the three are .199, .521, and
  .050. No argument restores the 1.0.x results of this function or of
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md).

- **A full-model R2 that falls below the squared semipartial correlation
  only by rounding is accepted, with a warning.** A semipartial
  correlation reported as .46 has a square of .2116, and the full-model
  R2 beside it may be reported as .21. The 1.0.x call
  `var_semipartial_r(.46, 100, 1, R2_full = .21)` (one variable
  partialed out, `J = 1` by position) returned .00814433 in DMAR 1.0.0.
  The pair is checked in this release, since a full-model R2 cannot be
  below the squared semipartial correlation. A pair that two-decimal
  rounding can produce, `R2_full + .005 >= max(0, |r_sp| - .005)^2`,
  passes with a warning of class `dmar_semipartial_r_rounded` (fields
  `R2_full` and `r_sp`):
  `var_semipartial_r(.46, 100, p = 2, R2_full = .21)` returns .00814433,
  as it did (`p = 2` is the 1.0.x count of 1 plus 1). What the warning
  says follows what is computed. The squared standard error of the *t*
  test (the default, `under_null = TRUE`) is (1 - `R2_full`) / (N - p -
  1), which does not involve `r_sp`, so the warning says that the value
  uses `R2_full` as given. The first-order variance
  (`under_null = FALSE`), the planner, and the sensitivity function
  compute from the part of the full-model R2 that the partialed
  variables explain, which is then taken as zero, and their warning says
  that the variables partialed out are taken to explain none of the
  outcome. A pair further apart (`R2_full = .15` with `r_sp = .46`) is
  refused as before, with the class `dmar_semipartial_r_incoherent`. The
  same rule applies in
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md).

- **The variance on
  [`?var_partial_r`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_partial_r.md)
  and
  [`?ss_aipe_partial_r`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r.md)
  is named for what it is, and the variance of the semipartial
  correlation is credited to the article that prints it.** The pages
  called (1 - rho²⁾2 / (N - p) the “Olkin-Finn (1995) asymptotic
  variance”. Olkin and Finn (1995, Equation 3, p. 157) give the
  first-order variance of a simple correlation, (1 - rho²⁾2 / N; the
  article has no variance of a partial correlation and no N - p form.
  The pages now say “first-order variance”, state that the sample
  partial correlation given p - 1 variables is distributed as a simple
  correlation from N - (p - 1) observations, and say that the divisor
  N - p is the package’s and differs from that at order 1/N^2; the
  message of
  [`var_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_partial_r.md)
  for too small an N reads “Need N \> p for the first-order variance of
  the partial correlation.”
  [`?var_semipartial_r`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md)
  and
  [`?ss_aipe_semipartial_r`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  name the first-order variance of Aloe and Becker (2012, Equation 4,
  p. 284), which they obtain from Alf and Graf (1999), with N - p in
  place of their n, and show that its numerator is the one the functions
  compute. No number changes.

### The Order-Based Effect Sizes Share One Contract

- **[`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md),
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md),
  and
  [`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  read their observations through one check, and say what they will not
  order.** The three statistics depend on the data only through the
  order of the observations. They accept numeric and logical vectors,
  and now ordered factors with the same levels in the same order, which
  are read through their order: a five-category item supplied as an
  ordered factor gives the value its integer codes give, and the value
  any increasing rescoring of the categories gives. A one-column matrix
  (the result of [`scale()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/scale.html)) and a
  one-dimensional array (the result of
  [`tapply()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/tapply.html)) are read as the
  vectors they are, and `Date` and `POSIXct` vectors are ordered by
  their numeric values.
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  did so before;
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  and
  [`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  refused logical vectors and dates (“must both be numeric vectors”) and
  now accept them. Infinite values have their place in the order in all
  three functions. When an infinite value was compared with an equal
  infinite value,
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  stopped (“missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”) and the paired
  function returned a table of `NA`; a single infinite value was already
  ordered correctly. Input with no common order is refused with an error
  of class `dmar_scores_not_ordered`, a `dmar_refusal` (see
  [`?dmar_metadata`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_metadata.md)):
  an unordered factor, an ordered factor beside anything else or beside
  an ordered factor with other levels, two `difftime` objects in
  different units or one beside anything else, a `Date` beside a
  `POSIXct`, and character, complex, list, and matrix input.

- **Missing values are removed and counted in all three.**
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  has always removed them group by group.
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  stopped on a missing value with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE
  needed”, and
  [`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  returned a table in which every row was `NA`, with no message.
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  now removes them group by group and the paired function removes every
  pair with a missing member. Each result carries the numbers removed in
  its `n_missing` attribute: `c(group_1 = , group_2 = )` for the
  two-group functions (through the formula interface of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  as well), one count of pairs for the paired function. A `conf_level`
  that is missing or not a single number gets the worded error in all
  three; `cliff_delta(x, y, conf_level = c(.90, .95))` stopped with
  “‘length = 2’ in coercion to ‘logical(1)’”.

- **A grouping factor with an unused level is accepted by the formula
  interface of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md).**
  The two groups are the two levels observed with an outcome;
  `vargha_delaney_A(y ~ g, data = d)` with `levels(d$g)` of `"a"`,
  `"b"`, `"c"` and no row in `"c"` stopped with “Grouping variable must
  have exactly two levels.”

- **An estimated variance of 0 is reported the same way by all three,
  with a classed warning.** The estimated variance is 0 exactly when the
  groups are completely separated (every observation in one group
  exceeds every observation in the other; for pairs, every pair favors
  the same member) or every observation has the same value.
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  already reported both limits at the estimate with a warning under
  complete separation. `vargha_delaney_A(c(4, 5, 6), c(1, 2, 3))`
  returned *A* = 1 with limits \[1, 1\] and no warning, and
  `probability_of_superiority_paired(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(4, 5, 6, 7))`
  returned `NaN` limits and no warning. All three now report both limits
  at the estimate and warn, with class `dmar_interval_degenerate` and a
  `reason` element (`"complete_separation"` or `"no_variation"`), that
  the limits are degenerate and are not a confidence interval with the
  stated coverage. The warning of
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  keeps its 1.0.x opening words through “completely separated (\|delta\|
  = 1)” and gains the class;
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  and the other two also warn when every observation has the same value,
  where the limits are both at 0 (0.5 for *A* and the paired
  probability). Each help page has a paragraph on the case.

- **The pairwise comparisons are computed from ranks, not from a matrix
  of every pair.**
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  and
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  built the matrix of all pairwise comparisons with
  [`outer()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/outer.html), about 36 bytes a pair.
  The placements and the proportions of pairs won, lost, and tied now
  come from the mid-ranks, minimum ranks, and maximum ranks of the
  pooled and the separate samples. The estimators, the variance
  estimators, and the tie conventions are the same, and the results
  agree with the earlier ones to rounding (see “Changes to Earlier
  Results”). With 6,000 observations per group,
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  took 0.52 s and about 1,240 MB, and now takes 0.03 s and under 30 MB;
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  took 0.57 s and about 960 MB, and now takes 0.02 s and under 30 MB.

- **[`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  refers its test to Student’s *t* by default, and offers a studentized
  permutation test.** The new argument
  `test = c("t", "permutation", "z")` chooses the reference distribution
  of the statistic *W* = (*A* - 1/2) / SE, which is the same under all
  three and is reported in the column `test_statistic` (`z_value` in
  1.0.x, a name that is wrong under the *t* and permutation references;
  see the breaking changes). `"t"`, the default, uses Student’s *t* with
  the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of the two placement variances,
  the Brunner-Munzel test as Schüürhuis, Konietschke, and Brunner (2025,
  Equations 7 and 8) give it. `"z"` uses the standard normal
  distribution, as DMAR 1.0.x did. `"permutation"` recomputes *W* over
  reassignments of the pooled scores to the two groups, with the
  arguments `exact`, `n_resamples`, and `seed` of
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  and its rules: every reassignment when there are at most 50,000,
  random ones otherwise, and a *p*-value that is the share of
  reassignments at least as extreme in absolute value. The three
  arguments are read and checked only under `"permutation"`. Two columns
  are added after the nine of 1.0.x, `df` and `test`; `tidy()` and
  `glance()` give them after `p_value`; the table records the
  reassignments in a `resampling` attribute and prints “Permutation
  test: all 252 reassignments” or “Permutation test: 10000 random
  reassignments”. The function reproduces the statistic 3.1375 on 17.683
  degrees of freedom, *p* = 0.005786, of the pain score example in the
  help of `lawstat::brunner.munzel.test()`, and the estimate 0.8 and *p*
  = 0.0239 of Table 2 of Schüürhuis et al. The permutation *p*-value
  equals a brute-force enumeration in 400 small data sets with and
  without ties. The normal reference rejects a true *A* = 1/2 too often
  in small samples. At a nominal .05 with normal data (10,000 samples a
  condition for *z* and *t*, Monte Carlo standard error .002; 2,000 for
  the permutation test, standard error .005) the rates for *z*, *t*, and
  the permutation test were .086, .071, and .047 with 5 per group; .073,
  .056, and .047 with 10 per group; .090, .062, and .063 with 8 and 20
  and the larger standard deviation, three times the other, in the
  smaller group; and .060, .052, and .046 with 20 per group. The
  permutation test is exact when the two distributions are equal and
  approximate when they differ in spread with *A* = 1/2. With completely
  separated groups it is the only one of the three that gives a
  *p*-value (2/252 for 5 and 5 untied scores). The help has the
  formulas, the table, and a paragraph on why the test and the logit
  interval can disagree. See “Changes to Earlier Results”.

- **Each refusal of input with no common order says why, what would have
  been computed, and what to supply.** The class is still
  `dmar_scores_not_ordered`. For an unordered factor the message names
  the argument and shows the levels of the object and the codes R stores
  for them (“here the levels are high, low, mid, stored as 1, 2, 3”),
  says how the statistic would have ranked them, and gives the call that
  states the order. A character vector has a message of its own (“10”
  sorts before “9”); it was told only that it was of class character. An
  ordered factor beside anything else is told what the other group is
  and that the comparison would be of positions in a list of levels with
  scores. Two ordered factors with different levels are shown both lists
  and, where the two share a label under two codes, that label and its
  codes. Every message says “Nothing was computed.” The condition of an
  unordered factor or a character vector carries the argument at fault
  as `arg`. Each help page has a paragraph “What is refused, and why”,
  and
  [`?vargha_delaney_A`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  and
  [`?cliff_delta`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  an example: for the ratings low, mid, high, high against low, low,
  mid, high, the codes of the unordered factors give *A* = 0.406 where
  the ordered levels give 0.656.

- **The warning of an estimated variance of 0 explains the case, and
  states the limit Feng and Cliff (2004) give for it.** The class is
  still `dmar_interval_degenerate`, and the reported limits do not
  change. The message now says what the two reported limits are, why a
  sample without overlap gives a variance estimate of 0, that this
  describes the sample and not the population, how large the samples
  are, what to report, and that the randomization test remains valid.
  For completely separated groups
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  and
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  state the limit of Feng and Cliff (2004, p. 324, Equations 6 to 8),
  (n_b - z^2) / (n_b + z^2) for a delta of 1 with n_b the smaller group
  size: 0.131 at the 95 percent level with five in the smaller group,
  and 0.566 on the scale of *A*. That limit is not the one the functions
  report. The condition carries `estimate`, `n`, and `limit_feng_cliff`
  beside `reason`. The help of each function has a section “When the
  estimated variance is zero” that names every case and what is
  returned: complete separation, no variation, separation produced by
  infinite values, two constant groups, groups that only touch (an
  ordinary, wide interval), and, for pairs, wins with ties and fewer
  than three pairs.

- **A table whose limits are not a confidence interval carries the mark
  with it.** When the estimated variance is 0 the three functions set
  the attribute `interval_degenerate` to `"complete_separation"` or
  `"no_variation"`;
  [`dmar_metadata()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_metadata.md)
  returns it in a field of that name; the printed table adds “Limits are
  not a confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0.”; and `tidy()`
  and `glance()` have a logical column `interval_degenerate`, so that a
  stack of rows keeps the mark.
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  and
  [`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  return tables of the classes `dmar_cliff_delta` and
  `dmar_probability_of_superiority_paired` (before `dmar_tbl`) for this.
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reads the mark; see “Changes to Earlier Results”.

- **The help of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md),
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md),
  and
  [`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  is rewritten in full.** Each page states the estimand, the sampling
  unit, and the kind of interval; the assumptions; the estimator and the
  variance estimator with their formulas and sources; how the interval
  is formed; what each column or row is; what is refused; every case of
  a zero variance; and a reading of an example in words.
  [`?cliff_delta`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  states that the variance is the sample version of Feng and
  Cliff’s (2004) Equation 2 (p. 323), whose printed coefficients
  (n_1 - 1) and (n_2 - 1) are transposed, with the argument that shows
  it, and that their Equation 4 is not used; it no longer cites
  Cliff (1996) or says what other R implementations do.
  [`?vargha_delaney_A`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  no longer calls the DeLong, DeLong, and Clarke-Pearson (1988)
  estimator “the standard nonparametric variance (Brunner & Munzel,
  2000)”; it says that Schüürhuis, Konietschke, and Brunner (2025) state
  the two estimators to be identical. The two pages show that their
  intervals are the same construction on two scales with different
  variance estimates: for `1:5` against `3:7`, *A* = 0.18 with limits
  0.034 and 0.576, which are -0.931 and 0.151 on the scale of delta,
  where
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  gives -0.64 with limits -0.935 and 0.177.
  [`?probability_of_superiority_paired`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  derives its variance as that of a mean of independent scores and no
  longer attributes it to Brunner and Munzel (2000).

- **[`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  gives the degenerate-interval warning under its own name.** When the
  Cliff’s delta rows have no variation or the groups are completely
  separated, the warning of class `dmar_interval_degenerate` began
  “cliff_delta():”, a function the user did not call. It now begins
  “randomization_test(): for the Cliff’s delta rows (computed by
  cliff_delta()),”, with the same class and elements.

- **The examples of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md),
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md),
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md),
  and
  [`randomization_test_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test_paired.md)
  show the accepted call.** The call that is refused is described in a
  comment and is no longer run under
  [`try()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/try.html).

### Mediation: Resamples in Which the Indirect Effect Is Defined

- **[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  codes its covariates once and decides in each resample whether the
  indirect effect is defined.** The two regressions were refit in every
  bootstrap resample from a formula, so the columns of a factor
  covariate were recoded from the rows drawn. Three things followed, and
  each is repaired. A covariate category with few cases stopped the call
  with R’s
  `contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or more levels`
  whenever a resample held no case of it; with 2 of 60 cases in a
  category and `B = 400` the call failed as a factor or a character
  covariate and returned 0.1857 \[0.0644, 0.3222\] as a 0/1 column. All
  four codings now return that table. A resample of this kind leaves the
  covariate column redundant, the paths *a* and *b* keep unique values,
  and the resample is kept; the new attribute `"n_covariate_redundant"`
  counts them. A resample in which *a* or *b* is not estimable (the
  predictor constant, or the predictor or the mediator a linear
  combination of the other predictors in the rows drawn) has no indirect
  effect. It is dropped and counted: the table has a new row `B_used`
  after `B` (the number of replications the interval rests on; `B` for
  the Monte Carlo interval, `NA` for Sobel), the attributes `"B"`,
  `"B_used"`, and `"n_dropped"` hold the counts,
  [`dmar_metadata()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_metadata.md)
  now records the bootstrap of a
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  result, and the one warning has the class
  `dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped` and carries `B`, `B_used`, and
  `n_dropped`. When too few replications remain the limits are withheld
  (see One Rule for Bootstrap Replications); through 1.0.x the call
  stopped when fewer than 100 remained. The interval then describes
  resamples in which the effect is defined; that is the package’s rule
  for a replication that returns no value, not a result that gives the
  interval its nominal coverage, and the help page says so. The decision
  does not depend on the units or the origin of a variable: a predictor
  with a large mean relative to its spread (`x + 1e9`) stopped with
  `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed` and now returns the table of
  the unshifted predictor.

- **`mediate(ci_method = "boot_bca")` refuses the interval when it is
  not defined.** The acceleration is estimated by the jackknife, which
  needs the indirect effect with each case left out in turn. When one of
  those was not estimable the value was removed without a word and the
  acceleration computed from the rest. The call now stops with an error
  of class `dmar_bca_undefined` (a `dmar_refusal`) that names the cases,
  and likewise when the bias correction or the acceleration is not
  finite; `ci_method = "boot_percentile"` does not need these
  quantities. This is DMAR’s rule for its jackknife acceleration.
