- **[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  takes column names as they are.** The names given as `x`, `m`, `y`,
  and `covariates` were pasted into a formula, so a name was read as
  formula syntax. A column named `predictor score` stopped the call with
  a parse error and one named `outcome$score` with
  `object 'outcome' not found`; a covariate column named `w^2` beside
  `w` was read as `w` a second time and the square left out of the model
  with no message (in the data of the independent check, N = 120, the
  path *a* was 0.831 where the model with the square gives 0.451); a
  column named `w:x`, `I(w)`, or `log(w)` was evaluated as an expression
  and could use an object `w` that was not in `data`; and a column named
  `.` put every analysis column, the outcome included, among the
  predictors of the mediator. No name reaches a formula now, and every
  such column is the column it names.

- **[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  says what it cannot use.** A factor or character `x`, `m`, or `y`, and
  a logical `x` or `m`, stopped with `subscript out of bounds`; the
  message now says the column must be numeric and that a predictor with
  two categories is supplied coded 0 and 1. A logical `y`, which was
  read as 0 and 1, is refused with the same message (see Changes to
  Earlier Results). A one-column matrix, such as
  [`scale()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/scale.html) leaves in a data frame,
  is read as its column, as before. A column named in two roles (`x` and
  `m` the same column, `y` among the covariates, a covariate named
  twice) stops with the name. An infinite value among the analysis
  variables stops with a message, as does a predictor that is constant
  or a linear combination of the covariates, and a model that leaves the
  outcome regression no residual degrees of freedom. A covariate with a
  single value in the complete cases, which stopped the call when it was
  a factor or a character column, is left out with a message. A Date,
  date-time, or time difference predictor is read as a number, as
  before; a mediator or an outcome of these classes, which stopped the
  call (“‘^’ not defined for”difftime” objects”), is now read the same
  way. `B` must be finite: `B = Inf` was accepted with
  `ci_method = "sobel"`.

- **[`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  gives at most one warning per call for its Monte Carlo intervals.** A
  call in which several effects lost draws gave one warning for each
  effect. It now gives one: of class `dmar_bootstrap_insufficient` if
  the interval of any effect is withheld, otherwise
  `dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped` if any effect lost draws,
  otherwise `dmar_bootstrap_exploratory`. The message has one line for
  each affected effect and then the full account of the effect with the
  fewest usable draws, and the condition carries the data frame
  `effects` (`term`, `B_used`, `n_dropped`, `formed`, `status`).

### Total and Partial Eta Squared and Omega Squared

- **[`eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared.md),
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md),
  and
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
  take `estimand = c("all", "total", "partial")`.** The default,
  `"all"`, reports every estimand; `"total"` or `"partial"` selects one.
  These four functions replace `eta_squared_partial()`,
  `omega_squared_partial()`, and `ci_eta_squared_partial()`, which are
  removed (see One Function for Each ANOVA Effect Size for the call that
  replaces each and the columns of the tables).

- **Total eta squared and total omega squared.**
  [`eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared.md)
  reports, beside the partial value SS_effect / (SS_effect + SS_error),
  the total value SS_effect / SS_total, with the corrected total sum of
  squares, and
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md)
  reports the total omega squared (SS_effect - df_effect MS_error) /
  (SS_total + MS_error) beside the partial value (SS_effect - df_effect
  MS_error) / (SS_effect + (N - df_effect) MS_error) (Olejnik & Algina,
  2000, Table 10; Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Eqs. 7.40 to 7.47).
  In a one-way design the two are the same number. For a fitted model
  the total uses the sums of squares of
  [`anova()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/anova.html); for an `aovlist` fit
  the total eta squared divides by the corrected total over every
  stratum, and the total omega squared, which is defined for designs
  whose factors are all between subjects, is `NA`.

- **Sums of squares from a published table.**
  [`eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared.md)
  takes `SS_effect` with `SS_total` (the total) and `SS_error` (the
  partial);
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md)
  takes `SS_effect`, `df_effect`, and the error mean square (`MS_error`,
  or `SS_error` with `df_error`), with `SS_total` (the total) and `N`
  (the partial). `SS_effect`, `df_effect`, and `F_value` may hold
  several effects of one analysis, named for the effects, and the table
  has a row for each: the 2 by 4 table of Kim (2016, Table 3) is
  `eta_squared(SS_effect = c(LIGHT = 34.716, MATERIAL = 1996.998, "LIGHT:MATERIAL" = 1570.389), SS_error = 2261.612, SS_total = 5863.715, df_effect = c(1, 3, 3), df_error = 72)`.
  Each interface takes exactly its own inputs: sums of squares with
  `F_value`, `MS_error` with `SS_error`, and a `SS_total` smaller than
  `SS_effect + SS_error` are refused, and so are summary statistics
  given with a fitted model (see Calls That Are Now Refused).

- **An estimand the inputs do not determine is `NA`, with the reason.**
  An *F* statistic and its degrees of freedom determine the partial
  value only, since the total also depends on the design’s other
  effects. With `estimand = "all"` such an estimand is `NA`, the
  `estimand_notes` attribute gives the reason, and the console prints it
  beneath the table. Asked for by name, it is refused with an error of
  class `dmar_estimand_undetermined`, which carries `estimand` and
  `reason`.

- **The interval functions report the total where an interval exists.**
  The noncentral *F* interval from an effect’s *F* is an interval for
  its partial value, which in a one-way design is the total, so
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  and
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
  of a fitted one-way model report it for both. For an effect of a
  design with other effects, and for an `aovlist` fit, the total is
  reported with `NA` limits, and `estimand = "total"` is refused.

- **[`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
  takes an `aovlist` fit**, computing the partial value of each effect
  and converting its limits with the size of its stratum, as
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  and
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md)
  do; through 1.0.x it took only a single-stratum fit.

- **[`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reads an interval held in columns named for its estimate**, such as
  `eta_squared_partial_ci_lower` and `eta_squared_partial_ci_upper` in a
  row of
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md).
  A row with one interval gives its sentence; for a row with two (a
  one-way model reports the same interval for the total and the partial
  value), `term` names the one to write.
  [`plot_ci()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_ci.md)
  draws each estimate of such a table that has limits, labeling the rows
  with the effect and the estimand when there are two.

- The estimand changes no value: every partial eta squared, partial
  omega squared, and interval is reported as the other entries of this
  release describe, under the column names of One Function for Each
  ANOVA Effect Size; the total values are new.

### The Assurance Method of the Sample Size Planners

- **`assurance_method` in
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md),
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md),
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),
  and their sensitivity functions.** With `assurance` it says how the
  planner finds the probability that the realized interval is no wider
  than `width`; without `assurance` it changes nothing. `"analytic"`,
  the default, computes without simulation.

  - Where that probability has an exact form, in
    [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md),
    [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md),
    [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md),
    and
    [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
    with its default `noncentral = FALSE`, the plan is the smallest
    sample size, not below the plan without `assurance`, at which the
    exact probability is at least `assurance`, and the row
    `assurance_attained` reports that probability. These plans differ
    from those of DMAR 1.0.x (see Changes to Earlier Results).
  - Where it has none, in
    [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),
    [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
    with `noncentral = TRUE`, and both intervals of
    [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md),
    the plan is the published approximation: that of Lai and
    Kelley (2012) for the ANCOVA contrast, that of DMAR 1.0.x and
    `MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef()` for the noncentral interval, and the chi
    square plan of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3) for the central
    interval for the standardized coefficient. It starts from this
    release’s plan without `assurance` (see Changes to Earlier Results)
    and draws no random numbers. It does not compute the probability it
    attains, which can be less than the request, so `assurance_attained`
    is `NA`, and the printed footer says so.
  - `"simulation"`, offered only where the probability has no exact
    form, returns the smallest sample size, not below the plan without
    `assurance`, at which the probability estimated from `G` simulated
    samples, with `seed`, is at least `assurance`. It reports the
    estimate as `assurance_attained`, with the row `G` and the Monte
    Carlo standard error of the estimate as the attribute
    `assurance_mc_se`. The same samples serve every sample size tried,
    so the estimate changes smoothly with the sample size, and the plan
    can be a case or two from the one the probability itself would give.
  - Where the probability is exact, a simulated estimate would only add
    Monte Carlo error, and `"simulation"` is refused, with or without
    `assurance`, with a condition of class `dmar_argument_invalid`
    (`arg = "assurance_method"`) whose message names where it is
    offered:
    [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),
    [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
    with `noncentral = TRUE`,
    [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md),
    and their sensitivity functions, among them
    [`ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity.md)
    and
    [`ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity.md)
    with `noncentral = TRUE`. Any other value is refused the same way,
    and an abbreviation is not matched.
  - The attributes `assurance_method` and `assurance_probability`
    (`"exact"`, `"simulation"`, or `"not computed"`) and a line of the
    printed footer record how `assurance_attained` was found. The
    sensitivity functions pass the argument to the planner they plan
    through. In the planners `G` and `seed` are used and checked only
    with `assurance` and `assurance_method = "simulation"`.

- **The exact probability in
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md).**
  The interval is no wider than `width` when the noncentral *t*
  statistic falls between the two values at which the width equals the
  target. In
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md)
  the probability of that event is an integral of the normal
  distribution function over the chi square, which does not depend on
  R’s noncentral *t*; in
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  it is the noncentral *t* probability, computed exactly (see Exact
  Noncentral *t* and Studentized Range Distributions). With equal tails
  it depends on the effect only through its magnitude. The plan is found
  by doubling a step upward from the plan without `assurance` and then
  bisecting. At `true_smd = 0`, `width = .8`, and `assurance = .95` it
  is 50 per group (.994636), where the published plan of DMAR 1.0.x, 49,
  attains .949878, and at `true_smd = 1`, `width = .5`, and
  `assurance = .99` it is 149 (.990260), where the published plan, 150,
  attains .994302.
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  at `true_std_contrast = 0` and `c_weights = c(1, -1)` gives the
  same 50. In 45 planning sets of
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md)
  (\|`true_smd`\| of 0 to 2, widths of .25 to 1, assurances of .80 to
  .99) and 96 of
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  (contrasts of -1 to 2, weights for two, three, and five groups, widths
  of .5 and 1, equal and unequal tails) the plan is the smallest sample
  size found by raising the sample size one case at a time from the plan
  without `assurance`, and the probability does not fall at any sample
  size from that plan to ten past the returned one. With `assurance`,
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  adds the rows `assurance` and `assurance_attained` to the one row DMAR
  1.0.x returned.

- **The simulated step of
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),**
  `assurance_method = "simulation"` with `G` (default 10000) and `seed`,
  returns the smallest sample size per group, not below the plan without
  `assurance`, at which the
  [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md)
  interval is no wider than `width` with at least that probability, for
  normal errors and a normal covariate distributed alike in every group.
  The probability is simulated from the exact sampling distribution of
  the five statistics the width depends on, so the covariate means term
  of the standard error and, with `divisor = "s_anova"`, the sampling of
  `s_ancova / s_anova` enter it, which the published plan of Lai and
  Kelley (2012, pp. 358–359) leaves out. This is the a priori simulation
  Lai and Kelley (2012, pp. 360–361) gave for the ANOVA divisor. A
  contrast and its negative get the same plan. Sample sizes per group,
  with the probability that the interval is no wider than the width:

  | standardized contrast, correlation, weights, width | divisor | assurance | 1.0.x and the default of 1.1.0 | `"simulation"`, `seed = 1` |
  |----|----|----|----|----|
  | .5, .5, `c(1, -1)`, .5 | `s_ancova` | .80 | 129 (.772) | 130 (.872) |
  | the same | `s_ancova` | .90 | 130 (.872) | 131 (.933) |
  | the same | `s_anova` | .80 | 98 (.547) | 104 (.842) |
  | the same | `s_anova` | .90 | 100 (.658) | 106 (.906) |
  | .8, .6, `c(.5, .5, 0, -1)`, .6 | `s_anova` | .90 | 47 (.691) | 51 (.937) |

  The simulated plan can differ by one from the smallest sample size at
  which the probability itself reaches the request (in the third row 103
  already gives .803). With `assurance`,
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md)
  returns the rows `assurance` and `assurance_attained` (`NA` for the
  published plan) and, for the simulated plan, `G`; DMAR 1.0.x returned
  one row. In
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity.md)
  the draws of the simulated step come from the stream before the
  replications, so under
  [`set.seed()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Random.html) the replications
  differ from those of the default even where the two plans agree.

- **The plans of the regression coefficient planners with `assurance`.**
  For the central interval for the coefficient in the units of the data,
  the plan of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  with `noncentral = FALSE` and of
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md),
  the probability is an exact *F* probability for random predictors from
  a multivariate normal population. For the standardized coefficient,
  the noncentral interval of `ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE)` and
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)
  and the central one of `ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE)`,
  `assurance_method = "simulation"` estimates it from `G`
  (default 20000) samples of the exact Wishart sampling distribution,
  with `seed`. Given squared multiple correlations, which leave the
  correlation of *Y* with the predictor open, the simulated step uses
  the least favorable value. The plans, and what they attain, are in
  Changes to Earlier Results. In
  [`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md),
  which now plans for the standardized coefficient at unit standard
  deviations, the default plan is the 1.0.x step only when the supposed
  variances of *Y* and of the targeted predictor are equal (for the
  noncentral interval, when both are 1; DMAR 1.0.x refused the
  noncentral plan otherwise): for `true_var_Y = 4`,
  `true_cov_YX = c(.8, .6)`, and unit predictor variances correlated .3,
  supposed correctly, `width = .3`, `noncentral = FALSE`, and
  `assurance = .9`, it gives 181 where DMAR 1.0.x planned 657 (see
  Changes to Earlier Results). DMAR 1.0.x stopped with an error on every
  plan of the three sensitivity functions with one predictor, so there
  is no 1.0.x plan for such a call to return.

- **`G` and `seed` in
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md),**
  for `assurance_method = "simulation"`; `G` must be a whole number of
  at least 100.

- **`noncentral` in
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md).**
  `TRUE` by default, the noncentral interval for the standardized
  coefficient that
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)
  planned in DMAR 1.0.x; `FALSE` plans the central interval for the
  standardized coefficient of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 1),
  whose standard error is formed from the two sample squared multiple
  correlations: their plan for the expected width without `assurance`
  (Equation 2), with `assurance` their chi square plan (Equation 3) by
  default, and with `assurance_method = "simulation"` the smallest
  sample size that attains it, simulated as the noncentral step is.

- **New rows in the result of the three regression coefficient
  planners:** `assurance` (the request) and `assurance_attained` (the
  probability at the returned sample size, `NA` for a published
  approximation) whenever `assurance` is given, and `G` when the step
  simulated.

### Calculators Given Population Values or Sample Summaries

- **[`cohen_f()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_f.md),
  [`ci_srsnr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_srsnr.md),
  and
  [`covmat_from_cfa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/covmat_from_cfa.md)
  say what they compute from each kind of input.** Each computes the
  same quantity from population values or from sample summaries and
  estimates, its help page says what the result is in each case, and its
  arguments carry quantity names without `true_` (see Renamed Arguments
  and the paragraph on these calculators under Old Names That R Still
  Matches). The values are unchanged: every call that still runs, with
  the arguments renamed, returns what it returned, and
  [`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md),
  which builds its population covariance matrix with
  [`covmat_from_cfa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/covmat_from_cfa.md),
  plans the same sample sizes.

### Exact Noncentral *t* and Studentized Range Distributions

- **The noncentral *t* distribution is computed exactly wherever R’s
  [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html),
  [`qt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html), and
  [`dt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) are not accurate.** R’s
  [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) sums a series up to a
  noncentrality of 37.62 and returns a normal approximation beyond it
  (and beyond 400,000 degrees of freedom), which was off by as much as
  .14 with one degree of freedom, .008 with 38, and .001 with 1,000;
  below one degree of freedom it is not accurate even inside 37.62. DMAR
  now takes the probability, quantile, or density from
  [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html),
  [`qt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html), or
  [`dt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) where they are accurate
  (within 1e-9 of the exact probability up to a noncentrality of 37.62
  with at most 2,000 degrees of freedom, and up to 33 with more) and
  otherwise from an integral of the normal distribution function against
  the distribution of the chi square (below one degree of freedom,
  against the standard deviation raised to the power `df`).
  [`ci_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_t.md)
  and every interval and planner built on it, the critical values of
  [`cv_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_t.md), the
  individual intervals of
  [`limits_of_agreement()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/limits_of_agreement.md),
  the power of the `ss_power_*()` planners whose test is a *t* test (of
  [`ss_power_indirect_effect()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_indirect_effect.md),
  only the power of the test of *a* with X fixed; its other powers
  average the noncentral *t* power over the sums of squares of its
  predictors) and of
  [`design_consequences()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/design_consequences.md),
  and the likelihood of the Bayesian *t* tests use these routines.
  Inside the range of [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) the
  results are those of [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) and
  [`qt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) (to 1e-13 for
  probabilities and powers). No warning about the range is given, since
  no limit is approximate. A limit outside the range takes about ten
  times as long to compute as one inside it:
  `ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = 3, width = .3, assurance = .9)` took 0.5 seconds
  and takes 2.1. Below one degree of freedom, should the integral or a
  search fail, the call stops with a condition of class
  `dmar_computation_failed` that names `df`. The values that change are
  in Changes to Earlier Results.

- **The studentized range is computed exactly wherever R’s
  [`qtukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) and
  [`ptukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) are not accurate.**
  There
  [`cv_tukey_hsd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_tukey_hsd.md),
  [`ci_tukey_kramer()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_tukey_kramer.md),
  [`ci_games_howell()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_games_howell.md),
  `contrast_test(adjust = "tukey")`,
  [`qbryant_paulson()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bryant_paulson.md),
  [`pbryant_paulson()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bryant_paulson.md),
  [`cv_bryant_paulson()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_bryant_paulson.md),
  and
  [`ci_c_ancova_bp()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c_ancova_bp.md)
  integrate the probability integral of the range against the chi square
  distribution of the error variance, take each critical value as its
  root, and take the adjusted *p*-values from the same distribution
  function; elsewhere the values are those of
  [`qtukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) and
  [`ptukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html), as before. Where the
  exact computation is used and the values that change are in Changes to
  Earlier Results.

### Teaching

- A new vignette, “Classical Tests as Path Models in lavaan”
  ([`vignette("anova_as_path_model")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/anova_as_path_model.md)),
  fits the single sample and paired *t* tests, the one way and two way
  analyses of variance (balanced and unbalanced), and the analysis of
  covariance as path models, and shows exactly where they reproduce the
  classical answers: a factor enters as a set of code variables tested
  jointly, and the likelihood divides by *N* where the classical test
  divides by the error degrees of freedom. It uses the `depression_bdi`
  and `pygmalion` data and draws its path diagrams with base graphics.
- The reliability vignette shows alpha falling below omega on the four
  spatial tests of `holzinger_swineford` in place of the first five
  `mtcars` columns, which are not a scale. The tests are scored on
  different scales, so their raw-score loadings on one factor are far
  from equal and the sum of the raw scores carries that inequality; the
  vignette prints the test standard deviations, the loadings, and the
  fit with the loadings free and constrained to be equal, then
  standardizes the tests and shows alpha and omega nearly agreeing on
  the sum of the standardized scores, so the reader sees that
  tau-equivalence is a property of the composite as scored. A second
  example, labeled as hypothetical, simulates six items that each have
  variance 1, three loading .9 on the factor and three loading .1; the
  vignette computes the population alpha (0.626) and omega (0.718) from
  the loadings and then estimates both from a sample of 300, so the
  reader sees a gap larger than the spatial tests’ on items that already
  share one variance, where standardizing leaves the gap in place. The
  vignette no longer draws on a data set from outside the package.
- Three more vignettes now use the package’s own data in place of base
  R’s. “Introduction to DMAR”
  ([`vignette("DMAR")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/DMAR.md))
  fits its one-way ANOVA, for omega squared and for the Tukey pairwise
  comparisons, to the `drinks_trial` outcome on its log scale in place
  of `PlantGrowth`, pooling the trial’s two cohorts and saying that the
  pooling is a simplification, and screens six spatial and verbal tests
  of `holzinger_swineford` in place of `attitude`, the same six its
  measurement model takes up. “Reading DMAR Result Tables”
  ([`vignette("dmar_output")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/dmar_output.md))
  and “Visualizing Effect Sizes and Distributions With DMAR”
  ([`vignette("effect-size-visualization")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/effect-size-visualization.md))
  show their two-factor table, and in the second its forest plot, on
  `pygmalion`, expectancy condition crossed with grade, in place of
  `ToothGrowth` and `warpbreaks`. Both say that the rows come from
  sequential (Type I) sums of squares, which with these unequal cells
  differ from Type II or III sums of squares for the earlier terms, and
  point to the help page that describes how to supply those statistics.
  The visualization vignette also shows the bloomers’ advantage grade by
  grade, concentrated in grades 1 and 2, which the omnibus interaction
  spreads over 5 degrees of freedom.
- The hypothetical example of the reliability vignette (six items, three
  loading .9 and three .1) is now a section of its own, “A Hypothetical
  Example: Items With Widely Unequal Loadings”, so it appears in the
  table of contents; its code and numbers are unchanged. “Introduction
  to DMAR”
  ([`vignette("DMAR")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/DMAR.md))
  shows
  [`anova_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/anova_within.md)
  on `pygmalion` in place of
  [`nlme::Orthodont`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/nlme/man/Orthodont.html), with
  the pretest and the two follow-up IQ scores as three occasions of a
  within-subjects factor, reports the partial eta squared for occasion
  with its confidence interval from
  `ci_eta_squared(estimand = "partial")` on the same analysis fitted by
  [`aov()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/aov.html) with an `Error()` term,
  and says that the analysis pools the two expectancy conditions.
  DESCRIPTION, the package citation (`citation("DMAR")`), the README,
  and the vignettes “Introduction to DMAR”, “Moving From MBESS to DMAR”
  ([`vignette("mbess_to_dmar")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/mbess_to_dmar.md)),
  and “Visualizing Effect Sizes and Distributions With DMAR” now
  describe DMAR in one phrase, as a more general and greatly expanded
  reimagining of MBESS. DMAR 1.0.x called it, in different places, a
  more modern, more general, and greatly expanded reimagining, the
  modern, more general reimplementation and expansion, and a modern and
  greatly expanded reimagining. The help pages of
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md),
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md),
  [`eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared.md),
  and
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md),
  which suggest `car::Anova(object, type = 3)` for Type III statistics,
  now say that Type III main-effect tests compare unweighted marginal
  means only when the factors are coded with sum-to-zero contrasts
  (`contr.sum`, set in the fit or with
  `options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))`), as the help page
  of [`car::Anova()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/car/man/Anova.html) warns, and
  that
  [`factorial_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factorial_anova.md)
  applies that coding itself.
- The README’s Related packages section gives the title of BUCSS as
  published, “Bias and Uncertainty Corrected Sample Size” (it read
  “Bias-Corrected Uncertainty Adjusted Sample Size”), and names its
  authors, Kelley, Anderson, and Maxwell.

### Every Function That Draws Random Numbers Takes a Seed

- **Every function that draws random numbers takes `seed`.**
  `seed = NULL` is now the last argument of the sensitivity functions
  that lacked it
  ([`ss_aipe_c_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_c_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c_ancova_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_r_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_icc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_icc_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_mixed_effects_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_mixed_effects_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_omega_squared_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_omega_squared_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_r_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sm_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sm_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_power_R2_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_power_reg_coef_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef_sensitivity.md),
  and, described in their own entries,
  [`ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity.md)),
  of
  [`procrustes_phi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/procrustes_phi.md),
  of
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_r.md)
  (whose assurance step is a simulation), and of the data generators
  [`simulate_ancova_data()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simulate_ancova_data.md),
  [`simulate_ancova_factorial_data()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simulate_ancova_factorial_data.md),
  [`simulate_longitudinal_polynomial()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simulate_longitudinal_polynomial.md),
  [`simulate_longitudinal_gompertz()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simulate_longitudinal_gompertz.md),
  [`simulate_longitudinal_logistic()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simulate_longitudinal_logistic.md),
  [`simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential.md),
  and
  [`simulate_longitudinal_richards()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simulate_longitudinal_richards.md).
  Where a function ends in `...`, `seed` follows it and is given by
  name. With the default every one of them draws from the caller’s
  stream exactly as before: for each of the 30 functions other than the
  six with entries of their own, a call under
  [`set.seed()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Random.html) returns the result
  it returned before the function had the argument, where no other entry
  of this release changes that result, and leaves the stream at the same
  point. A number makes the call reproducible, gives what
  [`set.seed()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Random.html) with that number
  followed by the call gives, and leaves the caller’s stream as it was.
  A seed that is not a single number is an error. For those six
  sensitivity functions the same holds wherever their results did not
  change for another reason (1,314 values of four of them compared under
  a common [`set.seed()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Random.html), largest
  difference 0, every run of
  [`ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity.md)
  without separated replications, and, for
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity.md),
  whose interval changed, the `mean_smd`, `median_smd`, and `sd_smd`
  rows and the stream after the call in 4 of 4 cases). In
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md)
  the seed is set before the plan, so it also fixes the simulated
  assurance step of the planner. With `assurance` and
  `assurance_method = "simulation"`,
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity.md)
  with `noncentral = TRUE` take that step from the caller’s stream when
  `seed` is `NULL`, so the stream after the call is not where 1.0.x left
  it; the default, `"analytic"`, draws nothing for the plan.
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  takes `seed` for its permutation test, and
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  with `noncentral = TRUE` for their simulated assurance steps.

### Tests and Maintainer Tools

- `tools/release_checks.R` fails when an export that can draw random
  numbers has no `seed = NULL` argument. `tools/precompute_vignettes.R`
  optimizes the PNG figures without loss after a knit, with `oxipng` or
  `optipng` when one is installed and otherwise, when `python3` can
  import Pillow, with `tools/optimize_png.py`. That script rewrites a
  figure only when the new file decodes, with Pillow and with the
  script’s own decoder, to the values and channels of the original, and
  it copies the iCCP, eXIf, and pHYs chunks byte for byte; it leaves
  16-bit images, APNGs, and files with other chunks (gAMA, cHRM, sRGB,
  sBIT, and others) as they are, and prints a line for each figure. The
  step says so when none of the three is available. The 42 vignette
  figures and `man/figures/logo.png` were passed through it: the figures
  went from 2,112,862 bytes as knitr wrote them to 1,380,358, and the
  logo from 90,909 bytes to 75,027. `tools/doi_audit.py` compares every
  DOI in the help with the metadata registered for it;
  `tools/release_gate.R` prints the number of references that disagree
  and does not fail on it.

- `tests/testthat.R` runs every test file only when `NOT_CRAN` reads as
  true the way testthat’s `skip_on_cran()` reads it
  (`isTRUE(as.logical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN")))`), and the curated CRAN
  subset otherwise. In DMAR 1.0.0 any nonempty value selected every
  file, so `NOT_CRAN = "false"` (or `"F"`, `"1"`, `"yes"`) ran the whole
  suite while `skip_on_cran()` still skipped its Monte Carlo blocks.

- `tools/release_gate.R` runs `R CMD check` on the CRAN path whatever
  the shell that starts it has set: `NOT_CRAN` unset,
  `TESTTHAT_CPUS = 2`, and one thread for OpenMP, OpenBLAS, MKL, and
  vecLib, for the check’s process only. In 1.0.0 the check inherited the
  caller’s values: from a shell with `NOT_CRAN = true` and
  `TESTTHAT_CPUS = 8`, the check’s tests ran the full suite on eight
  workers instead of the curated subset on two, and the gate timed that
  run.

- The release gate fails the full local test suite when a test was
  skipped, when a test file ran no test, when no expectation passed, or
  when the result cannot be read. A skip at the top of a file (eleven
  test files open with `skip_if_not_installed()` for lavaan or boot)
  leaves no result for that file, so the gate counts files as well as
  tests and its line says how many of the test files ran. It fails the
  oracle harness when a snippet was skipped, when none ran, or when the
  harness printed no summary line. In 1.0.0 only failures, errors, and
  warnings failed the suite, so an empty suite, a skipped test, and a
  file skipped from its top level all passed. Only a nonzero exit status
  failed the harness, and the harness exits 0 when an oracle package is
  missing (“oracle checks: 2 ok, 1 skipped, 0 failed” passed).

- When every gate passes, the release gate checks the copy it hands off
  against the `sha256` on its record and writes
  `DMAR_<version>.tar.gz.sha256` beside it, in the form
  `shasum -a 256 -c` reads (the hash, two spaces, the file name). A
  sidecar an earlier run left there is removed first (emptied where the
  folder allows no removal), so a failed delivery leaves no sidecar that
  vouches for an older tarball. A copy that fails or does not match, or
  a sidecar that cannot be written, ends the run with status 1, prints
  “DELIVERY FAILED”, and rewrites the record’s Result line as “ALL GATES
  PASSED, DELIVERY FAILED; the hand-off is not certified”. In 1.0.0 the
  result of the copy was not read: with an unwritable or missing
  destination the gate printed “ALL GATES PASSED” and exited 0 with no
  tarball delivered, and no sidecar was written.

- The release gate’s NOTE gate is named for what it allows: “no NOTE
  beyond incoming feasibility (new submission, spelling in DESCRIPTION,
  a URL server error that a re-probe clears) and HTML validation skipped
  by an old local HTML Tidy”. It reads each item of the feasibility NOTE
  against those three and fails on any other, naming it (an invalid DOI,
  a Title not in title case, a URL check that could not run, a CRAN URL
  not in canonical form). It allows the HTML manual NOTE only when its
  whole text is R’s message that the local HTML Tidy is too old. It
  lists every NOTE with its text, so a PASS shows what it tolerated; it
  judges a NOTE whose result R printed on a line of its own (after a
  network warning, say) with the step it belongs to; and a NOTE the
  Status line counts but the log does not show fails it. In 1.0.0 the
  gate was “no NOTE beyond new-submission and spelling” and passed the
  old-Tidy NOTE with no detail. It failed a feasibility NOTE only on
  five phrases (invalid file URIs, Non-FOSS, Insufficient package
  version, Size of tarball, Days since last update) or on a URL that
  stayed bad, so an invalid DOI, a Title not in title case, and a URL
  check that could not run all passed. It also passed an HTML NOTE that
  said math rendering was skipped as well, and, unlisted, a NOTE whose
  result was on a line of its own.

- Both `R CMD check` gates of the release gate (no ERROR or WARNING, and
  the NOTE gate) fail when the check printed no Status line. Given a
  tarball that does not exist, `R CMD check` warns (“is neither a file
  nor directory, skipping”), prints no Status line, and exits 0. In
  1.0.0 a check log with no feasibility step, that one among them,
  stopped the gate with the R error “‘from’ must be a finite number”
  before any record was written.

- The timing limits of the release gate are raised. The whole check may
  now take 720/403 (about 1.79) times the accepted release’s local time,
  the ratio that projects 720 s on the r-devel Linux flavor of the CRAN
  farm, and the CRAN-path tests may take 60 s; the limits were 600/403
  (about 1.49) and 30 s. The 1.1.0 candidate checked in 316 s locally
  (ratio 1.71), with the CRAN-path tests at 46 s; in 284 s (ratio 1.54,
  a projected 619 s) after the first trimming of the CRAN-path tests and
  examples; and in 250 s (ratio 1.35, a projected 545 s) after the cuts
  below, which take the CRAN-path tests to 16 files, prebuild the
  vignettes, and shorten twenty example pages, three of them for the
  second time. The anchors of the closed-form planners, added after
  those measurements, bring the subset to 40 files and add under a
  second to the CRAN-path tests. The gate still prints the 600 s line of
  the incoming pretest, which returned the package for overall check
  time on 5 September 2026, and says when the projection is over it.

- On CRAN the curated test subset runs in one process and holds 40 of
  the 362 test files. The promised detectors (`test-rd_hygiene.R` and
  `test-ss_sensitivity_filename.R`) run whole. Fourteen files each carry
  a published-value or oracle anchor for one family, which pins the
  package’s numerics across platforms: the pinned MBESS values, metafor,
  multcomp, car, lavaan, Equation 5.14 of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley,
  the example of Kelley (2007), for which the exact noncentral t gives
  the plans of 101 and 142 where the article reports 99 and 141 from R’s
  approximation, the exact noncentral t against its oracle, SIEVER’s
  recorded numbers, the published studentized maximum modulus, Yuan et
  al. (2016), Shrout and Fleiss (1979), Kelley and Rausch (2011), and
  Raudenbush and Liu (2001). Twenty-four more files each keep one block
  of a closed-form sample size planner (one that runs no Monte Carlo and
  fits no model) on CRAN: the G\*Power 3.1 manual for
  [`ss_power_R2_change()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_change.md),
  Kelley and Maxwell (2003) for
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md),
  the pinned plans of the published approximation of Lai and
  Kelley (2012) in
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),
  the exact probability of an
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  plan computed apart from the package, the exact noncentral t past the
  range of [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) for
  [`ss_power_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_c.md),
  [`ss_power_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_smd.md),
  [`ss_power_indirect_effect()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_indirect_effect.md),
  and
  [`ss_power_composite_ancova_2group()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_composite_ancova_2group.md),
  and, for the others, a closed form, a scan, or an integral written in
  the test file. Closed-form planners that no file of the subset tests
  are tested in the full local suite only, among them
  [`ss_aipe_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c.md)
  against the 1.0.0 search over a grid (4.5 s) and
  [`ss_aipe_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2.md)
  against MBESS (0.2 s), whose blocks take more than 150 ms,
  [`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  against lavaan,
  [`ss_power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_equivalence_c.md)
  against the noncentral t, and
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md),
  which calls
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md).
  In each anchor file but `test-numerical-correctness.R`, whose pinned
  values all run on CRAN except the
  [`ss_aipe_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2.md)
  search, the anchor comes at or near the top, and a top-level
  `skip_on_cran()` after it skips the rest of the file there with one
  skip; a `skip_on_cran()` inside a block costs about 8 ms under the
  check’s reporter, more than most blocks take to run. The per-family
  smoke files left the subset, and with them the published-value anchors
  of other functions (those of
  [`combine_p()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/combine_p.md),
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md),
  and
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md)
  among them). They, and every block the CRAN check skips, run in the
  full local suite and the release gate, which are unchanged. In the
  local check the CRAN-path tests take 5 to 6 s with 527 expectations,
  where they took 23 s with 4,678, and 47 s (93 s of CPU on two testthat
  workers) with 13,578 before the first trim. The `\donttest{}` detector
  collects the tags of the manual in 0.25 s rather than 0.7 s, with the
  same result on every page. The tests load lme4 only for the full
  suite. The release gate’s floor on CRAN-path expectations is the
  subset’s count, 527 (it was 2000), so a file that loses its anchor
  fails the gate.

- The vignettes go to CRAN as prebuilt HTML. Every vignette has been a
  precomputed twin since 1.0.0, so the check ran no vignette code, but
  its step “checking re-building of vignette outputs” still rendered the
  21 twins through rmarkdown and pandoc: 17 to 18 s of the local check,
  which win-builder has run at about three times the local time.
  `tools/release_gate.R` now runs `tools/asis_vignettes.R` on its
  archive of the commit before `R CMD build`. In that copy only, the
  script renders each twin by the call `R CMD build` makes, writes
  `<name>.html.asis` beside the HTML for the `R.rsp::asis` engine, and
  removes the twin and its figures. The check then copies the HTML
  instead of rendering it: the step takes 7 s locally (5 to 6 s of CPU)
  in place of 17 to 18 s (13 to 14 s of CPU). The HTML is byte for byte
  what the check rendered before, and the 21 vignettes keep their
  titles. Each vignette’s executable source,
  `vignettes/<name>.Rmd.orig`, ships in the tarball beside its
  `.html.asis` entry: it is the source that
  `tools/precompute_vignettes.R` knits to the twin from which the HTML
  is rendered. No vignette engine claims a file whose name ends in
  `.orig`, so `R CMD build` and `R CMD check` neither run nor render it,
  and `vignette(package = "DMAR")` lists the same 21 vignettes. The
  tarball is 1.5 MB smaller (7.2 MB against 8.7 MB), because the
  figures, and the twins’ markdown, no longer ship beside the HTML that
  holds them. A vignette’s source link in
  [`browseVignettes()`](https://rdrr.io/r/utils/browseVignettes.html)
  now shows its `R.rsp::asis` entry; the twins are in the GitHub
  repository. The source tree keeps the twins, and its `.Rbuildignore`
  still leaves out the HTML and the `.Rmd.orig` sources, so
  `devtools::build()` (with R.rsp installed) and pkgdown work as before,
  and no rendered output is committed. R.rsp joins Suggests and
  VignetteBuilder. The gate fails in each of these cases:

  - the tarball’s `vignettes/` holds anything other than one
    `.html.asis` entry and one `.Rmd.orig` source for each twin, or a
    shipped `.Rmd.orig` is not the committed one byte for byte;
  - an HTML in `inst/doc` is not the one rendered from its twin, or does
    not record the MD5 of its `.Rmd.orig` as committed;
  - the vignette index lacks a twin or its title, or lists anything
    else;
  - the check’s vignette step takes more than 10 s of CPU, which only
    rendering would take.

  A tarball built by hand goes through the same script, and the script’s
  header gives the commands.

- Twenty-seven help pages run their examples faster than in the first
  builds of 1.1.0, every demonstration kept and each comment still
  giving the count a reported analysis deserves. They were trimmed in
  two rounds, ten pages in the first and twenty in the second (three in
  both); six of the twenty-seven are new in 1.1.0, and for the other
  twenty-one the earlier counts below are those of 1.0.0. The bootstrap
  and Monte Carlo counts are lower:
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  with B = 10 (were 50 and 40),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md)
  with B = 10 (were 20),
  [`ss_power_composite_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_composite_sem.md),
  [`ss_aipe_composite_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_composite_sem.md),
  [`ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity.md)
  with G = 10 (were 20),
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  with B = 100 under `options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)` (was
  1000, the fewest it accepts otherwise),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md) with B
  = 500 (was 1000),
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  with `n_resamples = 2000` (was the default 10,000),
  [`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  with `G_initial = 20` and `G = 100` (were 50 and 200),
  [`ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md)
  with G = 100 (was 200), and
  [`ss_aipe_c_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c_ancova_sensitivity.md)
  with G = 25 (was 50); the permutation test of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  draws 2,000 reassignments, and the FIML check of
  [`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  runs G = 3. Where a page fitted the same model twice to show two
  settings, one call now shows both: the per-factor descriptor call of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  carries the equal loadings and its parallel call the tau-equivalent
  constraints,
  [`fa_exploratory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_exploratory.md)
  shows the target rotation on the ULS solution, the covariance matrix
  call of
  [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md) also
  names its items, the raw data figure of
  [`plot_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_smd.md)
  carries the group labels and the title, and the 90 percent limits of
  [`limits_of_agreement()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/limits_of_agreement.md)
  use the individual method. Fits that feed another function skip what
  it does not use: `point_estimates_only = TRUE` in the
  [`factor_congruence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_congruence.md)
  example, `effect_sizes = FALSE` in the
  [`df_missing()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/df_missing.md)
  example, and a fit to the covariance matrix of the complete tests in
  the
  [`covmat_from_cfa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/covmat_from_cfa.md)
  example.
  [`plot_trajectories()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_trajectories.md)
  panels six children (was twelve), and
  [`now()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/now.md) waits a
  twentieth of a second (was a fifth). The examples took 36 s of page
  time, where they took 44 s in the first builds. The comments of the
  [`ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity.md)
  examples no longer say that the share of intervals narrower than the
  target is about one half and that the mean width is at or under the
  target, which their output did not show, and the bias figures of
  [`?ci_bifactor_indices`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  say they are from the example run with B = 200.

- The interval and the plans for the coefficient of variation are tested
  against values computed apart from the package.
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) is
  checked against the interval Kelley (2007, p. 758) prints, against
  limits computed to 30 digits, and at each one-sided bound. The
  probability that the interval at an
  [`ss_aipe_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv.md)
  plan is no wider than the width is computed in base R from the
  noncentral *t* distribution, by integration over the normal variate:
  .5307 and .9966 at the two plans of the article’s worked example (101
  and 142), and .7436 at a plan that the assurance step leaves below a
  request of .80 (5, where Table 1 prints 6).
  `tools/kelley2007_table3_row.R` reruns the five plans of the Table 3
  row that shows a misprint, which take about six minutes of processor
  time (about two and a half minutes on five cores) and are not in the
  suite.

### References in the Help

- Every author-year mention in a help page now has its entry on the same
  page. A check of the release tooling parses every built page and finds
  the mentions in its text and examples (“Name (1970)”, “(Name, 1970)”,
  with chains of authors, et al., possessives, and particles such as
  von). The pages its first run flagged are fixed: ten gained the
  entries they name
  ([`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md) and
  [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md), for
  example, carry the seven estimator and interval references their
  inherited arguments cite), and on the others the mention was reworded
  instead (example comments that named the Holzinger and Swineford study
  now name the `holzinger_swineford` data, whose page carries the
  reference).

- The five-group example of the noncentral F interval pages
  ([`ci_pvaf()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_pvaf.md),
  [`ci_snr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_snr.md),
  [`ci_srsnr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_srsnr.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md),
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md),
  [`eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared.md),
  and
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md),
  and in 1.0.x `omega_squared_partial()`, now removed) and of the
  `one_way_anova_power` vignette, which 1.0.0 credited to
  Bargmann (1970) with his name spelled as Venables (1975) spells it,
  with one n, now spells it Bargmann; Venables, Fleishman (1980), and
  Steiger (2004) used the example in turn. Each of the seven pages gains
  the Bargmann (1970) entry, with its editors and pages, and the
  Venables (1975) entry, neither of which any of them carried in 1.0.0.
  The Fleishman (1980) entry gains its DOI, and
  [`eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared.md)
  and
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md)
  gain the entry itself. In the vignette the Bargmann entry gains its
  editors and pages, and Fleishman and Venables entries are added. A
  test pins
  [`ci_nc_F()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_F.md)
  to the .90 limits of Venables (19.381, 71.551) and of Steiger (19.380,
  71.549).

- The release tooling fails when a citation form corrected for this
  release appears again. It keeps a list of the wrong forms, each beside
  the form that replaced it, and first confirms that the pattern for
  each form finds examples of the wrong text and passes examples of the
  right. It then reads the R sources (help sources, comments, and
  messages), the help pages, the vignette sources, the tests,
  DESCRIPTION, the package citation, the spelling word list, and the
  README. The list holds the journal and subtitle of Kelley, Maxwell,
  and Rausch (2003), the title of the Steiger and Fouladi (1997)
  chapter, and the editions of Rencher and Christensen (2012) and of
  Anderson (2003) (all four under Changes to Earlier Results), the
  spelling of Bargmann above, and, on pages new in 1.1.0, the DOI of the
  Kiers (1994) entry and of the Saunders (1961) entry, the year and
  pages of Fieller’s (1941) insulin study, the equation number given for
  the incremental fit index of Bollen (1989), and the description of
  DMAR as a “reimplementation and expansion” of MBESS, replaced in the
  package citation, the README, and the MBESS vignette as described
  under Teaching. The list also holds seven forms corrected on 1.0.0
  pages: the DOI of the Owen (1968) entry, the first page of the
  Phillips (1990) entry, and the pages of the Hofmann (1977) entry (all
  three under Changes to Earlier Results), the citation of Sokal and
  Rohlf (1995) for the expected value of the sample coefficient of
  variation, which is Expression 3 of Sokal and Braumann (1980), and the
  entries for Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), for Lachowicz,
  Preacher, and Kelley (2018), and for Tofighi and Kelley

  2020. without their issue numbers.

- **[`?ss_power_R2`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  credits the random-predictor approximation as Lee’s (1971, Section
  5.1) three-moment noncentral *F* approximation.** The help called it a
  two-moment Patnaik (1949) approximation; the code is Lee’s Equation
  25, which fits three moments, and Lee (1971) does not cite Patnaik.
  The Patnaik (1949) reference is removed from the page. The pages of
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md),
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md), and
  [`ci_correlation()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md)
  said the distribution of the sample R^2 under random predictors “is
  given by Lee (1971)”; Lee (1971, p. 117) credits it to Fisher (1928),
  and the pages now do, with Lee credited for the approximation they
  use.

- **[`?vargha_delaney_A`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  no longer calls the DeLong, DeLong, and Clarke-Pearson (1988) variance
  estimator unbiased.** The estimator is consistent; it is not unbiased
  in general. Its expectation exceeds the variance of the estimate of
  *A* by a nonnegative term of order 1 / (n_1 n_2), which is zero when
  both variables take only two values; with three continuous
  observations per group from one distribution the variance is 7/108 and
  the estimator averages 8/108 (a test enumerates the 20 allocations).
  The page now says that *A* = 0.5 is stochastic equality (Vargha &
  Delaney, 2000, p. 102), which is weaker than equality of the two
  distributions, and that the reported test is of *A* = 0.5; cites
  Equation 14 on p. 107 for the rank formula, where it cited p. 109;
  says that the samples must be independent and points to
  [`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md);
  and says that the limits of
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  and of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  do not map onto each other exactly, since the two use different
  variance estimators. The sentence that credited Newcombe (2006a,
  2006b) with showing better coverage for the logit interval is removed
  with its two references, as the claim was not verified against the
  papers; the page cites Pohar Perme and Manevski (2019,
  <doi:10.1177/0962280218814556>), who conclude that the DeLong variance
  estimator is reliable and that the interval should be formed on the
  logit scale. The Hanley and McNeil (1982) entry, which no sentence
  cited, is removed, and the DeLong et al. reference gains its DOI.
  [`?cliff_delta`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  says that its analytic interval is “valid in large samples” where it
  said “exact in the large-sample limit”.

- The help of [`cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv.md)
  describes the `unbiased = TRUE` value as Kelley (2007, Equation 4)
  does, as a nearly unbiased estimate, and no longer as unbiased or as a
  first-order bias correction, and its title is now “Coefficient of
  Variation (Sample Value or Nearly Unbiased Estimate)”. The page gives
  the expected value of the sample coefficient from Expression 3 of
  Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 51), which Kelley (2007) reproduces, in
  place of the expansion with the single term 1/(4N) that 1.0.0 credited
  to Sokal and Rohlf (1995), and it bounds the statement that the sample
  coefficient is biased downward: that holds when the population
  coefficient is below about one half, and above it the sample
  coefficient is too large on average. The multiplier (1 + 1/(4N)) is
  credited to Haldane (1955), as both papers credit it. The page now
  says what the multiplier leaves (a relative bias of about kappa^2/N -
  9/(32 N^2), the second term derived for the page), gives the bias of
  both values at a coefficient of 0.1 and of 0.3 with 10 cases, and says
  that the corrected value is the more biased of the two once the
  coefficient exceeds about 0.35 to 0.4. The sentence that called the
  interval of
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) “the
  McKay (1932) noncentral *t* based interval” and the comparison with
  Vangel (1996) that 1.0.0 attributed to Kelley (2007), which does not
  cite Vangel, are replaced:
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md)
  inverts the noncentral *t* distribution (Johnson & Welch, 1940; McKay,
  1932; Kelley, 2007), and the chi square approximations of McKay (1932)
  and Vangel (1996) are ones it does not use. Where 1.0.0 pointed to
  “the corresponding asymptotic variances” in
  [`var_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_cv.md),
  the page names the one variance that function returns, the first-order
  variance of the sample coefficient under normality. The sample
  coefficient is written k = s / M, as on
  [`?var_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_cv.md) and
  [`?ss_aipe_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv.md),
  and the entry for Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) no longer points
  to Chapter 3. The page gains the Haldane (1955), Johnson and Welch
  (1940), and Sokal and Braumann (1980) entries and drops the Sokal and
  Rohlf (1995) entry, which nothing on it cites.
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md)
  describes its `cv_unbiased` row (`c_of_v_unbiased` in 1.0.x) as the
  nearly unbiased estimate, and the table of the `mbess_to_dmar`
  vignette describes
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) as
  the noncentral *t* interval. No value changes.

- `DESCRIPTION` no longer says that every estimation, inference, and
  planning function returns one data frame. Most do; the regression
  functions for incomplete data
  ([`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md),
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md))
  and a few others
  ([`correlations_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/correlations_test.md),
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md))
  return a list suited to their task, as
  [`?DMAR`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/DMAR-package.md)
  and the README already said.

- [`?ss_aipe_crd_es`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crd_es.md)
  opens with what the six planners take and return, and its `width`
  argument is described as the width of the interval for the
  standardized difference (the text said unstandardized).

- **[`?var_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_cv.md)
  says where its variance comes from and how accurate it is.** The 1.0.x
  page said the first row was McKay’s (1932) noncentral *t* based
  approximation, that Vangel (1996) showed the second gave better
  coverage, and that the first is what most planning tables use.
  McKay (1932) and Vangel (1996) give chi square approximations to the
  distribution of a function of the sample coefficient of variation,
  which [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md)
  does not use, and the variance the function returns is not taken from
  them. The page now gives the value as the first-order (delta method)
  variance under normality, kappa^2 (1/2 + kappa^2) / (N - 1), with its
  derivation. Expression 5 of Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 52) without
  its third-order term is kappa^2 / (2 (N - 1)) + kappa^4 / N; the
  function has N - 1 under both terms, so its value is larger by kappa^4
  / (N (N - 1)). The page states how close the value is to the variance
  of the sample coefficient under normality, computed with the sample
  mean kept away from zero: for a population coefficient of .30 or less
  and 10 or more cases it is too large, and the largest excess is 3.0
  percent to one decimal place; at .50 with 10 cases it is 5.7 percent
  too small. It also states how far the value can be from the
  large-sample variance of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018,
  Equation 30) when the population is not normal: in the limit it is 39
  percent too large for a gamma population with a coefficient of
  variation of .80 and 56 percent too small for a Laplace population
  with a coefficient of .30. The page gains the Sokal and Braumann

  1980. and Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) entries, and its
        entry for Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) no longer points
        to Chapter 3. Its example prints the variance to six decimal
        places and sets its square root beside the standard deviation of
        simulated coefficients, for normal data and for gamma data. The
        argument and the row have new names and the second row is
        removed (see Renamed Arguments, Renamed Output Rows and Columns,
        and Changes to Earlier Results).

- [`?ss_aipe_crd`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crd.md)
  has a title and a first paragraph that say what the six planners take
  and return (“Sample Sizes for a Cluster Randomized Design: Accuracy in
  Parameter Estimation for the Difference Between Condition Means”), in
  the words
  [`?ss_aipe_crd_es`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crd_es.md)
  uses for the standardized difference. No number changes.

- **[`?ss_seq_c`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_c.md)
  credits each part of the procedure to its source.** The stopping rule
  is that of Chow and Robbins (1965) applied to a contrast, and the
  allocation of the groups is the cost-optimal allocation of
  Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025, Theorem
  1). The page credited the whole fixed-width procedure to the 2025
  article, which plans for noninferiority and equivalence tests under a
  budget and has no fixed-width interval;
  [`?ss_seq_c_sensitivity`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_c_sensitivity.md)
  is corrected the same way.

- [`?mr_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_cv.md) gains
  the entries for Bao (2009) and for Bao’s erratum to it, which its part
  on Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) cites, and it cites
  Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) and Kelley (2007), which the page
  listed without citing.
  [`?mr_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_cv.md) and
  [`?mr_smd`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_smd.md) give
  the issue of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), 23(2);
  [`?ss_aipe_indirect_effect`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_indirect_effect.md)
  and
  [`?var_indirect_effect`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_indirect_effect.md)
  that of Lachowicz, Preacher, and Kelley (2018), also 23(2); and those
  two pages and
  [`?ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity.md)
  that of Tofighi and Kelley (2020), 25(4). Both minimum risk pages
  state the range of `m0` and of `gamma`, and
  [`?mr_smd`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_smd.md)
  describes `A` as the structural cost divided by the square of
  `epsilon` (it said that the maximum allowable difference was the
  square of epsilon).

- **[`?ci_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md)
  states that its interval assumes a normal population.** The interval
  is exact for a random sample from a normal population with a positive
  mean and is not robust to departures from normality, which a larger
  sample does not repair: in simulations of the 95 percent interval
  (coefficients of variation of .3 and .5, sample sizes of 30 and 200)
  coverage was .81 to .85 for Laplace data, .90 to .94 for lognormal
  data, and .96 to .97 for gamma data. The page says when the upper
  limit is infinite and why that interval has the stated coverage, and
  describes the tail columns as the requested tail areas. Its references
  gain Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), whose large-sample
  interval the page mentions, and lose the *Journal of Statistical
  Software* article, which the page does not cite.
  [`?ss_aipe_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv.md)
  writes Equation 3 of Kelley (2007) as the approximation it is (Sokal &
  Braumann, 1980, p. 51, Expression 3; for a coefficient of .25 it is
  above the expected value of the sample coefficient by 3.1 percent at N
  = 5 and 0.1 percent at N = 20), and it and
  [`?ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md)
  say what the plans deliver for gamma and lognormal populations. On the
  three pages the pointers to Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) name
  what they point to: Chapter 3 on confidence intervals for effect
  sizes, and on
  [`?ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md)
  Sections 3.9.1.5 and 4.9 in place of Section 3.5. No number changes.

### Bug Fixes

- **Sizes given as R integers no longer overflow.** R multiplies two
  integers as an integer, and the product becomes NA, with the warning
  “NAs produced by integer overflow”, once it passes 2^31 - 1 =
  2,147,483,647: with 46,341 or more in each of two groups, and also
  with unequal groups such as 40,000 and 60,000.
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md),
  [`ci_smd_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd_c.md),
  [`ci_mahalanobis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_mahalanobis.md),
  [`convert_d_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/convert_d_r.md),
  [`convert_r_d()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/convert_d_r.md),
  [`convert_delta_lambda()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/convert_t_smd.md),
  [`convert_lambda_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/convert_t_smd.md),
  [`cles()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cles.md),
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md),
  [`proportion_of_superiority()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/proportion_of_superiority.md),
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md),
  [`ss_power_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_smd.md),
  [`var_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_smd.md),
  and
  [`bayes_independent_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bayes_independent_t.md)
  multiplied the two group sizes this way when they were given as
  integers (such as `50000L`, or a count from
  [`length()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/length.html)), and
  [`plot_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_smd.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity.md)
  pass their sizes to
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md). In
  DMAR 1.0.0, at 50,000 in each group and at 40,000 and 60,000,
  `ci_smd(smd = .2, n_1 = 50000L, n_2 = 50000L)`,
  `ci_smd_c(smd_c = .2, n_C = 50000L, n_E = 50000L)`,
  [`cles()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cles.md),
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md),
  [`proportion_of_superiority()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/proportion_of_superiority.md),
  and `plot_smd(smd = .2, n_1 = 50000L, n_2 = 50000L)` then stopped with
  “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”,
  [`ci_mahalanobis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_mahalanobis.md)
  stopped with a message that its limits “could not be computed for the
  observed F-statistic NA”,
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md)
  with “Supply a positive sampling variance for each effect size.”, and
  [`bayes_independent_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bayes_independent_t.md)
  with “‘from’ must be a finite number”, while
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md) and
  [`ci_smd_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd_c.md)
  given `ncp`, the four conversion functions, and
  [`var_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_smd.md)
  returned NA.
  `ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_smd = .1, specified_n_per_group = 50000L, G = 3)`
  (`true_delta` and `n_per_group` in 1.0.x), which uses its one size for
  both groups, stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, as
  it did with `46341L` (with `46340L` it gave its table).
  [`ss_power_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_smd.md)
  overflowed even with sizes given as doubles, since it turned a given
  size into an integer, and reported the power as NA.
