  indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), named under the table. Ordered
  items, the least squares estimators, `se = "robust.sem"`, and the
  Satorra-Bentler kind of test, which FIML cannot accompany, are fitted
  as before when no item value is missing; when values are missing they
  ask for `missing = "listwise"` (or `"pairwise"` for ordered items)
  rather than deleting cases unasked, and
  [`fa_exploratory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_exploratory.md)
  now treats ordered items the same way. The `srmr` row is the SRMR of
  the covariance residuals alone whenever the model has a mean structure
  (lavaan’s `srmr_bentler_nomean`, as
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  reports it), so the intercepts, whose residuals are zero, do not lower
  it. With auxiliary variables (lavaan’s `aux` under FIML) the `srmr`
  row is over the items alone: lavaan averages the auxiliary variables
  in, whose residuals are also about zero, and for the three-factor
  model of the nine Holzinger and Swineford tests with 40 values missing
  per item the SRMR of .068 fell to .062 with one auxiliary variable and
  .058 with two. A fit whose observed information matrix is singular
  reports no standard errors, with a warning, as a listwise fit already
  did; lavaan inverts such a matrix without complaint and gives finite
  standard errors for parameters that are not identified.
  [`fa_exploratory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_exploratory.md)
  and
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  record the FIML method as `"fiml"` rather than lavaan’s `"ml"`.

- **[`cv_smm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_smm.md)
  is right at very small degrees of freedom.** In DMAR 1.0.0, with `df`
  below 1 at conventional levels (below about .8 at an `alpha_level` of
  .05, and below about .6 at .10) or with `df` of about 2 or less and an
  `alpha_level` of .02 or less, its integral over the chi squared
  variate missed a sliver of the integrand by the origin: the call
  stopped with “the integral is probably divergent”, or, at `df = 2` and
  `alpha_level = .001`, returned a critical value whose tail area was
  1.5 to 5 times `alpha_level` (32.80 rather than 40.43 for two
  comparisons). Each root is now checked against the upper tail computed
  by conditioning on the maximum modulus instead, and found on that tail
  when the two disagree. Every value that was right is returned
  unchanged, bit for bit.

- **[`design_consequences()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/design_consequences.md),
  [`sd_unbiased()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sd_unbiased.md),
  and
  [`var_ete()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_ete.md)
  are right at a very large `df` or *N*.** Each uses E(S)/sigma =
  sqrt(2/df) Gamma((df + 1)/2) / Gamma(df/2), the mean of a standard
  deviation on `df` degrees of freedom relative to sigma, or the
  variance 1 - (E(S)/sigma)^2 that goes with it. E(S)/sigma is below 1
  at every `df` and about 1 - 1/(4 df) for a large one, but each
  function computed it as a difference of two
  [`lgamma()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Special.html) values that nearly
  cancel there.
  [`design_consequences()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/design_consequences.md)
  multiplies the width it would have with the standard error known by
  E(S)/sigma for `mean_ci_width` and `expected_half_width`, and by the
  square root of the variance for `sd_ci_width`. The factor was off by
  4e-11 at `df = 1e5`, first reached 1 at `df = 10810066`, and was 1 or
  more at about half of all `df` above 1e8, which put `mean_ci_width`
  above the fixed width and `sd_ci_width` at 0. `sd_ci_width` lost more,
  because one minus the square of a number near 1 keeps only the digits
  the two do not share: it was off by 1e-12 at the 118 `df` of 60 per
  group, by 8e-6 at `df = 1e5`, by 0.1 percent at `df = 1e6`, and was 57
  times its value at `df = 1e9`. No other row involves them, and at the
  `df` of an ordinary design the mean rows move only in the last digits
  (by 4e-15 at 118 `df`).
  [`sd_unbiased()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sd_unbiased.md)
  divides by the same factor and returned `s` unchanged at *N* = 1e8 and
  .998 `s` at *N* = 1e12, where the correction is upward;
  [`var_ete()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_ete.md)
  with `covariate_value = "sd"` uses the variance and moves by 2e-13 or
  less at a few hundred cases and by 3e-6 at *N* = 1e6. Both are now
  formed from the logarithm of E(S)/sigma, the mean as its exponential
  and the variance through [`expm1()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Log.html)
  of twice it. From `df = 100` on the logarithm is its asymptotic
  expansion, and below that the expansion carried down two `df` at a
  time by an exact recurrence whose terms all have one sign, so nothing
  cancels at any `df`. Against a 320-bit evaluation, both are right to a
  few units in the last place: over some 490,000 `df` from 0.05 to 1e15,
  the largest relative error found is 5.5e-16, about 2.5 times the
  machine epsilon. E(S)/sigma is never above 1, and it never decreases
  as `df` grows on grids as fine as 1e-13 apart, including across every
  even `df` from 2 to 100, where the computation changes form; from one
  double to the next it can step back by a unit in the last place, as
  any value computed with a rounding error can.
  [`ss_aipe_mean()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_mean.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_two_phase()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_two_phase.md),
  both new in this release, use the same factor.

- **[`expected_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_r.md)
  and
  [`expected_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_partial_r.md)
  are right at a very large *N*.** E\[r\] = rho 2F1(1/2, 1/2; (N + 1)/2;
  rho^2) Gamma(N/2)^2 / {Gamma((N - 1)/2) Gamma((N + 1)/2)}, and the
  gamma ratio is the square of E(S)/sigma on N - 1 `df` (the entry
  above).
  [`expected_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_r.md)
  formed it from three [`lgamma()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Special.html)
  values that nearly cancel at a large *N*, and it was off by 1e-11 at
  *N* = 1e5 and 1e-7 at *N* = 1e8. The bias rho - E\[r\] is only about
  rho (1 - rho^2) / (2N), so its error was larger in proportion: at rho
  = .5 the `bias` column was 0.2 percent too small at *N* = 1e6, 26
  percent too large at *N* = 1e7, 31 times its value at *N* = 1e8, and
  of the wrong sign at *N* = 3e8, where E\[r\] came out above rho. The
  ratio now comes from the logarithm in the entry above, and the `bias`
  and `relative_bias` columns are formed directly rather than from rho -
  E\[r\]: `relative_bias` is one minus the product of the series and the
  ratio, formed from their logarithms, and `bias` is rho times it. The
  difference rho - E\[r\] keeps only the digits the two do not share,
  and with the ratio right to a few units in the last place it is still
  off by 3e-7, relative, at *N* = 1e8. Against a 320-bit evaluation the
  `bias` is now right to 2e-14, relative, for \|rho\| of .9 or less at
  *N* from 4 to 1e12. So that the series carries the digits the bias
  needs, the option `DMAR.expected_r.tol` now stops the sum once a term
  is below that fraction of the sum of the terms after the leading 1,
  rather than of the whole series, and the sum can run to more terms
  than in 1.0.x; the non-convergence warning still compares the last
  term with the whole sum, so it is given where it was. At *N* of 1000
  or less, E\[r\] moves by less than 2e-12, relative. A rho so small
  that rho^2 is 0 in double precision, below about 1.6e-162, gave E\[r\]
  = 0 and a `relative_bias` of 1; it now gives E\[r\] = rho c4(N)^2.
  [`expected_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_partial_r.md)
  calls
  [`expected_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_r.md)
  at *N* - (*p* - 1) and moves with it.

- **[`manova_split_plot()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/manova_split_plot.md)
  tests the within-subjects main effect averaged over the groups, as
  Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Section 14.6) do.** The default
  Type III `B` rows test whether the grand means of the within-subjects
  contrasts are zero. DMAR 1.0.x fitted the between-subjects factor
  under R’s default treatment coding, in which the intercept that Type
  III tests is the first group’s mean of each contrast, so its `B` rows
  were the simple effect of the within-subjects factor in the first
  group, tested against the error matrix pooled over the groups (the
  book’s Equation 14.66), rather than the main effect. The factor is now
  coded with sum-to-zero contrasts whatever `options("contrasts")` says,
  so Type III tests the unweighted grand means, which the book prefers
  and notes that SAS and SPSS test by default (Section 14.6.9 and note 6
  of Chapter 14), and `ss_type = 2` tests the weighted grand means, in
  which each group counts in proportion to its size. On the reaction
  times of the book’s Table 14.9 (10 young and 10 old participants at
  angles of 0, 4, and 8 degrees), DMAR 1.0.0 gave *F*(2, 17) = 36.22 for
  angle, the value the book reports for the simple effect of angle among
  the young participants (Equation 14.66, p. 810); the book’s angle main
  effect, *F*(2, 17) = 110.65 (Equation 14.54, p. 798), is what the
  function now returns. With only the 0 and 8 degree conditions (Table
  14.7), DMAR 1.0.0 gave *F*(1, 18) = 75.77 where the book gives 233.41
  (p. 792). The `A` and `interaction` rows are as before, as is every
  row under `ss_type = 2`, since none of them depends on the coding. The
  `B` rows were already the main effect whenever the contrasts in force
  for the between-subjects factor summed to zero: for an ordered factor
  under the default ordered coding, `contr.poly`, and for an unordered
  factor when `options("contrasts")` named `contr.sum` or
  `contr.helmert`. Under `contr.SAS` they were the simple effect in the
  last group. No argument gives the 1.0.x `B` rows. They are the `Time`
  rows of the call DMAR 1.0.x made under R’s default contrasts,
  `car::Anova(lm(Y ~ g), idata = data.frame(Time = factor(within, levels = within)), idesign = ~ Time, type = 3)`,
  with `Y` the matrix of the `within` columns and `g` the
  between-subjects factor. The help no longer says that Types II and III
  coincide for a single between-subjects factor: they give the same
  tests of `A` and of the interaction, and the same test of `B` only
  when the groups are of equal size. The model is now fitted to objects
  of its own, so a between-subjects column named `Time`, for which DMAR
  1.0.x reported the test of `A` in the `B` rows, is handled like any
  other, as are a between-subjects column named `Y` or with a name that
  is not syntactic and a within-subjects column named `Y`, with which it
  stopped with an error. The function no longer passes on car’s warning
  `HF eps > 1 treated as 1`, which comes from the univariate tests it
  does not report.

- **[`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md),
  and
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  take full information maximum likelihood as the default of `missing`
  as well**, so that the omega of
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  and that of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  agree on incomplete data, and
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md),
  which passes `missing` on only when it is supplied, follows them.
  `missing = "listwise"` gives the listwise deletion that DMAR 1.0.x
  applied by default. The default resolves by one rule in the four
  functions: the analysis is FIML whenever an item value is missing and
  the complete data analysis otherwise. That differs from
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
  which fits complete data by FIML too. Data in which no value is
  missing, and a covariance matrix, are analyzed as they stand, as DMAR
  1.0.x analyzed them, because the complete-data intervals of alpha and
  omega (the closed forms, `"adf"`, and `"likelihood"`, none of which
  FIML gives) need that analysis, and so no complete data result
  changes: FIML would give the same estimates, but its standard errors
  come from the observed information and the Huber-White sandwich,
  alpha’s bootstrap would refit a saturated model on every replication,
  about 70 times as long, and an MLR ladder’s robust indices would be
  the corrected ones of Zhang and Savalei (2023). A row with every item
  missing (every model variable, in
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md))
  does not count as a missing value, since listwise deletion and FIML
  both drop it, so data that are complete but for a blank row keep the
  complete data analysis. Incomplete items are analyzed by FIML, so the
  estimates, their standard errors, and N change; under FIML the
  analytic alpha’s default interval is `"ml"`, since Bonett’s needs
  complete cases. An option FIML cannot accompany (the complete-data
  closed form intervals, `"adf"`, and `"likelihood"` in alpha and omega;
  ordered items, estimators other than ML and MLR, `se = "robust.sem"`,
  and the Satorra-Bentler kind of test in
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md))
  is used as before when no item value is missing, and with missing
  values the call stops and names the options rather than deleting cases
  unasked; the checks of omega’s denominator and alpha’s estimator come
  first, so that neither option named meets another refusal. Auxiliary
  variables imply FIML, as before.
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  takes `data` for the first time in this release, and
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  keeps listwise deletion as its default. In
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md),
  under FIML by default or by name, a group that never observes a
  variable of the model, or never observes two of them together, is
  refused by name before any fit (an error of class
  `dmar_group_coverage`, a `dmar_refusal` carrying the variables and
  pairs), with what to do instead; lavaan stopped with “subscript out of
  bounds”, which the new default would have made the ordinary result for
  `holzinger_swineford`’s `t25_paper_form_board_r` and `t26_flags` by
  school. An explicit `missing = "fiml"` with `se = "robust.sem"` or a
  test of the Satorra-Bentler kind now stops, as in
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
  where through 1.0.1 lavaan fit the complete cases with a warning, and
  so does a ladder lavaan fitted by another treatment than the FIML
  asked for (it fits GLS, WLS, and ULS in two stages).

- **[`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  forms the default interval of the model implied omega on the logit
  scale.** The default `ci_method` is `"mlr_logistic"` where it was
  `"mlr"`: the same robust standard error, with the limits formed on the
  logit scale and transformed back to the scale of the coefficient
  (Browne, 1982; Kelley, 2007), so that
  `reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied")` and the omega row
  of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  give limits of the same form. It applies under listwise deletion,
  FIML, and two-stage estimation alike. The change rests on a Monte
  Carlo study (in the repository’s `methodology/reliability_limits`) in
  which the logit limits met every criterion fixed before the run, with
  normal data under listwise deletion and FIML and with nonnormal data
  fitted by MLR. The study formed both kinds of limits from the same
  standard error, the normal theory maximum likelihood one for normal
  data and the Huber-White one of MLR for nonnormal data, so it compared
  the scale on which the limits are formed: with normal data the logit
  limits covered from .939 to .956 in every cell, against .910 to .952
  for the limits on the scale of omega, whose misses fell mostly on one
  side. No cell used the `robust.sem` standard error of `"mlr_logistic"`
  with complete data, which estimates the same asymptotic variance as
  the Huber-White one. `ci_method = "mlr"` gives the limits of DMAR
  1.0.x; `ci_method = NULL` is the default, as it was through 1.0.x.
  Given a covariance matrix with `denominator = "model_implied"` and no
  `ci_method`,
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  now uses `"ml_logistic"`, the maximum likelihood standard error with
  the limits formed the same way, as
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  does, where through 1.0.x it stopped because its default needed raw
  data;
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md),
  which chose `"ml"` on that path, follows it. Under
  `wald_df = "missing_information"`, whose calibration covers the
  intervals on the scale of omega only, the default remains `"mlr"`
  (`"ml"` with a covariance matrix). The estimate and the `se` row do
  not change, nor do robust omega (whose default is no interval) and
  coefficient alpha’s defaults.

- **FIML and two-stage reliability fits count distinct cases that
  observe an item.** A row observed only on auxiliary variables informs
  their distribution, but not the items given them; a repeated row adds
  no dimension. The count must exceed the items plus auxiliary
  variables, in the data, every bootstrap replication, and each
  jackknife deletion. Fitted coefficients under listwise deletion count
  distinct complete rows. Listwise alpha is offered as an alternative
  only when it would accept those rows, with Feldt’s interval named when
  exactly two are complete. A standard error lavaan could not compute is
  `NA`, rather than zero.

- **FIML and two-stage reliability coefficients refuse a constant
  composite.** When complete rows outnumber the items, their sum is
  checked directly. A constant sum makes the saturated likelihood
  unbounded as its variance tends to zero. Otherwise the EM covariance
  estimate is checked with a tolerance reflecting EM convergence.
  Bootstrap replications follow the same rule. H’s weighted composite is
  exempt. For all Holzinger and Swineford pupils on visual perception,
  cubes, lozenges, and paragraph comprehension, center each pupil’s
  scores on that pupil’s mean, then delete the first ten visual
  perception scores. Version 1.0.1’s model implied FIML alpha was
  1.49e-13 with limits \[0, 9.23e-8\]. The data are now refused because
  the composite is constant in the 291 complete rows.

- **An indefinite supplied `S` is named as not a covariance matrix when
  its composite variance is not positive.** The message gives its
  negative eigenvalue, and the composite variance when clearly negative,
  rather than calling the matrix singular with a zero composite
  variance. For `S <- matrix(-.9, 3, 3); diag(S) <- 1`, version 1.0.1
  returned alpha 3.38 with limits \[4.31, 1\] at N = 100 with
  `ci_method = "feldt"`. This matrix is now refused; positive
  semidefinite ipsative matrices keep the constant-composite message.

- **The equal-loading factor analytic plan uses its fitted
  coefficient.** Let `S <- matrix(.3, 4, 4); diag(S) <- c(1, 1, 1, 4)`
  and `S[4, 1:3] <- S[1:3, 4] <- -.5`. At width .20,
  `ss_aipe_reliability(S = S, model = "True Score", type = "Factor Analytic", width = .20)`
  plans 244 cases, against 786 in 1.0.1, whose plan used alpha of the
  correlation matrix. The Parallel model gave 1669 and is now refused as
  far from parallel. Conversely,
  `S <- diag(c(10, 10, 1, 1)); S[1, 2] <- S[2, 1] <- 4; S[3, 4] <- S[4, 3] <- -.3`
  has positive alpha but a zero fitted loading. At width .30, 1.0.1
  planned 202 for Parallel and 386 for True Score; both now refuse it.
  Highly reliable congeneric populations are checked at a feasible
  estimation size: four loadings of .99 with error variances `1 - .99^2`
  at width .20 still plan 2 cases, as in 1.0.1. The closed form can
  remain below the minimum estimation size. Every assurance plan carries
  `no_interval`, including zero, and `glance()` adds `fmi`,
  `necessary_N_complete`, and `no_interval` when present. The closed
  form’s `tidy()` width is `NA`, as in 1.0.1.

- **[`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  refuses correlated factors no case observes together.** Their
  covariance does not enter the observed-data likelihood; a third factor
  observed with both does not identify it. Split the four spatial and
  three verbal Holzinger and Swineford tests between forms using
  `set.seed(3); form <- sample(1:2, 301, replace = TRUE)`, with the
  spatial block missing on form 1 and verbal on form 2. Version 1.0.1
  reported the correlation at its starting value, zero, and
  `omega_spatial` .650 with a standard error of zero and limits \[.650,
  .650\]. The fit is now refused by name; fit each factor alone or link
  the forms with common items. Orthogonal factors are fitted, since
  their correlation is fixed, and their coefficients and standard errors
  equal the separate fits. More generally a fit whose information cannot
  be inverted reports `NA` for standard errors, tests, and intervals in
  every table output, with a warning.

- **Zero degrees of freedom with a nonzero statistic gives no TLI or
  RMSEA.** A binding inequality can leave a positive statistic at zero
  degrees of freedom, which lavaan does not count as an equality. For a
  factor of three unit-variance variables correlated .8, .8, and .5, at
  N = 200 with `bounds = "pos.var"`, the statistic is 32.8 and CFI .925.
  Version 1.0.1 reported TLI and NNFI 1 and RMSEA 0 \[0, 0\]; those rows
  are now `NA`, since they divide by the degrees of freedom. CFI keeps
  .925. The RMSEA and following `delta_rmsea` of such an invariance rung
  are also `NA`. A rung’s CFI decides the version of its indices
  independently of its test. An exactly fitting saturated model keeps
  its earlier convention.

- **CFA summaries carry the method and reference of their results.**
  `glance()` adds `estimator`, `missing`, `test`, `fit_indices`, and
  `rmsea_ci_level` after its earlier columns. `tidy()` of CFA,
  reliability,
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md), and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  results carries `wald_df` per row, and reliability’s `glance()`
  carries it too. The default is `Inf`. Rows on a t reference can
  therefore be stacked with rows on the normal reference without losing
  which interval each has.
  `measurement_invariance(group_partial = character(0))`, refused in
  1.0.1, now frees nothing, as `NULL` does. Empty `group.partial` passed
  through `...` also frees nothing.

- **[`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  refuses a single-factor solution that leaves no reliability
  coefficient.** On three items whose correlations had a negative
  product, it returned an omega of 471, from a loading of 43.6 and an
  error variance of -1899, with only a warning about a Heywood case. A
  single factor implies that the product of the three correlations is
  the square of the product of the loadings, so no real loadings
  reproduce such correlations and the maximum likelihood estimate does
  not exist. The function now stops with a message that quotes the
  correlations, under either denominator, for covariance input, and
  under FIML. It also stops when the error variances of an improper
  solution sum below zero, so that the model implies a negative error
  variance for the composite and an omega above one, the signature of a
  solution that has run away (McDonald, 2004), and the model implied
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  does the same for the tau-equivalent model. An improper solution whose
  coefficient is still a proportion is returned with a warning, as
  before, and the warning now names the item, its error variance, and
  its observed variance; the observed denominator, which gave no warning
  of its own, now gives it. In a bootstrap, a replication with no
  coefficient is set aside under either `improper` setting (on 80 cases
  with one loading of .95, one such replication in 200 had put the
  bootstrap standard error at 1.02 rather than 0.049), and a replication
  of
  [`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  whose fit is now refused is set aside rather than returning an absurd
  interval. This is a deliberate, loud change for those samples: a
  number that described where the optimizer stopped is replaced by an
  error. lavaan’s own per-replication notices of improper solutions no
  longer reach the console.

- **Each confidence limit of a reliability coefficient is clamped into
  \[0, 1\], and a negative estimate is warned about.** Through 1.0.1 the
  lower limit was raised to 0 and the upper limit lowered to 1, each on
  its own. So when a negative coefficient alpha or KR-20 had an interval
  lying wholly below zero, the limits came back inverted, with the
  estimate outside them. On four binary items, one nearly the reverse of
  another
  (`set.seed(3); z <- rbinom(60, 1, .5); Xb <- cbind(i1 = z, i2 = 1 - z, i3 = rbinom(60, 1, .5), i4 = rbinom(60, 1, .5)); Xb[1:6, 2] <- z[1:6]`),
  `reliability_kr20(Xb)` gave -0.821 with Feldt limits \[0, -0.171\],
  and `reliability_alpha(as.data.frame(Xb))` gave Bonett limits \[0,
  -0.196\]. Both limits are now clamped into \[0, 1\], so they stay in
  order and that interval is \[0, 0\]. The estimate is returned as
  computed, with a warning (class `dmar_negative_reliability`) that it
  lies outside the range of a reliability coefficient and that an item
  keyed in the opposite direction is the usual cause. The `_logistic`
  intervals, which gave NA limits without a word, now say why. Only
  results whose upper limit, before clamping, was below zero change. In
  [`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  such a replication now has a width of 0 rather than a negative one,
  and the warning is muffled inside the loop. At `true_reliability = 0`
  such a replication also covers the true value, since \[0, 0\] contains
  zero, so none can miss high there; through 1.0.1 its inverted limits
  counted as a miss high. With four items, N = 40, and Bonett’s interval
  (`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(true_reliability = 0, n_items = 4, width = .3, specified_N = 40, ci_method = "bonett", G = 400)`
  after `set.seed(1)`), the share of intervals missing zero goes from
  .0400, .0325 of it high, to .0075, all of it low. With the `"ml"`
  interval it goes from .0425, .0100 of it high, to .0350, all of it
  low; its low misses move from .0325 to .0350 because that interval’s
  standard error now comes from the covariance matrix (see the next
  entry). The function evaluates the interval a study would report, and
  a miss high at zero would place the reliability below zero; its help
  says so. Above zero the counts do not change.

- **The `"ml"` interval of
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md)
  takes its standard error from the covariance matrix.** The van Zyl,
  Neudecker, and Nel (2000) variance was evaluated on the correlation
  matrix of the items, which is the variance of alpha of standardized
  items, and paired with alpha of the raw items. The paper defines it on
  the covariance matrix, as do Terry and Kelley (2012, Eq. 8) and Kelley
  and Pornprasertmanit (2016, Eq. 20), and the help already said it was
  computed from the covariance matrix. Whenever the item variances
  differ, the standard error was wrong in either direction. With equal
  loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2 at N = 206 it was
  .0256 where alpha-hat varies with a standard deviation of .0339, and
  the 95 percent interval covered .863 of 4,000 samples; it now covers
  .952. With item standard deviations from .8 to 1.9 it covered .889
  (.944 now), and with the large variances on the high loading items its
  standard error was twice the standard deviation and it covered .9998
  (.945 now). Items of equal variance are unaffected. On six binary
  items of unequal difficulty KR-20’s standard error moves from .0311 to
  .0279 against a sampling standard deviation of .0242. The default
  Bonett interval and the FIML and two-stage `"ml"` intervals, which
  already used the covariance matrix, are unchanged, and on complete
  data the listwise and FIML standard errors now agree up to the
  divisor. The code came from MBESS, whose `ci.reliability()` (through
  its internal `.interval.type31_32_type1()`) still evaluates the
  variance on the correlation matrix, so the two packages’ `"ml"` alpha
  intervals now differ when the item variances do.

- **Item names lavaan cannot parse no longer stop the single-factor
  coefficients.** Through 1.0.1,
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  (robust omega, the default, and the model implied omega), the model
  implied
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  and
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md)
  passed the column names to lavaan. lavaan stopped on a name such as
  “item 1” or “1a”, and the error was reported as a model that did not
  converge; under FIML the message also gave advice about small samples.
  The items now enter the fit as `y1`, …, `yJ`, and every result,
  message, and warning carries the user’s names. lavaan’s warnings, such
  as “some observed variables are perfectly correlated; … variables
  involved are”, are raised again with them. So are those of the
  saturated model behind FIML, which named the variables `v1`, `v2`, …
  or `y1`, `y2`, … even in 1.0.1, for analytic alpha under FIML and for
  the fits with auxiliary variables.
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  from data, new in 1.1.0, works the same way. On the five verbal tests
  of `holzinger_swineford` (`t5_general_information` to
  `t9_word_meaning`) renamed “item 1” to “item 5”, robust omega is
  0.900, the same as under the data’s names, where 1.0.1 stopped with
  “The single-factor CFA model did not converge.” A fit that lavaan
  stops with an error is reported with lavaan’s own message rather than
  as a convergence failure, and the message names the items and
  auxiliary variables as the data do, in
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  the model implied
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  and
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md);
  a fit that ran and did not converge is still reported as one, with the
  advice for FIML and two-stage estimation.
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  had reported every failure of its fit as “The single-factor
  categorical CFA model did not converge,” which sent the user looking
  for a problem with the sample. Its bootstrap sets a replication
  without a fit aside and counts it as before, so no estimate, interval,
  or count changes.
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)’s
  advice on requesting the robust omega interval now comes after the
  estimate, so a call that stops on its fit gives no advice first.

  A name given to two columns is refused by name wherever the columns
  are selected by name. Through 1.0.1, under FIML the first of two
  same-named columns was analyzed twice, and the call reported a model
  that did not converge; with auxiliary variables the second was dropped
  without a warning. On `t1_visual_perception`, `t2_cubes`,
  `t4_lozenges`, and `t6_paragraph_comprehension`, with the `t2_cubes`
  column also named `t1_visual_perception` and `t9_word_meaning` as an
  auxiliary variable,
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  returned 0.555 with J = 3, the alpha of the other three tests (0.606
  with J = 4 when the columns are named apart). An auxiliary variable’s
  name given to an item column as well is refused too.

- **[`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md)
  picks the coefficient from the items alone.** Auto-detection read
  every column of `data`, auxiliary variables included. So ordered items
  with a continuous auxiliary variable, or an integer one with more than
  10 values, went to continuous omega under FIML rather than categorical
  omega under multiple imputation, and a factor auxiliary stopped the
  call with a base R error. The rule now reads only the columns not
  named in `aux`.

- **[`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  reports the average variance extracted and coefficient H as `NA` for a
  factor with a negative error variance, and omega as `NA` when the
  factor’s error variances sum below zero.** An item whose error
  variance is negative has a communality above one. The AVE averages the
  communalities, and H, the largest reliability a weighted sum of the
  items attains, is at least that communality, since the item weighted
  alone attains it, so for such a factor neither is a proportion of
  variance. Through 1.0.1 both were reported beside the Heywood warning:
  on `holzinger_swineford`, a factor of visual perception and lozenges
  beside one of general information, paragraph comprehension, and
  sentence completion had H = 1.321 \[0.166, 2.476\] and an AVE of .726.
  Both rows are now `NA`, the estimate and its interval alike, with one
  warning that names the items and their communalities. Omega depends on
  the error variances only through their sum: while the sum is positive
  it is a proportion and is reported, as
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  reports it (.707 for that factor), and when the sum is negative the
  model implies a negative error variance for the sum score, so omega is
  `NA` too (visual perception and cubes beside three speed tests had
  omega 1.050, H 1.536, and an AVE of .788). For ordered items the
  communality is that of the latent response. Through 1.0.1 an improper
  ordered factor stopped the whole fit with the mvtnorm error “‘corr’ is
  not a correlation matrix”; its categorical omega, which is not defined
  for an improper solution, its AVE, and its H are now `NA`, named in
  the same warning. The classed Heywood warning is unchanged, and
  `output = "fit"` keeps lavaan’s defined parameters.

- **[`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  reports `NA`, with a warning, for a factor whose solution is improper,
  as
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  does.** An indicator whose error variance is estimated below zero has
  a communality above one, so the AVE of its factor, which averages the
  communalities, is not a proportion of variance.
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  now reports that factor’s `ave` row as `NA`, but
  `average_variance_extracted(fit)` averaged the squared standardized
  loadings regardless: for visual perception and lozenges beside a
  factor of general information, paragraph comprehension, and sentence
  completion in `holzinger_swineford`, where visual perception’s
  communality is 1.304, it reported .726. The factor’s `ave`, and its
  interval when one is requested, are now `NA`, with a warning that
  names each such indicator and its communality in the words of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)’s.
  The check reads the sign of the error variance and takes the
  communality as one minus the standardized error variance, so it gives
  the same answer whatever the identification of the fit, for the latent
  responses of ordered items under either parameterization, and in every
  group of a multiple group fit. Proper factors are unchanged (.705 for
  the verbal factor there). When every factor of the fit is improper,
  `ci_method = "percentile"` forms no interval: no bootstrap is run, and
  no confidence level is recorded or printed.

- **[`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  counts the improper replications its bootstrap keeps, and its warning
  gives the caution for each factor.** A replication whose resample
  solution is improper for a factor that is proper in the observed fit
  (an indicator with a negative error variance) is kept, as the
  reliability family’s default `improper = "keep"` keeps one. Through
  1.0.1 it was neither counted nor reported, though its AVE averages a
  communality above one and can exceed one.

  - The table now carries the reliability family’s `bootstrap` attribute
    (`attempted`, `returned`, `failed`, `improper_kept`, `refit_failed`,
    `caution`, `improper_kept_by_factor`, and the rest), and prints the
    family’s bootstrap line under the table, at the console and in a
    knitted report. When two or more factors have an interval, a second
    line gives the improper replications kept for each.
  - A caution is added when the replications set aside and the improper
    ones kept for a factor reach the tail area beyond a limit. With one
    factor the line keeps the reliability family’s wording; with two or
    more, it gives the share of each factor the caution holds for,
    counted for that factor alone. The bootstrap gives one warning, as
    the family does: the replications set aside, the improper ones kept,
    and the caution for each factor it holds for, with that factor’s
    count.
  - lavaan’s bootstrap cannot tell a refit that failed from one that did
    not converge. Such replications are counted among the non-finite
    ones and as `refit_failed`, and the line and the warning both say
    that they “failed to refit or did not converge” and were set aside,
    where 1.0.1’s warning said that they “failed to refit (or did not
    converge) and were dropped”.
  - Example: 80 pupils drawn from `holzinger_swineford`
    (`set.seed(113); d <- holzinger_swineford[sample(301, 80), ]`), fit
    by [`lavaan::cfa()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/lavaan/man/cfa.html) with a
    verbal factor of paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and
    word meaning and a spatial factor of visual perception, cubes, and
    lozenges, then
    `average_variance_extracted(fit, ci_method = "percentile", B = 200, seed = 113)`.
    The spatial factor is proper in the sample (AVE .449), yet 101 of
    the 198 replications that returned a value were improper for it, and
    its upper limit is 1.19. Version 1.0.1’s warning said only that 2 of
    200 replications failed to refit (or did not converge) and were
    dropped. The warning now says that they were set aside, that 101 of
    the 198 used came from an improper (Heywood) solution and were kept,
    and that for spatial 103 of 200 replications (51.5%) came from a
    solution improper for it or were set aside, against the 2.5% beyond
    each limit of a 95% interval. The line under the table says “for
    spatial, 51.5% of the replications came from a solution improper for
    the factor or were set aside, at least the 2.5% beyond each limit”,
    and the second line “spatial 101, verbal 0”.
  - The table gains the class `dmar_ave` ahead of `dmar_tbl` on every
    path. No interval changes.

- **[`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  reads a loading fixed or constrained to zero as none.** Through 1.0.1
  it averaged the squared standardized loading of every `=~` row of a
  fit, so a loading fixed at zero (`0*item`) or constrained to zero
  (`a*item` with `a == 0`) entered the factor’s average as a loading of
  zero. On `holzinger_swineford`
  (`lavaan::cfa(model, data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE)`), a
  visual factor of visual perception, cubes, and lozenges written with
  `0*t7_sentence` beside a verbal factor of general information,
  paragraph comprehension, and sentence completion is the same model as
  the one without that row (chi square 22.876 on 8 degrees of freedom
  for both), yet it had an AVE of .279 rather than the .371 of its three
  tests. The verbal factor written with `0*t1_visual_perception` beside
  the same visual factor had .529 (.705 times 3/4) rather than .705.
  Such a row is now left out of the average and out of the check for an
  improper solution described above, as
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md),
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md),
  and
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  read it. With a visual factor of visual perception and lozenges alone,
  whose visual perception error variance is negative, 1.0.1 gave the
  visual factor .726 and the verbal factor written with
  `0*t1_visual_perception` .529. The visual factor’s AVE is now `NA`
  under that check, and the verbal factor’s is the .705 of the model
  without the row, since visual perception is not one of its indicators.
  Fits without such a row are unchanged.

- **[`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
  [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md), and
  [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md)
  refuse `group` passed through `...`.**
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  labels every loading, error variance, intercept, and factor
  correlation, and lavaan holds a label shared by several groups equal
  across them. A `group` argument therefore fit one pooled model, every
  measurement parameter equal across the groups and each factor’s
  variance fixed at 1 in each: a model of complete invariance rather
  than a model by group. lavaan warned about the single labels, and the
  table repeated each labeled row once per group with the same estimate.
  The call is now an error that names the route:
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md),
  whose configural model frees every parameter in each group and whose
  fit gives `reliability_H(fit = , factor = , group = )` the H of one
  group, and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  on one group’s rows.

- **[`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  names the version of its fit rows after FIML, and its SRMR when the
  model has a mean structure.** Under `missing = "ml"` (or `"fiml"`),
  the `cfi`, `tli`, `nnfi`, `rmsea`, and RMSEA interval rows have always
  been lavaan’s robust indices. For a FIML fit these are the corrected
  indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), version 6 (version 3 with
  `estimator = "MLR"`), and they are not computed from the `chi_square`
  row beside them. The `srmr` row of a model with a mean structure is
  lavaan’s SRMR, which averages in the mean residuals, so it is not the
  SRMR
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  reports: .0229 against .0259 on the verbal and deduction tests of the
  help page (`hs_factors`) with 90 sentence completion scores deleted at
  random (`set.seed(1)`, then `t7_sentence[sample(301, 90)] <- NA`)
  under `missing = "ml"`. Lines under the table now say both, and the
  table carries them in a new `fit_rows` attribute, so a knitted report
  shows them too. When the robust indices of a fit are not available
  (lavaan computes none, and DMAR computes them only for the mean and
  variance adjusted statistic), every index row holds one other version
  and a line says which. That is the standard indices for a maximum
  likelihood fit of continuous items, and the scaled ones, or else the
  standard ones, after FIML or two-stage estimation, for ordered items,
  or by least squares. Another line names robust indices DMAR computed,
  for the mean and variance adjusted statistic. Whether the fit used
  FIML is read from the fit, so a fit lavaan made to the complete cases
  (with `missing = "ml"` and a test it cannot combine with FIML) is not
  labeled with the FIML corrected indices. An exactly fitting model with
  no degrees of freedom gets no version line under FIML or two-stage
  estimation; its SRMR and two-stage method lines stay. With a nonzero
  statistic the version line names CFI alone and another line explains
  the undefined TLI and RMSEA rows. A help paragraph says which version
  each fit row is. No number changes here; the next entry gives the rows
  that do.

- **[`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  reports one version of its fit indices, and the robust indices of a
  fit with the mean and variance adjusted statistic.**

  - Through 1.0.1 each of the `cfi`, `tli`, `nnfi`, `rmsea`, and RMSEA
    interval rows took the first of its robust, scaled, and standard
    versions that lavaan had computed, so a row whose robust version was
    `NA` could hold another version than the rows beside it.
  - With the older mean and variance adjusted statistic
    (`test = "mean.var.adjusted"` passed through `...`), for which
    lavaan computes no robust indices, every row held the scaled
    version, whose population value changes with the kurtosis of the
    data (Savalei, 2018). The rows now hold the robust indices, computed
    by DMAR as Savalei (2018) shows they can be. They equal lavaan’s
    under `estimator = "MLM"`, and a line under the table says that DMAR
    computed them.
  - On the verbal and deduction tests of the help page
    (`fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = hs_factors, test = "mean.var.adjusted")`),
    CFI .961 and RMSEA .046 \[0, .089\] become .993 and .047 \[0,
    .091\], both intervals at 90 percent, the level of 1.0.x and the
    default of `rmsea_conf_level`. On the three-factor model of nine
    tests (see the
    [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
    entry on the mean and variance adjusted statistic), CFI .734 becomes
    .932 and RMSEA .089 \[.068, .110\] becomes .091 \[.070, .113\].
  - Where neither lavaan nor DMAR computes robust indices for a maximum
    likelihood fit of continuous items, the rows hold the standard
    indices, never the scaled ones, and a line under the table says so.
  - An exactly fitting model with no degrees of freedom keeps the values
    1.0.1 gave it (CFI, TLI, and NNFI 1, RMSEA 0), under FIML and
    two-stage estimation as well, with no version line. A nonzero
    statistic keeps its CFI but gives `NA` for TLI, NNFI, and RMSEA, as
    the entry on zero degrees of freedom explains.

- **[`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  leave the covariances among the predictors free when auxiliary
  variables are supplied.** The saturated correlates of `auxiliary` were
  written as a covariance of each auxiliary with each predictor. That
  made the predictors endogenous to lavaan, whose automatic covariances
  among exogenous variables then no longer reached them, and nothing
  else freed them, so with two or more predictors every covariance among
  them was fixed at zero and the model that should be saturated
  (Graham, 2003) was not. The covariance of every pair of predictors is
  now written, and the model over the outcomes, the predictors, and the
  auxiliaries is saturated, with chi square 0 on 0 df. Its coefficients
  are the regression implied by the full information maximum likelihood
  means and covariances of every variable, auxiliaries included (what
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  returns), and on complete data they and R squared are those of
  [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html). A fit with one predictor,
  or none, is unchanged. When a predictor has missing values, the
  coefficients, standard errors, intervals, and *p*-values change. On
  `holzinger_swineford`, with t6 regressed on t7 and t9, t9 made missing
  at random given t7 for 110 of the 301 students (`set.seed(113)`), and
  t13 as the auxiliary, the model had chi square 129.5 on 1 df and an
  implied covariance of 0 between t7 and t9, whose correlation is .69.
  The t7 slope was 0.449 (SE 0.031) and is now 0.362 (SE 0.044), against
  0.362 without the auxiliary and 0.317 on the complete data, and the t9
  slope moves from 0.096 to 0.143 (0.167 on the complete data). The
  auxiliary example on the
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) page,
  where t26_flags is missing for 156 students, had chi square 14.1 on 1
  df; its intercept moves from -0.703 to -0.436 and its t7 slope from
  0.488 to 0.476. When the predictors are complete, the coefficients and
  their standard errors were already right, since their maximum
  likelihood estimates do not depend on the predictors’ covariance
  there, but every quantity that uses the model implied variance of the
  outcome was not. For t6 on t7 and t9 with complete data, R squared was
  .471 and is now .602, the value
  [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) gives; the standardized
  coefficients move from .541 and .423 to .469 and .367, and the
  semi-partial R squared from .141 and .086 to .106 and .065. The log
  likelihood moves from -4123.6 on 13 parameters to -4013.7 on 14, and
  AIC and BIC with it. The likelihood ratio test of
  [`anova()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/anova.html) for adding t9 in the
  first example was chi square 8.62 and is now 13.72. In
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  the first example gives t6 a t7 slope of 0.362 rather than 0.450 and
  t26_flags a t9 slope of 0.104 rather than -0.050, and with complete
  data the R squared of each outcome is now that of
  [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) (.602 and .474 for t6 and
  t8, where they were .471 and .379). The auxiliary simulation in the
  mlmr vignette, whose predictors are complete, prints the same values.
  With the model saturated, the three estimators of
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  now agree on such fits as they do without auxiliaries: in the first
  example the t7 slope’s unstructured and Hessian estimates were .016
  and -.559, and all three are now .254.
  `wald_df = "missing_information"` therefore gives that slope 221.5
  degrees of freedom rather than 293.1.

- **[`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  refuse an auxiliary variable under listwise or pairwise deletion.**
  lavaan’s listwise deletion drops every row missing any variable of the
  model, the auxiliaries included, so through 1.0.1 an incomplete
  auxiliary silently shrank the sample.
  `mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning, data = holzinger_swineford, missing = "listwise", auxiliary = "t26_flags")`
  fitted 145 of the 301 rows, with coefficients of 0.971, 0.313, and
  0.178 where [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) gives 1.117,
  0.317, and 0.167. An auxiliary carries information only through the
  full information likelihood, so the combination now stops and names
  the remedy (drop the auxiliary or set `missing = "fiml"`), as
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  stop. Under pairwise and available cases deletion
  (`missing = "pairwise"` or `"available.cases"`) the moments are
  computed from each pair of variables on its own. With the model
  saturated, the coefficients then depend on the moments of the outcomes
  and predictors alone, so an auxiliary can change nothing, while the
  result recorded it as used. In
  `mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning + t26_flags, data = holzinger_swineford, missing = "pairwise", auxiliary = "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals")`,
  1.0.1’s coefficients agreed with those of the fit without the
  auxiliary to within 5e-6; its standard errors differed only because
  the auxiliary also fixed the covariances among the predictors at zero
  (see the entry above), so the t7 slope’s was .0245 against .0355. That
  combination is now refused the same way.

- **Under `missing = "fiml"` with auxiliary variables, a case whose
  items are all missing is used when an auxiliary variable is observed
  on it.**
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  set aside every case with no observed item, with auxiliary variables
  or without. The saturated correlates model estimates the items and the
  auxiliaries jointly, so such a case informs the item moments through
  its auxiliaries, and lavaan’s own FIML fit of the model keeps it, as
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  does. Setting it aside made the analysis conditional on having an
  observed item, which depends on the auxiliaries when the items go
  missing together at random given them, and the estimates were then
  biased. On the nine tests of the three-factor model (visual
  perception, cubes, lozenges, paragraph comprehension, sentence
  completion, word meaning, addition, counting groups of dots, and
  straight and curved capitals), with the whole block set to `NA` for 77
  pupils at random given general information (`set.seed(113)`, the rows
  `sample(301, 77, prob = plogis(-1.5 + 1.2 * z))` with z the
  standardized `t5_general_information`, the auxiliary), `N` goes from
  224 to 301, alpha from .610 to .613, model implied omega from .350 to
  .358, and robust omega from .228 to .234.
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  from data, new in 1.1.0, uses such cases too. A result changes only
  when some case has every item missing and an auxiliary observed, and
  `N` now counts such cases. Two-stage estimation, new in 1.1.0, uses
  them as well: its first stage reads their auxiliaries, and the
  coefficients are computed on every case it reads, although lavaan’s
  two-stage estimator leaves such cases out of its N (see Two-Stage
  Maximum Likelihood for Incomplete Data). Under multiple imputation,
  also new,
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  imputes such a case from its auxiliaries.

- **The FIML item covariance matrix behind analytic alpha and robust
  omega is the EM estimate.** Under `missing = "fiml"`, analytic
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and the observed denominator of
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  apply their formulas to the maximum likelihood covariance matrix of
  the items under the saturated model. Through 1.0.1 that matrix came
  from lavaan fitting the saturated model from its default starting
  values, which on many items stops short of the maximum: on all 26
  Holzinger and Swineford tests, with the Pasteur students missing the
  last two, it took 2484 iterations and left covariances up to 0.0105
  from the maximum likelihood values, the log likelihood 3e-7 below its
  maximum. The matrix is now the EM estimate
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md)
  returns, the unrestricted moments lavaan computes for every FIML fit
  to the same variables (the EM runs on the standardized items, as in
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md),
  so the matrix does not depend on their units, and agrees with lavaan’s
  to about seven digits), and the standard error of the `"ml"` interval
  is the delta method one from the saturated model evaluated at that
  estimate, with no optimization run. On the Holzinger and Swineford
  examples checked (6, 9, 23, and 26 tests, with the Pasteur students’
  missing tests or with values deleted at random given general
  information, with and without an auxiliary variable), alpha changes by
  at most 1.5e-6, robust omega by at most 5.8e-6, and the standard error
  by at most 4.4e-8; on the 26 tests alpha is .8234684 rather than
  .8234689. The estimate no longer depends on the interval asked for,
  the FIML alpha of complete data equals the listwise one to machine
  precision (it differed by 2.3e-9 on nine tests), and the computation
  is faster: on 23 incomplete tests about three times for alpha with its
  interval and five to ten times for robust omega. Two-stage analytic
  alpha, which uses the same matrix, changes the same way, as does the
  fraction of missing information
  [`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  records for alpha. Model implied alpha and model implied omega are
  unchanged.

- **Under FIML and two-stage estimation, a pair of variables never
  observed together is refused by name.**
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  now stop, as
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  from data and
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md),
  new in 1.1.0, do, naming each pair of items or auxiliary variables
  that no case observes together and pointing to
  [`missing_coverage()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/missing_coverage.md).
  Through 1.0.1 lavaan only warned, and the covariance it returned for
  such a pair was arbitrary: on `t1_visual_perception`, `t2_cubes`,
  `t4_lozenges`, and `t6_paragraph_comprehension`, with
  `t1_visual_perception` deleted in rows 1 to 150 and `t2_cubes` in rows
  151 to 301, `reliability_alpha(missing = "fiml")` returned 0.536 with
  a standard error of 0 and the interval \[0.536, 0.536\]. In a
  bootstrap, a resample left with such a pair, or a jackknife deletion
  behind the BCa acceleration, is set aside with the message, under
  two-stage estimation as under FIML. A pair observed together only
  where one of them takes a single value, or by one row only, is refused
  the same way (see the next entry).

- **Under FIML and two-stage estimation, a pair of variables observed
  together only where one of them takes a single value is refused.**
  Rows in which one of two variables is constant say nothing about how
  the two vary together, so the estimate of their covariance rests on
  the form of the normal model, or is not determined at all.
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  now name such a pair and stop, as they do for a pair never observed
  together, and so do
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  from data and
  [`cov_fiml()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cov_fiml.md),
  new in 1.1.0. A pair that only one row observes is refused the same
  way, and in a bootstrap a resample that leaves such a pair is set
  aside.

  - Example: rows 1 to 100 of `t1_visual_perception`, `t2_cubes`,
    `t4_lozenges`, and `t6_paragraph_comprehension`, with
    `t1_visual_perception` deleted in rows 91 to 100 and `t2_cubes` set
    to 25 in rows 1 to 90, the rows that observe `t1_visual_perception`.
    Under `missing = "fiml"`, version 1.0.1 returned robust omega 1.06,
    the analytic alpha 0.113 with no interval, and the model implied
    omega 0.890 \[0.281, 1\].
  - Under listwise deletion 1.0.1 returned alpha 0.511, counting
    `t2_cubes` among the items. `t2_cubes` is now refused as constant in
    the 90 complete rows (see the entry on an item that does not vary),
    and the message says why FIML cannot help.

- **[`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  refuses fewer than three items.** With two ordered items the
  single-factor model is not identified: the one polychoric correlation
  determines only the product of the two loadings, while categorical
  omega depends on each. The value returned before depended on the start
  values of the optimizer and on the order of the columns, and its
  bootstrap interval reflected where the optimizer landed. The function
  now stops with the message
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  gives for two continuous items, and
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md),
  whose automatic routing sends two integer items to categorical omega,
  lets the error through rather than substituting another coefficient.

- **Categorical omega no longer drops an undetermined polychoric
  correlation from its total variance.** The unrestricted polychoric
  correlations behind the observed denominator came from a second,
  saturated fit (the approach `MBESS` also takes). When the data do not
  determine a polychoric correlation, as when two items are skewed in
  opposite directions and their bivariate table has empty cells, that
  fit gives the correlation no weight and returns its starting value, 0,
  so the pair was removed from the total variance without notice and the
  coefficient was too high, by about .035 for each such pair. In samples
  of 500 from the mixed-skew design of Green and Yang (2009), the help
  page’s example with `N <- 500` and seeds 1 to 100 in place of 113, 45
  of the 99 samples with a proper solution had at least one such pair.
  Against the coefficient with the model implied correlation in the
  pair, 1.0.1’s was .030 to .045 too high with one undetermined pair (38
  samples) and .065 to .088 with two whose loadings are identified (3
  samples). The correlations now come from the single-factor fit itself,
  which agrees with the saturated fit whenever every correlation is
  determined, so every other result is unchanged, and the computation
  needs one fit instead of two per bootstrap replication; that fit also
  no longer computes a test statistic it never used, which changes no
  number. Together the two cut the fitting time of a bootstrap
  replication by more than half. When a correlation is not determined,
  `reliability_omega_categorical(denominator = "observed")` stops with
  an error naming the pair. When the correlations the data do determine
  identify the single-factor loadings, it points to
  `denominator = "model_implied"`, which does not need the pair.
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  reports that factor’s categorical omega as `NA` with a warning naming
  the pair. A bootstrap meets such pairs far more often than the sample
  does, since a resample often leaves out the few respondents who
  determine the correlation (about half the replications on the help
  page’s example, whose sample has no such pair). Those replications are
  set aside, counted in the new `undetermined` element of the
  `bootstrap` attribute, and named in the printed line and the warning.
  The warning says that the interval then conditions on the replications
  that redrew the respondents who determine the correlation (on the help
  page’s example, 80, 95, and 97 of 200 in percentile bootstraps with
  `seed` 1, 2, and 3; with the improper ones, 80, 96, and 98 were set
  aside, close to the half beyond which no interval is reported, as the
  entry on a bootstrap of categorical omega that returns fewer than half
  describes), and that `denominator = "model_implied"` sets aside only
  the replications whose determined correlations leave the loadings
  unidentified (see Either Variance in the Denominator of Every Omega).
  This is a deliberate, loud change for those samples only: a number
  that rested on an arbitrary 0 is replaced by an error.

- **An improper categorical solution is named.** When the single-factor
  fit returns a standardized loading above one (a negative residual
  variance, a Heywood case), categorical omega is not defined, and the
  function failed with the error “‘corr’ is not a correlation matrix”
  from `mvtnorm`, under the model implied denominator only after a
  message advising that denominator. It now stops with an error naming
  each improper item and its loading, before anything is said about
  undetermined pairs. A bootstrap replication with an improper solution
  is set aside as a non-finite value and counted in the new `improper`
  element of the `bootstrap` attribute (it was counted as an error, with
  the message from `mvtnorm`), and the warning from `lavaan` about the
  negative variance no longer repeats once per replication.

- **[`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  says which sum its coefficient describes.** Categorical omega scores
  each item’s categories 0, 1, …, C - 1 in the order of its codes (Green
  & Yang, 2009, Eq. 11; Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016, Eq. 16), as
  MBESS and semTools do, and the help page now says so. When an item’s
  codes are not equally spaced, or items step by different amounts, the
  sum of the codes as given is a different composite, and a message
  names the items. In the examples behind the help page its reliability
  was 0.009 to 0.012 lower for codes -2, -1, 1, 2, and 0.034 lower for
  items coded 1, 3, 5 beside items coded 1, 2, 3. The coefficient is
  unchanged.

- **Listwise deletion that leaves too little to analyze says so.** With
  no complete row, only one, or an item that takes a single value in the
  complete rows,
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  printed lavaan’s table of variables and stopped with “The
  single-factor categorical CFA model did not converge.” It now stops
  before any fit, names the cause, and offers `missing = "pairwise"`
  (when every pair of items is observed together) or `missing = "mi"`.
  No estimate changes.

- **The reliability family treats SPSS user-defined missing values as
  missing.** A column read by `haven::read_sav(user_na = TRUE)` keeps a
  code declared missing in SPSS (999 for a test not given, 9 for a
  refusal) as a value of class `haven_labelled_spss`, which SPSS and
  haven’s [`is.na()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/NA.html) treat as missing.
  Through 1.0.1,
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  and [`icc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/icc.md)
  analyzed it as a score or rating.
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md)
  refused it as not 0/1, and
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  counted it as a further category.
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md)
  summed it as a count.
  [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md)
  dropped such a pair only when haven was loaded, and otherwise counted
  the code as a further category. These functions and
  [`reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability.md)
  now set, as
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  from data, new in 1.1.0, does, the declared values (`na_values` and
  `na_range`) to missing in every column before anything is deleted or
  fitted, as `read_sav()` does by default. A message names the columns
  and counts, and haven need not be loaded.
  [`icc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/icc.md) and
  [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md),
  which do not accept missing values, then refuse such a column as they
  refuse `NA`.

  - Five spatial tests of `holzinger_swineford`, `t1_visual_perception`,
    `t2_cubes`, `t3_paper_form_board`, `t4_lozenges`, and
    `t25_paper_form_board_r`, with the 156 missing scores of the last
    recoded to 999 and declared missing
    (`x <- holzinger_swineford$t25_paper_form_board_r; haven::labelled_spss(ifelse(is.na(x), 999, x), na_values = 999)`).
    Version 1.0.1 gave alpha 0.008 and omega 0.015; the functions now
    give 0.687 and 0.730 under listwise deletion
    (`missing = "listwise"`, the default through 1.0.x), the values for
    the same data with `NA`.
  - Three raters of 60 subjects (`set.seed(1); t <- rnorm(60)`, then
    `round(3 + t + rnorm(60, sd = .5))` for each rater in turn), with
    the first six ratings of the third declared missing as 9.
    [`icc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/icc.md) gave
    ICC(2,1) 0.318, against 0.668 on the complete rows, and now refuses
    the data.
    [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md)
    of the first and third raters gave 0.170 on 60 pairs and seven
    categories when haven was not loaded. It now gives 0.196 on 54 pairs
    and six, as it did with haven loaded.
  - Data read with `read_sav()`’s default, which already makes these
    values `NA`, are unaffected.

- **[`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  reads a factor’s labels as the numbers they name.** Through 1.0.1 a
  factor item passed only when its labels were 1, 2, …, K in order. A
  Likert factor labeled 0 to 4, or one whose lowest category no
  respondent chose (levels “2” to “5”), was refused with “column 1
  contains non-integer values”. The labels are now read as numbers, and
  the item is analyzed as those numbers under every treatment of
  `missing`. Listwise and pairwise deletion and multiple imputation
  therefore rank its categories alike, and the factor gives the result
  of its integer codes. For example, the items of the help page’s
  example recoded as factors labeled 0 to 4
  (`as.data.frame(lapply(as.data.frame(items - 1), factor))`) were
  refused by 1.0.1 and now give 0.720, the value of their codes. Two
  kinds of factor are refused, with a message that names the column and
  says what to do: one whose labels are words, and an ordered factor
  whose levels are not in the order of the numbers they name.

- **A bootstrap of categorical omega reports no interval when fewer than
  half of its replications return a value.** Through 1.0.1
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
  formed its interval from any two replications that returned a value.
  When most were set aside, the rest were a minority of the resamples,
  selected by whether they returned a value, and their spread described
  those resamples rather than the sampling distribution of the
  coefficient.

  - The standard error and the limits are now `NA` in that case, under
    every `ci_method` and every treatment of `missing`. A warning and
    the printed line say why.
  - This is the criterion by which the point estimate under multiple
    imputation stops when fewer than half of its completed data sets
    return a value (Lim & Cheung, 2022).
  - Example: six binary items of 60 respondents, one respondent alone
    endorsing the first item, so every resample without that respondent
    has a constant item
    (`set.seed(113); eta <- rnorm(60); y <- 1 * (outer(eta, rep(.7, 6)) + matrix(rnorm(360), 60) * sqrt(1 - .7^2) > 0); y[, 1] <- 0; y[1, 1] <- 1`).
    A percentile bootstrap (`B = 200`, `seed = 113`) set aside 106
    replications in 1.0.1 and gave \[0.660, 0.921\] from the other 94.
    It now reports no interval.
  - A larger sample is the remedy. Other callers keep the floor of two
    returned values, except when most resamples fail the distinct-case
    rule described under the bootstrap engine.

- **Listwise deletion that leaves fewer than two complete rows stops
  alpha, KR-20, and omega before anything is computed.**

  - Through 1.0.1, with no complete row, or only one,
    [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
    (either denominator) and the model implied
    [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
    passed the data to lavaan, which printed its table of the variables
    and stopped on a variance it could not compute, and the call
    reported a model that did not converge. The analytic
    [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
    returned NA with a warning that NaNs were produced, and
    [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md)
    returned NA for the estimate and every limit with two such warnings.
    Example: the first 40 pupils of `holzinger_swineford` on visual
    perception, cubes, lozenges, paragraph comprehension, and sentence
    completion, with one score deleted from every row
    (`d <- holzinger_swineford[1:40, c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges", "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence")]; for (i in 1:40) d[i, (i - 1) %% 5 + 1] <- NA`).
  - Each function now stops, says that listwise deletion leaves nothing
    to analyze, and offers `missing = "fiml"`, as
    [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md)
    offers its own treatments for its items. FIML is offered only when
    it can use the rows; otherwise the message says why it cannot, as
    when a pair of items is never observed together. An item that no row
    observes is named instead.
    [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
    from data, new in 1.1.0, does the same.
  - For KR-20 the message offers
    [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
    with `missing = "fiml"`, which computes the same coefficient (alpha
    of 0/1 items is KR-20) from the incomplete rows as well, when full
    information maximum likelihood can use them (otherwise the message
    says why it cannot). Example: the nine tests `t1_visual_perception`
    to `t9_word_meaning`, each scored 1 above its median
    (`as.integer(x > median(x))`), with each of the 301 pupils missing
    one test in rotation (pupil i misses test `i %% 9 + 1`). Version
    1.0.1 returned `NA`; the call the message offers gives 0.752, 95% CI
    \[0.709, 0.795\], against 0.756 for KR-20 of the complete data.
  - With two or more complete rows alpha and KR-20 are computed as
    before, and the single-factor coefficients reach the fit when the
    complete rows outnumber the items; any error lavaan stops with is
    quoted. An item or a total that takes a single value in the complete
    rows is now refused by name, and at two rows the intervals not
    defined there are refused while Feldt’s remains, for KR-20 as for
    alpha (see the entries below).

- **An item that is not numeric, or that does not vary, is refused by
  name.**
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md),
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  now stop before computing anything when an item takes a single value
  in the rows analyzed, and name it, as does
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  from data, new in 1.1.0. The rows analyzed are the complete rows under
  listwise deletion, and the rows that observe the item under FIML and
  two-stage estimation. A covariance matrix with a zero variance on its
  diagonal is refused the same way.

  - Such an item adds a constant to the composite, which leaves the
    composite’s variance and reliability as they are. Alpha and KR-20,
    however, counted it among the J items: with one such item, alpha is
    J(J - 2)/(J - 1)^2 times the alpha of the other items, which is the
    alpha of the same composite.
  - Examples. On the first 100 pupils of `holzinger_swineford` with
    `t2_cubes` set to 5, alpha of `t1_visual_perception`, `t2_cubes`,
    `t4_lozenges`, and `t6_paragraph_comprehension` was 0.487, against
    0.548 for the other three. On the first 20 pupils, with the nine
    tests `t1_visual_perception` to `t9_word_meaning` each scored 1
    above its 90th percentile among all 301 pupils
    (`as.numeric(x > quantile(x, 0.9))`), no pupil passes four of the
    tests, and KR-20 was 0.196, against 0.217 for the other five.
  - Through 1.0.1, omega (from data or from a covariance matrix) and the
    model implied alpha reported that the model did not converge; from
    data, lavaan first printed its table of the variables. The analytic
    alpha under FIML reported that the saturated model did not converge.
  - Under listwise deletion, the message says when the item varies in
    the rows deletion removed. It then offers `missing = "fiml"` (for
    KR-20,
    [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
    with `missing = "fiml"`) only when FIML could use those rows, and
    otherwise says why it cannot. A shared column name is a condition to
    fix first, rather than an obstacle in the data; fitted coefficients
    refuse shared names before checking the rows. FIML is not offered
    when the composite is constant in the complete rows and they
    outnumber the items.
  - An item column that is neither numeric nor logical is refused by
    name, with its class. Through 1.0.1, listwise deletion stopped with
