    [`stats::cov()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/cor.html)’s “is.numeric(x)
    \|\| is.logical(x) is not TRUE”, and FIML with the report about the
    saturated model. A logical item is still read as 0 and 1.

- **A bootstrap replication in which an item takes a single value is set
  aside, with the refusal.** The rule above now holds in every bootstrap
  replication of every continuous coefficient, and in the jackknife
  behind the BCa acceleration. Categorical omega already set such
  replications aside, but passed them to lavaan first. It now refuses
  them by item name before fitting, without printing lavaan’s variable
  table; their reason is counted as an error with the refusal rather
  than as an unnamed non-finite value. The same check applies to
  completed resamples after imputation.

  - A resample that leaves out every case on which a rare item differs
    from the rest raises the refusal. The bootstrap counts and quotes
    it, and the caution reports the share.
  - A resample leaves out a given case with probability (1 - 1/N)^N,
    about 0.37, so an item passed by one respondent loses its variation
    in about a third of the resamples.
  - Through 1.0.1, KR-20 and the analytic alpha of such a resample
    counted the item, at J(J - 2)/(J - 1)^2 times the coefficient of the
    same composite without it, and the replication was kept. Omega and
    the model implied alpha reached lavaan, which printed its table of
    the variables to the console for each such replication.
  - Example: the first 60 pupils of `holzinger_swineford`, with the nine
    tests `t1_visual_perception` to `t9_word_meaning` scored 1 above
    their medians among all 301 pupils, and `t20_deduction` scored 1 at
    the highest score among the 60 (one pupil). KR-20 is 0.689. Its
    percentile interval (`B = 1000`, `seed = 113`) was \[0.560, 0.779\],
    with 370 of the 1000 replications computed with `t20_deduction`
    constant. It is now \[0.564, 0.775\], from the other 630, with the
    caution.

- **A composite that does not vary is refused.** When the covariances of
  the items cancel their variances, the composite has no variance and no
  reliability. Ipsative items, whose scores sum to the same total in
  every row, are the usual case.
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md),
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  now stop and say so.

  - Through 1.0.1, alpha divided the item variances by a composite
    variance of zero, or by the rounding error left in its place.
  - Example: `t1_visual_perception`, `t2_cubes`, and `t4_lozenges`, each
    centered on the pupil’s mean of the three (`x - rowMeans(x)` for all
    301 pupils). Alpha was returned as 1.42e16, with a standard error of
    -1.42e15 and `NaN` limits.
  - KR-20 of the two rows (1, 0, 1, 0) and (0, 1, 0, 1) was returned as
    -Inf, with the limits 0 and -Inf.
  - Omega and the model implied alpha reported that the model did not
    converge.

- **The coefficients fitted by the single-factor model need more
  complete rows than items.** Under listwise deletion, N complete rows
  give a covariance matrix of rank at most N - 1. With no more complete
  rows than items it is singular, and the maximum likelihood fit is not
  defined. That fit lies behind robust and model implied omega and the
  model implied alpha, and behind
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  from data, new in 1.1.0.

  - Through 1.0.1 the call reported a model that did not converge, as on
    pupils 1 to 5 of `t1_visual_perception`, `t2_cubes`, `t4_lozenges`,
    `t6_paragraph_comprehension`, and `t7_sentence`.
  - The call now stops before the fit and says why. It offers
    `missing = "fiml"` when FIML could use the incomplete rows, and
    otherwise says why it cannot, or that the model needs more cases.
  - Alpha and KR-20 need only the trace and the sum of the covariance
    matrix, and are computed from two or more complete rows (alpha is
    0.351 on those five pupils, as in 1.0.1).

- **Full information maximum likelihood and two-stage estimation need
  more cases than variables.** Both first estimate the saturated model
  over the items and any auxiliary variables.

  - The count is of distinct cases that observe an item. Auxiliary-only
    cases and repeated rows do not add dimensions. With n such cases,
    their missing values filled in any way, the data lie in a space of
    at most n - 1 dimensions. With no more cases than variables, the EM
    estimate of the covariance matrix is therefore singular or nearly
    so, and it depends on where the algorithm stops.
  - [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
    and
    [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
    now stop before any fit and say so, as does
    [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
    from data. For the analytic alpha, listwise deletion is offered only
    when it would accept the complete rows, naming Feldt’s interval when
    exactly two are complete. Bootstrap and jackknife resamples obey the
    same rule.
  - Example: pupils 1 to 5 of the five tests above, with
    `t1_visual_perception` missing for pupil 4 and `t2_cubes` for
    pupil 5. Version 1.0.1 reported for alpha that the saturated FIML
    model did not converge, and for omega that the model did not
    converge.

- **At two complete rows, the intervals of alpha and KR-20 that are not
  defined there are refused.** Two rows give a covariance matrix of rank
  one, in which every pair of items correlates +1 or -1, whatever the
  items. Each interval is refused for its own reason, as `"fisher"`
  already is below N = 4:

  - Bonett’s variance, 2J/((J - 1)(N - 2)), is infinite at N = 2.
  - The `"ml"` and `"adf"` standard errors, and those of their
    `_logistic` variants, are zero for any data. The asymptotic variance
    of van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel vanishes at a matrix of rank one.
    Each case’s centered cross products are then proportional to the
    covariance matrix, which alpha does not change with.
  - Every bootstrap resample is one row drawn twice, or both rows.
  - Feldt’s interval remains, and every refusal names it. Its F
    reference is exact for any N of at least 2 under multivariate
    normality and parallel items; for KR-20’s 0/1 items it is an
    approximation (Feldt, 1965).
  - Hakstian and Whalen’s interval remains too, but at N = 2 its upper
    limit lies above one for every data set whose alpha is below one at
    any confidence level above about .90, and is clamped to one; at
    alpha = 1 its interval is \[1, 1\].
  - Example: rows 1 and 50 of `holzinger_swineford` (pupil ids 1 and
    54. on `t1_visual_perception`, `t2_cubes`, `t4_lozenges`,
        `t6_paragraph_comprehension`, and `t7_sentence` (alpha -0.475).
        Version 1.0.1 returned:

    - Bonett’s \[0, 1\], with an infinite standard error (alpha’s
      default interval);
    - NaN for `"ml"` and `"adf"` (a variance of zero, made negative by
      rounding error);
    - NA limits for their `_logistic` variants;
    - the inverted percentile interval \[0, -0.475\].
  - Feldt’s \[0, 0.998\] is unchanged.
  - KR-20’s default, Feldt’s interval, is computed from two complete
    rows as alpha’s is. An item the two rows answer alike is refused as
    constant, and two rows with the same total are refused as a
    composite that does not vary.

- **[`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  puts residual covariances in its model implied denominators and
  refuses correlated factors and multiple-group fits.** Each model
  implied denominator is now the sum of the corresponding block of the
  item correlations the fitted model reproduces. For every orthogonal
  fit without residual covariances that equals the earlier formula to
  machine precision, so those results are unchanged; for a fit that
  specifies residual covariances the earlier formula left them out, and
  a positive one made omega, omega_H, and omega_HS too high (omega_H
  .646 against .635 on a test sample with one cross-group residual
  covariance). A fit that correlates any two of the general and group
  factors, which the help page always excluded, is now refused with an
  error naming the pair. A multiple-group fit took its loadings from the
  first group and its residual variances from the last, so its table
  described neither group: for nine items with general and group
  loadings of .5 in two groups of 200 (`set.seed(11)`; the fixture of
  the package’s tests), the general factor’s omega was .865 and its
  omega_H .623, while the model fitted to the first group alone gives
  .862 and .621, and to the second group alone .874 and .674. Such a fit
  is now refused (see Calls That Are Now Refused); fit the model to each
  group’s data to obtain that group’s indices.

- **[`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  refuses an item on two group factors.** The help page, the argument,
  and the error message all required each item to load on exactly one
  group factor, but only an item on none was refused. An item on two
  took the loading and the membership of the group factor listed last,
  so its other loading dropped out of ECV, omega, omega_HS, H, and PUC,
  and the result depended on the order of the model syntax. On the
  15-test Holzinger and Swineford bifactor model with lozenges (t4) also
  on the verbal factor, the spatial row described three of its four
  tests (omega_HS .188, H .254), PUC counted lozenges as a verbal test,
  and ECV was .441, where every loading counted gives .432. Such a fit
  is now refused, with the items and factors named. A loading fixed or
  constrained to zero no longer counts, so a model written with `0*x3`,
  or with `a*x3` and `a == 0`, on a second group factor gets the indices
  of the same model written without that loading; through 1.0.1 the zero
  loading took the item from its real factor. An item listed under one
  group factor keeps that loading whatever its value, as before.

- **[`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  refuses a fit with one group factor.** DMAR 1.0.0 refused a fit with
  no group factor (“No group factors found; a bifactor model needs a
  general factor plus two or more group factors.”) and required every
  item to load on a group factor (“Every item must load on exactly one
  group factor.”), so it described a general factor beside a single
  group factor when every item was listed under that factor (some of
  them with loadings fixed at zero, and with `general` named, since both
  factors then listed every item), giving a table whose indices divide
  the common variance between those two factors alone. Such a fit is not
  a bifactor model with subscales, and it is now refused, with a message
  that names the group factor and any items on no group factor, as
  [`fa_bifactor()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_bifactor.md)
  and
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md),
  new in 1.1.0, refuse it. There is no warning period. The message for
  an item on two group factors now says that an item loads on one group
  factor at most, since an item on none is accepted when there are two
  or more group factors.

- **[`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  reports H as NA for a factor with a standardized loading at or beyond
  one.** The index counts 1 - l^2 as each item’s error, so such a
  loading leaves an item an error variance that is not positive and the
  index is not defined, as
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  treats an improper solution. Through 1.0.1 the loading was left out,
  and H described the factor’s other items, with only the general
  Heywood warning to show it. On nine simulated items
  (`set.seed(7); n <- 150; lg <- c(.9, rep(.6, 8)); ls <- c(.42, rep(.5, 8)); g <- rnorm(n); f <- list(rnorm(n), rnorm(n), rnorm(n))`,
  item i equal to
  `lg[i] * g + ls[i] * f[[ceiling(i / 3)]] + sqrt(1 - lg[i]^2 - ls[i]^2) * rnorm(n)`),
  fit as a bifactor model with three orthogonal group factors of three
  items each and `std.lv = TRUE`, the first general loading is 1.06, and
  the general factor’s H was .841, the H of the other eight loadings.
  That value was not a limit of nearby solutions: as that loading rose
  to .9999, H rose to .9998, and past one it fell to .841. It is now NA,
  and every other cell of the table is unchanged. In
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md),
  new in 1.1.0, such a replication yields no coefficient and is set
  aside under either `improper` rule.

- **[`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  says which H it reports and what its group rows mean, and gives the
  maximal reliability of each factor.** The help page called H “the
  construct reliability (maximal reliability) of Hancock and Mueller
  (2001)”. The column is the index Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016)
  report: Hancock and Mueller’s closed form on one factor’s standardized
  loadings, which treats the variance an item shares with the other
  factors as uncorrelated error. In a bifactor model that variance is
  correlated, so the index is not the maximal reliability of the factor
  under the fitted model, and it can lie on either side of it. In the
  help page’s example the general factor’s index is 0.769 and its
  maximal reliability 0.678, barely above omega_H (0.673), so no
  weighting of the items reaches the index; on the 15-test Holzinger and
  Swineford model they are .789 and .681; and with group loadings of
  mixed sign the maximal reliability is the larger. On a group factor’s
  row the maximal reliability is the larger when the items of the other
  subscales measure a strong general factor well, since the optimal
  weights remove it through them: with nine items in three subscales,
  general loadings .7, and group loadings .3, a group factor’s index is
  0.229 and its maximal reliability 0.279. That maximal reliability
  belongs to the group factor’s regression score from all nine items,
  which weights the other subscales’ items negatively. No score of the
  subscale’s own items reaches it, and their best weighting reaches only
  the omega_HS of 0.125. The maximal reliability, l’ R^-1 l with R the
  item correlations the model reproduces, is the square of the
  regression score determinacy that
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  reports. It is now returned in the new attribute `maximal_reliability`
  (NA for an improper solution), printed under the table, and given an
  interval by
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md);
  its sample value, like the index’s, runs upward, as the help page
  says. The ECV on a group factor’s row, which no page defined, is the
  general factor’s share of the common variance of that factor’s items.
  One minus it is the group factor’s own share, so .85 beside an
  omega_HS of .08 says the subscale is mostly general. The omega there
  is the reliability of the subscale’s total score. Both are now defined
  on the help page and in a line under the printed table, as they are
  for
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md).
  No value in the table changes.

- **[`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  returns the reliability family table for every call; the table of
  1.0.0 is gone.** In 1.0.0 the function took `loadings`, `se_loadings`,
  and `conf_level` and returned the row `reliability_H`, with
  `ci_lower`, `ci_upper`, and `var_H` when `se_loadings` was supplied.
  Such a call now returns the table every other input returns (rows
  `estimate`, `se`, `ci_lower`, `ci_upper`, `conf_level`, `N`,
  `N_complete`, `n_items`), with no warning period. With `se_loadings`
  it has the same estimate and the same logit interval, `var_H` being
  the square of `se`. Without `se_loadings` it has the estimate, with
  `se` and the limits `NA`, because standardized loadings alone carry
  nothing an interval can be formed from. Code that read
  `x$value[x$term == "reliability_H"]` reads
  `x$value[x$term == "estimate"]`. `factor`, `group`, `missing`, and
  `aux` do not apply to loadings and are refused. Every interval built
  from `se_loadings` warns, with class `dmar_H_marginal_se`, that it
  ignores the covariances among the loading estimates. The help page now
  attributes the logit interval to Browne (1982) rather than Browne
  (1968). It replaces the unverified statement that Hancock and Mueller
  proved H \>= omega \>= alpha, as does the function interactions
  vignette, which said that H is uniformly at least omega and omega at
  least alpha, with the bound that holds by construction: H is at least
  the model implied omega of the same single-factor fit; robust omega
  need not lie below it. Alpha is at most omega in the population for
  congeneric items with uncorrelated errors.

- **The `bootstrap` attribute names two causes.** Every reliability
  coefficient’s `bootstrap` attribute, and its `jackknife` element,
  gains `undetermined` and `improper`: the replications among the
  non-finite ones that were set aside because the resample left a
  polychoric correlation undetermined or gave an improper solution (zero
  outside categorical omega). The `reasons` vector keeps its 1.0.1
  shape.

- **A bootstrap whose returned replicates are all equal returns that
  value at both limits.** When every item is an exact linear function of
  the same variable, every resample gives the same coefficient. The
  percentile and BCa intervals of
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md)
  stopped with “argument is of length zero” (after boot printed “All
  values of t are equal”), or with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE
  needed” when some replications were set aside. They now return the
  common value at both limits, as `bootstrap_se` already did (and so
  does `bootstrap_se_logistic`, whose limits at a value of one,
  identical items, were `NA`, or one where rounding left the replicates
  just below it, since the logit is infinite there), with a warning that
  the bootstrap distribution is a single point. A BCa request falls back
  to that percentile interval and says why in `ci_method`. The engine
  also warns whenever fewer than two replications return a value, not
  only when some were set aside.

- **`B` is validated by
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md),
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md),
  [`reliability_kr20()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_kr20.md),
  and
  [`reliability_omega_categorical()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega_categorical.md).**
  When a bootstrap is requested, `B` must be a single whole number of at
  least 2, the fewest replications from which a standard deviation or a
  pair of quantiles can be formed, as
  [`reliability_H()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_H.md)
  and
  [`ci_bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_bifactor_indices.md)
  require. Through 1.0.1 `B = 0` or `1` returned NA limits without a
  warning (categorical omega did not check `B` at all, and `B = 1`
  returned its estimate with NA limits), and a fractional, negative, or
  missing `B` failed inside boot with an error that did not name it.
  Each function now stops before anything is computed, with one message.
  No estimate or interval changes.

- **A DMAR table prints to three decimal places, not to three
  significant figures.** A value in a DMAR table that is not a whole
  number printed to `digits` significant figures, 3 by default, and
  [`format()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/format.html) dropped its trailing
  zeros and wrote a small value in scientific notation: 13.018 printed
  as 13, 0.5596 as 0.56, 233.4107 as 233, 0.041234 as 0.0412, 1.5 as
  1.5, and 0.00001234 as 1.23e-05. It now prints to `digits` decimal
  places with its trailing zeros, never in scientific notation: 13.018,
  0.560, 233.411, 0.041, 1.500, and 0.000. A value that rounds to zero
  prints as 0.000 whatever its sign. Whole numbers, such as degrees of
  freedom and sample sizes, print without a decimal part as before. A
  measured quantity that lands on a whole number, at the bound of its
  range or where it is fixed, printed as a whole number too, and where
  the table shows that it is measured it now prints to the decimal
  places of the values beside it
  ([`?dmar_tbl`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_tbl.md)
  gives the rule):

  - the limits of an interval and the estimate they belong to, and the
    other bounds DMAR names with `_lower` or `_upper`, such as an
    equivalence margin: a lower limit of exactly 0, which printed as 0,
    prints as 0.000 beside an upper limit of 0.083, and a factor
    variance fixed at 1 prints as 1.000 beside its interval;
  - a fit index, a power, a proportion or probability (the `pct_` rows
    of a sensitivity analysis among them), a mean, median, standard
    deviation, or other moment, a test statistic, a standard error, a
    noncentrality parameter, the delta and the weights of a model
    comparison, and a heterogeneity index, wherever they appear: a CFI
    of 1 prints as 1.000 beside a TLI of 1.012, a power of 1 as 1.000
    beside a power of 0.840, and a standard deviation of the interval
    widths of 0 as 0.000 beside their mean of 1.176;
  - a whole value in a column that also holds values that are not whole,
    unless the column is named for a count: an *F* of 4 prints as 4.000
    beside 4.270, and a standard error of 0 as 0.000 beside 0.050, while
    degrees of freedom adjusted for sphericity still print 2 beside
    1.830;
  - the columns a function names as measured: the loadings, intercepts,
    and standard deviations of
    [`dmacs()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmacs.md),
    where an intercept given as 2 prints as 2.000 beside one of 2.300.

  Elsewhere a whole value prints as a count, as before, since nothing in
  a long table says which of its other whole numbers are counts: a
  planning value given as 15 prints as 15. *p*-values (`digits_p`, four
  decimal places, with the “\< 0.0001” floor) and the information
  criteria a table names in its `fixed_terms` (`digits_fixed`, three
  decimal places) print as before.
  [`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html),
  [`format()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/format.html), `knit_print()`, and
  [`as_kable()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  show the same table, and the displays that lay out cells of their own
  (those of
  [`fa_exploratory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_exploratory.md),
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md),
  and
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md))
  and the lines beneath a table print measured values the same way: a
  CFI of 1 prints as 1.000 in the display of
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md)
  as it does in the table of
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md),
  and a congruence coefficient of 1 as 1.000 in the table of
  [`factor_congruence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_congruence.md)
  and in the matrix beneath it. For code written against 1.0.x:

  - The `digits` argument of
    [`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) and
    [`format()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/format.html) for a DMAR table,
    and `options(dmar.digits = )`, now count decimal places, not
    significant figures: `print(x, digits = 5)` showed five significant
    figures and now shows five decimal places, in the table and in the
    numbers a display writes beneath it. `digits` must be a whole number
    of 0 or more; a fractional or negative value, which
    [`signif()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Round.html) accepted, stops with
    an error that says so.
  - `format(x)` returns the new display strings.
  - No stored value changes. `x$value`, the other columns, `tidy()`, and
    `glance()` return the numbers at full precision, as before; read the
    column, or print with more decimal places (`print(x, digits = 8)`),
    to see more of a number than the table shows.
  - [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
    keeps its own `digits`, two decimal places by default, which
    `options(dmar.digits = )` does not change. It now writes a value
    that rounds to zero without a minus sign, as the table does: a lower
    limit of -0.004 reads “95% CI \[0.00, 0.55\]”, where it read
    “\[-0.00, 0.55\]”.

- **A knitted result table carries every line the console prints.**
  `knit_print()` and
  [`as_kable()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  wrote only the sum-of-squares type and the confidence level, so a
  knitted omega lost its denominator and residual lines and a knitted
  bootstrap interval its replication count (missing since 1.0.1). The
  tables of
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md),
  [`equivalence_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_rmsea.md),
  [`sem_residual_fit()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_residual_fit.md),
  [`sem_information_criteria()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_information_criteria.md),
  [`compare_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/compare_sem.md),
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md),
  and
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  print lines of their own with the table (which version of a fit
  measure was reported and why, the sample size convention, the verdict
  of a test, what a model comparison checked, how a fraction of missing
  information was estimated), and a sample size plan for incomplete data
  prints the missing data it assumed. The console print and the knitr
  methods now read one footer, which every class extends through an
  internal generic; a knitted table sets each footer line as a paragraph
  beneath it (two lines no longer run together), and
  [`as_kable()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  joins them into the caption. A knitted
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  table leaves out the columns the console leaves out, and a knitted
  [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  result is the summary the console prints (the first rows of each
  factor, the reasons values are missing or borrowed, the determinacy of
  each missing data pattern, how to read the intervals) rather than
  every row. The console’s confidence level is formatted by the same
  helper as the knitted one, which prints every conventional level as
  before, and a blank line now separates it from the lines after it. The
  lines above a
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  table (the measurement structure each factor’s constraints imply, also
  for [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md)
  and [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md))
  and above a
  [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  table (the effects and N, the groups, the full model’s deviance, AIC,
  BIC, and R squared, how to read each `p_value`), which print methods
  of their own wrote and `knit_print()` never called, are set as
  paragraphs before a knitted table and first in the
  [`as_kable()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  caption. No stored value changes.

- **[`as_kable()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  and `knit_print()` escape the lines they write for LaTeX and HTML.**
  knitr escapes a table’s cells and column names but writes a caption as
  it is given, and
  [`as_kable()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  passed the table’s lines to it without escaping them. With
  `format = "latex"`, or the default format in an `.Rnw` document, the
  “%” of “Confidence level: 95%” started a LaTeX comment that swallowed
  the caption’s closing brace: a LaTeX document did not compile, and an
  R Markdown PDF printed the table’s LaTeX source as text. An underscore
  in an item name (the residual correlation line of an omega) or an
  ampersand in a citation (the pairwise deletion line) stopped the
  compilation as well. The caption is now escaped for the format knitr
  renders, and `knit_print()` writes its lines in that format’s markup:
  escaped paragraphs and a verbatim block for LaTeX, where a “%” had
  silently cut the rest of its line, and `<p>` and `<pre>` elements for
  HTML. Markdown output, the default in R Markdown, is unchanged. A
  `caption` passed through `...`, which R refused as an argument matched
  twice, is refused with a message that says how to caption the table
  otherwise.

- **Two DMAR tables knitted in one chunk stay apart.** `knit_print()`
  wrote its output with no blank line before or after it, and knitr
  writes a chunk’s outputs with nothing between them. In a chunk with
  `echo = FALSE` that printed two tables, the second table’s header row
  was appended to the first table’s last footer line (“Confidence level:
  95%\|term \|value \|”). Pandoc then read that line as the second
  table’s header, in R Markdown’s HTML and PDF output alike: the footer
  became a header cell, the second table lost its last column name, and
  the first table lost its footer paragraph. The output is now set off
  by a blank line on each side, as knitr sets off a kable of its own.

- **[`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reads an interval held as `ci_lower` and `ci_upper`, names the
  estimate the interval belongs to, and reports the interval’s own
  confidence level.** In DMAR 1.0.x it read an interval only from rows
  or columns then named `lower_limit` and `upper_limit`, and told every
  table that held one as `ci_lower` and `ci_upper` (a row of
  [`contrast_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/contrast_test.md),
  [`adjusted_means()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/adjusted_means.md),
  [`content_validity_index()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/content_validity_index.md),
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
  or the coefficient table of
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) or
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md),
  and the `tidy()` results that hold their limits as `ci_lower` and
  `ci_upper`) that it “carries no confidence interval”. Every table now
  names its limits `ci_lower` and `ci_upper` (see Breaking Changes), so
  the rows of
  [`common_method_adjusted_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/common_method_adjusted_r.md),
  new in 1.1.0, are read as well, from the columns of a one-row table, a
  row beside a generic `estimate` column is labeled by its `term` (so
  `results_sentence(tidy(ci_smd(...)))` writes what
  `results_sentence(ci_smd(...))` writes), and a table with neither pair
  is told what was looked for. Two earlier defects change sentences it
  wrote before. The estimate of a wide table was its first numeric
  column other than the limits, `N`, and the p-value, so the first row
  of the
  [`?responder_analysis`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/responder_analysis.md)
  example read “n = 60.00, 95% CI \[0.38, 0.62\]” and the second row of
  `simple_effects_AB(aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth))`
  “F_value = 13.33, 95% CI \[0.04, 0.35\], p = 0.0006”; the estimate is
  now the `estimate` or `value` column when there is one and otherwise
  the first numeric column that is not a limit, standard error, test
  statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, confidence level, or count
  (“estimate = 0.50” and “eta_squared_partial = 0.20” there). And the
  confidence level was read from the table’s attribute alone, which the
  reliability family does not set, so a 90% interval for omega was
  written “95% CI”; it is now read from the attribute, the `conf_level`
  row, or the `conf_level` column. A `tidy()` row that the default
  method builds from a wide table was labeled “estimate” through 1.0.1
  and is now labeled with the quantity it holds (see the entry on the
  default `tidy()` below). Every other change to a sentence is one of
  the entries that follow.

- **Every table that forms a confidence interval records its level, and
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  states no level a table does not record.**
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  took 95% when a table recorded no level, and many recorded none:

  - [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
    and
    [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
    (and `ci_eta_squared_partial()`, which this release removes);
  - [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
    and
    [`pairwise_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/pairwise_within.md);
  - every interval formed from `alpha_lower` and `alpha_upper`
    ([`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md),
    [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md),
    [`ci_mahalanobis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_mahalanobis.md),
    [`ci_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
    [`ci_R()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
    [`ci_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rc.md),
    [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md),
    [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md),
    [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md),
    [`ci_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sm.md),
    [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md),
    [`ci_smd_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd_c.md),
    [`ci_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_src.md));
  - and the `tidy()` and `glance()` results of every table the default
    methods handle.

  A 90% interval was therefore written “95% CI”. With
  `fit <- aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth)`,
  `results_sentence(ci_eta_squared(fit, conf_level = 0.90)[1, ], digits = 3)`
  gave “eta_squared = 0.224, 95% CI \[0.073, 0.350\]”, where the 95%
  interval is \[0.053, 0.377\]. With
  `set.seed(1); x <- rnorm(40, 0.5); y <- rnorm(40)`,
  `results_sentence(vargha_delaney_A(x, y, conf_level = 0.90), digits = 3)`
  gave “A = 0.674, 95% CI \[0.565, 0.767\], p = 0.0051”, where the 95%
  interval is \[0.543, 0.782\].

  Each of these tables now records its level: `conf_level`, or
  `1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper` when the tail areas are given, as
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md),
  [`ci_pvaf()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_pvaf.md),
  [`ci_snr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_snr.md),
  and
  [`ci_srsnr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_srsnr.md)
  already did.

  - The ANOVA intervals,
    [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md),
    [`pairwise_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/pairwise_within.md),
    and the intervals formed from tail areas print that level beneath
    the table, which they did not.
  - [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
    and
    [`pairwise_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/pairwise_within.md)
    return DMAR tables and print as the rest do; their columns are
    unchanged.
    [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
    gains `tidy()` and `glance()` methods whose row is named “A”.
  - `pairwise_within(bonferroni_ci = TRUE)` records `conf_level`, the
    level its Bonferroni intervals hold jointly, as
    `contrast_test(adjust = "bonferroni")` and the post hoc intervals
    record theirs. The line beneath the table of both functions names
    the adjustment and the level of each interval: “Confidence level:
    95%, simultaneous across the 3 comparisons (Bonferroni: each
    interval at 98.33%)”. With
    `set.seed(1); Y <- matrix(rnorm(60), 20) + rep(c(0, 0.3, 0.6), each = 20)`,
    the second row of
    `pairwise_within(Y, bonferroni_ci = TRUE, conf_level = 0.90)`, whose
    interval \[0.02, 1.07\] is the 96.67% interval of that comparison,
    was written “95% CI”; it is written “90% CI”.
  - [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
    recorded the default 0.95 beside the interval that
    `alpha_lower = 0.05` and `alpha_upper = 0.05` define; it records
    0.90.
  - The default `tidy()` of a wide table with an interval adds a
    `conf_level` column (`NA` when no interval was formed). The default
    `tidy()` of a long table with an interval adds a `conf_level` column
    that holds the level on the rows of the interval and `NA` on every
    other row. Those rows are its estimate and its two limits, or an
    estimate’s `<estimate>_ci_lower` and `<estimate>_ci_upper` rows at
    that interval’s own level. The rows therefore carry their level when
    `tidy()` results are stacked with
    [`rbind()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html): the rows of
    `tidy(ci_proportion(30, 60, conf_level = 0.99))` stacked under
    `tidy(ci_proportion(12, 40, conf_level = 0.90))` give “proportion =
    0.50, 99% CI \[0.34, 0.66\]”.
  - The default `glance()` of a long table with an interval adds
    `estimand` and `conf_level` columns (see the next entry):
    `results_sentence(glance(ci_proportion(30, 100, conf_level = 0.90)))`
    gives “proportion = 0.30, 90% CI \[0.23, 0.38\]”.
  - The tables
    [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
    reads for the first time in 1.1.0 carry their level as well. The
    coefficient tables of
    [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
    [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
    record it. The `tidy()` results of the reliability family,
    [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md),
    [`content_validity_index()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/content_validity_index.md),
    [`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md),
    [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md),
    [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md), and
    [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
    (with `conf.int = TRUE`) carry a `conf_level` column. For
    `m <- mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning, data = holzinger_swineford, conf_level = 0.90)`,
    `results_sentence(m$coef_table[2, ])` reads “t7_sentence = 0.32, 90%
    CI \[0.26, 0.38\], p \< 0.0001”.

  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  now refuses a table that records no level, such as one assembled by
  hand, unless its new argument `conf_level` gives the level. It also
  refuses a `conf_level` that differs from the level the table records.
  No interval changes.

- **[`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reports the estimate a long table’s interval belongs to.** In a table
  that holds its interval in `ci_lower` and `ci_upper` rows, the
  estimate was the first other row, and two tables list another quantity
  first.

  - `correction_for_attenuation(r = .3, reliability_x = .8, reliability_y = .7, N = 200)`
    gave “correlation_observed = 0.30, 95% CI \[0.22, 0.56\]”: the
    observed correlation beside the interval of the corrected one, .401.
  - `proportion_of_superiority(smd = .5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50)` gave “smd
    = 0.50, 95% CI \[0.54, 0.82\]”, an interval that does not contain
    the estimate it names.

  The two tables now name the row their interval belongs to in a
  `ci_estimate` attribute, which
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reads: “correlation_corrected = 0.40, 95% CI \[0.22, 0.56\]” and
  “proportion_of_superiority = 0.69, 95% CI \[0.54, 0.82\]”. Their rows
  are unchanged. The `tidy()` of a long table names the estimate in its
  rows, through its `conf_level` column, and its `glance()` names the
  column that holds the estimate in an `estimand` column, so the
  sentence of either is the table’s own. Through 1.0.1 the `glance()`
  sentence of the attenuation table also named the observed correlation.

- **[`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reports the TOST p-value of an equivalence test.** It appended the
  first p-value row of a long table. The tables of
  [`equivalence_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_r.md),
  [`equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_smd.md),
  and
  [`equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_c.md)
  list the p-values of the two one-sided tests before the TOST p-value,
  so a result that is not equivalent was written with the p-value of one
  one-sided test.

  - `equivalence_r(r = .15, N = 300, cor_lower = .2, cor_upper = .2)`,
    whose TOST p-value is .187 (not equivalent), gave “r = 0.15, 90% CI
    \[0.06, 0.24\], p = \< 0.0001” (the p-value of the lower test,
    5e-10). It now gives “r = 0.15, 90% CI \[0.06, 0.24\], p = 0.1870”.
  - For
    `equivalence_smd(smd = .3, n_1 = 100, n_2 = 100, smd_lower = .5, smd_upper = .5)`
    the sentence gives p = 0.0806 where it gave the lower test’s 3e-08.
  - For example 3 of
    [`?equivalence_c`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_c.md)
    it gives p = 0.0393 where it gave the lower test’s 3.9e-07.

  The three tables name `p_tost` in a `p_sentence` attribute, which
  `tidy()` and `glance()` carry, so their sentences give the same
  p-value. The meta-analysis tables, whose first p-value row is the
  pooled p-value, are unchanged.

- **[`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  writes “p \< 0.0001”, not “p = \< 0.0001”.** A p-value below the floor
  of
  [`format_p()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/format_p.md)
  was appended as “, p =” and then “\< 0.0001”. The sentence now writes
  the bound:
  `summary_t_test(mean_1 = 2, sd_1 = 1, n_1 = 30, mean_2 = 0, sd_2 = 1, n_2 = 30)`
  gives “mean_difference = 2.00, 95% CI \[1.48, 2.52\], p \< 0.0001”.
  Larger p-values are written as before.

- **The default `tidy()` of a wide table with an interval takes as its
  estimate the column the interval belongs to, and its sentence names
  that quantity.** It took the first numeric column. A row of
  [`simple_effects_AB()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simple_effects_AB.md)
  therefore gave its *F* statistic beside the limits for partial eta
  squared: for
  `simple_effects_AB(aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth))`,
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  on its second `tidy()` row wrote “estimate = 13.33, 95% CI \[0.04,
  0.35\], p = 0.0006”, where the estimate is 0.20. A table whose
  `estimate` column follows a count
  ([`responder_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/responder_analysis.md))
  lost the count.

  In a table that carries an interval, the estimate is now the table’s
  own `estimate` (or `value`) column. Otherwise it is the first numeric
  column that is not a limit, standard error, test statistic, degrees of
  freedom, *p*-value, confidence level, or count, the rule
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  follows. The other numeric columns follow under their own names (the
  *F* statistic as `F_value`, the count as `n`).

  When the estimate comes from a column with a name of its own, an
  `estimand` column after `estimate` keeps the name, and
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  labels the row with it; otherwise it labels the row with its `term`.
  The `tidy()` row’s sentence is then the table’s own.
  [`content_validity_index()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/content_validity_index.md)
  also gains the `estimand` column `"i_cvi"`:
  `content_validity_index(matrix(c(4, 4, 3, 4, 3, 1, 4, 3), nrow = 2), conf_level = .90)`
  gives “i_cvi = 1.00, 90% CI \[0.47, 1.00\]” on its first raw or tidy
  row, where 1.0.1 refused both as carrying no interval. A tidy FMI row
  labels its estimate `fmi` rather than the parameter’s name. For the
  existing examples:

  - “eta_squared_partial = 0.20, 95% CI \[0.04, 0.35\], p = 0.0006” for
    that row;
  - “D2 = 0.50, 90% CI \[0.03, 1.03\]” for
    `ci_mahalanobis(D2 = .5, n_1 = 40, n_2 = 40, p = 3, conf_level = .9)`;
  - `kappa` for
    [`fleiss_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fleiss_kappa.md)
    and
    [`cohen_kappa()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cohen_kappa.md),
    `mean_difference` for
    [`pairwise_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/pairwise_within.md),
    and `ave` for
    [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md);
  - the row’s `term` for
    [`icc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/icc.md)
    (“ICC(2,1)”),
    [`responder_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/responder_analysis.md)
    (“control”), and
    [`adjusted_means()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/adjusted_means.md)
    (the group).

  1.0.1 labeled the others “estimate”; it wrote no sentence for the
  `tidy()` rows of
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  and
  [`adjusted_means()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/adjusted_means.md),
  which hold their limits as `ci_lower` and `ci_upper`, and
  [`pairwise_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/pairwise_within.md)
  had no `tidy()` method. The `term` column is unchanged. A table
  without an interval is tidied as before.

- **The intervals of
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  for the effects of a fit with an `Error()` term are converted with the
  size of each effect’s stratum.** DMAR 1.0.x (in
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  and in `ci_eta_squared_partial()`, which this release removes)
  converted the noncentrality limits of every effect of an `aovlist` fit
  into limits for partial eta squared with the total number of rows,
  `lambda / (lambda + N)`. Within subjects that put the interval on a
  smaller quantity than the one the partial eta squared beside it
  estimates: for the three IQ occasions of `pygmalion` analyzed in
  [`vignette("DMAR")`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/articles/DMAR.md),
  930 rows against *F*(2, 618), the 95% interval was \[0.111, 0.194\]
  and lay below the estimate of 0.212. Each effect is now converted with
  the size of its own stratum. Within subjects that size is the
  stratum’s total degrees of freedom, here 2 + 618 = 620, which gives
  \[0.157, 0.265\]; the within-subjects example of
  [`?ci_eta_squared`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  goes from \[0.015, 0.322\] to \[0.023, 0.417\]. In the
  between-subjects stratum of a mixed design it is the number of
  subjects: with the expectancy treatment added to the `pygmalion`
  analysis as a between-subjects factor, the upper limit for treatment,
  converted with the 310 children rather than the 930 rows, goes from
  0.018 to 0.052. Fits without an `Error()` term convert with the total
  sample size and the raw-argument interface with the `N` it is given,
  as before, and their results are unchanged; for an effect tested
  between subjects the total sample size makes the interval exact for
  the population partial eta squared that Steiger (2004), Kelley (2007),
  and Smithson (2001, 2003) define. Smithson’s conversion with the
  effect and error degrees of freedom plus one, which Fidler and
  Thompson (2001) also used, agrees with that definition only in a
  one-way design. The help of
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  gives the reasons and the literature, which does not settle the
  within-subjects case. The raw-argument interface now accepts an `N` as
  small as `df_effect + df_error`, the size of a within-subjects stratum
  that tests one effect, which DMAR 1.0.x refused. It does not warn when
  `N` is the number of rows of a within-subjects design, since it cannot
  tell that number from the total sample size of a between-subjects
  factorial design.

- **The parametric interval of
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  for the effects of a fit with an `Error()` term is converted with the
  size of each effect’s stratum.** DMAR 1.0.x converted the
  noncentrality limits of every effect of an `aovlist` fit with the
  total number of rows, and within subjects the interval was for a
  smaller quantity than the one the estimate estimates: for the three IQ
  occasions of `pygmalion`, the 95% interval was \[0.019, 0.037\]
  against an estimate of 0.041. Each effect is now converted with the
  size of its stratum, as
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  converts it (the entry above), which gives \[0.029, 0.054\]. With that
  size the conversion maps each limit to the value of the population
  generalized eta squared of Olejnik and Algina

  2003. when the ratio of the other sums of squares in its denominator
        to the effect’s error sum of squares is at the value it
        converges to. In the between-subjects stratum of a mixed design
        the size is the number of subjects: with the expectancy
        treatment added to the `pygmalion` analysis between subjects,
        the upper limit for treatment goes from 0.015 to 0.044. The
        within-subjects example of
        [`?ci_eta_squared_generalized`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
        goes from \[0.005, 0.145\] to \[0.008, 0.203\]. Fits without an
        `Error()` term are converted with the number of observations, as
        before, and their intervals are unchanged. The help now sets out
        the quantity the conversion is made for and says that the
        interval cannot be exact when anything measured, or another
        stratum’s residual, enters the denominator: generalized eta
        squared then depends on a second parameter besides the
        noncentrality parameter, which alone determines the distribution
        of the effect’s *F*, and the interval takes that parameter’s
        sample value as known. The *F* interface now accepts an `N` as
        small as `df_effect + df_error`, the size of a within-subjects
        stratum that tests one effect, which DMAR 1.0.x refused.

- **[`eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared_generalized.md)
  and
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  stop when an effect of a fit with an `Error()` term is tested in more
  than one stratum.** When observations are missing within subjects, or
  a covariate varies within them,
  [`aov()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/aov.html) divides the effect’s sum
  of squares among strata and tests the effect in each of them. DMAR
  1.0.x then returned a row for every stratum each time the effect’s
  name came up, each computed from the effect’s share in the first
  stratum: for 20 subjects in two groups observed three times, with four
  observations missing, `aov(y ~ group * time + Error(subject / time))`
  gave nine rows for its five tests, `time` and `group:time` four times
  each, and the parametric interval stopped with an error from inside
  the noncentral *F* computation (“the condition has length \> 1”). No
  one stratum’s share is the effect’s sum of squares, and Olejnik and
  Algina (2003) define the estimate for balanced designs, so both
  functions now stop and name the effects and strata involved. A fit in
  which every subject is observed equally often in every within-subjects
  condition, and every covariate is constant within subjects, tests each
  effect in one stratum, whatever the sizes of the between-subjects
  groups, and its results are unchanged.

- **[`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  gives the parametric interval from sums of squares, and
  [`eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared_generalized.md)
  accepts the degrees of freedom that come with them.** The interval
  needs `df_effect`, `df_error`, and `N` beside the sums of squares.
  Without them DMAR 1.0.x stopped and asked for them; with them it
  stopped with “‘F_effect’ must be a single non-negative number”,
  because
  [`eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared_generalized.md),
  which computes the estimate, then read the call as the *F* interface
  as well; called directly with the same arguments, it stopped the same
  way. The sums of squares never gave an interval, and with the degrees
  of freedom present they gave no estimate either, whatever the method.
  Both functions now take `df_effect` and `df_error` with the sums of
  squares and read only `F_effect`, `F_observed`, and `df_observed` as
  the *F* interface. The estimate is computed from the sums of squares
  alone, which need no degrees of freedom, and the interval from the *F*
  they imply, (`SS_effect` / `df_effect`) / (`SS_error` / `df_error`),
  with `N` checked as the *F* interface checks it. That *F* is the
  effect’s test when `SS_error` is the sum of squares of the effect’s
  error term: the residual in a design without an `Error()` term, and
  otherwise the residual of the stratum in which the effect is tested,
  with the residuals of the other strata in `SS_observed`, beside the
  measured sources (Olejnik & Algina, 2003). The help of both functions
  now says so, and that each *F* of the *F* interface divides by the
  effect’s error mean square. For the one-way analysis of IQ gain by
  grade in `pygmalion`, the sums of squares of the
  [`anova()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/anova.html) table, with `N = 310`,
  give 0.118 \[0.048, 0.176\], the row of the fitted model and of the
  *F* interface. Given no fitted model and both interfaces,
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  answers, as DMAR 1.0.x did, when they describe the same test: the *F*
  that the sums of squares imply for the effect, and the ratio of
  `SS_observed` to `SS_error`, agree with the *F* interface’s to a
  relative tolerance of 1e-6, the tolerance
  [`eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared_generalized.md)
  applies to the two estimates, and the interval is formed from the
  *F*-values. When they disagree it now stops, whatever the method, and
  so it does when only part of the *F* interface comes with the sums of
  squares; a fitted model still sets every raw argument aside with a
  warning, and
  [`eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared_generalized.md),
  which computes no interval, still accepts the two interfaces together
  when they give the same estimate. DMAR 1.0.x accepted both interfaces
  whenever they gave the same estimate and built the interval from the
  *F*-values, but the two can agree on the estimate and still imply
  different *F* statistics for the effect. Sums of squares of 100 for
  the effect, 70 for the measured sources, and 200 for the error, on 2
  and 50 degrees of freedom, imply an *F* of 12.5; an *F* of 25 for the
  effect and of 85 for a measured source on 1 degree of freedom give the
  same estimate, 0.270. With `N = 53` the sums of squares give the
  interval \[0.089, 0.413\] and the *F*-values \[0.127, 0.381\], which
  DMAR 1.0.x reported for the two together. Both functions now also
  refuse a sum of squares, an *F*-value, or a number of degrees of
  freedom that is missing or infinite, and
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md)
  an infinite `N`. DMAR 1.0.x stopped on most missing values with R’s
  “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, returned an estimate of 0 or
  `NaN` for an infinite value, and gave the *F* interface the interval
  \[0, 0\] for an infinite `N`.

- **The partial omega squared of each effect of a fit with an `Error()`
  term is computed with the size of its stratum, and the stratum is
  named.** DMAR 1.0.x (`omega_squared_partial()`, which this release
  removes; `omega_squared(fit, estimand = "partial")` is its call)
  computed `df_effect (F - 1) / (df_effect (F - 1) + N)` with the total
  number of rows: for the three IQ occasions of `pygmalion`, 930 rows
  against *F*(2, 618), it gave 0.150, below the partial eta squared of
  0.212 and its interval \[0.157, 0.265\]. With the stratum’s 2 + 618 =
  620 the estimate is 0.209, an estimate of the quantity whose interval
  `ci_eta_squared(estimand = "partial")` gives; for treatment in the
  mixed design of the entry above, computed with the 310 children, it
  goes from 0.004 to 0.012. The value with the number of rows is the
  partial omega squared that Olejnik and Algina (2003) compute for a
  repeated measures factor, and the raw-argument interface given that
  number as `N` still returns it. The table of an `aovlist` fit gains a
  `stratum` column after the estimate, as in
  [`eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/eta_squared.md),
  which the description of the function promised; its `N` column still
  reports the number of observations, and the help says how to find the
  size of a stratum from
  [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html) of the fit. Fits
  without an `Error()` term are unchanged. The raw-argument interfaces
  of
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md)
  and
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
  now accept an `N` as small as `df_effect + df_error`, which DMAR 1.0.x
  refused, so that
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
  gives a row’s estimate and its interval from the row’s *F*, its
  degrees of freedom, and the size of its stratum, and
  [`omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/omega_squared.md)
  gives the same estimate.
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
  now takes an `aovlist` fit itself (see Total and Partial Eta Squared
  and Omega Squared).

- **The `tidy()` of an ANOVA effect size table returns every effect.**
  `tidy()` of
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md),
  `ci_eta_squared_partial()`,
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md),
  and
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md)
  in DMAR 1.0.x returned the first row of the table alone, so the
  `tidy()` of a factorial fit dropped every other effect, and `glance()`
  was the same row. For
  `fit <- aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth)`,
  `tidy(ci_eta_squared_partial(fit, conf_level = 0.90))` gave one row,
  the supp effect (.224 \[.073, .350\]);
  `tidy(ci_eta_squared(fit, estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90))`
  gives three, adding factor(dose) (.773 \[.659, .814\]) and the
  interaction (.132 \[.011, .246\]).

  The `term` names the effect size and, for
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md)
  and
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md),
  its estimand (`eta_squared_partial` or `eta_squared_total`, where
  1.0.1 named `eta_squared`; see One Function for Each ANOVA Effect
  Size), and an `effect` column after it names the effect; a `stratum`
  column follows it for a fit with an `Error()` term. A table of one
  effect and one estimand, as from summary statistics, therefore gives
  the row it gave with the `effect` column added. Its `glance()` is that
  row when `tidy()` gives one row. Otherwise it is one row with the
  effect size (`term`, the estimands separated by a comma when there are
  two), the number of effects (`n_effects`), `N`, and `conf_level`.

- **[`manova_split_plot()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/manova_split_plot.md),
  [`mixed_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mixed_anova.md),
  and
  [`anova_within_two_way()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/anova_within_two_way.md)
  return DMAR tables.** DMAR 1.0.x returned each result as a plain
  `data.frame`, so `class(x)` was `"data.frame"` and the table printed
  through
  [`print.data.frame()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.dataframe.html),
  which formats a column of numbers as a whole: one small *p*-value put
  the whole `p_value` column in scientific notation. In the example on
  the help page of
  [`mixed_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mixed_anova.md),
  the three *p*-values printed as 2.148782e-05, 1.817787e-12, and
  9.565106e-01. Each function now returns its table with the class
  `c("dmar_tbl", "data.frame")`, as
  [`anova_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/anova_within.md)
  and
  [`factorial_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factorial_anova.md)
  do, and it prints through the `dmar_tbl` display layer: whole numbers
  such as degrees of freedom without a decimal part, other values to 3
  decimal places, and *p*-values to 4 decimal places, with one below
  0.0001 printed as “\< 0.0001” (in that example, \< 0.0001, \< 0.0001,
  and 0.9565). Adding the class changes nothing else in the object, and
  `as.data.frame(x)` returns the table as a plain data frame. For
  [`mixed_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mixed_anova.md)
  and
  [`anova_within_two_way()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/anova_within_two_way.md)
  that is the 1.0.x data frame itself
  ([`identical()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/identical.html) to it): the
  columns, rows, and values are unchanged, as is the
  `sum_of_squares_type` attribute of
  [`mixed_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mixed_anova.md).
  For
  [`manova_split_plot()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/manova_split_plot.md)
  the columns and rows are those of 1.0.x, but not every value: its
  default Type III `B` rows now test the within-subjects main effect,
  where those of 1.0.x tested a simple effect (see the entry above on
  that test), and its other rows, with the `B` rows under `ss_type = 2`,
  agree with those of 1.0.x to rounding error (within 1e-12, relative,
  on the designs compared) rather than exactly. For code written against
  1.0.x:

  - `is.data.frame(x)` and `inherits(x, "data.frame")` are `TRUE` as
    before, and `x$p_value` and the other columns hold the table’s
    numbers at full precision. Code that tests the class itself sees the
    new one: `identical(class(x), "data.frame")` is `FALSE`;
    `class(x) == "data.frame"` has length 2, so `if ()` on it stops with
    “the condition has length \> 1” in R 4.2.0 and later (earlier
    versions warn and use the first element, `FALSE`); and against a
    saved 1.0.x result of
    [`mixed_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mixed_anova.md)
    or
    [`anova_within_two_way()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/anova_within_two_way.md),
    [`identical()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/identical.html) is `FALSE`
    and [`all.equal()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/all.equal.html) reports a
    difference in the class alone.
  - The data frame methods work on the table as they did on the plain
    data frame. `x[i, ]`,
    [`subset()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/subset.html), and
    [`rbind()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html) with `x` first keep
    the class, so their results print the new way too;
    [`merge()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/merge.html) still returns a plain
    data frame, and [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html)
    and [`as.matrix()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/matrix.html) return what
    they return for the plain data frame.
    [`print()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/print.html) and
    [`format()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/format.html) now dispatch to the
    `dmar_tbl` methods, so `format(x)` returns the display strings
    described above rather than those of
    [`format.data.frame()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/format.html). In an R
    Markdown document a table that a chunk prints is set by
    [`knit_print.dmar_tbl()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
    as a [`knitr::kable()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/knitr/man/kable.html)
    table of those strings where 1.0.x showed console text;
    `knitr::kable(x)` called directly formats the numbers itself, as
    before.
  - `tidy()` and `glance()` answer through the default methods for a
    wide DMAR table (see
    [`?dmar_tidiers`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_tidiers.md)).
    `tidy()` gives one row per row of the table, its `term` joining the
    label columns (`effect` with `statistic_name`, `denominator`, or
    `adjustment`), its `estimate` the first numeric column
    (`statistic_value`, `ss`, or `F_value`), and the other numeric
    columns after it under their own names. The last row of the `tidy()`
    of
    [`manova_split_plot()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/manova_split_plot.md)
    is the table’s record of the sum-of-squares type: its `term` is
    `"sum_of_squares_type:NA"` (the row’s `statistic_name` is `NA`), its
    `estimate` the type, 2 or 3, and its other columns `NA`, so code
    that summarizes the estimates of the tests leaves that row out, as
    it would from the table. `glance()` gives one row: the number of
    rows (`n_terms`), with `conf_level` and `B_used` `NA`, since no
    interval or bootstrap is formed. For the plain data frame of 1.0.x
    the generics package has no method, and where broom was loaded its
    data frame tidiers, which broom has deprecated, answered: `tidy()`
    stopped with an error on the character columns, and `glance()` gave
    `nrow`, `ncol`, `complete.obs`, and `na.fraction`.
    [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
    refuses these tables as before, since none holds a confidence
    interval.
    [`as_kable()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md),
    which stopped on the plain data frame of 1.0.x with “no applicable
    method”, now returns a
    [`knitr::kable()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/knitr/man/kable.html) table
    of the display strings, and
    [`dmar_metadata()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_metadata.md),
    new in 1.1.0 and taking only a DMAR table, accepts these tables.

  [`ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ancova.md)
  already returned a `dmar_tbl` in DMAR 1.0.x, and its result is
  unchanged.

- **`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(estimator = "omega")` returns
  intervals.** Since 1.0.0 it asked
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  for the `"mlr"` interval under the default observed denominator, for
  which no Wald interval is defined; every replication failed silently,
  and the table showed no widths and a non-coverage of zero. Omega is
  now computed with `denominator = "model_implied"`, the coefficient the
  planner’s interval is built on, with the `"ml"` interval the plan
  describes (see the entry on the interval its plan was made for). A
  replication that returns no interval is now set aside rather than
  counted as covering the true value; the proportions are over the
  replications that returned one, one warning states how many were set
  aside and why, and a run in which none returned an interval stops with
  the reason. The rule changes nothing for alpha with Bonett’s interval,
  its default through 1.0.1.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  evaluates the assurance plan at the planner’s defaults.** With an
  assurance, the plan whose N is simulated was searched at 50 and 200
  replications (`G_initial` and `G`, then `initial_iter` and
  `final_iter`) against the planner’s defaults of 500 and 5000, and the
  noise let a size below the one the assurance needs pass by chance. For
  four parallel items of reliability .80, a width of .15, and an
  assurance of .80, the evaluated N ranged from 93 to 101 over seeds 1
  to 30 (`set.seed(s)` before each call; mean 96.9) against 98 to 101
  (mean 99.2) at the defaults, so a correctly specified plan seemed to
  fall short of its assurance. The plan now runs at the planner’s
  defaults, as the rest of the sensitivity family does, which adds about
  a second. With `ci_method = "ml"` the replications’ alpha intervals
  change as
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)’s
  do, slightly for the unit variance items simulated here (mean width
  .1531 to .1527 in 1,000 replications at N = 74, after
  `set.seed(113)`); Bonett’s interval, the default through 1.0.1, is
  unchanged.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md)
  evaluates the interval its plan was made for.** The plan is
  [`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)’s
  for the parallel model with the normal theory interval, a Wald
  interval with the van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000) variance. The
  replications, however, computed Bonett’s (2002) interval for alpha and
  the `"mlr"` interval for omega, so a correctly specified plan was
  judged by an interval it was not made for. The default `ci_method` is
  now `"ml"` for both estimators, with complete or incomplete data. For
  alpha that is `reliability_alpha(ci_method = "ml")`, whose variance at
  a population of parallel items is the compound symmetry form the plan
  uses. For omega it is
  `reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml")`,
  whose delta method variance equals that form there to machine
  precision. Under missing data these are the Wald intervals with the
  FIML standard error that the `fmi` adjustment plans for.

  - Take four items, a true and planned reliability of .80, a width of
    .15, and an assurance of .80, with `set.seed(113)` before each call
    (`true_reliability = .8, supposed_reliability = .8, n_items = 4, width = .15, assurance = .8, G = 2000`).
    The plan of 99 cases gives intervals no wider than .15 in 81.3
    percent of the 2,000 replications, against 76.75 percent with
    `ci_method = "bonett"` on the same draws, and a mean width of .1312
    against .1346.
  - For omega (`estimator = "omega", G = 1000`), which returned no
    intervals in 1.0.x, the default gives 83.3 percent against 81.9 with
    `ci_method = "mlr"`.
  - The first example on the help page (`G = 20`) goes from a mean width
    of .1685 and a proportion of .40 to .1630 and .45.
  - For alpha, naming `ci_method = "bonett"` reproduces 1.0.x without an
    assurance, apart from the replications the entry on clamped limits
    describes. With an assurance the plan is now searched at the
    planner’s defaults (see the entry on the assurance plan), which
    draws other replications: the call above gave 78.65 percent and a
    mean width of .1337 in 1.0.1. Any other interval can still be named.

- **Noncentral chi square intervals stay right for a statistic in the
  millions.** R’s [`pchisq()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Chisquare.html)
  with a noncentrality stops its series after 10^6 terms, and above a
  noncentrality of about 2e6 it returns wrong probabilities (0 where the
  value is .19 at 3e6), with a warning that was suppressed.
  [`ci_nc_chisq()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_chisq.md),
  and through it
  [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md),
  [`ecvi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ecvi.md), and
  the intervals of
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  and
  [`equivalence_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_rmsea.md),
  then returned limits collapsed onto one value below the statistic. For
  a statistic of 3e6 on 3000 df the 90 percent limits were 2979734 twice
  and are now 2991307 and 3002700; the RMSEA interval at N = 1e5, with
  the multiplier N, was \[0.09966, 0.09966\] around an estimate of
  0.09995 and is now \[0.09986, 0.10004\]. Above a noncentrality of 1e5,
  the distribution function is now summed as the Poisson mixture of
  central chi square distributions it is, accurate to rounding. At and
  below 1e5 nothing changes.
  [`equivalence_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_rmsea.md)
  and the close fit tests of
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  use the same function: a bound of .10 at a statistic of 3e6 had a
  p-value of 0 and was declared met, where the p-value is .193. For a
  fitted model,
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  computes the limits and tests itself once the statistic, or the
  noncentrality of a close fit bound, exceeds 1e5. The robust limits and
  tests of a FIML, ordered data, or two-stage fit, which it cannot
  rebuild, become `NA` with a warning past 1e6.

- **[`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md)
  gains `sample_size_convention = c("N-1", "N")`.** It sets the
  multiplier with which the reported RMSEA was computed; lavaan’s
  default likelihood and Mplus use N. The default keeps every earlier
  result. The help page now says correctly that the lower limit of the
  90 percent interval settles the test of close fit and the upper limit
  the test of not close fit (it had described the upper limit as the
  test of close fit), and that the function assumes one group.

- **[`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md)
  refuses zero degrees of freedom and a sample size that leaves no
  multiplier.** A saturated model (lavaan reports an RMSEA of 0 on 0 df)
  had returned limits of Inf with no warning, the lower one above the
  estimate. N = 1 under the default convention had given an upper limit
  of Inf, and N between 0 and 1 an `NA`. `df` must now be greater than
  0; it need not be whole, since a mean and variance adjusted statistic
  has fractional degrees of freedom. `N` must make the multiplier
  positive. An invalid `conf_level` is refused in its own name rather
  than as `alpha_lower` and `alpha_upper`.

- **[`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md)
  forms a 90 percent interval by default.** The default `conf_level` is
  0.90, where DMAR 1.0.x had 0.95, since a 100(1 - 2 alpha) percent
  interval decides the one-sided tests of close and not close fit at
  level alpha (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996, p. 136), so the
  limits of the 90 percent interval are those tests at .05 (see Every
  RMSEA Interval at 90 Percent by Default). For an RMSEA of .035 on 40
  df with N = 425, the interval of the help page’s first example, the
  limits were .008 and .055 and are .015 and .052. `conf_level = 0.95`
  restores the 1.0.x interval. An interval given by `alpha_lower` and
  `alpha_upper` is unchanged.

- **[`ss_aipe_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea.md)
  plans a 90 percent interval by default.** The default `conf_level` is
  0.90, where DMAR 1.0.x had 0.95, so that the plan is for the interval
  [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md)
  now forms by default. A lower level needs a smaller sample for the
  same width: for an RMSEA of .045 on 5 df and a width of .060,
  `necessary_N` was 1068 and is 802. `conf_level = 0.95` restores the
  1.0.x plan.

- **[`ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity.md)
  simulates 90 percent intervals by default and forms each as lavaan
  does, from the replication’s statistic with lavaan’s multiplier.**

  - The default `conf_level` is 0.90, where DMAR 1.0.x had 0.95, as in
    [`ss_aipe_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea.md)
    and
    [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md).
    `conf_level = 0.95` restores the level.
  - Each replication’s interval was formed from lavaan’s RMSEA, which
    lavaan computes with the multiplier N under its default likelihood,
    as though it had been computed with N - 1, the default convention of
    [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md).
    The interval matched neither convention and was slightly too wide,
    that of a sample one case smaller. It is now formed with lavaan’s
    own multiplier (N under the default likelihood, N - 1 under
    `likelihood = "wishart"` or a least squares estimator passed through
    `...`). This was a defect, and no argument restores it.
  - Each interval was also formed from the replication’s RMSEA, which
    lavaan truncates at 0 when the statistic is at or below its degrees
    of freedom. From an RMSEA of 0 the statistic can be rebuilt only as
    equal to its degrees of freedom (see
