    [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md)),
    so every such replication was given the interval of that statistic,
    wider than the interval of its own. Each interval is now formed from
    the replication’s chi square statistic, as lavaan and
    [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
    form it, and equals the interval lavaan reports for the sample
    whatever the statistic; its upper limit is 0 when the statistic is
    at or below the (1 - `conf_level`) / 2 quantile of the central chi
    square, the convention the two share. A model that fits well, many
    of whose replications fall below their degrees of freedom, gets
    narrower intervals: for the two-factor population of the help page
    fit by its own two-factor model (8 df), with N = 200, `G = 40`,
    `conf_level = 0.90`, and `set.seed(113)`, 21 of the 40 statistics
    fell below 8, the mean width, .0920 in DMAR 1.0.x, is .0802, and the
    proportion of intervals narrower than a width of .05, 0 before, is
    .10. This was a defect too, and no argument restores it. A
    replication whose statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom gets the
    interval it had, so a markedly misspecified model, such as that of
    the help page’s example, is not affected.
  - The simulated sample is still the planner’s `necessary_N`, the size
    a study would collect. The width depends on the sample size only
    through the multiplier, and
    [`ss_aipe_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea.md)
    plans with N - 1 (Kelley & Lai, 2011), so under lavaan’s default,
    whose multiplier is N, the realized intervals are a little narrower
    than the planned width, by an amount of order 1/N.
  - For the help page’s example (a population RMSEA of .204 on 9 df, a
    width of .05, `set.seed(113)`, `G = 20`), DMAR 1.0.x evaluated a
    sample of 695 and reported a mean width of .05002; the default now
    evaluates 493 for the 90 percent interval, with a mean width of
    .04990, and `conf_level = 0.95` evaluates 695, with a mean width of
    .04998.

- **`ecvi(fit)` divides by the multiplier lavaan used to form the
  statistic.** For a fit under `likelihood = "wishart"` or a least
  squares estimator (GLS, WLS, ULS, DWLS) that multiplier is N - G, and
  the earlier divisor N disagreed with
  [`lavaan::fitMeasures()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/lavaan/man/fitMeasures.html);
  the three-factor Holzinger and Swineford model under the Wishart
  likelihood gave 0.4220 and now gives lavaan’s 0.4234, and the interval
  limits move with it. Results for ML under the default normal
  likelihood, and for summary input, are unchanged. The help page now
  states the identity N ECVI = AIC + 2 l_s only for the likelihood ratio
  statistic.

- **[`ecvi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ecvi.md)
  applies the checks of the SEM fit family and states its boundary
  cases.** A fitted model with an inadmissible solution is now refused,
  as
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  and
  [`sem_information_criteria()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_information_criteria.md)
  refuse it; a 60 case two-factor fit of the Holzinger and Swineford
  tests with a latent variance of -72.9 had an ECVI of 1.116 \[0.799,
  1.598\]. A well fitting model, whose statistic is below the upper
  alpha/2 quantile, no longer warns about a `prob_greater` row that
  [`ecvi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ecvi.md) does
  not return. When the statistic lies at or below the lower alpha/2
  quantile, the upper limit is still `NA`, now with a warning in
  [`ecvi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ecvi.md)’s own
  terms. The help page says why that limit is not set to the lower one,
  and that the untruncated estimate lies below the interval when the
  statistic is below its degrees of freedom. `n = 0`, which returned Inf
  and NaN, is refused.

- **An ML fit is read as ML under lavaan 0.7-3.** lavaan 0.7-3 lists
  Browne’s residual based statistic beside the standard one for an ML
  fit by default, and
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md),
  which asked whether the test option was exactly `"standard"`, labeled
  an ML ladder as using the scaled difference test and robust fit
  indices. It now sets aside the standard statistic and every Browne
  residual statistic (alternative tests, not corrections) when deciding
  whether a fit carries a robust test. The profile likelihood interval
  for model implied omega and alpha no longer warns at every refit that
  lavaan cannot compute Browne’s statistic under its equality
  constraint. No number changes.

- **[`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  reports one version of the test and of the fit indices at every rung,
  and its attributes name the versions.** Outside FIML the ladder read
  the names of its measures from its first rung alone. In the examples,
  `hs_factors` is the verbal and deduction model of the help page.

  - With the older mean and variance adjusted statistic
    (`test = "mean.var.adjusted"`), for which lavaan computes no robust
    indices, the `cfi` and `rmsea` columns held the standard indices
    while the `fit_indices` attribute said `"robust"`. The columns now
    hold the robust indices, which DMAR computes because they do not
    depend on which corrected statistic accompanies them (Savalei,
    2018); they equal lavaan’s under `estimator = "MLM"`, and a line
    under the table says so. On the help page’s first ladder
    (`measurement_invariance(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors, group = "school", test = "mean.var.adjusted")`)
    the configural CFI was .9916 and is .9928, the configural RMSEA was
    .0520 and is .0478, and the metric `delta_cfi` was -.0127 and is
    -.0134. A ladder whose configural rung is saturated gets them too:
    on the three verbal tests
    (`model = "verbal =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning"`,
    configural, metric, and scalar) the metric `delta_cfi` was -.0109
    and is -.0100.
  - With a bootstrap test (`test = "bollen.stine"`), the `chi_square`
    column and the difference test were the standard ones, while
    `fit_indices` said `"robust"` and `test` named a scaled difference
    test. Those numbers stand, and the attributes now say `"standard"`.
  - Where the robust indices of a maximum likelihood ladder of
    continuous items cannot be had, the columns hold the standard
    indices, which estimate the population values the robust ones
    estimate with the bias corrected as if the data were normal; the
    scaled ones do not (Savalei, 2018).
  - An ordered ladder under the default delta parameterization reported
    the robust CFI and RMSEA of its configural rung beside `NA` at every
    later rung, and no `delta_cfi`. lavaan leaves the robust indices
    `NA` at the rungs that constrain the thresholds. Every rung now
    reports the scaled indices, and `fit_indices` says `"scaled"`. On
    the help page’s ordered example (the verbal and deduction tests cut
    at their quartiles, configural and thresholds rungs):
    - the configural CFI was .980 and is .999;
    - the configural RMSEA was .084 and is .029;
    - the thresholds rung’s CFI and RMSEA were `NA` and are .996 and
      .040;
    - `delta_cfi` was `NA` and is -.0023.
  - A line under the table names any fallback.
  - A saturated rung (no degrees of freedom) no longer decides the
    version, since lavaan forms its robust CFI there from a ratio of
    zeros (1 on one data set and `NA` on another) or does not compute
    it. Such a rung now reports a CFI of 1, which every version implies
    (see the entry on a saturated rung).

- **`measurement_invariance(missing = "fiml")` reports the FIML
  corrected fit indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), and a line under
  the table says so.** The corrected indices estimate the values
  complete data would give, the values a cutoff for a change in fit
  (Cheung & Rensvold, 2002) is a statement about, where lavaan’s
  standard `cfi` and `rmsea` move with the amount and kind of missing
  data;
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  reports the corrected indices for the same kind of fit. Under FIML the
  `cfi` and `rmsea` columns, and `delta_cfi` and `delta_rmsea` with
  them, are lavaan’s robust versions, chosen as
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  chooses them: Zhang and Savalei’s version 6, or version 3 with
  `estimator = "MLR"`.

  - Through 1.0.1 an ML ladder under FIML reported the standard indices
    with lavaan 0.7-2, the oldest lavaan it accepted. With lavaan 0.7-3
    it reported the corrected ones, but only because it read every ML
    fit as robust (see the entry on lavaan 0.7-3), and with
    `estimator = "MLR"` it reported them with either lavaan; those
    numbers stand.
  - On the verbal and deduction tests with 90 sentence completion scores
    deleted at random (`set.seed(113)`, then
    `t7_sentence[sample(301, 90)] <- NA`), the standard and the
    corrected indices are:
    - configural CFI .9936 and .9930;
    - configural RMSEA .0426 and .0473;
    - the metric rung’s delta CFI -.0106 and -.0104, and its delta RMSEA
      .0195 and .0193.

    On the help page’s FIML example the metric RMSEA is .137 and .140.
  - One version holds every rung. When lavaan cannot compute the
    corrected indices at some rung with degrees of freedom, every rung
    falls back to the scaled indices of a scaled fit or to the standard
    ones. A saturated rung does not decide the version: its robust CFI,
    formed from a ratio of zeros, can be `NA`, and that rung reports a
    CFI of 1, which every version implies. On visual perception, cubes,
    and lozenges by school
    (`model = "visual =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges"`)
    with 60 cube scores deleted at random (`set.seed(1)`, then
    `t2_cubes[sample(301, 60)] <- NA`), configural, metric, and scalar,
    lavaan’s robust CFI of the saturated configural rung is `NA`. Every
    rung reports the corrected indices (scalar CFI .852 and RMSEA .172,
    where the standard indices are .861 and .159), and the configural
    CFI is 1.
  - Whether a ladder used FIML is read from its fits: lavaan fits the
    complete cases instead, with a warning, when FIML meets a test it
    cannot combine with it (`test = "satorra.bentler"` or
    `"mean.var.adjusted"`), and such a ladder is reported and labeled as
    the listwise ladder it is.
  - The `fit_indices` attribute names the version (`"robust"`, or
    `"scaled"` or `"standard"` in the fallback). A line under the table,
    kept in the new `fit_columns` attribute, says which indices the
    columns hold, at the console and in a knitted report. Complete data
    and listwise and pairwise deletion are not affected by this entry.

- **A saturated rung of
  [`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  has a CFI of 1.**

  - A rung with no degrees of freedom and a statistic of zero reproduces
    the moments exactly. A binding inequality can give a nonzero
    statistic instead, as the entry on zero degrees of freedom explains.
    Its statistic is zero in every version, and so is the model term of
    the CFI, whatever the scaling constant, which is 0/0 there.
  - lavaan’s robust CFI of such a rung is `NA` or 1 by rounding. The
    table reported the `NA`, and the next rung’s `delta_cfi` with it. On
    the verbal tests of `holzinger_swineford` under `estimator = "MLR"`
    (`items = c("t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning")`,
    `group = "school"`; configural, metric, and scalar), the configural
    CFI was `NA` and is 1, and the metric `delta_cfi` was `NA` and is
    -.0097. The three visual tests with 60 cube scores deleted under
    FIML (see the entry above) behaved the same way.
  - The RMSEA of a saturated rung is 0/0, which no version defines. It
    keeps lavaan’s 0, the convention lavaan applies in every version to
    a model that fits exactly.

- **[`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  reports no fit index or difference test of a ULS ladder of continuous
  items that is formed from the ULS statistic and changes with their
  units.** The examples are the help page’s first ladder, the verbal and
  deduction tests by school.

  - The ULS statistic, (N - G) times the ULS fit function, is in the
    units of the squared covariances. With `estimator = "ULSM"` or
    `"ULSMV"` and continuous items, the `rmsea` column held lavaan’s
    robust RMSEA, which lavaan forms by putting that statistic into a
    correction derived for the ML fit function. It was 1.57, 4.92, and
    4.50 at the configural, metric, and scalar rungs of a ULSM ladder,
    and 0.0157, 0.0492, and 0.0532 with every score divided by 10. The
    `rmsea` and `delta_rmsea` columns are now `NA`.
  - At the scalar and strict rungs, which restrict the means, the ULS
    fit function adds the squared mean residuals to the squared
    covariance residuals, which are in other units, so the statistic,
    the loadings, and the CFI change with the units too. The scalar CFI
    was .9885, against .9840 with the scores divided by 10, and the
    scalar `delta_cfi` was -.00005 against -.0046: a judgment against
    the cutoff of Cheung and Rensvold (2002) that turned on the units.
    The `cfi` and `delta_cfi` of those rungs are now `NA`. The
    configural and metric CFI (.9991 and .9886) do not depend on the
    units and are unchanged. So are the `chi_square` column and the
    scaled difference test, whose reference distribution does not depend
    on the units, though their values do.
  - With `estimator = "ULS"` and `test = "standard"`, the `cfi` and
    `rmsea` columns held the standard indices formed from the ULS
    statistic: CFI .9956 and .9818 and RMSEA 3.51 and 6.37 at the
    configural and metric rungs, and CFI 1 and RMSEA 0 at both with the
    scores divided by 10. Both columns are now `NA`.
  - With `estimator = "ULS"`, alone or with `test = "standard"`,
    lavaan’s difference test refers the difference of the ULS statistics
    to the chi square distribution. The metric rung’s `delta_chi_square`
    was 91712 (p \< .0001), against 9.17 (p = .057) with the scores
    divided by 10, and the `test` attribute named a scaled difference
    test (a standard one with `test = "standard"`). `delta_chi_square`,
    `p_value`, and `test` are now `NA`.
  - With `estimator = "ULS"` alone, Browne’s residual statistic remains
    a valid test. CFI and RMSEA at configural and metric rungs, which
    leave the means free, are unchanged. At scalar and strict rungs,
    restrictions link means and covariances through the latent means, so
    the ULS estimates change with the units. Browne’s statistic at those
    estimates and its indices change too: CFI, RMSEA, and their
    differences are now `NA` there. On the help page’s first ladder,
    `measurement_invariance(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors, group = "school", estimator = "ULS")`,
    the scalar CFI was .8874 and its RMSEA .0680 in 1.0.1; both are now
    `NA`.
  - Lines under the table say which columns are `NA` and why.
    `estimator = "MLR"` is the estimator for nonnormal continuous items.

- **[`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  under FIML leaves an auxiliary variable’s mean and variance free at
  every rung.** An auxiliary variable passed through `...` as lavaan’s
  `aux` enters a FIML fit as a saturated correlate (Graham, 2003).
  lavaan makes its mean and variance parameters of each group, and the
  ladder’s `group.equal` reached them. The scalar rung equated the
  auxiliary’s means across the groups and the strict rung its variances,
  so each of those rung tests also tested, with one more degree of
  freedom, whether the auxiliary is distributed alike in the groups.
  They are now added to `group.partial` at every rung, beside any
  `group_partial` terms. The ladder then has the degrees of freedom of
  the ladder without the auxiliary, and its differences are those of the
  same ladder with the auxiliary’s moments free.

  Example: a spatial factor of visual perception, cubes, and lozenges
  and a verbal factor of paragraph comprehension, sentence completion,
  and word meaning by school, with 60 sentence completion scores deleted
  at random (`set.seed(1)`, then `t7_sentence[sample(301, 60)] <- NA`)
  and general information as the auxiliary (means 44.8 and 36.6 in the
  two schools).

  - The scalar test was 57.59 on 5 df (p \< .0001) with a delta CFI of
    -.081. It is now 23.88 on 4 df (p = .0001) with -.031; without the
    auxiliary it is 24.03 on 4 df with -.031.
  - The strict test goes from 10.85 on 7 df to 11.04 on 6.

  Under two-stage estimation the auxiliaries enter the first stage only,
  so its ladders hold no such parameters.

- **[`measurement_invariance()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/measurement_invariance.md)
  merges lavaan’s `group.partial` passed through `...` into
  `group_partial`, and refuses `group.equal` there.** Each rung passes
  lavaan one `group.partial`, so through 1.0.1 a call that gave both
  `group_partial` and `group.partial` stopped with lavaan’s error that a
  snake_cased name is duplicated. The terms of both are now freed at
  every rung, beside those of an auxiliary variable under FIML. On the
  six tests by school above under FIML, without the auxiliary,
  `group_partial = "t2_cubes ~ 1"` with
  `group.partial = "t4_lozenges ~ 1"` gives a scalar test of 1.56 on 2
  df, where 1.0.1 stopped.

  `group.equal` in `...` constrained the configural rung, which was
  still reported as configural, and a ladder that went past it stopped
  with the same error. On the six tests by school above under listwise
  deletion, `group.equal = "loadings"` with `levels = "configural"` gave
  a configural rung of 25.62 on 20 df against the configural model’s
  15.27 on 16. It is now an error that names `levels` and
  `group_partial`.

- **[`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md)
  returns the same four columns whatever `B`.** `ci_upper` existed only
  when `B > 0`, so the shape of the table depended on an argument. It is
  now always present, `NA` when no bootstrap is run. A bootstrap bound
  also carries the `B_used` attribute (the resamples left after any were
  dropped), which `glance()` reports. No value changes.

- **[`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md) takes
  the absolute value of every correlation, the monotrait correlations
  within each block as well as the heterotrait correlations between
  blocks.** Through 1.0.1 only the heterotrait correlations were
  absolute, a mix that matches neither the signed ratio nor the absolute
  one `semTools::htmt()` computes. A reverse keyed item that was not
  recoded then lowered its block’s average within-construct correlation
  while the numerator kept its size, so the ratio was inflated. Take one
  such item in a block of four:

  ``` r

  set.seed(113); n <- 300
  f1 <- rnorm(n); f2 <- 0.5 * f1 + sqrt(0.75) * rnorm(n)
  d <- data.frame(a1 = .8 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                  a2 = .7 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                  a3 = .8 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                  a4 = -.6 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .8),
                  b1 = .8 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                  b2 = .7 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                  b3 = .6 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .8))
  blocks <- list(A = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4"),
                 B = c("b1", "b2", "b3"))
  htmt(d, blocks)
  fa_confirmatory(d, factors = blocks, output = "measurement")
  ```

  The two constructs, which correlate .5 in the population, had an HTMT
  of 1.346, a discriminant validity failure that is not there, and
  `fa_confirmatory(output = "measurement")` reported it beside phi =
  .473 without a word; a block of three with such an item stopped the
  call. Every correlation now enters as an absolute value, so the ratio
  does not depend on how an item is keyed (1.346 becomes .463, the value
  of the recoded data). When no correlation within a block is negative,
  as with consistently keyed items, the point estimates are unchanged,
  the example of
  [`?htmt`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md) and
  three factors of `holzinger_swineford` included. The bootstrap bound
  can move, though: a resample that draws a negative correlation within
  a block now enters it with its size, where 1.0.1 averaged it with its
  sign or dropped the resample. Take two blocks whose within-block
  correlations for B are .04, .11, and .20:

  ``` r

  set.seed(4); n <- 80; f <- rnorm(n); g <- rnorm(n)
  d <- data.frame(a1 = f + rnorm(n, sd = .5),
                  a2 = f + rnorm(n, sd = .5),
                  b1 = .45 * g + rnorm(n), b2 = .45 * g + rnorm(n),
                  b3 = .45 * g + rnorm(n))
  htmt(d, list(A = c("a1", "a2"), B = c("b1", "b2", "b3")), B = 200,
       seed = 113)
  ```

  The HTMT is .408, as before, and the bound .728 from 200 resamples,
  where it was .869 from 198. The bound of the
  [`?htmt`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md) example
  is unchanged. On complete data the values agree with
  `semTools::htmt(htmt2 = FALSE, absolute = TRUE)`. On incomplete data
  they agree only when semTools is given the same pairwise-complete
  correlations through `sample.cov`, since by default it deletes
  incomplete rows listwise. The help page no longer credits the absolute
  form to a 2021 paper missing from its references, and a pair whose
  ratio cannot be computed is reported as the next entry describes.

- **[`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md)
  reports a pair whose ratio cannot be computed as `NA`, with a warning,
  and `fa_confirmatory(output = "measurement")` keeps its table.** A
  correlation that cannot be computed leaves a pair’s ratio undefined.
  That happens with two items never observed together, as in a planned
  missing data design whose forms give two blocks to different
  respondents, or with a constant item. Through 1.0.1 such a pair across
  two blocks was `NA` without a word, and a pair undefined within a
  block stopped the call with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”.

  The pair is now `NA`, as is its bootstrap bound, with a warning that
  names the pair and the reason, and the other pairs are reported. The
  call stops, with a message that says why, only when no pair is
  defined. A call with only two blocks whose one pair is undefined,
  which returned `NA`, therefore stops.

  `fa_confirmatory(output = "measurement")` keeps every phi, omega, AVE,
  and *H* row and reports the undefined `htmt` row as `NA` with the
  warning, as 1.0.1 did without the warning. Take two three-item factors
  of 300 cases with a1 and b1 on different forms:

  ``` r

  set.seed(113); n <- 300
  f1 <- rnorm(n); f2 <- 0.4 * f1 + sqrt(.84) * rnorm(n)
  d <- data.frame(a1 = .8 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                  a2 = .7 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                  a3 = .7 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                  b1 = .8 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                  b2 = .7 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                  b3 = .7 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .7))
  d$a1[c(TRUE, FALSE)] <- NA; d$b1[c(FALSE, TRUE)] <- NA
  fa_confirmatory(d, factors = list(A = c("a1", "a2", "a3"),
                          B = c("b1", "b2", "b3")),
        missing = "fiml", output = "measurement")
  ```

  This gives phi .380 \[.239, .521\], omega .793 and .784, AVE .558 and
  .549, and *H* .798 and .792.

- **[`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md)
  returns the same seven rows whatever `boot`.** The `ci_lower`,
  `ci_upper`, and `B_used` rows existed only when `boot = TRUE`, so the
  shape of the table, and of its `tidy()` and `glance()`, depended on an
  argument, as
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md)’s did.
  They are now always present, and `NA` when no bootstrap is run, which
  is the default: the nominal ratings of Krippendorff (2011, Table 1)
  give seven rows where they gave four, with alpha .743 and every other
  value unchanged. As in
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md) and
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  the confidence level is recorded, and printed, only beside an interval
  that was formed. A script that tested for the rows by name
  (`"ci_lower" %in% x$term`) should test for a finite value instead.
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  now refuses a table whose limits are `NA` rather than writing “95% CI
  \[NA, NA\]”.
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  has returned its `ci_lower` and `ci_upper` columns under every
  `ci_method` since 1.0.0, and its tests now pin the columns of its
  `tidy()` and `glance()` as well.

- **[`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md)
  checks `B` and reports the bootstrap resamples it drops.** `B` must
  now be a whole number that meets the rule for bootstrap replications
  when `boot = TRUE` (400 at the 95 percent level; see One Rule for
  Bootstrap Replications); through 1.0.1 any value was accepted, and
  `B = 10` gave a percentile interval from ten resamples. A resample on
  which alpha cannot be computed (too few pairable values, or values all
  alike) is dropped as before, but now with one warning that gives the
  count, and the limits are withheld when too few resamples remain. When
  the data themselves leave alpha undefined (every value alike), no
  bootstrap is run: the interval rows stay `NA` and no confidence level
  is recorded, where the table had said `B_used = 0` beside “Confidence
  level: 95%”. Intervals are unchanged.

- **The bound for close fit in
  [`sem_residual_fit()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_residual_fit.md)
  is credited to the paper that proposed it.** The help page attributed
  the bound of .05 times the average R squared to Ximénez,
  Maydeu-Olivares, Shi, and Revuelta (2022). It is the bound of Shi,
  Maydeu-Olivares, and DiStefano (2018). Their criterion also requires
  the largest absolute standardized residual covariance to be at most
  .10 (with .10 times the average R squared and .15 for acceptable fit),
  and they apply both as population values through an interval or a
  test. The page and the SEM fit vignette now say so, and say that the
  function tests the first part and reports the second as a sample
  value. Ximénez et al. (2022) are cited for finding that the bound
  works reasonably well for the unbiased SRMR in finite samples, except
  when the loadings are small. The
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  page and the vignette now also cite Steiger (1990, p. 178), which
  states in print the result of Steiger (1989) behind gamma hat: gamma
  hat and adjusted gamma hat estimate the population values of the GFI
  and the adjusted GFI.

- **The Steiger and Fouladi (1997) chapter is cited by its title.** The
  help pages of
  [`smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/smd.md),
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md),
  [`ci_smd_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd_c.md),
  [`ci_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sm.md),
  [`cles()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cles.md),
  [`ci_mahalanobis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_mahalanobis.md),
  [`ci_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_t.md),
  [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md),
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md),
  [`ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sm.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sm_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sm_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity.md)
  gave its title as “Noncentrality interval estimation and the
  evaluation of statistical methods”; the chapter is “Noncentrality
  interval estimation and the evaluation of statistical models”
  (pp. 221–257). The help page of
  [`sem_fit_measures()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_fit_measures.md)
  and the SEM fit vignette, both new in 1.1.0, cite it by that title for
  the intervals of gamma hat.

- **The journal and subtitle of Kelley, Maxwell, and Rausch (2003) are
  given as published.** The help pages of
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md),
  [`design_consequences()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/design_consequences.md),
  [`ss_aipe_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c.md),
  [`ss_aipe_c_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c_ancova.md),
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_r.md),
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd.md),
  [`ss_aipe_mean()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_mean.md),
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md),
  and
  [`ss_power_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_smd.md)
  gave the journal as “Evaluation and the Health Professions” and the
  subtitle as “Delineating methods of sample size planning”; the journal
  is *Evaluation & the Health Professions* and the subtitle is
  “Delineating methods of sample-size planning”, as the DOI record of
  the article (10.1177/0163278703255242) has them. The volume, issue,
  and pages, 26(3), 258–287, already matched the record and are
  unchanged.

- **The edition of Rencher and Christensen (2012) is given as
  published.** The help page of
  [`manova_split_plot()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/manova_split_plot.md)
  gave *Methods of multivariate analysis* (Wiley, 2012) as the fourth
  edition; the 2012 book is the third edition, as the catalog record of
  its print edition (ISBN 978-0-470-17896-6) and the Crossref record of
  its review in *International Statistical Review*, 81(2), 328–329, have
  it. The entry gains the book’s DOI, 10.1002/9781118391686.

- **The edition of Anderson (2003) is given as published.** The help
  pages of
  [`ci_eigenvalue()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eigenvalue.md)
  and
  [`ci_mahalanobis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_mahalanobis.md)
  gave *An introduction to multivariate statistical analysis*
  (Wiley, 2003) as the fourth edition; the 2003 book is the third
  edition, as the publisher’s page for it (ISBN 978-0-471-36091-9) and
  catalog records of the print edition have it, and as the pages of
  [`expected_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_r.md)
  and
  [`expected_partial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_partial_r.md)
  already cite it. The entry on the
  [`ci_mahalanobis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_mahalanobis.md)
  page also sets the title in sentence case, as the other entries do.
  Crossref holds no record of the book, so the entries carry no DOI.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  returns the AIPE planner class with an assurance.** The closed form
  plan carried class `dmar_ss_aipe` and the assurance plan did not, so
  `tidy()` and `glance()` answered differently by path: for an assurance
  plan `tidy()` gave five term and estimate rows rather than the planned
  N beside the width. Both paths now carry the class, so an assurance
  plan’s `tidy()` is one row (`term = "sample_size"`, `estimate`,
  `width`) and its `glance()` adds `assurance`, `assurance_attained`,
  and `G` as columns. The values of the table are unchanged (its rows
  are renamed; see Breaking Changes in 1.1.0). Two arguments are now
  checked before they are used: a vector `true_residual_var` for the
  Parallel model stopped with R’s “the condition has length \> 1” and
  now stops with the function’s own message, and a True Score plan from
  `true_factor_loading` without `n_items` stopped with “argument is of
  length zero” and now says that `n_items` is needed. A vector
  `true_factor_loading` for the Parallel model was recycled across the
  items, so it planned the congeneric pattern it describes under the
  Parallel label without saying so (loadings .8, .7, .7, and .8 with
  `true_residual_var = .4` returned N = 96). It is now an error, as it
  already was for the True Score model, with a message that names the
  Congeneric model, and both models refuse any `true_factor_loading`
  that is not one number.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  plans for the coefficient of the raw items.** The tau equivalent model
  on every route, and the congeneric model given by `S`, turned the
  population covariance matrix into a correlation matrix before the
  closed form and the Monte Carlo draws. That plans for alpha or omega
  of standardized items rather than for the coefficient
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  estimate, and the same congeneric population entered by loadings or by
  `S` got different searches. Every route now uses the covariance matrix
  itself. With equal loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2,
  the normal theory plan for a width of .10 goes from 206 to 367 cases
  (the factor analytic one to 242; see the entry on that interval). At
  367 the corrected interval averages .1004 wide and covers .941, while
  at 206 the 1.0.1 interval was as narrow as planned (.1008) but covered
  .869 (1,000 samples of each size, drawn as in the entry on that
  interval and analyzed by
  `reliability_alpha(S = S, N = N, ci_method = "ml")`). A correlation
  matrix still plans for standardized items, and items of equal variance
  keep the closed form they had.

  Seeded assurance searches with the normal theory interval of the tau
  equivalent model move a little for any population. Each sample’s
  interval now takes its standard error from that sample’s covariance
  matrix, whose variances differ even when the population’s do not, and
  a population whose equal variances are not one is now drawn from its
  covariance matrix. With `true_item_covariance = .3` and error
  variances of .2 on five items, a width of .10, an assurance of .85,
  `G_initial = 50`, `G = 200`, and seed 113, the plan goes from 81 cases
  (empirical assurance .905) to 79 (.885). The True Score example of the
  1.0.1 help page (`true_item_covariance = .3`,
  `true_residual_var = c(.2, .3, .3, .2, .3)`, width .10) goes from a
  closed form of 84 to 86 and, with an assurance of .85
  (`G_initial = 50`, `G = 200`, seed 113), from 115 to 118. The page now
  plans for items near unit variance (`true_item_covariance = .5`,
  `true_residual_var = c(.4, .5, .6, .4, .6)`): 108 cases, or 140 with
  that assurance (106 and 138 under 1.0.1). Its plan from a correlation
  matrix (`pop_mat`, width .15) with that assurance goes from 120 cases
  (empirical assurance .85) to 121 (.855), because its Monte Carlo
  intervals now use the sample covariance matrix. The Parallel examples
  give the plans they gave (38 cases, and 57 with an assurance of .85).

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  plans coefficient omega from omega’s own variance.** Without an
  assurance the congeneric model returned Terry and Kelley’s (2012) Eq.
  19, the variance of alpha, which they used only as a starting value
  for a Monte Carlo search on omega’s mean width (p. 390). The closed
  form is now the delta method variance of the model implied omega from
  the expected information of the single-factor model at the population
  (Raykov, 2002), the variance behind
  `reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml")`.
  When the population is given by `S` or `data`, the model is first fit
  to it by maximum likelihood. Eq. 19 was too large when standardized
  items have unequal loadings and could be far too small when the item
  variances differ. At width .15, loadings .9, .8, .3, and .2 of
  standardized items go from 297 to 177 (the interval averages .114 wide
  at 297 and .153 at 177); loadings .3, .5, 1, and 2 with error
  variances .1, .3, 1, and 3 go from 75 to 151 (.211 wide at 75, .148 at
  151); and the help page’s example goes from 53 to 52. At width .10,
  loadings 2, 1, .6, and .4 with unit error variances go from 360 to
  229, and six standardized items with loadings from .4 to .8 from 197
  to 183. The widths come from 1,000 samples of each size, drawn as in
  the next entry and analyzed by
  `reliability_omega(S = S, N = N, denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml")`;
  three of those at 177 return no interval.

  The first-order approximation can miss the mean width when samples at
  the planned size approach improper solutions or empirical
  underidentification. The median can also exceed the target. The
  loadings, item count, and sample size act together; no lower bound on
  individual loadings separates these populations. Three-item models are
  just identified, and a sample covariance near zero can make their
  estimated loadings run away. Wider targets can create the same problem
  with more items. The help describes these cases and points to an
  assurance above one half, whose search counts the realized widths. A
  congeneric population with two items is refused.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  plans the factor analytic interval of the tau equivalent model for
  that interval.** Without an assurance the True Score model returned
  the normal theory size whatever `type` was, so
  `type = "Factor Analytic"` planned for the van Zyl, Neudecker, and
  Nel (2000) interval of alpha, which through 1.0.1 was evaluated on the
  correlation matrix. It did not plan for the interval the user asked
  for: the delta method interval of the coefficient implied by the
  single-factor model with equal loadings. That is the interval of
  `reliability_alpha(estimator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml")` and
  the one the assurance search draws. That coefficient is the maximum
  likelihood estimator under the model, so its variance is no larger
  than the normal theory variance of alpha. The closed form now takes
  its delta method variance, with the information and gradient of the
  one loading summed over the items. A population given by `S` or `data`
  is first fit by the equal loadings model. Take equal loadings .7 and
  error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2 at a width of .10. 1.0.1 returned 206
  cases, too few for this interval, which averages .108 wide at 206
  cases; about one sample in eight gives an interval no wider than .10.
  The normal theory plan for these items is 367, and the factor analytic
  plan is now 242, at which that interval averages .10 wide. These
  widths come from 1,000 samples of each size drawn after `set.seed(1)`
  as the assurance search draws them, each
  `S <- var(MASS::mvrnorm(N, rep(0, 4), Sigma))` from the population
  matrix `Sigma`, and analyzed by
  `reliability_alpha(S = S, N = N, estimator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml")`.
  With equal error variances the two variances coincide, so the Parallel
  model keeps its closed form, and no normal theory plan is affected.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  refuses a population it cannot plan for.** Through 1.0.1 each of the
  following was planned without a word:

  - Every error variance in `true_residual_var` must now be above zero
    for the Congeneric model and for the True Score model with the
    factor analytic interval, as it already had to be for the Parallel
    model. These plans fit the single-factor model, at whose boundary an
    error variance of zero lies. At a width of .15, loadings .7, .6, .5,
    and .5 with error variances .51, -.1, .75, and .75 gave 81 cases for
    the congeneric model, and one loading of .7 on all four items with
    those error variances gave 46 for the tau equivalent one.
  - With the normal theory interval of the True Score model nothing is
    fit. The loading and error variances only build the covariance
    matrix the plan is made from, which must be a covariance matrix, as
    `S` must. The plan is the one the same matrix gives as `S`: 74 cases
    for that tau equivalent population at a width of .15, by either
    route.
  - A matrix with a negative eigenvalue, which no population has, is
    refused, whether it is given as `S` or implied on that normal theory
    route. Loadings .7, .6, .5, and .5 with error variances .51, -.3,
    .75, and .75 imply a matrix whose smallest eigenvalue is -.144;
    given as `S` at a width of .15, it gave 25 cases for the True Score
    model and 115 for the Parallel model.
  - A congeneric population given by `true_cov_matrix` or `data` whose
    single-factor fit is improper or has no solution is refused.
  - A population with fewer than three items whose loading is not zero
    is refused, since the congeneric model is not identified there.
    `true_factor_loading = c(.7, .6, 0)` with
    `true_residual_var = c(.51, .64, 1)` gave 937 cases at a width of
    .15.
  - With the factor analytic interval of the Parallel and True Score
    models, the fitted equal-loading model decides whether the common
    factor is absent for a population supplied as `true_cov_matrix` or
    `data`. Alpha at or below zero is equivalent only when the item
    variances are equal: at a zero loading, the likelihood weights each
    covariance by the inverse of the two item variances, and alpha does
    not. A population supplied through `true_item_covariance` or
    `true_factor_loading` is refused when its loading is zero. A
    Parallel plan whose alpha is not positive despite a nonzero fitted
    loading is refused as far from parallel, with the True Score model
    named as the alternative. The normal theory interval still plans for
    alpha of such items.
  - The congeneric closed form is refused where its delta method is
    degenerate. Omega grows with the square of the sum of the loadings.
    When that sum is small relative to its standard error, as when
    loadings of opposite sign nearly cancel, the first-order variance
    understates the width of the interval, and where they cancel it
    vanishes. For standardized items at a width of .10, loadings .7,
    -.7, .5, and -.5 have an omega of zero, for which the delta method
    gives one case (1.0.1, with alpha’s closed form: 14078). Loadings
    .7, -.7, .5, and -.4 (omega .0038) give 49 cases, at which the
    interval averages .20 wide for a target of .10 (12 of the 1,000
    samples return none), and about 95 are needed (1.0.1: 12606).
  - The closed form is checked at the N it gives, rounded up, or at one
    more case than there are items when it gives fewer. Take the sum of
    the loadings to be normal. The interval the estimation functions
    report, clamped at zero, then averages less than the target until
    the standard error of that sum is about 1.5 times the sum at 95
    percent confidence (1.36 at 90 percent, 1.66 at 99), and the plan is
    refused beyond that. In simulation the rule errs a little toward
    refusing: loadings .7, -.7, .5, and -.35, whose sum has a standard
    error 1.52 times its size at the 110 cases of the closed form, give
    intervals averaging .099 wide for a target of .10.
  - The refusal says to reverse score items when the loadings differ in
    sign, and in any case to give an assurance. An assurance plan is
    never refused, since its search counts the widths of the intervals
    themselves. Loadings of one sign with a small omega are planned as
    in 1.0.1: four loadings of .1 at a width of .10 still take 3787
    cases.

  The widths in this entry come from 1,000 samples of each size, drawn
  as in the previous entry and analyzed by
  `reliability_omega(S = S, N = N, denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml")`.
  With the factor analytic interval, the assurance search now starts at
  no fewer than one more case than there are items, the fewest a
  single-factor model can be fit to. A highly reliable population
  planned for a wide interval can have a closed form below that:
  loadings .95 on four items need two cases for a width of .2. The
  search used to stop there.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  warns when the loadings of a congeneric population differ in sign.**
  The warning names the items that load in the direction opposite to the
  others. Such items lower omega of the unweighted sum, as an item keyed
  in the opposite direction does when it is not reverse scored, and the
  plan is for omega of the sum of the items as given. Standardized items
  with loadings .7, -.7, .5, and .5 at a width of .10 now plan 1419
  cases with the warning; 1.0.1, with alpha’s closed form, planned 4884
  without one.

- **The assurance of
  [`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  counts a simulated study that returns no interval as one whose
  interval is too wide.** The assurance is the probability of an
  interval no wider than desired (Terry & Kelley, 2012), and a study
  that ends without an interval has not had one. Through 1.0.1 a Monte
  Carlo sample whose single-factor fit did not converge was set aside,
  and the proportion was taken over the rest. A sample whose solution
  had run away (error variances summing below zero, a model implied
  coefficient above one) was kept, and its interval, often inverted (an
  estimate of 104 between 104 and 1), was counted as narrow or wide.
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  now returns no coefficient for a runaway solution, and the search
  treats each sample as the estimation functions treat it. A sample that
  returns no interval, whether its fit did not converge, had no
  solution, or ran away, counts as wide. Every assurance plan carries
  their count in `no_interval`, zero when all samples returned an
  interval, and `glance()` carries the count as a column. A nonzero
  count is printed under the table. Both confidence limits are clamped
  into \[0, 1\], as the estimation functions clamp them, which changes
  no count. The rule changes nothing in a search in which every sample
  returns an interval, as every normal theory search does. Samples
  without an interval are rare unless several loadings are .3 or below.
  Take standardized items with loadings .8, .3, .2, and .2 and a width
  of .40 (200 samples of each size, drawn and analyzed as in the entry
  on the populations the planner refuses):

  - At 100 cases, 47 of 200 samples return no interval. The share of
    studies with an interval no wider than .40 is .410, against .536
    among the samples that return one.
  - At 140 cases, 49 return none, and the two shares are .545 and .722.
  - With an assurance of .5 (`G_initial = 50`, `G = 200`, seed 1), 1.0.1
    returned 110 cases at an empirical assurance of .626, taken over the
    samples whose fit converged. The plan is now 118, at .545, and 39 of
    the 200 samples of the final pass return no interval.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)’s
  assurance search can go below its starting size, says why it stops,
  and works from data.** The search started at the closed form size and
  only went up. When that size already met the assurance, as with an
  assurance near one half or below, or with the factor analytic interval
  of the tau equivalent model, which is narrower than the normal theory
  interval 1.0.1’s closed form described, the search returned the closed
  form size whatever the assurance needed. For the tau equivalent
  population of equal loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2
  with the factor analytic interval, a width of .10, and an assurance of
  .80, 1.0.1 planned from the correlation matrix and returned its start,
  207 cases, at an empirical assurance of .99 for standardized items.
  That is too few for alpha of the items as they are: at 207 cases .156
  of the samples give an interval no wider than .10 (1,000 samples,
  drawn as in the entry on that interval). The plan is now 263
  (`G_initial = 100`, `G = 400`, `seed = 1`), searched up from the
  factor analytic closed form of 242. The search now moves down to where
  the widths it drew would meet the target and then up one case at a
  time; a search whose start falls short, and in which every sample
  returns an interval, draws what it drew before from the same matrix (a
  tau equivalent population whose variances are not one is now drawn
  from its covariance matrix rather than its correlation matrix, and so
  draws differently). A size at which no Monte Carlo sample returns an
  interval stops with the first error, where the search stopped with
  “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. How a sample that returns no
  interval counts is in the entry on the assurance of
  [`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md).
  The congeneric model with `type = "Normal Theory"`, which the help
  already called an error, is refused at once (the closed form returned
  an N without reading `type`). A population given by `data` now sets
  the number of items, so an assurance plan from data no longer stops
  with “invalid ‘times’ argument”.

- **[`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  names the common covariance of the items for what it is.** The
  argument was `cor_est` and was called the presumed inter-item
  correlation, but the function takes its square root as the common
  loading beside the error variances, so it is the common inter-item
  covariance, and it is the correlation only when
  `true_residual_var = 1 - true_item_covariance`, Terry and Kelley’s
  standardized design. It is now `true_item_covariance`, and the help
  says what it is. The Parallel examples planned from a covariance of .3
  with error variances of .2, items that correlate .6; they now give the
  same populations as standardized items (`true_item_covariance = .6`,
  `true_residual_var = .4`) and say so, and their plans are the same.
  The True Score example now plans another population (see the entry on
  the coefficient of the raw items). The page also says that a
  correlation matrix plans for standardized items, and how the closed
  forms and the assurance search work.

- **The help says what `seed = NULL` does.** The pages of the
  reliability family,
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md),
  [`randomization_test_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test_paired.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md),
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`plot_trajectories()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_trajectories.md),
  and
  [`plot_trajectories_fitted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_trajectories_fitted.md)
  said that a `NULL` seed leaves the random number state intact. In fact
  the draws come from, and advance, the caller’s stream; it is a
  supplied seed that leaves the state as it was. The help of
  [`reliability_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_alpha.md)
  and
  [`reliability_omega()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/reliability_omega.md)
  also now names the delta method behind `bootstrap_se_logistic` (Kelley
  & Pornprasertmanit, 2016, Eq. 32). No number changes.

- **Suggested packages.** lavaan’s floor rises from 0.7-2 to 0.7-3, the
  version every two-stage and factor score result was checked against
  ([`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
  refuses ordered fits under 0.7-2 in any case); `mice` (3.18.0 or
  newer, which keeps ordered factors ordered when it augments the data)
  is added for multiple imputation in categorical omega; and `mvtnorm`
  is no longer suggested.

- **A confidence level is displayed with the digits it needs, never as
  100% when it is below 1, and whatever `getOption("digits")` is.**
  Through 1.0.1 the labels of
  [`plot_ci()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_ci.md),
  [`plot_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_smd.md),
  [`plot_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_R2.md),
  and
  [`plot_mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_mediation_mbco.md)
  and the caption of
  [`correlations_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/correlations_test.md)
  rounded the level to a whole percent, so a 97.5% interval was labeled
  98% and a 99.9% interval 100%, a level only an unbounded interval has:
  `plot_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.975)` read
  “98% CI \[0.043, 0.954\]” and now reads “97.5% CI \[0.043, 0.954\]”,
  `plot_R2(R2 = 0.25, N = 100, p = 5, conf_level = 0.999)` read “100% CI
  \[0.017, 0.477\]” and now reads “99.9% CI \[0.017, 0.477\]”, and a
  [`correlations_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/correlations_test.md)
  result at `conf_level = 0.975` is captioned “Correlations (Pearson,
  97.5% CI)”, where it read “98% CI”.

  - [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
    wrote the level with `getOption("digits")` significant digits: under
    `options(digits = 2)`,
    `results_sentence(ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.975))`
    gave “smd = 0.50, 98% CI \[0.04, 0.95\]”; it gives “smd = 0.50,
    97.5% CI \[0.04, 0.95\]”.
  - The line beneath the table and the sentence wrote a level within
    5e-8 of 1 as 100:
    `ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.99999995)`
    printed “Confidence level: 100%” and the sentence “100% CI \[-0.61,
    1.61\]”. Digits are now added until a level below 1 no longer reads
    100 (“99.999995%”).
  - The line beneath the table follows `getOption("OutDec")`, as the
    table’s numbers and the sentence already did: under
    `options(OutDec = ",")` it reads “Confidence level: 97,5%” beneath a
    table of 0,043 and 0,954, where it read “97.5%”.
  - [`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html) of an
    [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) fit
    and [`confint()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/confint.html) of
    [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md) and
    [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
    wrote the level and the interval columns with `getOption("digits")`:
    under `options(digits = 2)`, a fit with `conf_level = 0.975` gave
    its intervals at “level = 0.97” over columns “1.3 %” and “99 %”. It
    gives them at “level = 0.975” over “1.25 %” and “98.75 %”, the
    labels [`stats::confint()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/confint.html)
    writes. At the default settings nothing changes.
  - The texts that are new in 1.1.0 write the level the same way: the
    Bonferroni line of
    [`pairwise_within()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/pairwise_within.md)
    and
    [`contrast_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/contrast_test.md)
    (each of 28 intervals at a family level of .999 is at 99.996%, which
    four significant digits would have written as 100%), the interval
    columns of a printed
    [`factor_scores()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_scores.md)
    table, and the interval that
    [`equivalence_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_rmsea.md)
    names.

  No interval and no stored level changes; only the display does.

- **An interval formed from unequal tail areas says so, and a one-sided
  interval is written as the confidence bound it is.** An interval with
  tail area `alpha_lower` below its lower limit and `alpha_upper` above
  its upper limit has confidence coefficient 1 - `alpha_lower` -
  `alpha_upper` whatever the split (Neyman, 1937), and that is the level
  the table records, but “95% CI \[L, U\]” is read as the equal-tailed
  interval. Through 1.0.1 nothing recorded the split:
  `ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, alpha_lower = 0.01, alpha_upper = 0.04)`
  gave the sentence “smd = 0.50, 95% CI \[0.03, 0.85\]”, read as the
  equal-tailed 95% interval, which is \[0.10, 0.90\]. Each constructor
  that takes `alpha_lower` and `alpha_upper`
  ([`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md),
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md),
  [`ci_mahalanobis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_mahalanobis.md),
  [`ci_omega_squared()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_omega_squared.md),
  [`ci_pvaf()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_pvaf.md),
  [`ci_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
  [`ci_R()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md),
  [`ci_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rc.md),
  [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md),
  [`ci_rmsea()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rmsea.md),
  [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md),
  [`ci_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sm.md),
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md),
  [`ci_smd_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd_c.md),
  [`ci_snr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_snr.md),
  [`ci_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_src.md),
  and
  [`ci_srsnr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_srsnr.md))
  now records the two areas when they differ, and:

  - the line beneath the table reads “Confidence level: 95% (unequal
    tail areas: 0.01 below the lower limit, 0.04 above the upper
    limit)”, and
    [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
    writes “smd = 0.50, 95% CI \[0.03, 0.85\] (unequal tail areas: 0.01
    below, 0.04 above)”;
  - an interval with a tail area of 0 is a one-sided confidence bound,
    whose other limit (infinite, or the parameter’s own bound, 0 for an
    RMSEA or 1 for a squared multiple correlation) carries no
    information, and the sentence writes the bound alone. With
    `alpha_lower = 0` and `alpha_upper = 0.05` the sentence of the
    [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md)
    call above was “smd = 0.50, 95% CI \[-Inf, 0.83\]” and is “smd =
    0.50, one-sided 95% upper confidence bound 0.83”;
    `ci_rmsea(rmsea = 0.06, df = 24, N = 300, alpha_lower = 0.05, alpha_upper = 0)`
    was “rmsea = 0.06, 95% CI \[0.04, Inf\]” and is “rmsea = 0.06,
    one-sided 95% lower confidence bound 0.04”; and
    `ci_R2(R2 = 0.2, N = 100, p = 3, alpha_lower = 0.05, alpha_upper = 0)`
    was “R2 = 0.20, 95% CI \[0.08, 1.00\]” and is “R2 = 0.20, one-sided
    95% lower confidence bound 0.08”. The line beneath the table says
    which limit is the bound (“one-sided: the upper limit is the 95%
    upper confidence bound, with tail area 0.05 above it and none below
    the lower limit”). An interval is taken to be one-sided only from a
    tail area of 0, never from a limit, since an equal-tailed interval
    can have a lower limit of 0 because the statistic fell below its
    critical value;
  - `tidy()` and `glance()` add `alpha_lower` and `alpha_upper` columns
    after `conf_level`, holding the two areas on the rows of the
    interval (`NA` on the other rows of a long `tidy()`), so that rows
    stacked from several results keep their own split and their sentence
    states it. A stack built with
    [`rbind()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html) from an equal-tailed
    and an unequal-tailed result stops on their different columns rather
    than state either split for the other’s rows, and one built with
    [`dplyr::bind_rows()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/bind_rows.html)
    holds `NA`, read as equal tails, on the equal-tailed rows;
  - [`plot_ci()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_ci.md)
    names the split in a subtitle (see the entry on
    [`plot_ci()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_ci.md)).

  An equal-tailed interval, the usual one, is unchanged: it records no
  areas, prints and reads as before, and its `tidy()` and `glance()`
  gain no column. No limit changes.

- **[`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md),
  [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md),
  [`ci_c_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c_ancova.md),
  [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md),
  and
  [`ci_c_ancova_bp()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c_ancova_bp.md)
  require the standard deviation of the errors and refuse one that is
  not a single positive, finite number.** The standard error of a
  contrast is that standard deviation times a function of the weights
  and the sample sizes (and, in ANCOVA, of the covariate means), and it
  cannot be recovered from the means. Through 1.0.1 it was checked only
  on some paths:

  - `ci_c(means = c(1, 2, 3), c_weights = c(1, -1, 0), n_per_group = c(10, 10, 10))`,
    with no `s_anova`, returned a zero-width interval at the estimate,
    -1, -1, and -1, labeled “Confidence level: 95%”, with the sentence
    “contrast = -1.00, 95% CI \[-1.00, -1.00\]”;
  - `ci_c_ancova(adj_means = c(7.5, 12, 14), c_weights = c(1, -1, 0), n_per_group = c(10, 10, 10), cov_means = c(5, 6, 7), SSwithin_x = 750)`,
    with no `s_ancova`, returned -4.5, -4.5, and -4.5 labeled 95%, and
    `s_ancova = 0` returned the same;
  - a negative value swapped the limits: `s_anova = -1` in the
    [`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md) call
    gave a lower limit of -0.08 above an upper limit of -1.92, and
    `s_ancova = -2` in the
    [`ci_c_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c_ancova.md)
    call gave -2.66 above -6.34;
  - [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md)
    with means and no `s_anova`, and
    [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md)
    with no `s_ancova`, stopped with “argument is of length zero”;
    [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md)
    with `s_ancova = 0` stopped with “lower \< upper is not fulfilled”;
  - [`ci_c_ancova_bp()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c_ancova_bp.md)
    stopped on an `NA` with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” and
    returned infinite limits for `Inf`.

  Each of these is now refused with a message that names the argument
  and says what it is: `s_anova` for
  [`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md) and
  [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md) on
  every path, `s_ancova` for
  [`ci_c_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c_ancova.md)
  (either procedure),
  [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md),
  and
  [`ci_c_ancova_bp()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c_ancova_bp.md),
  and `s_anova` for
  [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md)
  when it is the standardizer. A call with neither the means nor the
  contrast, which failed with “arguments imply differing number of rows:
  3, 0” in
  [`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md), is
  refused in words. Every interval formed from a valid standard
  deviation is unchanged.

- **[`plot_ci()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_ci.md)
  titles a DMAR table with the level the table records.** The title came
  from the `conf_level` argument, used only for the label, so a table
  formed at another level was titled with its default:
  `plot_ci(ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.90))`
  was titled “95% Confidence Interval” above the limits of a 90%
  interval, and a 97.5% table the same. The level the table records (its
  `conf_level` attribute, or a `conf_level` column holding one value) is
  now used when `conf_level` is not given (“90% Confidence Interval”),
  and a `conf_level` that differs from it is refused, since the plot
  draws the limits it is given and cannot change their level; rows that
  record several levels are refused as well. A frame that records no
  level, and explicit `estimate`, `lower`, and `upper` values, keep the
  argument’s level, .95 by default. An interval with unequal tail areas
  is drawn with a subtitle in the words of
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  (“Unequal tail areas: 0.01 below, 0.04 above”, or “One-sided: the
  upper limit is the 95% upper confidence bound”). The limits drawn are
  unchanged.

- **[`equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_c.md)
  has one more row and one more verdict.** An interval that contains
  `-contrast_lower` and whose upper limit is below `contrast_upper`
  (`delta_lower` and `delta_upper` in 1.0.x) was labeled “Inconclusive”
  through version 1.0.1 and is now “Not relevantly superior only”, in
  the `verdict` attribute and in
  [`plot_equivalence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_equivalence.md)’s
  colors. The second example of the help page,
  `equivalence_c(contrast = -5.28, se = 2.49, df_error = 399, contrast_upper = 5)`,
  with 90% limits -9.39 and -1.17, reads so now. “Inconclusive” is left
  for an interval that contains both bounds. Code that reads the rows by
  `term` is unaffected; code that reads them by position meets an 18th
  row, `nonsuperior`, after `inferior`, and the first 17 keep their
  places. No estimate, limit, or p-value changes.

- **[`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  stops when `null_R2` is not 0, and the test of an increment in R^2 has
  its own function.**
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  plans the omnibus test that the population squared multiple
  correlation coefficient of all `p` predictors is zero. A nonzero
  `null_R2`, which DMAR 1.0.x accepted, is now an error of class
  `dmar_null_R2_unsupported` (a `dmar_refusal`) whose message says what
  MBESS calculated with a nonzero `null_R2` and writes the call to
  [`ss_power_R2_change()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2_change.md)
  with the values given. No value is returned for such a call, in place
  of the following.

  With fixed predictors, 1.0.x and MBESS formed (`true_R2` - `null_R2`)
  / (1 - `true_R2`), which is Cohen’s

  1988. f^2 for the increment when predictors are added to a model that
        already explains `null_R2`, and referred it to an *F*
        distribution with `p` and N - `p` - 1 degrees of freedom and
        noncentrality N f^2. With `p` read as the number of predictors
        added, that is Cohen’s calculation for a total sample size of N
        plus the number of predictors in the restricted model:
        `true_R2 = .30`, `null_R2 = .25`, `p = 4`, `alpha_level = .01`,
        and `specified_N = 85` gave a power of .2225 with a
        noncentrality of 6.071, which is the value Cohen’s formula gives
        at N = 90 with five predictors in the restricted model, and the
        search gave 242 where Cohen’s form gives 247. With `p` read as
        all of the predictors, as the function defines it, the number is
        not the power of the test of the increment, whose numerator
        degrees of freedom are the number of predictors added: for .25
        against .20 with `p = 5` and `specified_N = 200` it was .8047,
        where the test of one predictor added to four has power .953 and
        the test of two added to three .911 (fixed predictors; .945 and
        .901 with random predictors), and the search for power .80 gave
        199, where those two tests need 120 and 148 (127 and 154 with
        random predictors). With random predictors, the default, 1.0.x
        did not form that effect size: given `true_R2` it returned
        `alpha_level` when `true_R2` was at or below `null_R2` and the
        power of the omnibus test above it (.0500 at `true_R2 = .20` and
        .9999 at .200001 with `p = 5`, `specified_N = 200`, and
        `null_R2 = .20`; a search for .25 against .20 returned 47, the
        sample size of the omnibus test of .25), and given `true_f2` it
        took the population value as (`true_f2` + `null_R2`) / (1 +
        `true_f2`) and returned the power of the omnibus test at it
        (.9975 for `true_f2 = .1`, `null_R2 = .2`, `p = 5`, and
        `specified_N = 100`, where the same call without `null_R2` gave
        .6378). The argument alone cannot say which calculation is
        meant, because the test of an increment needs the number of
        predictors in the restricted model.

  What to call instead. The test of the increment:
  `ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_full = a, true_R2_restricted = b, p_full = , p_restricted = )`.
  The number 1.0.x returned with fixed predictors, and MBESS returned:
  `ss_power_R2(true_f2 = (a - b) / (1 - a), p = p, random_predictors = FALSE)`,
  which gives .8047 and 199 for the second design above and .2225 and
  242 for the first. A call that gave `true_f2` with a nonzero `null_R2`
  is refused in the same way. With fixed predictors 1.0.x took that
  `true_f2` as the effect size of the increment, so the same call
  without `null_R2` returns its number; with random predictors
  `ss_power_R2(true_R2 = (true_f2 + null_R2) / (1 + true_f2), p = p)`
  returns the number 1.0.x gave (.9975 in the case above). When
  `true_R2` is at or below `null_R2` there is no increment to test:
  1.0.x returned `alpha_level` (MBESS returns `NaN`), and the message
  says so in place of the two calls, which would stop on a negative
  effect size. Whether the population squared multiple correlation
  coefficient exceeds a stated value above zero is a third question, for
  which DMAR has no planner in this release; that test rejects when the
  one-sided lower confidence limit from
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md)
  exceeds the value. `null_R2` stays in the signature so that an
  existing call is answered with the explanation, and `null_R2 = 0` is
  accepted. An invalid `null_R2` (not a single number of at least 0 and
  below 1) keeps its own message.

  A search with `true_R2 = 0` stops with “With ‘true_R2’ of 0 the null
  hypothesis is true, so power equals ‘alpha_level’ at every sample size
  and no sample size attains ‘desired_power’.” The sample size search
  doubles the size and then bisects, so a small effect returns promptly
  (`true_R2 = .00005` with `p = 5`, `desired_power = .80`, and fixed
  predictors gives 256,545); the size it returns is the smallest that
  attains `desired_power`, as before, and the search stops with an error
  at ten million. No power is returned from an evaluation at which R’s
  noncentral *F* warned of lost accuracy (“full precision may not have
  been achieved in ‘pnbeta’”); with a null value of zero no call was
  found that reaches that warning. Results with `null_R2 = 0` are
  unchanged from DMAR 1.0.0: on 1,500 combinations of `true_R2` (from
  .000001 to .999), `p`, `specified_N`, `alpha_level`, and predictor
  model, and 500 searches, version 1.0.0 and this version returned the
  same sample size in every search and powers that differ by at most
  6e-11 (the entry below on a very small `true_R2` describes a `true_R2`
  near 1e-8).

- **[`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  checks its arguments.** `alpha_level` must be a single number strictly
  between 0 and 1 (0 and 1 were accepted and returned `NaN`, 0, or 1);
  `true_R2` and `null_R2` must be single numbers of at least 0 and below
  1 (`true_R2 = 1` returned `NaN` with an infinite effect size, and
  `null_R2 = 1` a power of .05 with an effect size of -1); `p` must be a
  whole number of at least 1 (`p = 5.5` was accepted); `true_f2` must be
  nonnegative; and a call with neither `true_R2` nor `true_f2` says so,
  where it stopped with “object ‘f_Squared’ not found”.
  `random_predictors` must be `TRUE` or `FALSE`; 1, 0, and the character
  strings “TRUE” and “FALSE” were accepted and are now refused.

- **The random-predictor power of
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  no longer returns `NaN` for a very small nonzero `true_R2`.** The
  parameters of Lee’s approximation need the square root of a difference
  that cancels when rho^2 is small, and near rho^2 = 1e-8 the difference
  came out negative:
  `ss_power_R2(true_R2 = 1e-8, p = 10, specified_N = 12)` returned `NaN`
  with the warning “NaNs produced” and now returns .05. The root has a
  closed form with no subtraction, which the function shared by
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md),
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md), and
  [`ss_aipe_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2.md)
  now uses. The limits of
  [`ci_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_R2.md) and
  the sample sizes of
  [`ss_aipe_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2.md)
  did not change on the grids compared (1,500 and 65 calls). The power
  of
  [`ss_power_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_R2.md)
  changes by less than 1e-13 for a `true_R2` of .001 or more and by up
  to 9e-11 at 1e-6, where the earlier square root carried the larger
  rounding error.

- **[`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  without `true_R2_full` returns a larger sample size when `true_r_sp`
  squared is above 1/2.** DMAR 1.0.x planned with (1 - r_sp²⁾2, the
  variance when the variables partialed out explain none of the outcome.
  That is the largest the variance can be when r_sp^2 is at most 1/2,
  and there the plan is unchanged. Above 1/2 it is the smallest, and the
  1.0.x plan was too small unless the variables partialed out explained
  none of the outcome: for r_sp = .8, one variable partialed out
  (`p = 2`), and a width of .10 it gave 202, where an interval of that
  width needs 331 when the full-model R2 is .94 (at N = 202 the mean
  width in 4,000 replications was .127). The plan without `true_R2_full`
  now uses the largest variance over every possible full-model R2,
  r_sp^2 (1 - r_sp^2) when r_sp^2 is above 1/2: `necessary_N` for that
  call was 202 and is 357; for r_sp = .9, `p = 3`, and a width of .10 it
  was 59 and is 240; and for r_sp = .75, `p = 2`, a width of .10, and
  `assurance = .90` it was 329 and is 386 (with `seed = 113`; the plan
  with `assurance` is now found by simulation, as the entry on the
  assurance step describes). `true_R2_full = true_r_sp^2` restores the
  1.0.x plan made without `assurance` (with `assurance` it does not: the
  same call then returns 363, because the assurance step changed too).

- **[`ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md)
  simulate `p - 1` variables partialed out, the count their planners
  plan for, where DMAR 1.0.x simulated one fewer for the same model.**
  In 1.0.x the count was the argument `J` (`p = J + 1`). It was
  documented there as the total number of predictors and the simulated
  data had `J + 1` columns, while the planner each function calls, and
  the standard error of the interval each one formed, took the same `J`
  as the number of variables partialed out. With `J = 1` the “partial”
  correlation simulated was the simple correlation of two variables,
  given the interval of a partial correlation with one variable removed.
  Both functions now simulate the model the rest of the family
  describes: *Y*, *X*, and `p - 1` variables partialed out, so the
  simulated data have `p + 1` columns. The planner call and `total_N`
  are unchanged, and the results at a given seed change, by little,
  since the interval already allowed for the variables partialed out:
  with `set.seed(113)`, `true_cor = .40`, `specified_N = 30`, three
  variables partialed out (`p = 4`; `J = 3` in 1.0.x), a width of .40,
  and `G = 2000`, the standard deviation of the partial correlations was
  .1666 and is .1717, and with `fisher_z = TRUE`, the interval 1.0.x
  formed, the proportion of intervals that missed the true value was
  .048 and is .057 (Monte Carlo standard error .005). With the default
  interval of this release, on the raw scale, that proportion is .091,
  which also reflects the change of interval described in the entry on
  `fisher_z`. This was a defect, and no argument restores the earlier
  results; a model with nothing partialed out is
  [`ss_aipe_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_r_sensitivity.md).

- **[`ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity.md)
  forms the interval the planner plans for.** Each replication’s
  interval was formed on Fisher’s *Z* scale with standard error 1 /
  sqrt(N - p - 1), by analogy with the partial correlation. No function
  of a semipartial correlation alone stabilizes its variance, which
  depends on the full-model R2, and
  [`ss_aipe_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_semipartial_r.md)
  plans the width of a Wald interval on the correlation’s own scale.
  Each interval is now that Wald interval: the estimate plus and minus
