  the normal critical value times the square root of the first-order
  variance
  ([`var_semipartial_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_semipartial_r.md)
  with `under_null = FALSE`) at the sample semipartial correlation and
  the sample full-model R2, with the limits not truncated at -1 and 1.
  In the population 1.0.x simulated, in which the controls explain none
  of the outcome, the two intervals nearly coincide: with
  `set.seed(113)`, `true_r_sp = supposed_r_sp = .30`, `p = 4` (`J = 3`
  in 1.0.x), a width of .20, and `G = 2000`, the mean width was .1988
  and is .1986 at the same `total_N` of 323. With `true_r_sp = .80`,
  `p = 2` (`J = 1` in 1.0.x), and a width of .10 the planner’s change
  above moves `total_N` from 202 to 357 and the mean width from .1007 to
  .0754. This was a defect, and no argument restores the earlier
  interval.

- **[`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  and
  [`randomization_test_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test_paired.md)
  count tied reassignments by the rounding of the arithmetic, and the
  studentized statistic no longer drops the reassignments with no
  within-group spread.** A reassignment whose statistic equals the
  observed one counts as at least as extreme. Earlier versions compared
  with a tolerance relative to the largest reference statistic, formed
  each variance as a sum of squares less *n* times a squared mean, and
  set a statistic with a zero standard error to 0. The comparison now
  allows the rounding bound of the statistic compared, which is
  proportional to the size of the scores; variances come from residuals
  about each group’s own mean; and a reassignment in the reference set
  whose standard error is zero is ordered as an infinite statistic with
  the sign of its difference (0 when every score is equal). When the
  observed data themselves have a zero standard error and a nonzero
  difference, `statistic = "t"` is refused (see the entry on that
  refusal below). The *p*-values that change:

  - Studentized statistic, two-valued or tied scores.
    `randomization_test(group_1 = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 0), group_2 = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1), statistic = "t")`
    gave 0.198413 and gives 52/252 = 0.206349. For
    `g_1 <- c(4.800000002, 4.8, 4.800000003, 4.800000001, 4.800000002)`
    and
    `g_2 <- c(8, 8.000000001, 8.000000003, 8.000000003, 8.000000003)` it
    gave 0.003968, half the smallest value ten scores can produce, and
    gives 2/252 = 0.007937 (the statistic reported for that call was
    -339,547,000 and is -3,938,927,000, the value of the Welch formula
    for those scores).
    `randomization_test_paired(rep(0, 6), c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, -1), statistic = "t")`
    gave 0.1875 and gives 14/64 = 0.21875 (0.09375 and 7/64 = 0.109375
    with `alternative = "greater"`).
  - Paired test, constant differences, `statistic = "t"`.
    `randomization_test_paired(1:5, 1:5 + 2, statistic = "t")` gave a
    statistic of 0 and *p* = 1. The paired *t* has a zero standard error
    there and no value, so the call is now refused (class
    `dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined`) with a message that says why
    and gives the *p*-value of the mean difference, 2/32 = 0.0625, which
    `statistic = "mean"` returns.
  - Difference in means, scores with many digits. For
    `x <- c(1000000.002, 1000000.005, 1000000.000, 1000000.002, 1000000.001, 1000000.001)`
    and
    `y <- c(1000000.003, 1000000.007, 1000000.002, 1000000.001, 999999.999, 1000000.001)`,
    `randomization_test_paired(x, y)` gave 0.75 and gives 0.8125, the
    value for the same scores in thousandths without the offset. The
    independent test was too small in the same way:
    `randomization_test(group_1 = 1000000 + c(2, 2, 2, 0) / 1000, group_2 = 1000000 + c(3, 3, 0, 7, 4) / 1000)`
    gave 0.214286 and gives 28/126 = 0.222222.
  - Difference in means, one score far larger than the rest.
    `randomization_test(group_1 = c(3e9, 4, 7, 2), group_2 = c(3, 5, 6, 9, 1))`
    gave 0.444444 and gives 35/126 = 0.277778;
    `randomization_test_paired(c(3e9, 4, 7, 2, 5), c(3, 5, 6, 9, 1))`
    gave 1 and gives 0.6875.
  - Differences that are distinct by more than rounding are no longer
    merged.
    `randomization_test_paired(rep(0, 6), c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1 + 1e-12, -1))`
    gave 0.21875 (and 1 with `statistic = "t"`) and gives 12/64 = 0.1875
    with either statistic.

  Scores with no ties and no extreme offsets give the *p*-values they
  gave: 3,240 seeded calls on continuous data (exact and Monte Carlo,
  both statistics, three alternatives, and
  [`procrustes_phi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/procrustes_phi.md))
  returned the same *p*-value before and after the change. The limits of
  the shift interval move by up to about two millionths of a standard
  error, because the earlier tolerance counted near ties at the edge of
  the interval. Checked against rational arithmetic in 1,800 comparisons
  on unbalanced designs, the studentized *p*-value is exact for binary,
  three-valued, Likert, three-decimal (with and without an offset of a
  million), and constant scores; with one score of 3e9 among single
  digits, or scores within a millionth of one of two values, statistics
  closer than the rounding bound are counted as tied and the *p*-value
  was above the exact one in 96 of 600 comparisons and below it in none.
  [`?randomization_test`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  says so under “Ties”. The repaired statistic costs time, since each
  reassignment now keeps the scores of both groups and forms its own
  residuals: with the default 10,000 reassignments and the shift
  interval, a call with 150 scores per group and `statistic = "t"` takes
  about 2.8 s where it took 0.16 s, and one with 1,500 per group about
  26 s where it took 1.7 s (`statistic = "mean"`: 0.30 s against 0.11 s,
  and 3.0 s against 1.1 s). Most of the time is the inversion for the
  shift interval: with `shift_ci = FALSE` the two studentized calls take
  0.27 s and 1.3 s.

- **[`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  with `statistic = "t"` reports the whole line as the shift interval
  where no shift can be rejected.** With three scores per group the
  smallest two-sided *p*-value is 2/20, so the 95 percent interval is
  unbounded, as the help says. Under the studentized statistic the
  earlier arithmetic lost the reassignments with no within-group spread
  at large shifts and returned limits such as -77,486,400 and 78,526,226
  for `group_1 = c(80, 84, 79)`, `group_2 = c(72, 75, 68)`; the limits
  are now `-Inf` and `Inf`, as they were for `statistic = "mean"`. The
  studentized statistic is now computed on scores divided by a power of
  2 near their largest absolute value, so scores near 1e-200 or 1e200,
  whose squared residuals underflow or overflow, give the statistic and
  *p*-value of the same scores in ordinary units
  (`c(3, 5, 9, 4) * 1e-200` against `c(1, 2, 2, 6, 3) * 1e-200` stopped
  with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”). The division is exact,
  and no other result changes.

- **`statistic = "t"` is refused in
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  and
  [`randomization_test_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test_paired.md)
  when the observed standard error is zero and the observed difference
  is not.** The studentized statistic is the mean difference divided by
  its standard error. When both observed groups are constant at
  different values, or every paired difference is the same nonzero
  value, that standard error is 0 and the statistic has no value. DMAR
  1.0.0 reported a paired *t* of 0 with *p* = 1 for such differences
  (`randomization_test_paired(1:5, 1:5 + 2, statistic = "t")`) and, for
  two constant groups
  (`randomization_test(group_1 = rep(5, 4), group_2 = rep(3, 4), statistic = "t")`),
  stopped with an error raised while the standardized mean difference
  was computed. Both calls now stop with an error of class
  `dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined` (a `dmar_refusal`), made before
  any arrangement is enumerated or drawn, so a refused Monte Carlo call
  leaves the random number stream where it was. The message says that
  the denominator is zero, that the observed data lie at the boundary of
  the reference set (of the 32 sign patterns, only the observed one and
  its mirror image have a zero standard error; of the 70 reassignments
  of 4 and 4 scores, only the observed one and the one that exchanges
  the groups), that this concerns the statistic and not the evidence,
  and what `statistic = "mean"` gives: the mean difference 2 with the
  exact *p*-value 2/32 = 0.0625 for the first call and 2/70 = 0.02857
  for the second. The condition carries that value as `p_value_mean`,
  with `reason` (`"constant_differences"` or `"constant_groups"`),
  `alternative`, and `n` or `n_1` and `n_2`. The value is the smallest
  the design allows in the direction of the data: 1/2^*n* one-sided and
  2/2^*n* two-sided for *n* pairs; for a first group of `n_1` among *N*
  scores, 1/choose(*N*, `n_1`) one-sided, and two-sided 2/choose(*N*,
  `n_1`) with equal group sizes and 1/choose(*N*, `n_1`) otherwise (1/56
  for 3 against 5); it is 1 for the alternative that points away from
  the data. When the call would have been run by Monte Carlo sampling
  the message adds that such a run estimates the value and cannot report
  less than 1/(`n_resamples` + 1): for 30 against 30 constant scores the
  exact value is 2/choose(60, 30), about 1.7e-17, and
  `statistic = "mean"` reports 1/10001 = 0.00009999.
  `statistic = "mean"` is unchanged in every case. What is kept: a
  reassignment inside the reference set whose standard error is zero is
  still ordered as `Inf` or `-Inf`, because such reassignments occur in
  ordinary two-valued and coarsely measured data and the limit puts them
  where the difference in means does (`group_1 = c(1, 1, 1, 0)` against
  `group_2 = c(0, 0, 0, 1)` with `statistic = "t"` returns *t* = 1.4142
  and *p* = 34/70 = 0.4857, with one `-Inf` and one `Inf` among the 70
  reference values, the same *p* as the difference in means;
  `randomization_test_paired( rep(0, 5), c(2, 2, 2, -2, 2), statistic = "t")`
  returns *t* = 1.5 and *p* = 12/32 = 0.375); and when every score is
  equal the statistic is 0 and *p* is 1 under either statistic, as
  before. The comparison that decides whether the observed data are
  constant uses the tolerances already in place, so
  `c(5, 5, 5, 5 + 1e-12)` against `rep(3, 4)` is not refused and returns
  *t* = 8.0e12.
  [`?randomization_test`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  and
  [`?randomization_test_paired`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test_paired.md)
  have a paragraph, “When the studentized statistic is undefined”, and
  an example of the refusal.

- **The shift interval of
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  rejects a shift whose *p*-value equals 1 - `conf_level`.** A shift is
  in the interval when its *p*-value is above alpha, and alpha was
  computed as 1 - `conf_level`, which for 0.90 is 0.09999999999999998 in
  binary arithmetic, just below the *p*-value 1/10 that the test at the
  0.10 level rejects. Shifts with exactly that *p*-value were therefore
  kept, and the interval was too wide whenever alpha times the number of
  reassignments is a whole number (at 0.90 with 10, 20, 70, or 210
  reassignments; at 0.80 likewise). For `group_1 = c(-1.5, 3.6, 0)` and
  `group_2 = c(4.2, 3.0, -1.7)` the 90 percent limits were `-Inf` and
  `Inf` and are -5.7 and 5.3, and the 80 percent limits were -5.7 and
  5.3 and are -4.5 and 1.7. The comparison now allows a few units of
  rounding in alpha. Intervals at 0.95 and 0.99 are unchanged; the
  defect was in 1.0.0 as well, and an interval was never too narrow.

- **[`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  returns its table when the standardized mean difference is
  undefined.** With no within-group variance (`group_1 = c(1, 1, 1)`,
  `group_2 = c(2, 2, 2)`, or every score equal) the call stopped inside
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md)
  with “lower \< upper is not fulfilled” or with “missing value where
  TRUE/FALSE needed”. It now reports the test, the shift interval, and
  Cliff’s delta, with the rows `smd`, `smd_ci_lower`, `smd_ci_upper`,
  `cles`, `cles_ci_lower`, and `cles_ci_upper` as `NA` and a warning of
  class `dmar_smd_undefined`. For `rep(1.1, 4)` against `rep(0.2, 4)`
  with `statistic = "mean"` the statistic is 0.9, *p* is 2/70, and both
  shift limits are 0.9; `statistic = "t"` is refused there, since both
  groups are constant. A response that is not finite (`Inf`, `-Inf`) is
  refused in both randomization tests (“must be finite”), where it gave
  a base R error or a *p*-value of `NA`.

- **[`plot_randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_randomization_test.md)
  shades the reassignments the *p*-value counted.** The figure used an
  absolute tolerance of 1e-12 of its own. For the scores of the first
  help example multiplied by 1e-13 it shaded every reassignment (share
  1.000 beside *p* = 0.0238), and for `1e5 + c(.1, .4, .7, .2)` against
  `1e5 + c(.3, .5, .6, .9)` it shaded 0.2571 beside *p* = 0.3143.
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  now stores the logical vector it counted as the attribute
  `reference_extreme`, and the plot shades those. A reassignment with an
  infinite studentized statistic is not drawn, and the subtitle says how
  many are not, on a second line. Infinite values occur in the reference
  distribution only: the observed statistic is always finite, since
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  refuses the one case in which it is not, and its line is always drawn.
  When every reassignment the *p*-value counted is infinite, which can
  happen only in a Monte Carlo sample (under enumeration the observed
  assignment is among those counted), the subtitle gives *p* without
  calling it a shaded area and says that none is shaded.

- **[`procrustes_phi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/procrustes_phi.md)
  counts a permutation tied with the observed arrangement.** A
  permutation that exchanges two items with the same loading reproduces
  the observed coefficient, but was compared with it exactly and could
  fall one unit in the last place below. With
  `l1 <- c(0.6, 0.72, 0.65, 0.72, 0.81)`,
  `l2 <- c(0.61, 0.76, 0.64, 0.68, 0.85)`, and `set.seed(113)`,
  `procrustes_phi(l1, l2, n_resamples = 60000)` gave 0.00772 and gives
  0.01637; 2 of the 120 permutations are at least as extreme, 0.01667.
  The denominator is computed once and the comparison allows 4(*n* + 2)
  units of machine precision. A call with no tied loadings gives the
  *p*-value it gave.

- **`n_resamples` must be a whole number.**
  `randomization_test_paired(x, y, exact = FALSE, n_resamples = 4.5)`
  drew four sign patterns and divided by 5.5, and
  `procrustes_phi(l1, l2, n_resamples = 2.5)` drew two permutations and
  divided by 3.5;
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  truncated 4.5 to 4, and `procrustes_phi(n_resamples = -3)` returned
  the coefficient with no message. Each now stops with an error of class
  `dmar_count_invalid` unless the count is a single whole number of at
  least 1 (the two randomization tests) or at least 0
  ([`procrustes_phi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/procrustes_phi.md),
  where 0 skips the test). A whole count gives what it gave. The count
  is checked whether or not the call draws:
  `randomization_test_paired(x, y, n_resamples = NULL)` with eight
  pairs, which enumerates, returned its table and now stops, as
  [`randomization_test()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  already did. The check of `n_resamples` applies under exact
  enumeration as well, where the count is not used.

- **Help corrections for the randomization tests and
  [`procrustes_phi()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/procrustes_phi.md).**
  [`?randomization_test_paired`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test_paired.md)
  said that the paired *t* is more robust to pair-to-pair variability
  than the mean difference. Over the sign patterns the paired *t* is an
  increasing function of the mean difference, so the two give the same
  *p*-value for every data set and differ only in the statistic
  reported; the page now says so, and says that exact enumeration is the
  default through 20 pairs and available through 25.
  [`?randomization_test`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/randomization_test.md)
  said that the mean difference and the studentized statistic agree in a
  balanced design with equal variances “to within the discreteness of
  the reference distribution”; they give the same *p*-value in every
  balanced design, whatever the variances, and differ only when the
  groups are unequal in size, and the second example’s comment no longer
  recommends the studentized statistic for two groups of five.
  [`?procrustes_phi`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/procrustes_phi.md)
  called the permutation distribution a sampling distribution and said
  the function reports the coefficient “with its uncertainty”; the test
  takes the two sets of loadings as given, and the function reports the
  coefficient and the permutation *p*-value, with no standard error or
  interval.

- **[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md):
  the bootstrap limits of the indirect effect change in data where a
  resample makes the predictor or the mediator a linear combination of
  the covariates.** [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) returned a
  finite product *a b* in such a resample, by dropping a covariate
  column in place of the predictor, and that product entered the
  interval although the effect is not estimable there. These resamples
  are now dropped and counted (see
  “[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  codes its covariates once” above). With a binary predictor (8 of 40
  cases) and a binary covariate that differs from it in two cases,
  `B = 2000`, `seed = 113`: 248 of the 2000 resamples are of this kind;
  the percentile limits were \[-0.0401, 0.7202\] over all 2000 and are
  \[-0.0369, 0.6800\] over the 1752 in which the effect is defined, with
  the warning of class `dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped`. The
  estimate (0.1925) and every other row are the same. The same holds in
  a small sample with several covariates, where a resample can hold
  fewer distinct cases than the model has coefficients: with 12 cases,
  three continuous covariates, and `B = 600`, 12 resamples are dropped
  and the limits, which were \[-1.397, 2.023\] with 127 warnings from
  [`lm()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) about a perfect fit, are
  \[-1.177, 1.881\]. A call whose resamples all leave *a* and *b*
  estimable returns the limits it returned before, to rounding error
  (relative difference below 1e-10; up to 1e-9 for a date-time
  predictor, where the earlier fit lost digits to the size of the
  origin). No argument restores the earlier limits.

- **[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  refuses a logical outcome.** A logical `y` was read as 0 and 1 and the
  linear model fit to it; the call now stops and says that the column
  must be numeric. [`as.numeric()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/numeric.html)
  of the column gives the earlier table. (A logical `x` or `m` stopped
  before, with `subscript out of bounds`.)

- **[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  returns 18 rows, not 17**: `B_used` follows `B`. Code that reads rows
  by `term` is not affected; code that reads the table by position past
  row 17 is.

- **`mediate(ci_method = "boot_bca")` stops where it returned an
  interval from an incomplete jackknife.** With one case carrying all
  the variation in the predictor (`x = c(3, rep(0, 19))`, `B = 300`,
  `seed = 113`) it returned \[-0.1173, 0.4605\]; it now stops with
  `dmar_bca_undefined`, naming case 1.

- **[`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md)
  stops when a column is named more than once.** A covariate named twice
  returned the answer for the covariate entered once; `y` among the
  covariates returned a table from a model with the outcome among the
  predictors of the mediator. Both now stop.

- **[`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md)
  reports the confidence set for the number needed to treat correctly
  when the interval for the standardized mean difference includes zero,
  where DMAR 1.0.0 returned its two ends in reversed order as if they
  bounded an interval.** The reciprocal of an interval for the success
  rate difference (SRD) that includes zero is two intervals that meet at
  infinity, the NNT of no effect (Altman, 1998). DMAR 1.0.0 put the two
  finite ends of that set in the rows `nnt_lower` and `nnt_upper`, the
  lower above the upper and the estimate outside them, with nothing to
  mark the case:
  `nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.3, smd_lower = -0.10, smd_upper = 0.70)`, the
  fourth example of the help page (now
  `nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.3, smd_ci_lower = -0.10, smd_ci_upper = 0.70)`),
  returned `nnt` 5.953, `nnt_lower` 2.636, and `nnt_upper` -17.739, and
  `nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.1, n_1 = 30, n_2 = 30)` returned 17.739, 3.015,
  and -4.417. In that case the NNT limits, now the rows `nnt_ci_lower`
  and `nnt_ci_upper`, are `NA`, as the NNT limits of
  [`responder_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/responder_analysis.md)
  are, the set is in the new `nnt_confidence_set` attribute (for the
  first call, the rows (`-Inf`, -17.739) and (2.636, `Inf`)), the new
  `nnt_set` attribute is `"two_intervals"`, and the table prints the set
  beneath it: “NNT \<= -17.739 (harm) or NNT \>= 2.636 (benefit), joined
  at infinity (Altman, 1998)”. Read as an interval, the two rows of
  1.0.0 held the true NNT in none of the samples when the population
  difference is zero and in 34 percent of them at a population
  standardized mean difference of 0.5 with 20 per group (95 percent
  intervals); the set of two intervals holds it at the stated level.
  When the upper limit of the standardized mean difference is exactly
  zero, the lower NNT limit is now `-Inf`, where 1.0.0 gave `Inf`
  (`nnt_from_smd(smd = -0.3, smd_lower = -0.7, smd_upper = 0)` returned
  `nnt_lower` `Inf` and `nnt_upper` -2.636, and
  `nnt_from_smd(smd = -0.3, smd_ci_lower = -0.7, smd_ci_upper = 0)`
  returns `-Inf` and -2.636). A result whose interval excludes zero, or
  has a lower limit of exactly zero, is unchanged in its first seven
  rows, with one exception at the edge of the arithmetic: the SRD is
  computed without the subtraction that lost digits for a standardized
  mean difference near zero, so results for \|d\| below about 1e-8
  differ from 1.0.0 in their later digits (at d = 1e-12 the NNT was
  1.772373e12 and is 1.772454e12, which is sqrt(pi) / d), and a d so
  small that the SRD rounded to zero keeps its sign
  (`nnt_from_smd(-1e-200)` gave an NNT of `Inf` and gives `-Inf`). Every
  result has the leading class `dmar_nnt`, which prints the set, ahead
  of `dmar_tbl` and `data.frame`, and `dmar_metadata()$result` is
  `"dmar_nnt"`; code that tests `inherits(x, "dmar_tbl")` is unaffected.
  `tidy()` and `glance()` return the rows without the two attributes;
  the finite ends of a set of two intervals are 1 / `srd_ci_lower` and 1
  / `srd_ci_upper`.

  - Two rows, `srd_ci_lower` and `srd_ci_upper`, are appended after
    `nnt_ci_upper`: the confidence interval for the SRD, which is an
    ordinary interval in every case and is the interval Kraemer and
    Kupfer (2006) prefer. The seven rows of 1.0.0 keep their positions;
    four are renamed (see Renamed Output Rows and Columns).
  - The arguments are checked. `smd` must be a single finite number,
    `conf_level` a single number in (0, 1), the limits and the sample
    sizes each given as a pair or not at all, and `smd_ci_lower` not
    above `smd_ci_upper`; DMAR 1.0.0 returned the point estimate without
    an interval and without a message when one limit or one sample size
    was given, accepted reversed limits, and printed “Confidence level:
    700%” for `conf_level = 7`. An estimate outside its supplied limits
    is accepted with a warning. Supplied limits are still used in place
    of `n_1` and `n_2`.
  - With supplied limits, a confidence level is recorded and printed
    only when `conf_level` is given in the call; DMAR 1.0.0 printed
    “Confidence level: 95%” for limits whose level it did not know.
  - The help page states what is estimated: the SRD of Kraemer and
    Kupfer (2006), the probability that a randomly chosen treated person
    has the better outcome minus the probability of the reverse, and its
    reciprocal. It no longer describes a median cut, which the
    conversion does not use. It distinguishes this NNT from the NNT at a
    response threshold, corrects the title of Furukawa and Leucht (2011)
    (“Comparison of two methods”) and what they found (the control event
    rate conversion was closer to the observed NNTs, where the page had
    said they recommended the conversion computed here), and adds Altman
    (1998).

- **The
  [`responder_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/responder_analysis.md)
  help page no longer cites Altman (1998) for withholding the NNT
  limits.** The page said that an interval on the NNT scale would
  mislead when the interval for the difference includes zero.
  Altman (1998) argues for reporting it: the confidence set is then two
  intervals that meet at infinity, with the reciprocals of the
  difference limits as its two finite ends. The page now says that, and
  that one lower and one upper limit cannot hold such a set, which is
  why the two NNT limits are `NA`. No result changes.

- **[`responder_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/responder_analysis.md)
  carries the confidence set for the number needed to treat, as
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md)
  does, and the help pages of both functions are written out in full.**
  When the interval for the difference of the two responder proportions
  includes zero, the NNT limits are `NA`, as before, and the set they
  could not hold is now in the result. With two groups the table has the
  attributes `nnt_set` (`"interval"` or `"two_intervals"`, one value per
  threshold) and `nnt_confidence_set` (columns `lower` and `upper`, with
  `threshold` first under `sweep`), on the signed scale 1 / difference,
  and `group_labels`; for two intervals a line under the table states
  the set. For the first example of the help page (30 of 60 control and
  35 of 60 treated participants at a threshold of 10; difference 0.083,
  interval -0.093 to 0.252; NNT 12 with `NA` limits), earlier versions
  printed the table alone, and the table is now followed by “NNT \<=
  -10.806 (control responds more often) or NNT \>= 3.966 (treatment
  responds more often), joined at infinity (Altman, 1998)”, the
  reciprocals of the two limits of the difference. Every result has the
  leading class `dmar_responder`, which prints that line, ahead of
  `dmar_tbl` and `data.frame`, and `dmar_metadata()$result` is
  `"dmar_responder"` where it was `"dmar_tbl"`; code that tests
  `inherits(x, "dmar_tbl")` is unaffected. No row of any table changes
  (152 calls compared with the build before this change: largest
  difference 0).
  [`?responder_analysis`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/responder_analysis.md)
  now states what is estimated and how it differs from the NNT of
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md);
  the assumptions, among them that the threshold is fixed before the
  data are seen and that `sweep` describes dependence on the threshold
  and is not a search; the Wilson and Newcombe formulas as computed; the
  construction of the confidence set; what is returned when the
  proportions are equal, when no one or everyone responds in one group
  or in all (in the last case the chi square statistic is 0/0 and is
  reported as `NaN`), for a group of one, for outcomes at the threshold,
  for missing values, and for more than two groups; what each row is;
  the example read number by number; and what dichotomizing costs, from
  MacCallum, Zhang, Preacher, and Rucker (2002): a split at the mean
  multiplies a correlation by 0.798 and its square by 0.637, about the
  loss of 36 percent of the sample.
  [`?nnt_from_smd`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md)
  now states the estimand in words; which assumptions serve the point
  conversion and which the interval; the conversion with a table of the
  SRD and the NNT for standardized mean differences of 0.1 to 1.0, which
  agrees with Table 1 of Kraemer and Kupfer (2006); case by case why the
  reciprocal of an interval that includes zero is two intervals and why
  one pair of limits cannot hold it; the edge cases; the threshold NNT
  beside this one in numbers (at a standardized mean difference of 0.5:
  3.62 here, and at least 5.07 at any threshold under the same normal
  model); and two worked examples. No result of
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md)
  changes (154 calls compared: largest difference 0).

- **[`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  stops on input it used to order by a rule the user did not choose.**
  It converted whatever it was given with
  [`as.numeric()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/numeric.html). An unordered
  factor was read through its integer codes, which follow the
  alphabetical order of its labels:
  `vargha_delaney_A(factor(c("10", "9", "8")), c(10, 9, 8))` returned
  *A* = 0 with limits \[0, 0\], and a five-category agreement item
  supplied as an unordered factor through `outcome ~ group` returned the
  value of its alphabetical codes. Two time differences in different
  units were compared as bare numbers:
  `vargha_delaney_A(as.difftime(c(1, 2, 3), units = "hours"), as.difftime(c(30, 90, 150), units = "mins"))`
  returned *A* = 0 with limits \[0, 0\], where the value is 0.667. A
  `Date` beside a `POSIXct` was compared as days against seconds. A
  matrix outcome in a formula, `cbind(s, t) ~ g`, was strung out column
  after column under a recycled row index, so that 3 rows per group were
  reported as 6 observations per group. Each of these calls now stops
  with an error of class `dmar_scores_not_ordered` that says what to
  supply. Two time differences in the same units, and a time difference
  outcome in the formula interface, are on one scale and are ordered as
  before. Convert time differences in different units with
  `as.numeric(x, units = "hours")`, and supply an ordinal response as an
  ordered factor or as numeric scores.

- **[`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  reports both limits at the estimate, with a warning, when every pair
  favors the same member.** It returned `NaN` for both limits and no
  warning:
  `probability_of_superiority_paired(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(4, 5, 6, 7))` gave
  an estimate of 1 with limits `NaN`, `NaN`, and now gives 1 with limits
  1, 1 and the warning of class `dmar_interval_degenerate`, which says
  that the limits are not a confidence interval with the stated
  coverage. With a missing value it returned a table of `NA`; it now
  removes the pair.

- **[`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  and
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  agree with their earlier values to rounding, not to the last bit.**
  The rank-based computation gives the same *A* bit for bit. On 3,000
  samples with and without ties (2 to 60 observations per group), the
  largest differences from the earlier results were 8e-17 in the
  standard error of *A*, 8e-16 in its limits, 8e-15 in Cliff’s delta,
  2e-16 in its variance, and 2e-14 in its limits; the proportions of
  pairs won, lost, and tied were identical. These are the largest
  differences on the samples compared, not bounds. Cliff’s delta is now
  the difference of two exact proportions where it was the mean of the
  signs of all pairs (on one sample of 3,000 per group it was
  0.170807999999525 and is 0.170808, the exact ratio). The *z* statistic
  of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  moved by at most 1e-13 and its *p*-value by at most 4e-16.

- **[`meta_es()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_es.md),
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md),
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md),
  and
  [`plot_forest()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_forest.md)
  warn when the effect sizes are identical under the Hartung-Knapp
  adjustment, and the warning states what the conventional analysis
  gives.** When every effect size is the same, exactly or up to rounding
  error, the weighted residuals are zero and so is the adjusted standard
  error: `meta_es(rep(.5, 4), rep(.04, 4))` returns a standard error of
  0, a *t* of `Inf`, and confidence and prediction limits of 0.5 and
  0.5. Those numbers are unchanged (they are what `test = "knha"` in
  metafor returns). Earlier versions returned them with no message. The
  functions now give one warning of class `dmar_meta_hk_zero_se`. It
  says that the adjustment multiplies the conventional standard error by
  the square root of *q*, the weighted mean square of the effect sizes
  about the pooled estimate, and that *q* is 0 when the effect sizes do
  not differ; it shows the limits (0.5, 0.5); it says that this is not
  evidence that the effect is known exactly, since each effect size has
  a sampling variance that agreement among four estimates does not
  remove; and it states the conventional standard error and the normal
  interval at the level of the call, 0.1 and 0.304 to 0.696 for that
  call, which `hartung_knapp = FALSE` reports. The condition carries
  `n_studies`, `estimate`, `se_conventional`, `lower_conventional`, and
  `upper_conventional` (4, 0.5, 0.1, 0.3040036, 0.6959964). When the
  common effect size is 0 the message says that the *t* statistic is
  undefined (0 divided by 0), and when the standard error is only
  numerically zero (`meta_es(c(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, 0.3), rep(.04, 3))`,
  standard error 2e-17) it says that the statistic is the estimate
  divided by a rounding error. For
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md) the
  limits and the normal interval in the message and in the condition are
  correlations, as the reported rows are, and the conventional standard
  error is on the Fisher *Z* scale and is labeled so
  (`meta_r(r = c(.3, .3, .3), n = c(40, 60, 90))`: 0.07433 on the Fisher
  *Z* scale, normal interval 0.1624 to 0.4262). Effect sizes that
  differ, however little (0.5, 0.5, and 0.5 + 1e-9), do not raise the
  warning, and no warning is given for a *q* between 0 and 1, which is
  the method working as defined.

- **Meta-analysis results record *q* and the conventional standard
  error.** Whenever the Hartung-Knapp adjustment is applied, the tables
  of
  [`meta_es()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_es.md),
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md),
  and [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md)
  carry two new attributes: `hartung_knapp_q`, the weighted residual
  mean square on *k* - 1 degrees of freedom, and `se_conventional`, the
  standard error without the adjustment (both on the Fisher *Z* scale
  for
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md)).
  The adjusted standard error is the square root of the first times the
  second. For effect sizes of .30, .32, .29, .31, and .33 with variances
  of .04, .05, .03, .06, and .04 they are 0.006860532 and 0.0912870929,
  and the reported standard error is 0.007561158. The tables keep their
  20 rows, and no reported number changes (1,104 fits compared with the
  build before this change: largest difference 0).
  [`?meta_es`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_es.md)
  has two new paragraphs. “When q is small” says that the adjusted
  interval is narrower than the normal interval exactly when *q* is
  below the squared ratio of the normal quantile to the *t* quantile on
  *k* - 1 degrees of freedom (0.02, 0.21, 0.50, and 0.75 at *k* = 2, 3,
  5, and 10 for a 95 percent interval), that a small *q* belongs to the
  reference distribution of the method, and that both intervals should
  be reported when the adjusted one is much the narrower. “Identical
  effect sizes” describes the case the warning is for.

- **The help of
  [`meta_es()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_es.md)
  no longer says that the Hartung-Knapp adjustment keeps the confidence
  interval near its nominal coverage.** It now gives the adjusted
  standard error, the conventional one times the square root of the
  weighted residual mean square *q* (Röver, Knapp, & Friede, 2015), and
  says that the function applies the unmodified method: *q* is not
  replaced by max(1, *q*), so when *q* \< 1 the interval is narrower
  than the normal interval. For effect sizes of .30, .32, .29, .31, and
  .33 with variances of .04, .05, .03, .06, and .04, *q* is 0.0069 and
  the interval is 0.287 to 0.329, against 0.129 to 0.487 with
  `hartung_knapp = FALSE`. The help says where the coverage of the
  adjusted interval is at or near the nominal level (homogeneous or
  equally precise studies) and where it falls below it (studies that
  differ greatly in precision, with heterogeneous effects, where the
  normal interval covers less still), and that the prediction interval
  uses the same standard error. No result changes.

- **The REML estimate of the between-study variance is now carried to
  the maximum of the restricted likelihood, in whatever units the effect
  sizes are.**
  [`meta_es()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_es.md),
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md),
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md),
  and
  [`plot_forest()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_forest.md)
  with `method = "reml"` (the default) searched over `tau2` itself with
  the default tolerance of
  [`optimize()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/optimize.html), the fourth root
  of the machine epsilon. That search stops within about 0.00003 of the
  maximum in the units of `tau2`, whatever the size of the effects. The
  search is now made on `tau2` divided by the scale of the data (the
  largest sampling variance plus the variance of the effect sizes),
  stopping at a distance relative to the estimate, so the estimate for
  effect sizes multiplied by a constant c is c squared times the
  estimate for the original ones. The change is small for effect sizes
  of the order of 1. On 600 random sets of 2 to 15 studies with sampling
  variances between .005 and 3, the largest distance of `tau2` from the
  solution of metafor run to convergence
  (`control = list(threshold = 1e-12)`) fell from 0.00003 to 0.0000004
  (598 sets drawn afresh; the remaining distance is the flatness of the
  restricted likelihood at its maximum), and no estimate moved between
  zero and positive; on those sets `tau2` changed by at most 0.000028,
  the pooled estimate by at most 0.00006, and its standard error by at
  most 0.00003 (0.04% of its size). These are the largest changes on the
  sets compared, not bounds. For the 12 simulated studies of the
  package’s tests, `tau2` was 0.0279437 and is 0.0279387, the pooled
  estimate was 0.416452 and is 0.416453, and its Hartung-Knapp standard
  error was 0.080996 and is 0.080995. The change is large for effect
  sizes in small units, where 0.00003 is of the size of `tau2`: the
  earlier estimate could be zero where the maximum is positive, or
  several times too large. For ten simulated risk differences near .02
  with 4,000 to 40,000 per group (sampling variances near 1e-5;
  `set.seed(2718)` in the test file), `tau2` was 0 and is 0.0000090755,
  which is metafor’s converged value; the pooled estimate was 0.021151
  and is 0.021255, I2 was 0 and is 52.2 percent, and the prediction
  interval was 0.0181 to 0.0242 and is 0.0137 to 0.0289. On 300 random
  sets with sampling variances between 1e-6 and 1e-4, the earlier
  estimate disagreed with metafor on zero against positive in 76 and was
  off by more than 1 percent in 184; the estimate now disagrees in none
  and is within 0.002 percent in all. An analysis of risk differences,
  proportions, or other effect sizes with sampling variances below about
  .001 should be rerun. The estimate is now accurate relative to itself,
  including when one study’s sampling variance is far above the others’
  (1.0.0 stopped within about 0.00003 of the maximum in the units of
  `tau2`, about 0.5 percent of a `tau2` near .01): for the twelve
  studies of the package’s tests with one sampling variance of 1e6
  (`.outlier_yivi()` in the test file), `tau2` was 0.012048 and is
  0.012058, the root of the score equation; the pooled estimate,
  -0.0510, and its Hartung-Knapp standard error, 0.0328, are unchanged
  to the digits shown. The results of the other estimators are unchanged
  by this entry (the Paule-Mandel estimate and the Q-profile interval
  for `tau2` are the subject of an entry under Bug Fixes). metafor at
  its default threshold of 0.00001 gives 0.0279436 for the 12 studies
  above, so a comparison with its default output can differ in the fifth
  significant digit of `tau2` where it agreed before.

- **[`meta_es()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_es.md),
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md),
  and
  [`plot_forest()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/plot_forest.md)
  refuse an infinite effect size or sampling variance with a message
  that says so, and
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md) and
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md)
  an infinite sample size.** Under `method = "reml"`,
  `meta_es(c(.1, Inf, .3), rep(.1, 3))` stopped with “invalid ‘xmin’
  value” from the search and an infinite variance with “invalid ‘xmax’
  value”; under `"pm"` and `"dl"` both stopped with “missing value where
  TRUE/FALSE needed”. They now stop with “Supply finite effect sizes”
  and “Supply a finite sampling variance for each effect size”. Under
  `method = "fe"` these calls returned a result and now stop as well:
  `meta_es(c(.1, .2, .3), c(.1, Inf, .1), method = "fe")` gave an
  estimate of 0.2 (the study with an infinite variance had a weight of
  zero), and an infinite effect size gave an infinite estimate. To pool
  without a study, leave it out. An infinite `n` in
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md)
  stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” or, under
  `method = "fe"`, returned an estimate of `NaN` with a standard error
  of 0 and no message; an infinite `n_1` or `n_2` in
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md)
  stopped with a message about the effect sizes. Each now stops with its
  “must give an integer sample size” message.

- **[`moments_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/moments_nc_t.md)
  is right at large degrees of freedom and at a large noncentrality
  parameter, where DMAR 1.0.0 lost digits, changed the sign of the
  excess kurtosis, or returned a negative variance.** DMAR 1.0.0 formed
  the variance, skewness, and excess kurtosis as differences of the raw
  moments, which grow with the noncentrality parameter while the
  differences do not, so the digits left fell as either argument grew:
  the excess kurtosis was off by 1e-7 of its value at 1000 degrees of
  freedom and a noncentrality parameter of 5 and by 4e-4 at 2000 and 30,
  and `moments_nc_t(df = 1e4, ncp = 100)` returned -0.0022675 where the
  value is 0.0013340. `moments_nc_t(df = 1e16, ncp = 2.5)` returned a
  mean of 1.97e14 and a variance of -3.9e28 (now 2.5 and 1),
  `moments_nc_t(df = 20, ncp = 1e80)` an excess kurtosis of `NaN`, and
  `moments_nc_t(df = Inf, ncp = 2)` `NaN` for the mean, variance,
  skewness, and excess kurtosis and `NA` for the standard deviation. The
  mean now comes from the logarithm of the chi mean factor that
  [`sd_unbiased()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sd_unbiased.md)
  uses, and the other three from the central moments of the square root
  of the degrees of freedom over a chi square variate, so that no raw
  moments are subtracted; from 100 degrees of freedom on, the third
  central moment and fourth cumulant of that square root are their
  expansions in the reciprocal of the degrees of freedom. Against values
  computed to several hundred digits, for degrees of freedom from just
  above each boundary (1, 2, 3, and 4) to 1e300 and a noncentrality
  parameter up to 1e6 in magnitude, the largest relative errors found
  are 3e-16 for the mean, 9e-16 for the variance, 4e-14 for the
  skewness, and 1.3e-12 for the excess kurtosis; the same limits hold at
  a noncentrality parameter of 1e10, 1e100, and 1e300. `df = Inf` now
  returns the normal distribution with mean `ncp` and variance 1, and an
  infinite `ncp` is refused. For degrees of freedom up to 300 and a
  noncentrality parameter up to 5 in magnitude the values differ from
  those of 1.0.0 by at most 1.5e-8 of their size (`df = 20`, `ncp = 2.5`
  agrees to ten digits).

- **[`cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv.md),
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md),
  [`sd_unbiased()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sd_unbiased.md),
  [`ci_proportion()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_proportion.md),
  and
  [`power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_c.md)
  refuse inputs for which DMAR 1.0.0 returned a number that meant
  nothing or an error from inside base R.** Each refusal names the
  argument. In
  [`cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv.md): a negative
  `sd` (`cv(mean = 2, sd = -1)` returned -0.5), a mean of 0
  (`cv(mean = 0, sd = 1)` returned `Inf`), `cv` given with one of `mean`
  and `sd` (`cv(cv = .2, mean = 999)` returned 0.2 and ignored the
  mean), a `cv` that is not one finite number (`cv(cv = "a")` returned a
  table holding “a”), an `N` of 1 or less, or an infinite `N`, with
  `unbiased = TRUE` (`cv(cv = .2, N = 0, unbiased = TRUE)` returned
  `Inf`, and `N = Inf` returned the uncorrected 0.2), and an `unbiased`
  that is not `TRUE` or `FALSE` (`unbiased = "yes"` returned the
  uncorrected value).
  [`cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv.md) documented
  single values and now requires them: a vector `cv`, `mean`, `sd`, or
  `N`, and `unbiased = 1`, were accepted and are refused
  (`cv(cv = .2, N = c(10, 20), unbiased = TRUE)` returned two rows). A
  negative mean still gives a negative coefficient. In
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md): a
  coefficient of variation that is not positive, whether given as `cv`,
  through `sd`, or by the data (`ci_cv(cv = -.2, N = 20)` and
  `ci_cv(mean = 10, sd = -2, N = 20)` returned the limits -0.298 and
  `Inf`, and `ci_cv(data = c(-1, -2, -3, -4))` returned -6.859 and
  `Inf`), data with a missing or infinite score or fewer than two
  scores, data that are not numeric (a logical vector was read as 0 and
  1), and an `N` that is not one finite number above 1;
  `ci_cv(cv = 0, N = 20)`, `ci_cv(cv = .2, N = Inf)`, and
  `ci_cv(data = c(1, 2, NA, 4))` stopped with “missing value where
  TRUE/FALSE needed”. A fractional `N` above 1 is still accepted. In
  [`sd_unbiased()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sd_unbiased.md):
  a negative or infinite `s` (`sd_unbiased(s = -1, N = 20)` returned
  -1.013, and `s = Inf` returned `Inf`), `s` without `N` (which stopped
  with “arguments imply differing number of rows”), a single score as
  `X` (`sd_unbiased(X = 5)` returned `NA`), scores `X` that are not
  numeric (a logical vector was read as 0 and 1), an `N` of 1 or less, a
  single `s` or `N` that is missing, and vectors `s` and `N` of
  different lengths other than 1. One inadmissible element refuses the
  whole call: `sd_unbiased(s = 2, N = c(10, 1))` returned 2.056 and
  `NaN` and now stops. A missing element of a vector still gives a
  missing row (`sd_unbiased(s = c(1, NA), N = 10)` returns 1.028 and
  `NA`). A fractional `N` and vectors of equal length give what they
  gave in 1.0.0; an infinite `N` gives `s` (1.0.0 returned `NaN`). In
  [`ci_proportion()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_proportion.md):
  an infinite count (`ci_proportion(1, Inf)` returned the limits 0 and
  0). In
  [`power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_c.md):
  a missing or infinite `true_contrast`, `n_per_group`, `true_sd`,
  bound, or `df_error`, and a missing `alpha_level`
  (`true_psi = NA_real_`, an infinite per-group size, and
  `delta_upper = Inf`, in the 1.0.x names, each returned a power of 0,
  where `n_per_group = 1e12` and `contrast_upper = 1e6` return 1; a
  missing per-group size, `true_sd`, `df_error`, or `alpha_level` given
  as `NA_real_` stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”). A
  fractional `n_per_group` or `df_error` gives what it gave.

- **[`ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md)
  leaves a replication whose sample mean is not positive out of its
  width and coverage summaries, where DMAR 1.0.0 entered it with the
  limits
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) gave
  for a negative coefficient, an infinite upper limit among them.** Such
  a sample has no confidence interval for the coefficient of variation,
  which [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md)
  now refuses. The replication is left out of every statistic row,
  `mean_cv`, `median_cv`, and `sd_cv` included (see the next entry): all
  ten are taken over the replications that have an interval; one warning
  of class `dmar_replications_without_interval` states how many were
  left out, and the count is `attr(x, "simulation")$failed`. The case
  needs a large coefficient of variation and a small sample: with
  `true_cv = 1` and `specified_N = 10` the sample mean is not positive
  in about 8 of 10000 replications. With `set.seed(7)` and `G = 3000`
  there, 3 replications are left out: `pct_ci_miss_low` was 0.0287 and
  is 0.0277, `total_type_I_error` was 0.0553 and is 0.0544, and
  `median_ci_width` was 3.743 and is 3.735. `mean_ci_width` was `Inf`
  there in 1.0.0, since
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) has
  no finite upper limit for some samples with a positive mean, and is
  now taken over the finite widths (see the next entry). A study in
  which every sample mean is positive, which is every study at the
  coefficients of variation the help page and the vignette use, differs
  from DMAR 1.0.0 only where the limits of
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md)
  changed with the exact noncentral *t* (see Exact Noncentral *t* and
  Studentized Range Distributions).

- **[`ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md)
  summarizes the same replications in every row.** A replication whose
  sample mean is not positive has no interval, and its sample
  coefficient is negative. All ten statistic rows, `mean_cv`,
  `median_cv`, and `sd_cv` among them, describe the replications with a
  positive mean (DMAR 1.0.0 entered such a replication in every row; see
  the entry above). An interval with an infinite upper limit made
  `mean_ci_width` infinite and `sd_ci_width` undefined; the two are now
  over the finite widths, `median_ci_width` stays over every width, an
  infinite width counts as not meeting the target (as it did), and the
  number of infinite widths is `attr(, "simulation")$n_infinite_width`.
  DMAR 1.0.0 repeated the warning
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) gave
  for such an interval in every replication that had one.
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) no
  longer gives that warning (see the entry on
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md) and
  an infinite upper limit), and the sensitivity function gives one
  warning of its own, of class `dmar_replications_with_infinite_limit`,
  that states how many replications had an infinite upper limit and how
  they enter the rows (the count is also the field `n_replications` of
  the condition). With `set.seed(88)`, `true_cv = 3`, `specified_N = 5`,
  `width = .5`, and `G = 500` (114 replications without an interval, 346
  infinite widths): `mean_cv` -3.499 in DMAR 1.0.0 and 4.870 now,
  `median_cv` 1.400 and 1.884, `sd_cv` 118.98 and 22.16, `mean_ci_width`
  Inf and 14.85, `sd_ci_width` NaN and 37.25. With `true_cv = 1`,
  `specified_N = 10` (no replication without an interval, 96 infinite
  widths): `mean_ci_width` Inf in DMAR 1.0.0 and 15.55 now,
  `sd_ci_width` NaN and 188.3. A simulation in which every mean is
  positive and every width finite differs from DMAR 1.0.0 only through
  the exact noncentral *t* limits of
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md). The
  table also carries the `simulation` attribute (replications attempted,
  with and without an interval, and exact binomial limits for the share
  that met the width) and prints the counts beneath it. In the first
  example the coverage rows differ from those of DMAR 1.0.0 as well, for
  the reason of the entry above.

- **The number of replications `G` must be a whole number, in every
  function that has the argument.** The 31 sensitivity functions with a
  `G` argument,
  [`ss_aipe_indirect_effect()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_indirect_effect.md),
  [`ss_aipe_composite_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_composite_sem.md),
  and
  [`ss_power_composite_sem()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_composite_sem.md)
  check it with the one check of a count (an error of class
  `dmar_count_invalid`), before anything is simulated. The smallest `G`
  is what it was: 10 for the three planners, 2 for
  [`ss_seq_c_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_c_sensitivity.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity.md),
  and 1 elsewhere. In DMAR 1.0.0 most of them did not check `G`:
  `ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(G = 0)` returned a full table from one
  replication and `G = 2.7` ran two, `ss_aipe_r_sensitivity(G = 0)`
  returned a table of `NA`, `ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(G = 0)` stopped with
  “subscript out of bounds”, and `G = -3`, `Inf`, `NA`, or a vector
  stopped with “invalid ‘times’ argument”;
  [`ss_seq_c_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_c_sensitivity.md)
  accepted `G = 2.5`. The messages of the functions that did check `G`
  now read “‘G’ must be a single whole number of at least 1.” (or 2, or
  10), in place of “‘G’ must be a positive integer.”, “‘G’ must be a
  single positive whole number.”, “‘G’ must be a single number of at
  least 2.”, and “‘G’ must be a positive whole number of attempted
  studies.”.

- The six `ss_aipe_crd_es_*()` planners check `G` (`nrep` in 1.0.x) the
  same way at entry: a fractional number, 0, a negative number, `NA`, a
  character string, an infinite value, or more than one value is an
  error of class `dmar_count_invalid`, before any simulation starts
  (earlier such a value reached the simulation unchecked). `G = NULL`
  remains the default of the two planners that fix a size and a budget,
  where it skips the simulation. Results for a valid `G` are unchanged.

- **The Hofmann (1977) entry of
  [`simple_structure()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/simple_structure.md)
  gives the issue and pages of the article.** The help page gave *The
  Journal of General Psychology*, 96, 58–66; the DOI record of the
  article (10.1080/00221309.1977.9920803) has 96(1), 103–110. The entry
  now gives that issue and those pages with the DOI, and the
  Hofmann (1978) entry on the same page gains its DOI,
  10.1207/s15327906mbr1302_9, which
  [`fa_exploratory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_exploratory.md)
  already cites. The title, the journal, and the 1978 volume, issue, and
  pages, 13(2), 247–250, already matched the records and are unchanged.

- **The Owen (1968) entry of
  [`moments_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/moments_nc_t.md)
  gives the DOI of the article.** The entry carried the DOI of a letter
  to the editor in the preceding issue (10.1080/00401706.1968.10490590);
  it is now 10.1080/00401706.1968.10490594.

- **The Phillips (1990) entry gives the first page of the article.** The
  help pages of
  [`power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_c.md),
  [`power_equivalence_md()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_md.md),
  [`power_density_equivalence_md()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_density_equivalence_md.md),
  and
  [`power_equivalence_md_plot()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_md_plot.md)
  gave the pages as 139–144; they are 137–144.

- **The correction factor of Hedges (1981) is right at a very large
  sample size, in
  [`smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/smd.md),
  [`smd_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/smd_c.md),
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md),
  [`expected_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_smd.md),
  and
  [`var_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_smd.md).**
  The factor J(df) = Gamma(df/2) / {sqrt(df/2) Gamma((df - 1)/2)} was
  computed as a difference of two
  [`lgamma()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Special.html) values that nearly
  cancel at a large `df`, the form that
  [`design_consequences()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/design_consequences.md),
  [`sd_unbiased()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sd_unbiased.md),
  and
  [`var_ete()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_ete.md)
  gave up earlier in this release (the entry on E(S)/sigma). It is now
  formed from the logarithm of E(S)/sigma on `df - 1` degrees of
  freedom, log J(df) = L(df - 1) + log1p(-1/df)/2, two negative terms
  with nothing to cancel, through one internal helper that the five
  functions share. Against a 60-digit evaluation J is right to a
  relative 3.4e-16 from 2 `df` to 1e14; the earlier form was off by a
  relative 5e-11 at 1e5 `df` and 8e-9 at 1e7, and at 1e8 it returned a J
  above 1. At ordinary sample sizes nothing a user sees moves: over 272
  planning sets with at most 10,000 per group the largest change in any
  reported value is 2.6e-10 (in
  [`var_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_smd.md)),
  except in
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md)
  under REML, whose iteration stops at a tolerance that lets the
  estimate move by about 1e-9 and I^2 by about 4e-6 of a percentage
  point (no printed digit moves), and with 20 per group
  `smd(unbiased = TRUE)` and
  [`expected_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_smd.md)
  agree with 1.0.x to all printed digits. Two results that subtract
  nearly equal numbers were wrong much sooner than J itself, and are now
  taken from the logarithm with
  [`expm1()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/Log.html): the `bias` row of
  [`expected_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/expected_smd.md),
  `true_smd` (1/J - 1), and the exact variance in
  [`var_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_smd.md),
  which is now computed as df/(df - 2) + lambda^2 {2/(df - 2) - (1/J^2 -
  1)}. `expected_smd(true_smd = 0.5, n_1 = 1e8, n_2 = 1e8)` reported a
  bias of -1.19e-07 (the wrong sign) and now reports 1.875e-09;
  `var_smd(true_smd = 3, n_1 = 1e8, n_2 = 2e8)` reported an exact
  variance of -8.5e-06 and now reports 3.0e-08;
  `var_smd(true_smd = 0.5, n_1 = 1e8)` reported 1.42e-07 and now reports
  2.06e-08; with 100,000 per group the bias of
  `expected_smd(true_smd = 0.5)` moves from 1.875105e-06 to
  1.875029e-06. Against the 60-digit values the bias and the exact
  variance are now right to a relative 7e-16 over 344 planning sets with
  up to 2e8 observations; the earlier relative errors there reached 190
  and 285. No argument is added.

- **[`moments_nc_F()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/moments_nc_F.md)
  is right at large degrees of freedom.** The variance, skewness, and
  excess kurtosis were formed as differences of raw moments, which agree
  in their leading digits when the degrees of freedom are large, so the
  digits that remained were rounding error.
  `moments_nc_F(df_1 = 1e6, df_2 = 1e6)` returned an excess kurtosis of
  -5.285e-05 where the value is 6.60006e-05, and a skewness of
  0.0060000263 where the value is 0.0060000230. The function now writes
  the statistic as (df_2/df_1) X Y with X the noncentral chi square and
  Y the reciprocal of the central one, and forms the central moments of
  F/E(F) from those of X/E(X) - 1 and Y/E(Y) - 1, which are independent
  and have mean 0: every term of each sum is nonnegative, so nothing
  cancels (the expressions are on the help page; they were derived for
  DMAR and checked against exact rational arithmetic). In 14 cases with
  degrees of freedom up to 1e12 and noncentrality up to 1e6 the four
  moments are right to a relative 5e-16, where the earlier form was off
  by a relative 1.8 at (1e6, 1e6, 0) and 0.36 at (3, 1e6, 1e6). At
  ordinary degrees of freedom nothing a user sees moves: over 918
  combinations with both degrees of freedom at most 200 and
  noncentrality at most 50 the largest relative change is 8.5e-12, and
  the moments that do not exist are `NA` in the same places. The mean is
  unchanged.

- **[`rbind()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html) of DMAR tables no
  longer carries the first table’s confidence level over rows computed
  at another.** A `dmar_tbl` keeps its confidence level, and the other
  facts its printed lines are written from, as attributes, and
  [`rbind()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html) kept the attributes and
  the class of the first table:
  `rbind(ci_smd(..., conf_level = 0.90), ci_smd(..., conf_level = 0.95))`
  was a table of class `dmar_ci_smd` that printed “Confidence level:
  90%” beneath six rows, three of them 95 percent limits, and
  [`dmar_metadata()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_metadata.md)
  of it gave 0.90. [`rbind()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/cbind.html) now
  has a method for these tables. When every table stacked is a DMAR
  table and all have the same classes and attributes, the stack is a
  DMAR table with those attributes, as before. In every other case
  (different confidence levels, different functions, or a DMAR table
  stacked with a plain data frame, in either order) the result is an
  ordinary `data.frame` with the same rows and columns and none of the
  DMAR attributes, and no warning: the numbers are all there, and no
  printed line states a level that does not hold for every row. To
  compare results across levels, stack `tidy()` rows, which carry the
  level in a column: `rbind(tidy(x_90), tidy(x_95))`.
  [`dplyr::bind_rows()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/bind_rows.html)
  does not call the method. Code that relied on the class of a mixed
  stack (`inherits(rbind(a, b), "dmar_tbl")` with tables at two levels)
  now gets `FALSE`.
  [`?dmar_tbl`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_tbl.md)
  has a section on stacking.

- **[`ss_aipe_R2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2.md)
  with `assurance` returns a sample size for a small population R2,
  where it stopped with “invalid ‘xmin’ value”.** The procedure inverts
  the expected value of R2 by matching a value rounded to two decimals
  against a grid of expected values. When the one-sided lower limit it
  uses is 0, which happens for a small population R2, no grid value has
  an expected R2 that low, the match was missing, and
  [`optimize()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/optimize.html) was given a
  missing end point. A missing match is now replaced by the end of the
  grid when the target lies beyond it and by the grid value with the
  nearest expectation otherwise.
  `ss_aipe_R2(true_R2 = .03, p = 1, width = .2, assurance = .9)` returns
  113; of 30 conditions drawn at random with a `true_R2` of .03 to .90,
  the 8 that stopped now return (107 to 173) and the 22 that returned
  give the same sample sizes, as do 40 further conditions that returned
  before and 48 without `assurance` (largest difference 0).

- **The default *p*-value of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md)
  is larger.** The test statistic is referred to Student’s *t* with
  Satterthwaite degrees of freedom where DMAR 1.0.x referred it to the
  standard normal distribution (see “The Order-Based Effect Sizes Share
  One Contract”). The estimate, its standard error, the statistic, and
  the confidence interval are unchanged, and `test = "z"` gives the
  1.0.x *p*-value: on 240 data sets by three levels and two interval
  methods the eight numbers of a `test = "z"` row equal the earlier ones
  exactly. For the first example of the help (`set.seed(113)`, 40 per
  group) the *p*-value is 0.0082 on 77.96 degrees of freedom where it
  was 0.0067; for `vargha_delaney_A(iq_8 ~ treatment, data = pygmalion)`
  it is 0.0892 on 92.48 degrees of freedom where it was 0.0858; and for
  `x = c(3.5, 5, 6, 7, 8)`, `y = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4.2)` it is 0.0033 on
  6.63 degrees of freedom where it was 0.0000076 (the exact permutation
  *p*-value is 8/252 = 0.032).
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reports the *p*-value of the test that was run. The table has two more
  columns, `df` and `test`, after the nine it had.

- **Every sensitivity function summarizes its replications over one
  denominator and records the counts.** The proportion of intervals that
  met the width target (`pct_ci_less_width`), the proportions that
  missed the true value, and the summaries of the widths are taken over
  the replications that produced a confidence interval, in every
  `ss_aipe_*_sensitivity()` function; a replication without an interval
  is in none of those rows. In
  [`ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity.md),
  where a simulated study can end without an interval, DMAR 1.0.0 took
  the width rows over the studies that returned one, as now, and the
  three rows for intervals that missed the true value
  (`pct_ci_miss_low`, `pct_ci_miss_high`, `total_type_I_error`) over all
  `G`, so that a study without an interval counted as one whose interval
  held the value: with two of four simulated studies returning an
  interval and one of the two missing the value, the row is 1/2 where
  DMAR 1.0.0 gave 1/4, and with no study returning an interval the three
  rows are `NA` where it gave 0.
  [`ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity.md)
  have entries of their own. The rule changes nothing in a run in which
  every replication has an interval. All 31 sensitivity functions, the
  two `ss_power_*_sensitivity()` functions and
  [`ss_seq_c_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_seq_c_sensitivity.md)
  included, now attach the attribute `simulation`, a list with
  `attempted` (`G`), `returned` (replications with an interval, or a
  test), `failed` (those without), `denominator` (which is `returned`),
  `width_target_probability` (the `pct_ci_less_width` row), and
  `width_target_mc_ci` (exact binomial limits for it over `returned`,
  which describe simulation error); the two width entries are `NA` for a
  function with no width target.
  [`ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity.md)
  adds `n_redrawn`, the data sets whose fit did not converge and were
  drawn again (such a data set is replaced, so it is not among the
  replications without an interval; the help says how the count is
  read). The record is the one place the counts are kept: the rows
  `suc_rep` of
  [`ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity.md)
  and `num_probs_with_cis` of
  [`ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity.md),
  which held the same counts in DMAR 1.0.x, are removed (`returned` and
  `failed` hold them). The line “Replications” beneath each printed
  table gives `G`, and the three counts when a replication was without
  an interval.
  [`dmar_metadata()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_metadata.md)
  returns the record as `simulation`.

- **[`ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity.md)
  no longer counts a completely separated replication as an interval of
  width 0.** When the two simulated groups do not overlap, the estimated
  variance of Cliff’s delta is 0 and
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  reports both limits at the estimate, which are not a confidence
  interval. DMAR 1.0.x took them as an interval of width 0, which met
  every width target, and scored its coverage from the point estimate.
  Such a replication now has no interval: its estimate still enters
  `mean_cliff_delta`, `median_cliff_delta`, and `sd_cliff_delta`, and
  the width, width-target (`pct_ci_less_width`), and coverage rows
  describe the replications with an interval. One warning of class
  `dmar_replications_without_interval` gives the count (fields
  `n_without_interval` and `G`), the per-replication warnings are not
  passed on, the table carries the `simulation` attribute with the
  counts and exact binomial limits for the width proportion, and the
  file named in `filename` records such a replication with its estimate
  and `NA` elsewhere. With `set.seed(113)`,
  `ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity(true_delta = 0.9, specified_N = 12, width = 0.4, G = 400)`
  has 162 separated replications of 400. `pct_ci_less_width` is 0 where
  it was 0.405; `mean_ci_width` 0.966 where it was 0.575;
  `median_ci_width` 0.909 where it was 0.867; `sd_ci_width` 0.112 where
  it was 0.483; `pct_ci_miss_low` 0 where it was 0.405;
  `pct_ci_miss_high` 0.025 where it was 0.015; and `total_type_I_error`
  0.025 where it was 0.420. The three rows of the estimate are unchanged
  (0.904, 0.944, 0.119). A run in which no replication is separated
  returns what it returned: 36 conditions under a common seed are
  identical. No argument restores the earlier result.

- **[`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  does not write limits that are not a confidence interval as one.** For
  a table of
  [`vargha_delaney_A()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/vargha_delaney_A.md),
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md),
  or
  [`probability_of_superiority_paired()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/probability_of_superiority_paired.md)
  whose estimated variance is 0, the sentence gives the estimate and the
  reason. `results_sentence(vargha_delaney_A(c(4, 5, 6), c(1, 2, 3)))`
  is “A = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the groups are completely
  separated, so the estimated variance is 0)” where it was “A = 1.00,
  95% CI \[1.00, 1.00\]”; for
  [`cliff_delta()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cliff_delta.md)
  on those groups “cliff_delta = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the
  groups are completely separated, so the estimated variance is 0)”
  where it was “cliff_delta = 1.00, 95% CI \[1.00, 1.00\]”; for
  `probability_of_superiority_paired(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(4, 5, 6, 7))`
  “probability_of_superiority = 1.00 (no confidence interval: every pair
  favors the same member, so the estimated variance is 0)” where DMAR
  1.0.0 wrote “probability_of_superiority = 1.00, 95% CI \[NaN, NaN\]”;
  and for `vargha_delaney_A(c(2, 2, 2), c(2, 2, 2))` “A = 0.50 (no
  confidence interval: every score is equal, so the estimated variance
  is 0)” where it was “A = 0.50, 95% CI \[0.50, 0.50\]”. A *p*-value is
  appended only when the table has one (the permutation test). The
  sentence of a `tidy()` or `glance()` row of such a table reads “A =
  1.00 (no confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0)”. The
  sentence of every other table is unchanged.

- **A bootstrap or Monte Carlo interval asked for with fewer
  replications than the rule requires is refused** (see One Rule for
  Bootstrap Replications): fewer than 200, 400, or 2000 at the 90, 95,
  or 99 percent level for a percentile or Monte Carlo interval, fewer
  than 1000, 2000, or 10000 for a BCa interval, and fewer than 100 for a
  bootstrap standard error interval or a Bollen-Stine *p*-value. Calls
  that ran in 1.0.x and now stop include
  `reliability_alpha(ci_method = "percentile", B = 40)` (0.6083
  \[0.5231, 0.6846\] before; with `B = 400` the function returns
  \[0.5203, 0.6709\], as it did),
  `reliability_alpha(ci_method = "bca", B = 500)` (\[0.5204, 0.6692\]
  before; with `B = 2000`, \[0.5348, 0.6768\], as it did),
  `reliability_alpha(ci_method = "bootstrap_se", B = 50)`,
  `htmt(B = 100)` to `htmt(B = 199)`, `parallel_analysis(B = 20)`,
  `sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(B = 20)` (*p* = 0.05 from 20 samples before),
  `R2_mixed_effects(ci_method = "boot", B = 20)`, and
  `mlmr(ci_method = "boot", B = 20)`. The error has class
  `dmar_count_invalid` and names the number;
  `options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)` runs the call and marks
  the result.

- **An interval formed from fewer than half of the replications
  requested is no longer reported.** The estimate is returned with `NA`
  limits and a warning of class `dmar_bootstrap_insufficient`. In
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  the kappa functions,
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md), the
  ratio functions,
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  and
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md)
  an interval was formed from any 100 replications that remained (two in
  the last), and in the reliability family through 1.0.1 from any two.
  An interval from at least half of those requested is reported as
  before, since the number required is held to the request and not to
  the replications that remain, and the warning now has a class, states
  the counts, and says when those that remain are fewer than the number
  required. With two raters and eight subjects, six of whom both raters
  place in one category,
  `cohen_kappa(ci_method = "percentile", B = 400, seed = 113)` returns
  0.6 \[0.0, 1.0\] from the 361 resamples in which kappa is defined, as
  1.0.x did (and `ci_method = "bca", B = 2000` returns \[0.0, 1.0\] from
  1787); `krippendorff_alpha(boot = TRUE, B = 400, seed = 113)` on five
  units of which four are alike returns \[1, 1\] from 254 resamples;
  `htmt(B = 200, seed = 113)` with an item that is nonzero in one of 12
  cases returns the bound 1.1723 from 130 resamples; and
  `ci_ratio_of_means(ci_method = "percentile", B = 400, seed = 113)`
  with a denominator group that is nonzero in one of 12 cases returns
  3.0 \[0.3333, 6.0\] from 269 replications. Each of these now warns
  that fewer than the number required remained and says to request more.

- **[`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md), and
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md)
  drop a replication for every statistic when it has no value for one.**
  Each statistic’s limits were the quantiles of its own finite values,
  so one missing value moved the interval of that statistic alone and
  the intervals of one call rested on different replications. With 500
  replications of which three lack the marginal and two the conditional
  R-squared (the fixture of `test-dmar_bootstrap.R`), the marginal
  limits were the quantiles of 497 values and the conditional limits of
  498; both are now the quantiles of the same 495. When every
  replication returns every statistic, which is the usual case, the
  limits do not change:
  `R2_mixed_effects(ci_method = "boot", B = 400, seed = 113)` on the
  `sleepstudy` random intercept model returns 0.2799 \[0.1880, 0.4072\]
  and 0.7043 \[0.5838, 0.7964\] in both builds.

- **No interval that is still reported changes for any other reason.**
  On 75 calls that the rule accepts and in which every interval is still
  reported (1311 reported numbers;
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  the kappa functions,
  [`krippendorff_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/krippendorff_alpha.md),
  [`htmt()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/htmt.md), the
  two ratio functions, the reliability family,
  [`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  [`fraction_missing_information()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fraction_missing_information.md),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`ci_eta_squared_generalized()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_eta_squared_generalized.md),
  [`mlmr()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr.md),
  [`mlmr_mv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mlmr_mv.md),
  [`parallel_analysis()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/parallel_analysis.md),
  [`factor_count()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factor_count.md),
  and
  [`sem_exact_fit_bootstrap()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.md),
