  each with a seed), the largest absolute difference between this build
  and the earlier one is 0.

- **[`ci_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_t.md)
  computes the noncentral *t* distribution exactly where R’s
  [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) is not accurate, so every
  interval built on it is exact.** DMAR 1.0.x inverted
  [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) everywhere and warned
  only when the observed `ncp` passed 37.62, so an interval whose upper
  limit alone passed it was approximate without a warning. Limits inside
  the accurate range are unchanged. The interval of
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md) for
  two groups of 20 at d = 10 with 99 percent confidence was \[7.003,
  12.999\] and is \[7.003, 13.099\]; `ci_nc_t(ncp = 34.5, df = 38)` gave
  \[26.511, 42.273\] and gives \[26.511, 42.447\];
  `ci_nc_t(ncp = 100, df = 1, conf_level = .99)` gave \[-107.157,
  257.157\] and gives \[0.394, 280.717\]; `ci_cv(cv = .05, N = 15)` was
  \[0.0369, 0.0818\] and is \[0.0366, 0.0790\]; and
  `ci_sm(sm = 10, N = 30)` was \[7.315, 12.512\] and is \[7.412,
  12.580\].
  [`ci_smd_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd_c.md),
  [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md),
  [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md),
  [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md),
  [`ci_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_rc.md),
  [`ci_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_src.md),
  [`smd_trimmed()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/smd_trimmed.md),
  and the sensitivity functions of the AIPE planners inherit the exact
  limits. The warning “The observed noncentrality parameter exceeds
  37.62 in magnitude” is gone, and the planners that passed it on
  ([`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  425 times for `true_std_contrast = 4`, `width = .5`, `assurance = .9`)
  are silent. With more than 1e7 degrees of freedom the integral is
  taken over the standardized chi square: its density is computed
  without forming the chi square value, and the argument of the normal
  distribution function, *q* *s* - ncp, is formed as (*q* - ncp) +
  *q*(*s* - 1) with *s* - 1 computed without forming *s*, since a double
  holds neither the chi square value nor *s* finely enough there.
  Against a 256-bit oracle, at 13 values of the degrees of freedom from
  1e7 to 1e32, with *q* times the standard deviation of *s* from .001 to
  10, both tails of the distribution function, P(\|*T*\| \<= *k*), and
  the density are within 2.0e-14, the probability the integral leaves
  out past the 1e-14 and 1 - 1e-14 quantiles of the chi square. A plan
  of
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  or
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md)
  up to 2^53 per group with *J* groups has at most *J*(2^53 - 1) degrees
  of freedom, fewer than 4.1e31 for any vector of contrast weights R can
  hold.

- **The AIPE planners built on
  [`ci_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_t.md)
  plan for the exact interval, and some plans change by one or two.**
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sm.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md)
  plan for the interval
  [`ci_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_t.md)
  now reports, with exact noncentral *t* probabilities in the published
  quantile assurance steps (that of
  [`ss_aipe_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sm.md),
  and of
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md)
  by default; the plans of
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  with `assurance` are now the exact ones of the entries below). Of 116
  plans scanned with those steps (standardized effects of 1 to 10,
  widths of .1 to 2.5, with and without an assurance of .90), 11
  changed, among them `ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = 5, width = 1)` from 127 to
  128, `ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = 3, width = .5, assurance = .9)` from 277
  to 278, `ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = 3, width = 1, assurance = .9)` from 102
  to 104,
  `ss_aipe_sc(true_std_contrast = 8, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = 1, assurance = .9)`
  from 300 to 299, and
  `ss_aipe_sc_ancova(true_std_contrast = 2, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .25)`
  from 738 to 739. The two plans with `assurance` of
  [`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  quoted here are also their exact plans.

- **[`cv_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_t.md)
  returns exact noncentral critical values.** With `alpha_level = .05`,
  `df = 3`, and `ncp = 50` the critical values were 29.0756 and 429.1783
  and are 28.2828 and 186.4939; with `df = 10` and `ncp = 45` they were
  31.7440 and 83.9369 and are 31.3532 and 79.0839; and with one degree
  of freedom and `ncp = 38` the upper value was infinite and is
  1212.586. The `area_less` and `area_greater` columns are exact as
  well.

- **[`cv_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_t.md) and
  [`ci_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_t.md)
  with fewer than one degree of freedom are exact, and the critical
  values of
  [`cv_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cv_t.md) there
  change, by orders of magnitude with `df` of 0.3 or less.** DMAR 1.0.x
  took them from [`qt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html), which
  inverts [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html), and below one
  degree of freedom [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) with a
  noncentrality is not accurate even inside 37.62. The critical values
  moved by factors up to 2e47 with `df = 0.05` and 39 with 0.3, by as
  much as 15 percent with 0.5, and by less than 1e-4 of themselves with
  0.6 and above (noncentralities up to 37.5 in absolute value,
  `alpha_level` .001 and .05): `cv_t(.05, 0.1, ncp = 0.5)` gave
  -33554432 and 305284064 and gives -1.0428e10 and 5.7095e13, and
  `cv_t(.001, 0.5, ncp = 38)` gave -Inf and Inf and gives 8.478261 and
  92490299.0. A critical value beyond the largest double is -Inf or Inf.
  The limits of
  [`ci_nc_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_nc_t.md)
  with `df < 1` change by at most 1.5e-10 of themselves.

- **The individual intervals of
  [`limits_of_agreement()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/limits_of_agreement.md)
  are exact for large samples.** Their noncentrality, k sqrt(n), passes
  37.62 from n = 369 at 95 percent coverage, and past it each confidence
  limit was too far from the mean difference, by as much as 0.0011
  standard deviations of the differences. For
  `set.seed(1000); a <- rnorm(1000, 100, 15); b <- a + rnorm(1000, 0.5, 3)`,
  the interval on the upper limit of agreement was \[6.05197, 6.68620\]
  and is \[6.05119, 6.68513\]. The pair intervals (the default) are
  unchanged.

- **Power past a noncentrality of 37.62 is exact.** The power planners
  whose test is a *t* test
  ([`ss_power_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_smd.md),
  [`ss_power_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_c.md),
  [`ss_power_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_sc.md),
  [`ss_power_c_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_c_ancova.md),
  [`ss_power_contrast()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_contrast.md),
  [`ss_power_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_mixed_effects.md),
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md),
  [`ss_power_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_rc.md),
  [`ss_power_pcm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_pcm.md),
  and, for the test of *a* with X fixed,
  [`ss_power_indirect_effect()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_indirect_effect.md)),
  the marginal powers of
  [`ss_power_composite_ancova_2group()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_composite_ancova_2group.md),
  the noninferiority power of
  [`power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/power_equivalence_c.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_equivalence_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_equivalence_c.md),
  and
  [`design_consequences()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/design_consequences.md)
  take the noncentral *t* probabilities from the exact routines. No
  planned sample size changes, since a search stops far below a
  noncentrality of 37.62; the power reported for a specified sample size
  changes where the noncentrality passes 37.62 and the test has few
  degrees of freedom (by as much as .28 with one degree of freedom and
  .034 with two; with 10 or more it was and is 1 to within 4e-11).
  `ss_power_smd(true_smd = 40, n_1 = 2, alpha_level = .001)` reported a
  power of .7823613 and reports .7981440; the marginal power of the
  group test of
  `ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 40, true_cor = .3, specified_n_per_group = 2, composite_terms = c("group", "covariate"), include_interaction = FALSE, alpha_level = .001)`
  was .1666 and is .0525; and
  `design_consequences(true_effect = 40, se = 1, df = 2, alpha_level = .001)`
  reported a power of .7823613, a Type S error of 1.2e-5, and an
  exaggeration ratio of 1.0207, and reports .7981440, a Type S error
  below 1e-300, and 1.0005. The power of a negative effect at a
  specified sample size (`ss_power_smd(true_smd = -1, n_1 = 50)`, and
  the same in
  [`ss_power_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_c.md),
  [`ss_power_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_sc.md),
  [`ss_power_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_mixed_effects.md),
  and an example of
  [`ss_power_composite_ancova_2group()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_composite_ancova_2group.md))
  passed on the warning of [`pt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html)
  `full precision may not have been achieved in 'pnt{final}'`; these
  calls are now silent, with the same values.

- **The Bayesian *t* tests use the exact noncentral *t* density.**
  [`bayes_one_sample_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bayes_one_sample_t.md),
  [`bayes_paired_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bayes_paired_t.md),
  and
  [`bayes_independent_t()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bayes_independent_t.md)
  integrate the noncentral *t* likelihood over the prior, and R’s
  [`dt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html) with a noncentrality
  rests on the normal approximation past 37.62 and loses accuracy near
  *t* = 0 and with many degrees of freedom. It is now used only with at
  most 1,000 degrees of freedom, a noncentrality of at most 37.62, and
  \|*t*\| of at least .1, where results are unchanged, and the density
  is integrated exactly elsewhere, except at *t* = 0, where it is
  exp(-ncp^2 / 2) / {B(df / 2, 1/2) sqrt(df)}. R’s
  [`dt()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/TDist.html), which DMAR 1.0.x used
  there, computes it at a nonzero noncentrality by differencing two log
  gammas, and is off by as much as 3.4e-8 of it short of 1e7 degrees of
  freedom (at 9,832,229.8): `dt(0, 5.6e6, 1.5)` is 0.12951758933 where
  the density is 0.12951758988, and
  `bayes_one_sample_t(mean = 0, sd = 1, N = 5600001)` gave a Bayes
  factor `bf_01` of 2097.196624 in DMAR 1.0.0 and gives 2097.196615.
  `bayes_one_sample_t(mean = 5.7, sd = 1, N = 50)` (*t* = 40.3) gave a
  posterior median of 5.6038, a 95 percent interval of \[4.4709,
  6.7759\], and a Bayes factor of 5.3589e35, and gives 5.5967, \[4.4709,
  6.7901\], and 5.3537e35. Such calls take about 0.4 seconds, up from
  0.05 to 0.1.

- **The Tukey and Games-Howell procedures, and the Bryant-Paulson
  distribution with no covariates, use the exact studentized range
  wherever R’s [`qtukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) and
  [`ptukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) are not accurate**
  (see Exact Noncentral *t* and Studentized Range Distributions). R
  documents [`qtukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) as accurate
  to the fourth decimal place. It falls short of that at small error df,
  by more as the number of means and the confidence level grow (with 10
  means and 2 df its .999 quantile is 41 percent too small, so intervals
  built on it have a familywise error rate of about .0029 rather than
  .001); at large df; far in either tail; below the .75 point with more
  than 50 means; and where its search stops short of the root of
  [`ptukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html). The exact
  computation is used below 9 error df with up to 6 means, 11 with up to
  10, 15 with up to 20, 21 with up to 50, 31 with up to 100, 41 with up
  to 250, 47 with up to 400, 57 with up to 700, 71 with up to 1000, 81
  with up to 1500, 91 with up to 2000, 101 with up to 3000, and 111 with
  more (measured to 10000 means and extrapolated beyond); above 10000
  and up to 10^8 df; for every quantile at a probability above .999 or
  below .001; with more than 50 means, below the .75 point (the .80
  point with more than 1000 means); and wherever
  [`qtukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) fails or is more than
  2e-6 from the root of
  [`ptukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html). Elsewhere the values
  are those of [`qtukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) and
  [`ptukey()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/Tukey.html) (above 10^8 df, their
  infinite-df values), which were within 9.6e-6 of the exact quantile
  and 9.1e-7 of the exact probability at every point checked where they
  are kept. The changed values:

  | call | DMAR 1.0.x | now |
  |----|----|----|
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.01, df = 2, n_groups = 20)` | 31.485 | 26.830 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.01, df = 3, n_groups = 20)` | 14.105 | 13.976 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.05, df = 2, n_groups = 20)` | 11.867 | 11.857 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.001, df = 2, n_groups = 10)` | 41.612 | 71.063 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.001, df = 12, n_groups = 50)` | 8.0894 | 8.0897 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.05, df = 30000, n_groups = 10)` | 3.16368 | 3.16392 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(1e-4, df = 11, n_groups = 10)` | 8.491265 | 8.491348 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(1e-5, df = 1000, n_groups = 2000)` | 9.1427 | 6.9804 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.001, df = 41, n_groups = 1000)` | 7.282740 | 7.282842 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.025, df = 12, n_groups = 10)` | 4.245304 | 4.245333 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.0025, df = 23, n_groups = 5)` | 4.255839 | 4.255754 |
  | `cv_tukey_hsd(.025, df = 15000, n_groups = 100)` | 4.479376 | 4.479297 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.99, n_covariates = 0, n_groups = 20, df = 2)` | 44.526 | 37.943 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.00001, n_covariates = 0, n_groups = 3, df = 150)` | 0.000092 | 0.006023 |
  | [`ci_tukey_kramer()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_tukey_kramer.md), 20 groups, 2 error df, `conf_level = .99`: lower limit of “2 - 1” | -4.718 | -3.784 |
  | the same, adjusted *p* of “2 - 1” | .10649 | .10647 |
  | [`ci_games_howell()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_games_howell.md), the three small groups of the entry under Bug Fixes: lower limit of c - b (2.55 df) | -6.03754 | -6.03731 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.99, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 20, df = 10)` | 8.815518 | 8.815520 |

  Every example and vignette result DMAR 1.0.x printed is unchanged, as
  are the Bryant and Paulson (1976) Table 1 values the tests check. The
  probability integral of the range, which the Bryant-Paulson functions
  with covariates used below 7 error df in DMAR 1.0.x, is now taken in
  two pieces, since in one it could miss the peak of the integrand with
  many means (with 7000 means it returned 2.3e-17 where the probability
  is 9.5e-6), and with covariates the quantiles and probabilities beyond
  .999 and below .001 integrate the exact studentized range
  (`qbryant_paulson(.9999, 1, 10, 11)` was 12.977072 and is 12.977142).
  An exact critical value costs a few milliseconds, after about half a
  second the first time a number of means is used in a session:
  [`ci_games_howell()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_games_howell.md)
  with 10 groups of 3 takes about 0.6 s rather than 0.07 s.

- **Bryant-Paulson values with covariates where DMAR 1.0.x computed
  them.** The new range of the integral (see Bug Fixes) moves the nodes
  of the quadrature, which moves the values by about 10^-9 at most below
  10^5 error df and by less than 10^-6 above, at most in the seventh
  significant figure (the most for quantiles beyond .999 above 10^7 df).
  No printed result changes: the examples, the vignettes, and the
  published Table 1 values the tests check are unchanged. Where DMAR
  1.0.x returned about 0, stopped, or returned a wrong critical value,
  the values are those of the bug fix. Compared with DMAR 1.0.x, the
  values above 10000 df also carry the change to the exact studentized
  range in the entry above.

  | call | DMAR 1.0.x | now |
  |----|----|----|
  | `pbryant_paulson(3.7, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 4, df = 1e8)` | 5.6e-25 | 0.9559514 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.95, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 4, df = 1e8)` | error | 3.6331597 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.95, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 4, df = 4.09e7)` | 4.5327092 | 3.6331598 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.95, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 4, df = Inf)` | error | 3.6331596 |
  | `pbryant_paulson(3.5, n_covariates = 150, n_groups = 3, df = 1e6)` | 0 | 0.9644250 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.95, n_covariates = 200, n_groups = 3, df = 1e6)` | error | 3.3148295 |
  | `qbryant_paulson(.9999, n_covariates = 3, n_groups = 4, df = 1e7)` | 6.0828639 | 6.0828670 |

- **[`ss_aipe_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_r.md)
  with `assurance` returns the smallest sample size that attains it,
  computed from the distribution of the sample correlation.** The
  Fisher’s *Z* interval is no wider than the target exactly when \|*r*\|
  is at least a value the function solves for, and the probability of
  that event is taken from the exact distribution function of *r* under
  bivariate normality; the new rows `assurance` and `assurance_attained`
  give the request and that probability. DMAR 1.0.x multiplied the plan
  by qchisq(assurance, N - 2) / (N - 2). At `true_cor = .90` and
  `width = .10` it returned 72 for `assurance = .80` and 92 for `.99`,
  where the probabilities are .672086 and .887068; the plans are now 83
  and 122 (.807291 and .990268). At `true_cor = 0` it returned 1585 for
  `width = .10` and `assurance = .80`, where the plan without
  `assurance`, 1538, already attains a probability of 1 and is now
  returned.
  [`ss_aipe_r_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_r_sensitivity.md)
  with `supposed_cor` and `assurance` changes with it.

- **[`ss_aipe_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd.md)
  with `assurance` returns the smallest per-group sample size, not below
  the plan without `assurance`, at which the exact probability that the
  interval is no wider than `width` is at least `assurance`, for
  \|`true_smd`\|.** DMAR 1.0.x and `MBESS::ss.aipe.smd()` returned the
  plan of the procedure of Kelley and Rausch (2006, pp. 372–374), which
  does not compute that probability (see The Assurance Method of the
  Sample Size Planners).

  - It could be larger than the smallest sample size that attains the
    request: at `true_smd = 1`, `width = .5`, and `assurance = .99` it
    was 150 per group (.994302) and is 149 (.990260). In 45 planning
    sets (\|`true_smd`\| of 0 to 2, widths of .25 to 1, assurances of
    .80 to .99) the published plan attained the request in every set and
    was one case larger in 7, six of them at .99.
  - It could fall short: at `true_smd = 0`, `width = .8`, and
    `assurance = .95` it was 49 (.949878) and is 50 (.994636).
  - DMAR 1.0.x worked on the signed `true_smd`, so reversing the groups
    changed the plan: at `width = .5` and `assurance = .90` it returned
    125 per group at `true_smd = -.5` and 133 at `-1`, below the plans
    without `assurance`, where the probability is .146146 and .064400.
    They are now 130 and 144 (.915627 and .904165), as for .5 and 1.
  - No argument restores the earlier plans.
    [`ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity.md)
    changes with it.

- **[`ss_aipe_equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd.md)
  plans for the interval
  [`equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_smd.md)
  reports,** d -/+ t SE(d) with the Student *t* quantile on n_1 + n_2 -
  2 degrees of freedom, where DMAR 1.0.x planned with the narrower
  standard normal quantile, so the analysis at the planned size could
  report an interval wider than `width`. The search starts at 2 per
  group, the smallest size
  [`equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_smd.md)
  accepts (1.0.x never returned fewer than 4). For `true_smd = 0` and
  `width = 2.5` the plan was 4 per group, with an `expected_width` of
  2.3262, where
  [`equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_smd.md)
  at 4 per group reports 2.7481; it is now 5, with 2.3522. For
  `width = 0.5` the plan was 87 and is 88. The table records the
  confidence level of the interval, 1 - 2 alpha, in its `conf_level`
  attribute.

- **[`ss_aipe_equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd.md)
  computes the probability for `assurance` from the distribution of the
  sample standardized mean difference, and reports it** in the new rows
  `assurance` and `assurance_attained`, by numerical integration (the
  form of Kelley and Rausch, 2006, Equation 20). DMAR 1.0.x simulated
  2,000 widths of the narrower normal-quantile interval at each size, so
  its plans fell short of the request and differed from run to run. With
  `true_smd = 0.5`, `width = 0.5`, and `assurance = 0.80` it returned 91
  per group, where the probability is .671; the plan is now 92 (.828).
  With `true_smd = 0` it returned 87 or 88; the plan is now 88 (.839).
  The function draws no random numbers and has no `seed` argument.

- **[`ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity.md)
  simulates the interval
  [`equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_smd.md)
  reports**, at `conf_level`, where DMAR 1.0.x simulated the noncentral
  *t* interval of
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md),
  which is usually narrower; the width, miss, and equivalence rows
  change with it. With `true_smd = 0.3`, `specified_n_per_group = 61`,
  `conf_level = 0.90`, and `set.seed(113)`, the first simulated sample
  (d = 0.670) was scored with the limits 0.363 and 0.975 and is now
  scored with 0.362 and 0.979; with `true_smd = 0`, `supposed_smd = 0`,
  `width = 0.3`, `smd_upper = 0.5`, `G = 2000`, and `seed = 113`,
  `pct_ci_less_width` was .856 at 342 per group and is .736 at 343. The
  simulated samples are the ones 1.0.0 drew, so the `mean_smd`,
  `median_smd`, and `sd_smd` rows are unchanged under a common seed and
  size. No argument restores the earlier results of
  [`ss_aipe_equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_equivalence_smd.md)
  or of its sensitivity function.
  [`equivalence_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/equivalence_smd.md)
  returns what it returned before, except for sizes given as integers or
  counted from raw data whose product passes 2^31 - 1 (46,341 or more in
  each group, or 40,000 and 60,000), for which it returned `NA` (see Bug
  Fixes).

- **The plans of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md),
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)
  without `assurance` are the smallest sample size whose interval meets
  the width, with the expected squared multiple correlation of the
  targeted predictor on the other p - 1 predictors.** DMAR 1.0.x, like
  `MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef()`, did two things differently. It took the
  expected squared multiple correlation of X_j with the other predictors
  to be that of a regression on *p* predictors, which overstates it and
  so the planned width. And it searched upward one case at a time from a
  start, for the central interval the larger of 2p + 1 and nine below
  the normal approximation rounded up, and for the noncentral one the
  larger of 2p + 2 and five below the central plan, so it returned the
  start when a smaller sample size already met the width. The
  expectation now has p - 1 predictors (0 with one predictor), and the
  search, by doubling and bisection, covers every sample size from p +
  2, one residual degree of freedom. Examples, old to new:

  - `true_R2_Y_X = .8`, `true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0`, `p = 10`,
    `true_reg_coef_j = .3`, `width = 2`: the central plan was 21 and is
    14. 
  - `true_R2_Y_X = .1`, `true_R2_j_X_without_j = .2`, `p = 2`,
    `true_reg_coef_j = 0`, `width = .4`, `noncentral = TRUE`, tails of
    .0002: the noncentral plan was 358 and is 355.
  - Two predictors correlated .3, correlated .4 and .3 with *Y*,
    `width = .3`: the central plan was 157 and is 156, and the
    noncentral plan was 165 and is 164.
  - The examples of Kelley and Maxwell (2008, p. 186) were 250 and 264
    and are 249 and 263.

  In 1,530 central planning sets (*p* from 1 to 15, squared multiple
  correlations from 0 to .9, widths from .05 to 2, tails of .025 and
  .025, .005 and .005, and .01 and .04) the plan is one case smaller in
  1,329, 2 to 13 smaller in 104, and unchanged in 97. In 810 noncentral
  sets it is one smaller in 596, 2 to 10 smaller in 177, and unchanged
  in 37. Every plan equals the smallest sample size from p + 2 that a
  scan of every *N* finds, and a noncentral plan takes about half the
  time it did.

  The published approximations with `assurance` start from these plans
  and change with them. They are the chi square plan of Kelley and
  Maxwell (2003, Equation 3), DMAR 1.0.x’s plan for the central interval
  and now the default of `ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE)`, and the
  noncentral approximation, the default of
  `ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE)` and
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md):

  - The chi square plan is 181 where it was 182 for the two predictors
    at an assurance of .90 (for the interval in the units of the data it
    attains .852, where it attained .862), 486 where it was 487 for
    Kelley and Maxwell’s five exchangeable predictors at .80 (.765, was
    .773), and 277 where it was 278 for the 2008 example at .85.
  - Over the 1,530 sets at .80, the chi square plan is 1 to 3 cases
    smaller in 1,302, unchanged in 106, and 1 to 20 larger in 122. The
    larger ones are where the plan without `assurance` fell to a few
    residual degrees of freedom and Equation 3 takes its *t* quantile
    there. At .95 it is smaller in 1,315, unchanged in 80, and 1 to 26
    larger in 135. At .80 it attains the request for the interval in the
    units of the data in 752 of the sets, where it did in 797.
  - The noncentral approximation is 179 where it was 180 for the two
    predictors. Over the 810 sets at .80 it is 1 to 4 smaller in 620,
    unchanged in 149, and 1 to 13 larger in 41.

  The plans that compute the probability (the exact central plan and
  those of `assurance_method = "simulation"`) change only where their
  answer was the earlier plan without `assurance`. In the 1,530 sets, 83
  exact plans at .80 and 49 at .95 are 1 to 12 cases smaller, each still
  the smallest *N* at or above the plan without `assurance` whose
  probability meets the request. The exact and simulated plans in the
  table of the next entry are unchanged by it, and in 120 noncentral
  sets with `G = 2000` no simulated plan changed. The sensitivity
  functions plan through these planners and change with them
  ([`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md)
  in an entry below: 157 to 156). No argument restores the earlier
  plans.

- **[`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md)
  with `assurance` return, for the central interval, the smallest sample
  size at which the interval is no wider than `width` with at least that
  probability, computed exactly.** DMAR 1.0.x used the chi square factor
  of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3; 2008, Equation 37) for the
  central interval and, for the noncentral one, a lower confidence limit
  of the squared multiple correlation in place of its population value;
  neither computes the probability it attains, which can be more or less
  than the request. Three intervals are planned for in 1.1.0:
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  with `noncentral = FALSE` (the default) and
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md)
  plan the central interval for the coefficient in the units of the
  data, even at unit standard deviations;
  `ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE)` and
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)
  the noncentral interval for the standardized coefficient; and
  `ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE)` (new) the central interval for the
  standardized coefficient, Kelley and Maxwell’s (2003) Equation 1. For
  the central interval in the units of the data the new argument
  `assurance_method`, `"analytic"` by default and the only method
  offered there, gives the smallest sample size, at or above the plan
  without `assurance`, at which that probability, an exact *F*
  probability for random predictors from a multivariate normal
  population, is at least `assurance` (280 for the example of Kelley and
  Maxwell, 2008, p. 186, where DMAR 1.0.x and
  `MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef()` gave 278). For the standardized
  coefficient `"analytic"` gives the approximations of 1.0.x, from the
  plans without `assurance` of this release (see the entry on those
  plans), with `assurance_attained` `NA`, and
  `assurance_method = "simulation"` estimates the probability from `G`
  samples (default 20000) of the exact Wishart sampling distribution,
  with `seed`, and gives the smallest sample size at which the estimate
  reaches `assurance`; `assurance_attained` is the estimate at the
  returned size, its Monte Carlo standard error is the attribute
  `assurance_mc_se`, and the plan can be a case or two from the one the
  exact probability gives. Given squared multiple correlations, which
  leave the correlation of *Y* with the predictor open, the simulated
  step uses the least favorable value.

  - Old and new sample sizes, with the probability each attains for the
    interval in the second column: “raw central”
    ([`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
    with `noncentral = FALSE`,
    [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md)),
    “std noncentral” (`ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE)`,
    [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)),
    and “std central” (`ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE)`, whose 1.0.x
    plan is the chi square plan of
    `ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = FALSE)`). Each probability is exact
    or the proportion of 50,000 or more simulated samples (Monte Carlo
    standard error at most .0014). The simulated plans are those of
    `seed = 1` and the default `G`; another seed can give a plan a case
    away. Variances are 1 unless stated:

    | planning set, width, assurance | interval | 1.0.x *N* (attains) | 1.1.0 *N* (attains) | 1.1.0 `"simulation"` *N* (attains) |
    |----|----|----|----|----|
    | two predictors correlated .3, correlations .4 and .3 with *Y*, .3, .90 | raw central | 182 (.862) | 187 (.902) | not offered |
    | the same, .3, .80 | raw central | 174 (.777) | 176 (.801) | not offered |
    | the same, .3, .99 | raw central | 203 (.974) | 213 (.990) | not offered |
    | the same, .3, .90 | std central | 182 (.989) | 181 (.987) | 171 (.914) |
    | the same, .3, .90 | std noncentral | 180 (.957) | 179 (.947) | 176 (.909) |
    | the same, .3, .80 | std noncentral | 177 (.923) | 176 (.907) | 172 (.818) |
    | five exchangeable predictors (.4 among them, .3 with *Y*; Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, pp. 312–313), .2, .80 | std central, the interval of the article | 487 (.884) | 486 (.877) | 478 (.807) |
    | the same, .2, .80 | raw central | 487 (.773) | 491 (.800) | not offered |
    | the same, .2, .99 | std noncentral | 498 (.944) | 497 (.940) | 517 (.989) |
    | Kelley and Maxwell’s (2003, p. 313) three predictors, the first, .3, .90 | raw central | 271 (.859) | 278 (.904) | not offered |
    | the same, the first, .3, .99 | std noncentral | 314 (.952) | 313 (.949) | 330 (.990) |
    | one predictor correlated .4 with *Y*, .2, .90 | raw central | 362 (.841) | 373 (.904) | not offered |
    | the same, .2, .90 | std noncentral | 377 (1.000) | 376 (1.000) | 364 (.911) |
    | Kelley and Maxwell’s (2008, p. 186) example (*p* = 5, R^2 .5 and .2, sigma_Y / sigma_X = 10), 2, .85 | raw central | 278 (.838) | 280 (.853) | not offered |
    | its standardized analog (coefficient .3, unit standard deviations), .2, .85 | std noncentral | 296 (.894) | 295 (.886) | 291 (.854) |

    The default plans for the standardized coefficient are the 1.0.x
    approximations, a case smaller through the plans without
    `assurance`; the probabilities they attain were simulated from
    200,000 or more samples of the exact sampling distribution (Monte
    Carlo standard error at most .0011). The five exchangeable
    predictors are Kelley and Maxwell’s (2003) example, planned with the
    central interval of their Equation 1 (485 in the article, which uses
    the normal quantile); at .99 for them the simulated plan’s own
    estimate is .990 and the simulation’s .989, within the Monte Carlo
    error. The plan is the same for a coefficient and its negative. The
    three sensitivity functions plan through these planners, each for
    the interval it simulates, and change with them.

  - No argument restores the central plans of DMAR 1.0.x with
    `assurance`; for unequal tails see the next entry. The default plans
    for the standardized coefficient change only through the plans
    without `assurance`. DMAR 1.0.x stopped with an error on every plan
    of the three sensitivity functions with one predictor.
    `ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE)` is new and has no earlier result.

- **With unequal tails, the central plans of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md)
  are for the interval
  [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md)
  reports** (and so are those of `ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE)`, new
  in this release). That interval runs from b_j + t(alpha_lower) SE to
  b_j + t(1 - alpha_upper) SE, so its width is t(1 - alpha_lower) +
  t(1 - alpha_upper) times the standard error. DMAR 1.0.x took both
  quantiles at the average of the two tails, t(1 - (alpha_lower +
  alpha_upper)/2), in the plan without `assurance` and in its chi square
  step with `assurance` (Kelley and Maxwell, 2003, Equation 3), and so
  planned an interval narrower than the one reported. For two predictors
  correlated .3, correlated .4 and .3 with *Y*, and a width of .3:

  | tails (lower, upper) | plan | 1.0.x *N* | 1.1.0 *N* |
  |----|----|----|----|
  | .01, .04 (or .04, .01) | without `assurance` | 157 (the interval .3108 wide) | 169 (.2992) |
  | .001, .049 | without `assurance` | 157 (.3634) | 228 (.2996) |
  | .01, .04 | `assurance = .90` | 182 (attains .709) | 201 (attains .902) |
  | .001, .049 | `assurance = .90` | 182 | 266 (attains .905) |
  | .025, .025 | without `assurance`; `assurance = .90` | 157; 182 | 156; 187 |

  The widths are those of the reported interval at the expected squared
  multiple correlations, and the probabilities are exact. Without
  `assurance` equal tails give the plans they gave, but for the change
  in the entry on the plans without `assurance`; with `assurance` the
  plan is the exact one of the entry above. The noncentral plans used
  the two tails as given and are unchanged by this correction. The chi
  square step with both quantiles, the default of
  `ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE)` with `assurance`, gives 194
  (attaining .847 for the interval in the units of the data) and 258.
  With unequal tails no argument restores the 1.0.x central plans of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  and
  [`ss_aipe_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_rc.md)
  (or the plan of `MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef()`).
  [`ss_aipe_src()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src.md)
  is not affected: its noncentral plans used both tails in 1.0.x, so
  this correction does not change them, and its central plans are new.
  The sensitivity functions plan with equal tails, so it does not change
  them either.

- **The limits of the central
  [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md),
  [`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md), and
  [`ci_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md)
  move, by up to 1.25e-7 of themselves near the floor.** With the upper
  quantile taken in the upper tail (see Bug Fixes) each limit is the
  exact one, and the change grows as the tail shrinks. In 2,160 calls of
  these three functions, at levels from .90 to .999999998 and tails from
  .05 down to 1e-9, against the development versions of 1.1.0, the
  limits moved by at most 6.1e-14 of themselves at levels of .90 to .999
  and tails of 0 to .05, 2.2e-11 at a tail of 1e-6, 1.1e-9 at a level of
  .9999999, and, at a tail of 1e-9 or a level of .999999998, 1.1e-8
  ([`ci_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_c.md) and
  [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md))
  and 1.25e-7
  ([`ci_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_correlation.md),
  whose lower quantile changed as well). Near the floor a limit moves in
  about its eighth or ninth significant digit.
  `ci_c(means = c(1, 0), s_anova = 1, c_weights = c(1, -1), n_per_group = c(20, 20), conf_level = .999999998)`
  (`n` in 1.0.0) has an upper limit of 3.4711584085612, symmetric with
  its lower limit of -1.4711584085612, where DMAR 1.0.0 and the
  development versions gave 3.47115840279224, and
  `ci_r(r = -.9, N = 20, conf_level = .999999998)` (`n` in 1.0.0) has an
  upper limit of -0.0175358196414772, where they gave
  -0.0175358218277256. The `assurance_attained` of the exact central
  assurance step of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  moves the same way:
  `ss_aipe_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = .3, true_R2_j_X_without_j = .2, p = 4, true_reg_coef_j = .2, width = .3, assurance = .8, conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = .04, alpha_upper = 1e-9)`
  reports 0.80195028591575, where the development versions reported
  0.801950281617816, for the same plan of 643. The 768 noncentral
  intervals of
  [`ci_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_reg_coef.md)
  among those calls were unchanged, as were
  [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md),
  [`ci_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc_ancova.md),
  [`ci_sm()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sm.md),
  [`ci_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_cv.md),
  [`ci_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_smd.md),
  and every sample size in 1,944 further calls, the plans of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md),
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md),
  [`ss_aipe_c()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_c.md),
  and
  [`ss_aipe_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_r.md)
  among them, and the 1,530 central plans of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  over a grid of squared multiple correlations, predictors, widths, and
  tails and the 1,080 plans of
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md)
  over a grid of contrasts, correlations, divisors, weights, widths, and
  levels. (Other entries change some of these plans: those on the plans
  without `assurance` of
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  and of
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md).)

- **[`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md)
  plans the sample size for the standardized coefficient, for the
  interval it simulates.** The plan came from
  [`ss_aipe_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reg_coef.md)
  with the supposed standard deviations, so `width` was taken in the
  units of the data while the simulated intervals were standardized. For
  `true_var_Y = 4`, `true_cov_YX = c(.8, .6)`, unit predictor variances
  correlated .3 (correlations of .4 and .3 with *Y*), supposed
  correctly, `width = .3`, and `noncentral = FALSE`, the plan was 610,
  with a mean width of .150, and is 156 (mean width .300). With
  `assurance = .90` it was 657 (182 with unit supposed variances). It is
  181 by default, the chi square plan of Kelley and Maxwell (2003,
  Equation 3) for the central interval for the standardized coefficient,
  which the replications compute (.987 of those intervals are no wider
  than .3 at 181), and 171 with `assurance_method = "simulation"` and
  `seed = 1`, the smallest sample size at which that interval is no
  wider than .3 with probability at least .90 (.914 at 171). No argument
  restores the 1.0.x plans. With equal variances of *Y* and of the
  targeted predictor, true and supposed, whatever the variances of the
  other predictors, and two or more predictors, the default plans are
  made as in 1.0.x, a case smaller (see the entry on the plans without
  `assurance`). The noncentral plan, the default interval, was refused
  whenever the supposed variance of *Y* or of the targeted predictor was
  not 1, and every other plan with one predictor stopped with “argument
  is of length zero”; such calls now plan (the noncentral plan is 164
  here). The numbers for `noncentral = FALSE` are also those of DMAR
  1.0.x’s `ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(standardize = TRUE)`.

- **The standardized regression coefficient in the sensitivity functions
  is judged against the standardized coefficient.**
  [`ss_aipe_src_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.md)
  standardizes the data of every replication, but the true and supposed
  values the intervals were judged against were unstandardized; both are
  now the standardized coefficient (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, p. 316). For
  the structure above with `specified_N = 200`, `width = .3`, `G = 300`,
  and seed 2026, the true value was .681 beside a mean estimate of .334,
  and every interval missed (`total_type_I_error` 1); it is now
  `true_std_reg_coef_j` .341, with `total_type_I_error` .017 (.033 with
  `noncentral = FALSE`). A call with `specified_N` changes as well, as
  does one with one predictor (`true_var_Y = 4`, `true_cov_YX = .8`,
  `true_cov_XX = matrix(1)`, and `specified_N = 100`: .8 in DMAR 1.0.x,
  .4 now).

- **[`ss_aipe_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc.md)
  with `assurance` returns the smallest sample size per group, not below
  the plan without `assurance`, at which the exact probability that the
  [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md)
  interval is no wider than `width` is at least `assurance`.** DMAR
  1.0.x returned, in one row, the plan of the step of Kelley and
  Rausch (2006) as Lai and Kelley (2012, pp. 358–359 and 361) apply it
  to a standardized contrast, which does not compute that probability
  (see The Assurance Method of the Sample Size Planners).

  - It could fall short: at `true_std_contrast = 0`,
    `c_weights = c(1, -1)`, `width = .8`, and `assurance = .95` it was
    49 per group (.949878) and is 50 (.994636).
  - It could be larger than the smallest sample size that attains the
    request: in 96 planning sets (contrasts of -1 to 2, weights for two,
    three, and five groups, widths of .5 and 1, assurances of .80 and
    .99, equal and unequal tails) the published step attained the
    request in every set and was one case or more larger in 17.
  - With unequal tails and a negative `true_std_contrast` it planned the
    magnitude with the tails as given (see Bug Fixes). At
    `true_std_contrast = -2.5`, `width = .4`, `alpha_lower = .001`,
    `alpha_upper = .049`, and `assurance = .90` it was 522 per group
    (.890) and is 523 (.902); at -3, width .5, and tails .001 and .099
    it was 342 (.842) and is 346 (.902).
  - The result gains the rows `assurance` and `assurance_attained`. The
    plan without `assurance` is unchanged.
  - No argument restores the earlier plans.
    [`ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity.md)
    changes with it.

- **[`ss_aipe_sc_ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md)
  without `assurance` returns the smallest sample size per group whose
  interval at the planning value is no wider than `width`.** DMAR 1.0.0
  started its search at the fixed point of the central *t*
  approximation, n = C r^2 (t_l + t_u)^2 / w^2 with *t* on J(n - 1) - 1
  degrees of freedom, and searched only upward. At a small contrast the
  central quantiles are farther apart than the noncentral limits, so the
  start could already meet the width, and the plan was then the start:
  `ss_aipe_sc_ancova(true_std_contrast = 0, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .5)`
  (`psi_standardized` in 1.0.0) gave 125 per group, though the interval
  is .49985 wide at 123 and .50190 at 122. It now gives 123. The search
  now starts at 2 per group, the smallest sample size with positive
  error degrees of freedom, and the width falls as the sample size grows
  from there (checked on 420 combinations of contrast, ratio of the two
  error standard deviations, weights for two to five groups, and level).
  Of 1,080 plans over contrasts of 0 to 2, correlations of 0, .5, and
  .9, both divisors, weights for two to four groups, widths of .1 to
  3.6, and levels of .95 and .99, 446 are smaller: 304 by 1 per group,
  141 by 2, and 1 by 3. None is larger, and no plan at a contrast of 2
  changed. At widths of 1 or less, 198 of 720 are smaller, by 1 or 2.
  Each plan meets the width, and one fewer does not. The published
  assurance step, the default (`assurance_method = "analytic"`), plans
  from this plan and changes with it. On the same grid, 302 plans at an
  assurance of .80 are 1 or 2 smaller. At .90, 227 are 1 or 2 smaller
  and 7 are 1 larger: the call above with `assurance = .9` gave 125 and
  gives 124. The step plans without `assurance` at a contrast it adjusts
  for the assurance, so its plan can move by a case or two per group, in
  either direction, even where the plan without `assurance` at the
  planning values did not: at `true_std_contrast = 2`, `true_cor = .5`,
  `c_weights = c(1, -1)`, `width = .3`, and `assurance = .99` it was 545
  per group and is 546. The simulated step
  (`assurance_method = "simulation"`, new in 1.1.0) also searches upward
  from this plan. With `conf_level = .99` the call above gave 215 per
  group without `assurance` and gives 213, and with `assurance = .8` it
  gave 215 and gives 213 by default and 214 with
  `assurance_method = "simulation"` and `seed = 1` (`assurance_attained`
  .886). The default plans in the table of the ANCOVA entry under The
  Assurance Method of the Sample Size Planners are those of 1.0.x.
  [`ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity.md)
  plans through the planner and changes with it. Past about 1e11 per
  group the plans rest on the precision of doubles, and they move as
  well (Details of
  [`?ss_aipe_sc_ancova`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_ancova.md)).
  No argument restores the earlier plans.

- **[`ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity.md)
  standardizes each simulated contrast by the pooled standard
  deviation,** the square root of the mean square error, which is the
  `s_anova` that
  [`ci_sc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ci_sc.md)
  takes. DMAR 1.0.x divided by the mean of the group standard
  deviations, which is never larger, so its contrasts ran about 2
  percent large with three groups of 10. After `set.seed(113)`,
  `ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity(true_std_contrast = .5, specified_n_per_group = 10, c_weights = c(.5, .5, -1), width = .8, G = 2000)`
  gave `mean_std_contrast` .527 and `total_type_I_error` .070 and gives
  .517 and .064. No argument restores the 1.0.x result.

- **[`ss_power_indirect_effect()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_indirect_effect.md)
  computes power from the exact sampling distribution of the two path
  *t* statistics, with X random by default** (see Bug Fixes). Every
  result changes, and no argument restores the 1.0.x results:
  `random_predictors = FALSE` fixes X as 1.0.x did, and with it
  `power_a` is the 1.0.x power of the test of *a*, but the mediator is
  random in every design, so the 1.0.x `power_b` and `power_ab` are the
  powers of no study. `power_ab` is no longer `power_a` times `power_b`
  but the probability that both tests reject, which is below that
  product. The Sobel power need not rise with N, since the test refers
  *t* statistics on few degrees of freedom to the normal: with paths of
  .9 and .05 it falls from .0729 at N = 10 to .0562 at N = 59, and with
  paths of .8 and .02 and `alpha_level = .5` it is .5072 at N = 12 and
  .5035 at N = 59, and does not reach .507 again until N = 216. The
  search no longer takes one case at a time; it passes over a range of
  sample sizes only where an upper bound of the power shows that none in
  it reaches `desired_power`, so the plan is the smallest N of at least
  10 that attains `desired_power`, whether or not the power rises
  with N. It still stops with an error at ten million. The values
  (1.0.x, now with X random, now with X fixed):

  | call | 1.0.x | now | now, `random_predictors = FALSE` |
  |----|----|----|----|
  | `ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, specified_N = 65)`: `power_ab`, `power_a`, `power_b` | .8017, .9196, .8719 | .7675, .9046, .8503 | .7804, .9196, .8503 |
  | `ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, specified_N = 75)`: `power_ab` | .8706 | .8436 | .8537 |
  | `ss_power_indirect_effect(.3, -.25, .1, specified_N = 120)`: `power_ab` | .7056 | .6876 | .6936 |
  | `ss_power_indirect_effect(.6, .5, .2, specified_N = 12)`: `power_ab` | .2367 | .1631 | .1826 |
  | the same four with `method = "sobel"`: `power_ab` | .6380, .7001, .5639, .3165 | .6157, .7272, .5067, .1226 | .6305, .7410, .5135, .1367 |
  | `ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, specified_N = 96, method = "sobel")` | .8026 | .8818 | .8907 |
  | `ss_power_indirect_effect(.2, .1, specified_N = 10, alpha_level = .999, method = "sobel")` | .9990 | .9983 | .9983 |
  | `necessary_N`, `ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, desired_power = .80)` | 65 | 69 | 68 |
  | the same with `method = "sobel"` | 96 | 84 | 82 |
  | `necessary_N`, `ss_power_indirect_effect(.14, .39, desired_power = .80)`, joint significance and Sobel | 395, 438 | 398, 412 | 395, 410 |
  | `necessary_N`, `ss_power_indirect_effect(.3, -.25, .1, desired_power = .80)`, joint significance and Sobel | 144, 210 | 148, 179 | 147, 178 |
  | `necessary_N`, `ss_power_indirect_effect(.1, .59, desired_power = .95)`, joint significance and Sobel | 1289, 1312 | 1293, 1296 | 1289, 1292 |
  | `necessary_N`, `ss_power_indirect_effect(-.3, .2, desired_power = .50)`, joint significance and Sobel | 116, 141 | 119, 157 | 118, 155 |
  | `necessary_N`, `ss_power_indirect_effect(.0044, .5, desired_power = .80)` | 405411 | 405414 | 405411 |
  | `necessary_N`, `ss_power_indirect_effect(.8, .02, desired_power = .507, alpha_level = .5, method = "sobel")` | 229 | 12 | 10 |

- **[`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md)
  with reliabilities gives each corrected correlation the sampling
  variance of a corrected correlation.** Each correlation corrected for
  attenuation, r / sqrt(rxx ryy), was given on the Fisher *Z* scale the
  variance of an uncorrected correlation, 1 / (n - 3), which is too
  small (by a factor of 1.96 for r = .40 with both reliabilities .80).
  The variance is now the delta method variance (1 - r²⁾2 / (rxx ryy
  (1 - r_c²⁾2 (n - 3)), with r_c the corrected correlation, at each
  study’s observed correlation; it sets the weights and every result.
  Without reliabilities nothing changes. For five studies with r = .40,
  n = 100, and both reliabilities .80 (`method = "fe"`,
  `hartung_knapp = FALSE`), the standard error on the Fisher *Z* scale
  was 0.0454 and is 0.0636, and the interval for the construct
  correlation was .430 to .564 and is .401 to .588. For
  `meta_r(r = c(.21, .35, .42, .18, .30, .47), n = c(48, 120, 75, 300, 60, 150), reliability_x = c(.72, .85, .78, .90, .65, .80), reliability_y = c(.80, .70, .88, .75, .82, .90))`,
  the pooled correlation was .4095 and is .4051, Q was 20.14 and is
  12.05, and I2 was 69.0 percent and is 54.1 percent.
  [`?meta_r`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md)
  states the variance and that the reliabilities are treated as known
  constants. An analysis that gave reliabilities to
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md)
  should be rerun.

- **[`var_alpha()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/var_alpha.md)
  returns each variance in the row named for its source.** DMAR 1.0.x
  returned 2*J*(1 - alpha)^2/((*J* - 1)(*N* - 2)) in the row
  `var_alpha_van_zyl` and 2*J*(1 - alpha)^2/((*J* - 1)(*N* - 1)) in the
  row `var_alpha_bonett`. Van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000,
  Equation 13) give the second, and Bonett (2003, Equations 2 and 4)
  gives the first, on the scale of the logarithm of 1 - alpha; the van
  Zyl variance that `reliability_alpha(ci_method = "ml")` and
  [`ss_aipe_reliability()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_reliability.md)
  use is, at a compound symmetric covariance matrix, the *N* - 1 form.
  The two values now sit in the rows their names attribute; the pair is
  unchanged. No argument restores the earlier rows.

- **`fa_confirmatory(output = "standardized")` (and
  [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md),
  [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md), and
  [`cfa_k()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md))
  computes the standardized `loading_sum`, `error_sum`, `omega`, `ave`,
  and `H` rows of a factor with `equal_loading` or `equal_error` from
  each item’s own standardized loading and error variance,** with delta
  method standard errors. lavaan’s `standardizedSolution()`, the earlier
  source, evaluates a defined parameter at the first item’s standardized
  value of a shared label. For four items with unstandardized loadings
  of .7 and error variances of .1, .2, 1, and 2 (a covariance matrix, N
  = 500), equal loadings gave a standardized AVE, H, and omega of .6583,
  .9094, and .8730 and give .5166, .8899, and .7988; equal error
  variances gave .3155, .6642, and .6523 and give .3816, .7710, and
  .7007. lavaan’s ambiguity warning no longer reaches the caller. Other
  factors and the `"measurement"` and `"verbose"` tables are unchanged.

- **`fa_bifactor(output = "standardized")` computes each index that uses
  a label several items share in the same way.** On
  `holzinger_swineford` with the three groups of the example, equal
  loadings on `spatial`, and equal error variances on `memory`,
  `omega_general`, `omega_HS_spatial`, `H_spatial`, and `omega_memory`
  were .9113, .1222, .1972, and .8995 and are .8731, .2195, .4025, and
  .7233; with equal loadings on the general factor, `ECV_general` and
  `H_general` were .0879 and .3627 and are .1443 and .5133, the values
  of the `"measurement"` table.
  `fa_second_order(output = "standardized")` no longer passes on
  lavaan’s warning about the index rows it leaves out.

- **The tables of
  [`fa_confirmatory()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md)
  (and of
  [`cfa_1()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_1.md),
  [`cfa_2()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cfa_2.md), and
  [`cfa_k()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/fa_confirmatory.md))
  withhold every standard error, test, and interval of a fit whose
  expected information is singular,** with the warning of class
  `dmar_result_qualified`, as they did for a singular observed
  information. A two-test factor uncorrelated in the sample with another
  factor, fitted by listwise deletion with equal loadings on that
  factor, had an H of .853 with a standard error of .028 and the
  interval \[.790, .900\]; the standard errors and intervals are now
  `NA`.

- **[`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md)
  refuses a multiple-group or multilevel fit,** with an error of class
  `dmar_argument_invalid` that names the groups (as `groups`) or the
  levels (as `levels`). DMAR 1.0.0 averaged the squared standardized
  loadings of every group, or of both levels, into one row: a factor
  whose AVE is .810 in one group and .090 in the other (three items with
  equal correlations of .81 and .09, groups of 1000 and 100) had an AVE
  of .450, which describes neither group. The AVE of one group or level
  is `average_variance_extracted(loadings = )` given its standardized
  loadings.
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  refuses a multiple-group fit the same way (see Calls That Are Now
  Refused).

- **[`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md)
  refuses a multilevel fit** with an error of class
  `dmar_argument_invalid`. DMAR 1.0.0 read the loadings of the within
  level and the residual variances of the between level: for nine items
  in three subscales with a general factor `g` at both levels (200
  clusters of 8, `set.seed(113)`), the general factor’s omega was .942
  and its omega_H .740, where the within level’s own solution gives .885
  and .695.

- **[`average_variance_extracted()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/average_variance_extracted.md),
  [`bifactor_indices()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/bifactor_indices.md),
  and [`dmacs()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmacs.md)
  refuse a fit whose optimizer did not converge**
  (`lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "converged")` is `FALSE`), with an error of
  class `dmar_not_converged` that carries `fn` and `iterations`. DMAR
  1.0.0 read the point where the optimizer stopped as a solution: a
  one-factor fit to three items whose correlations are all .81 (N =
  200), stopped after one iteration, had an AVE of .412, where the
  converged fit has .810. A fit that converged to an improper solution
  is treated as before.

- **The standardized cluster randomized planners (`ss_aipe_crd_es_*()`)
  measure the width of each simulated interval from its lower limit to
  its upper limit.** The width was the estimate minus the lower limit,
  about half the interval, so every width these planners report is about
  twice the earlier one, and a plan made for a width is larger. With
  `G = 2, seed = 113`,
  `ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20, cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5)`
  reports an `expected_width` of 0.672 where it reported 0.335; with
  `G = 12, seed = 113`,
  `ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 0.40, cluster_size = 20, true_es = 0.5, true_icc = 0.10, pr_treat = 0.5)`
  returns 67 clusters where it returned 14, and
  `ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 0.60, n_clusters = 60, ...)`
  a cluster size of 5 where it returned 2.

- **The standardized cluster randomized planners use only the intervals
  of converged fits, count a failed data set as an infinite width under
  `assurance`, and bracket the target before they bisect.** The interval
  of a data set is used only when the optimizer status code of the fit
  and of each limit’s search is 0 or 1, the diagnostic OpenMx gives each
  limit is “success”, and the limits are finite and bracket the
  estimate; any two limits that were numbers were used before. The
  assured width is the `assurance` quantile of all `G` widths, with the
  data sets without a usable interval at infinity: with two of four data
  sets failed and the other two at 0.2, the assured width at 0.8 was
  0.2, and the call is now refused. The searches upward for a size
  stepped up one cluster or one individual at a time and now step up 1,
  3, 7, 15, and so on, and then halve the gap. When the simulated width
  falls as the size grows the design is the same (the calls above still
  return 67 clusters and a cluster size of 5); with a small `G` the
  simulated width rises and falls, and the two searches can stop at
  different sizes near the target (with `G = 6, seed = 99`,
  `ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 0.7, cluster_size = 2, true_es = 3, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.2, pr_treat = 0.5)`
  returns 233 clusters after simulating 16 designs, where stepping one
  at a time stopped at 203 after 107).

- **[`ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crd_es.md)
  with `es_type = 1` plans targets it refused, refuses unreachable ones
  before simulating, and starts its search lower.** With a fixed number
  of clusters the width levels off, at a value with a closed form, as
  the clusters grow. The search started from the cluster size the
  unstandardized difference needs, which uses the *t* quantile and with
  few clusters needs far more: with 10 clusters and an intraclass
  correlation of 0.2 it needed more than 100,000 per cluster for every
  target from 1.19 to about 1.458, and 1,875 for 1.46, which about 10
  reach with `true_es = 0.5`. It now starts from the smaller of that
  size and the size at which the closed-form width, with the
  within-cluster standard deviation known, falls below the target; with
  equal cluster sizes, no covariate, and no assurance that start is a
  lower bound on the size the target needs.
  `width = 1.30, n_clusters = 10, true_es = 0.5, true_icc = 0.2, pr_treat = 0.5, G = 20, seed = 5`
  returns a cluster size of 18, and `width = 1.46` (`seed = 11`)
  returns 9. Targets whose search started at 500 or less are now
  searched upward from the smaller start. When the simulated width falls
  as the cluster grows the design is the same; with a small `G` it can
  differ, and far fewer designs are simulated: with `G = 20, seed = 5`,
  `width = 1.50` returns 8 after simulating 2 designs, where stepping
  down one size at a time from 70, as DMAR 1.0.x searched, stops at 16
  after 56. A target at or below the level (1.187 there) is refused
  without a simulation (class `dmar_argument_invalid`, `reason`
  `"width_not_reachable"`, the level as `width_limit`), and so is one
  whose start is above 500 (from 1.187 to about 1.1914 there; `reason`
  `"cluster_size_beyond_reach"`).

- **The cluster randomized searches over the number of clusters keep the
  floor of two clusters in each condition and return a number they
  tested.** The floor,
  `ceiling(2 / min(pr_treat, 1 - pr_treat)) + n_covariates` (MBESS: “at
  least two groups in each condition”), is where the search starts when
  every number from 100 to 1000 meets the target. There the search
  returned `3 + n_covariates`, which it had not tested:
  `ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 100, cluster_size = 20, pr_treat = .1, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8)`
  returned 3 clusters, none treated, with an `expected_width` of `Inf`,
  in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0, and returns 20
  (1.534). Where the floor is above 100 (`pr_treat` below .02) the
  search stopped with “wrong sign in ‘by’ argument” (`pr_treat = .01`,
  now 200 clusters, 1.373) or returned a number below the floor
  (`pr_treat = .005`: 101 clusters, one treated, now 400, 1.365). With
  unequal cluster sizes the same call with `diff_size = c(-2, 0, 2)`
  returned 3 clusters with a width of `NaN` in both, and returns 20.
  Every number returned meets the target and is at least the floor. In a
  grid of 6,912 calls (`pr_treat` from .005 to .9, 18 widths from .12 to
  8 that are not the width of a design, `n_covariates` 0 to 2,
  `assurance` `NULL` and .8, equal sizes and two `diff_size` patterns)
  the 3,989 results of the development versions that met the target from
  the floor are unchanged; the 2,923 others change: 919 that stopped
  with an error, 1,693 returns of `3 + n_covariates` whose width did not
  meet the target, and 311 that met it below the floor. With equal
  cluster sizes and no `assurance` the width falls as clusters are
  added, and the number returned is the first from the floor that meets
  the target. With `diff_size`, or with an `assurance` below .5, the
  width need not fall at every step, and the number returned can be
  larger than the first that meets the target, as before:
  `ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 0.363312492117768, cluster_size = 50, pr_treat = .9, true_var_between = 1, true_var_within = 4, conf_level = .9, diff_size = c(.5, 1, 1.5))`
  returns 1002, although 999 meets the target (1000 and 1001 do not). In
  3,000 calls at targets set from the widths of designs, 152 results
  were larger than the first such number, 150 of them with `diff_size`
  and 2 at `assurance = .3`. The two `both` planners consider the same
  floor:
  `ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width(width = 3, cluster_cost = 1000, individual_cost = 1, pr_treat = .005, ...)`
  returned 101 clusters of 3 (budget 101,303, one cluster treated) and
  returns 400 clusters of 2 (budget 400,800). The standardized planners
  start their search over the number of clusters from this plan, so a
  standardized plan that started from the untested `3 + n_covariates`
  changes: with `G = 10, seed = 113`,
  `ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 6, cluster_size = 10, true_es = .5, true_icc = .2, pr_treat = .5)`
  returned 3 clusters (one of them a control cluster) and returns 4; at
  `pr_treat = .3` it returned 3 (one treated) and returns 5. DMAR 1.0.0
  also returned 3 in both. Eleven standardized calls whose start was not
  the untested one, among them the calls the entries on the standardized
  planners cite (67 and 233 clusters, and a cluster size of 18), are
  unchanged.

- **A target equal to the width of a cluster randomized design is met by
  that design.** A width meets the target when it is no larger than the
  target, inside a bracket of the search as at its ends (see “Bug
  Fixes”). DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0 asked for a
  width below the target inside a bracket, so the width a plan reported,
  given back as `width`, gave the next size:
  `ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_size = 20, pr_treat = .5, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8)`
  plans 18 clusters with an expected width of 0.979142316129524, and
  that width as the target gave 19 clusters and gives 18;
  `ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 1, n_clusters = 30, ...)`
  plans a cluster size of 4 (0.946118731780349), which gave 5 and gives
  4; and the first call with `assurance = .8` plans 22 clusters
  (0.975082804893471), which gave 23 and gives 22. Only a target equal
  to a width the search computes is affected: in 3,000 calls of
  [`ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crd.md)
  at targets set to the width of a design and a part in 1e9 above or
  below it, 741 of the 2,536 results of the development versions that
  met the target from the floor change, every one at a target equal to a
  design’s width (in 672 the number they returned was one more), and
  none at the others; in 500 calls of
  [`ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_width()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_aipe_crd.md)
  at targets set from the widths of designs 100 plans change (28 of them
  with equal cluster sizes), all at a target equal to a design’s width,
  and 24 that stopped with “‘from’ must be a finite number” return a
  size. A standardized plan starts from these searches, so its start can
  move by one where the target equals the unstandardized width of a
  design. The budget searches already counted a cost equal to the budget
  as within it inside a bracket.

- **A between-cluster proportion of variance explained no longer shrinks
  a cluster randomized plan without a covariate.** With
  `n_covariates = 0` the six unstandardized planners took
  `true_R2_between` out of the between-cluster variance. The six
  standardized planners started their search from that smaller plan,
  while the data they simulated left it out. DMAR 1.0.0 (`R2_between`
  with `num_predictors = 0`) and the development versions of 1.1.0 gave
  these plans with `true_R2_between = 0` and `.9`:
  `ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_size = 20, pr_treat = .5, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8)`
  18 clusters (expected width 0.979) and 7 (0.962);
  `ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 1, n_clusters = 20, ...)`
  a cluster size of 10 (0.994) and 4 (0.881); and
  `ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_cost = 10, individual_cost = 1, ...)`
  22 clusters of 7 (budget 374) and 8 clusters of 13 (budget 184). In
  the development versions
  `ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_size = 20, true_es = .5, true_icc = .2, pr_treat = .5, G = 20, seed = 113)`
  planned 18 clusters (0.982) with either value. Its search started at
  22 or at 8 and simulated 6 or 8 designs. The calls with `.9` are now
  refused (see Calls That Are Now Refused). In 216 calls of the six
  unstandardized planners (`true_R2_between` 0, .3, and .9,
  `true_R2_within` 0 and .5, `n_covariates` 0 to 2, `pr_treat` .3 and
  .5), the 48 with a nonzero `true_R2_between` and `n_covariates = 0`
  are refused and the other 168 are unchanged.

- **[`mediation_mbco()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediation_mbco.md)
  statistics change where the fits were wrong, and some calls of it and
  of
  [`ss_power_reg_coef()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_reg_coef.md)
  and
  [`ss_power_rc()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ss_power_rc.md)
  that returned a result are refused** (see Bug Fixes for the calls and
  values).
  `ss_power_reg_coef(true_cor_XX = diag(2), true_cor_YX = c(.3, .2), which_predictor = 1.5)`
  returned `necessary_N` = 89, the plan for the first predictor, and is
  refused.

- **`tidy()` and
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  read the intervals of
  [`ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ancova.md),
  [`factorial_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factorial_anova.md),
  [`variance_components_mls()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/variance_components_mls.md),
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  [`R2_mixed_effects()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/R2_mixed_effects.md),
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md),
  [`cles()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cles.md),
  [`meta_es()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_es.md),
  [`meta_r()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_r.md),
  and
  [`meta_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/meta_smd.md),
  whose limits are now named `<estimate>_ci_lower` and
  `<estimate>_ci_upper`** (see Renamed Output Rows and Columns). The
  values are unchanged. `tidy()` of
  [`ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ancova.md),
  [`variance_components_mls()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/variance_components_mls.md),
  [`mediate()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mediate.md),
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md),
  and [`cles()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cles.md) has
  a third column, `conf_level`, on the rows of each interval (DMAR 1.0.x
  returned `term` and `estimate` alone), and in `tidy()` of the
  meta-analysis functions that column also marks `tau2` and `I2` and
  their limits.
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  on these tables stopped (“this table has none of these”); it now
  writes the sentence of the estimate `term` names or, by default, of
  the first estimate with limits (for
  [`ancova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/ancova.md) of
  the Pygmalion example, “eta_squared_partial = 0.02, 95% CI \[0.00,
  0.06\]”), and on one row of
  [`factorial_anova()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/factorial_anova.md)
  with `term = "eta_squared_partial"` it writes that row’s sentence. A
  table that records no level
  ([`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md)
  with supplied limits and no `conf_level`) is refused with the message
  that asks for `conf_level`.

- **[`cles()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/cles.md),
  [`nnt_from_smd()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/nnt_from_smd.md),
  and
  [`proportion_of_superiority()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/proportion_of_superiority.md)
  still report their own interval.** Now that the limits on *d* are
  named for *d*, each table holds two intervals named for their
  estimates, and a new attribute, `ci_source`, names *d* as the estimate
  whose interval the function’s own is computed from.
  [`results_sentence()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/dmar_output_helpers.md)
  reports the common language effect size, the SRD, and the proportion
  of superiority, and `tidy()` gives `NA` as the confidence level on the
  rows of *d*, as in DMAR 1.0.x; `results_sentence(x, term = "smd")` now
  gives the interval for *d*, which DMAR 1.0.x refused.

- **The renames themselves change no value.** A call that gives the new
  names returns what the DMAR 1.0.x call returned, except where another
  entry of this release changes the result; renamed rows and columns
  hold the values they held under their 1.0.x names.

- **[`mr_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_cv.md)
  estimates the variance of the sample coefficient of variation by
  Equation 32 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), so its results
  differ from those of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) and of MBESS for
  nearly any data.** DMAR 1.0.x used Equation 22 of the 2016 article, as
  `MBESS::mr.cv()` does. Written with the skewness gamma_1 and the
  excess kurtosis gamma_2 of the scores, that equation estimates kappa^2
  / 2 + kappa^4 - kappa^3 gamma_1 + kappa^4 gamma_2 / 4, the first-order
  term of Bao (2009, Equation 3) as printed, and the kurtosis term
  should be kappa^2 gamma_2 / 4 (Equation 30 of the 2018 article, and
  the erratum Bao posted for his Equation 3, which
  [`?mr_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_cv.md)
  describes). The two population values are equal only when the excess
  kurtosis is 0 or the coefficient of variation is 1; for gamma scores
  with a coefficient of variation of .8 the value of Equation 22 is
  0.304 and the corrected value is 0.525. In a sample the two estimates
  differ by (k^2 / 4)(1 - k^2)(mu4_hat / s^4 - 3), so the stopping point
  changes with normal scores too: in 4,000 simulated runs with A =
  5,000,000, c = 10, and a coefficient of variation of .3 it changed in
  95 percent of the runs, by 8 observations on average, while the mean
  final sample size changed little (172 with Equation 22, 170 now). For
  scores with positive excess kurtosis and a coefficient of variation
  below 1 the population value of Equation 22 is the smaller of the two,
  and with strongly skewed scores DMAR 1.0.x could stop well short of
  the large-sample value sqrt(A / c) xi. In 20,000 simulated runs with
  the same A and c, the mean final sample size for gamma scores with a
  coefficient of variation of .8 was 375 with Equation 22 and is 480
  now, where the large-sample value is 512; for lognormal scores with a
  coefficient of variation of .6 it was 220 and is 440, where that value
  is 545. For the article’s example (35 observations, A = 400,000, and a
  sampling cost of 75) DMAR 1.0.x reported a risk of 4891.284 and a
  stopping rule that was met, as the article does.
  [`mr_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_cv.md) now
  reports a risk of 4977.259 and a criterion of 1261.332 against N^2 =
  1225: the rule is not met, and another observation is collected.
  [`?mr_cv`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_cv.md) has a
  part on Equation 22.

- **[`mr_cv()`](https://yelleknek.github.io/DMAR/reference/mr_cv.md)
  does not stop sampling on a zero or negative variance estimate.** The
  estimate can be zero or negative in a small sample, and DMAR 1.0.x put
  it into the stopping rule as it was, which lowered the criterion.
  `mr_cv(data = c(2.3, 0.61, 1.6, 0.54, 0.51, 0.41, 0.67, 0.37), A = 485, sampling_cost = 1)`,
  a pilot sample of the size the function plans for those costs, gave an
  estimate of -0.058, a risk of 4.468 (less than the 8 already spent on
  sampling), and a rule that was met; 18 equal scores gave an estimate
  of 0 and a rule that was met. Such an estimate now means that the rule
  is not met: `is_satisfied` is `FALSE`, the risk and the criterion are
  `NA`, the new attribute `variance_unusable` is `TRUE`, and a line
  under the table says to collect another observation. Scores that
  differ only by rounding error (a range of at most 1e-10 times the
  largest absolute score), such as equal gains computed as posttest
